Use when: Multi-entity arrangement problems with optional participants, position constraints, and several conditional team/slot rules.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when every entity is definitely included or when rules are unconditional global requirements.

Transfer rule: If a passage presents several harms from a behavior and frames one as the overall effect, then choose the option stating that broad effect, not a single example of harm.
Error pattern: I narrowed the main idea to one concrete consequence instead of the author’s higher-level evaluative claim.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the thesis in 8–12 words and verify the option covers all supporting points, including audience/context and overall outcome.
Use when: The passage has one central judgment supported by multiple consequences, examples, or mechanisms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, cause, or one explicitly highlighted consequence.

Transfer rule: If asked how a stated fact functions, then map conclusion, premises, and intermediate claims before matching the fact’s role.
Error pattern: Success came from role analysis—distinguishing support for possibility/plausibility from proof, refutation, or the main conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase the conclusion in one sentence, then ask of the cited fact: “Does it support this, restate it, or oppose another view?”
Use when: Relevant in argument-role questions with historical/scientific claims where one fact is used analogically to make an earlier occurrence seem plausible.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for truth, outside knowledge, or a direct causal mechanism rather than argumentative function.

Transfer rule: If a definition targets periodic change in a lake’s water regime, then select the option describing water level/area or inflow variation, not temperature or basin climate statistics.
Error pattern: I matched a time-pattern word to the wrong variable, confusing hydrological regime with other environmental rhythms.
Diagnostic check: Underline the required object and behavior; verify the option mentions lake water state changing over time and identify a driver tied to water input/output.
Use when: The stem defines a concept by both variable type and temporal pattern, especially in environmental or geography multiple-choice items.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept explicitly includes temperature, precipitation totals, or broader climatic indicators rather than water-regime changes.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires an active process that coordinates conflicting social parts into equilibrium, then exclude choices that merely describe a group, condition, or byproduct without coordination.
Error pattern: Mistook a content area related to order or society for the defined process, instead of checking whether the option is itself an integrative action.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Who is coordinating what contradictions, by what mechanism, toward system-wide balance?” If no process is present, reject it.
Use when: Relevant for definition questions contrasting dynamic processes or policies with static categories, populations, or outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the target concept is a status, trait, demographic label, or result rather than an action/process.

Transfer rule: If evidence for a causal prediction can be explained by an alternative mechanism, then prefer the choice that supplies that mechanism and undercuts the prediction.
Error pattern: I treated a merely neutral fact as weakening, instead of seeking a stronger rival cause for the observed effect.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option explain the reduced outcome without the predicted property?” If yes, it is a serious weakener.
Use when: An argument infers a hidden property from an intervention’s effect on outcomes in an experimental comparison.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only add side facts, baseline comparisons, or other harms without addressing the intervention-to-outcome pathway.

Transfer rule: If a passage says one concept is “more comprehensive” and lists stages it contains, then choose the option expressing inclusion, not stronger effects like prevention or importance.
Error pattern: I overextended a broad definition into an unsupported causal claim instead of matching the stated part-whole relation.
Diagnostic check: Mark every verb the passage explicitly supports; reject any option adding outcome words such as prevent, guarantee, core, most important, or stronger than.
Use when: Relevant for definition or scope questions comparing a broad term with a narrower sub-process across stages or components.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly states causation, necessity, hierarchy, or effectiveness beyond simple inclusion.

Transfer rule: If an argument says one source helps, so another source cannot help, then test whether the favored cases also include the allegedly useless source.
Error pattern: False exclusivity; treating categories as mutually exclusive when they may overlap, so support for one can indirectly support the other.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Can some examples fit both labels?” If yes, substitute an overlapping case and see whether the conclusion becomes self-undermining.
Use when: Relevant in weaken/assumption questions with comparative hiring, credential, origin, or category claims that infer “A helps, therefore B does not.”
Boundary: Ignore when the categories are explicitly defined as disjoint or the conclusion concerns relative degree of help rather than any help.

Transfer rule: If one person is fixed on a day and another must occur immediately after someone, then enumerate all possible adjacent-day placements before assigning any repeated person.
Error pattern: I forced the repeated-duty person onto the fixed day pair without proving uniqueness, causing unsupported deductions and contradictions.
Diagnostic check: List day slots 1–4, mark fixed appearances, place every legal consecutive pair, then verify which person appears in all surviving schedules.
Use when: Use for scheduling/ordering problems with fixed days, adjacency constraints, a single repeated participant, and “must be” option choices.
Boundary: Ignore when repeats are unrestricted, adjacency is absent, or the task asks only for one possible schedule rather than a necessary one.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a report source highlights cases because the event is uncommon, then check whether that premise already assumes the event is uncommon.
Error pattern: I missed circular reasoning and chased an unsupported side issue about bias instead of the premise-conclusion relationship.
Diagnostic check: Restate the conclusion, then ask: “Would the key premise make sense only if I already accepted that conclusion?”
Use when: Relevant for flaw questions where a premise explains evidence by asserting the same underlying fact the conclusion tries to prove.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the premise is independently supported by data or when the argument attacks representativeness without assuming its conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts political periods with art-historical trends, then choose the option matching the stated artistic continuity or contrast, not a broader inference.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from a methodological remark and picked an abstract principle instead of the directly supported comparison.
Diagnostic check: List each dynasty/period pair and mark whether the text says “different” or “often grouped together”; accept only an option restating one mark.
Use when: Apply this to reading-comprehension items about historical categories, especially when the text separates political lineage from artistic development.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an implied cause, evaluation, or external background not explicitly compared in the passage.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects one cited cause because one observed instance seems insufficient, then check whether it assumes there were no additional similar instances.
Error pattern: I focused on local survival effects instead of the hidden uniqueness assumption needed to move from “this one is inadequate” to “therefore that kind of cause is impossible.”
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: could the conclusion fail if multiple events of the same type occurred; if yes, select the option that rules that out.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where evidence targets the size, timing, or sufficiency of a single event yet the conclusion excludes an entire causal category.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already explicitly states uniqueness or when options concern side effects unrelated to the sufficiency inference.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires creating dependence by imposing unnecessary care, then choose the case with sustained intrusive support that reduces another person’s independence.
Error pattern: I matched emotional neediness alone, ignoring the required mechanism of forced care plus induced reliance.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify all core elements: unsolicited care, pressure to accept it, the other person’s autonomy being limited, and the caregiver gaining worth from dependence.
Use when: Apply this to behavior-definition questions involving caregiving, control, dependence, autonomy, or relationship dynamics.
Boundary: Ignore this when the case shows only affection, worry, proximity, or dependence without imposed help that undermines independence.

Transfer rule: If an insurance question asks how to minimize losses on a low-premium policy, then prefer the strategy that delays claims while collecting premiums earlier.
Error pattern: Success came from matching profit risk to claim timing and adverse selection, not from judging choices by generosity or fairness.
Diagnostic check: For each option, compare expected premium years before first likely claim and whether it attracts higher-risk applicants; choose the longest delay with lower risk.
Use when: Apply to insurance, warranty, subscription, or lending scenarios involving pricing, payouts, and customer risk mix.
Boundary: Ignore when the goal is maximizing enrollment, equity, legal compliance, or care quality rather than minimizing insurer losses.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a claim is “not deceptive because it is true,” then look for a principle that treats literally true statements as deceptive when they predictably induce a false takeaway.
Error pattern: Success pattern: distinguished truth-value from communicative effect and matched the principle to the dispute’s exact gap.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, state the advocate’s needed bridge as “Even true statements can count as deceptive when ___,” then pick the option filling that blank most directly.
Use when: Relevant in principle-strengthen questions involving advertising, omission, framing, or misleading comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore when the dispute is about factual accuracy itself, speaker belief alone, or morality unrelated to deception criteria.

Transfer rule: If an argument says exclusion makes a process unfair, then look for evidence that the excluded group would introduce bias, making exclusion fairness-preserving.
Error pattern: I weakened by showing the remaining participants are less capable, instead of attacking the assumption that inclusion of the excluded group would improve fairness.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Does this fact make the exclusion justified on impartiality grounds, or does it merely worsen competence after exclusion?”
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions about fairness, selection rules, eligibility, or whether excluding experts/specialists undermines a decision process.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is about accuracy, efficiency, or cost rather than fairness/impartiality of who is allowed to decide.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts a human development with before/after wildlife conditions, then infer the option summarizing that development’s effects, not a narrower detail.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the main causal theme and resisting distractors that restate only examples, trends, or outcomes for one subgroup.
Diagnostic check: List cause, affected subjects, and reported consequences; choose the answer covering all three at the highest supported level of abstraction.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions with contrast words, causal links, and multiple examples used as evidence for one broader claim.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a directly stated detail, definition, chronology, or the examples are independent rather than evidence of one cause.

Transfer rule: If a definition lists several required traits and one allowed exception, then verify every required trait and don’t reject cases that still fit the stated exception.
Error pattern: Misread a permissive clause as disqualifying and overweighted one positive feature while ignoring failed required conditions.
Diagnostic check: Make a checklist from the definition; mark each required condition yes/no and separately ask whether any mentioned issue is explicitly allowed.
Use when: Applying strict verbal definitions in multiple-choice items, especially with mixed physical, cognitive, behavioral, and social criteria.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for best explanation, typicality, or causal inference rather than exact membership by definition.

Transfer rule: If a support question gives two correlated groups, then favor new evidence that links them through the proposed causal mechanism.  
Error pattern: I chose a superficially similar extension to another population instead of integrating all stated facts into one causal story.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option by asking: does it explain both observations at once without adding a new comparison class?  
Use when: The stem combines observational evidence, a hypothesis about a required factor, and a second fact about timing, development, or exposure.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for analogy, scope expansion across populations, or a direct experiment outweighs mechanism-linking evidence.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the EXCEPT in a causal explanation set, then rate each choice by how directly it explains the stated group difference and pick the least connected one.
Error pattern: Overweighting plausibility or correlation instead of checking whether the factor specifically accounts for the contrast between the groups.
Diagnostic check: For each option, complete “This would make group X differ from group Y because ___”; eliminate any option that cannot fill that blank without extra assumptions.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items asking which statement does not explain a surprising comparison, trend, or disparity.
Boundary: Ignore when choices are definitions, necessary assumptions, or evidence-strength questions rather than explanatory causes.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a policy “failed” because outcomes remain below a target, then test whether evidence shows the policy improved results relative to no-policy baseline.
Error pattern: I judged by absolute trend/level instead of the needed counterfactual effect of the intervention.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this choice compare actual outcomes with what would have happened without the policy?” Prefer options giving that comparison.
Use when: Relevant in weaken/refute questions about whether a program achieved expected results despite still-poor indicators.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is about trend description, timing only, or when no causal policy-effect evaluation is at issue.

Transfer rule: If a causal claim is drawn from one event’s correlation, then test it against comparable replications across time or settings before accepting causation.
Error pattern: Success pattern: weakening by showing the reported advantage fails to persist in a closely matched repeat case.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Is there a similarly structured comparison where the effect reverses or disappears?” If yes, that strongly weakens the claim.
Use when: The argument generalizes from a single dataset, season, tournament, or sample to a broad benefit or causal advantage.
Boundary: Ignore when strong controls, random assignment, or a stated mechanism already rule out coincidence and make replication evidence irrelevant.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a feared harmful effect is unnecessary, then prefer evidence showing the activity directly improves or at least does not reduce the targeted offline outcome.
Error pattern: Strengthen questions are won by matching the conclusion’s causal claim, not by choosing background facts or fixed-time tradeoff statements.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this option make the feared harm less plausible by linking the activity to equal-or-better real-world behavior?”
Use when: The stimulus generalizes from subgroup findings to a broad reassurance that a new behavior will not damage a traditional one.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task is to weaken, explain methodology, or compare prevalence rather than support the causal reassurance.

Transfer rule: If a statement is “if P, then not Q,” then accept any case where P is false or Q is false; do not treat the conditional as requiring P.
Error pattern: Misread a conditional as fixing one specific outcome instead of recognizing all truth-making cases under material implication.
Diagnostic check: Test all four P/Q combinations and eliminate only the one with P true and Q true; any remaining option is compatible.
Use when: Relevant for logic items with “if,” “only if,” “unless,” negation, and answer choices describing combinations of two conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when the statement is biconditional, causal/temporal, or uses domain facts that make material-implication truth tables inappropriate.

Transfer rule: If a ranking puzzle says exactly one statement is false, then test each possible liar separately and force all others true to complete the permutation.
Error pattern: I reasoned by loose plausibility and skipped exhaustive case completion, so I missed that every liar case could determine a full order.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate liar, write the fixed positions from the true statements, place the remaining person in the only open slot, and verify uniqueness.
Use when: Use this on single-liar logic problems with exclusive positions, orderings, or assignments where each person claims one slot-related fact.
Boundary: Ignore this when statements are not jointly exhaustive, can all be partly true, or positions are not one-to-one.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “unused/serves no current purpose” to “therefore it can produce major benefits,” then test for an unsupported assumption about latent positive capacity.
Error pattern: Treating absence of current function or observed effects as evidence of a specific valuable potential.
Diagnostic check: Underline each premise and the conclusion; ask, “Which new property appears only in the conclusion?” If that property is never supported, flag a gap.
Use when: Claims infer hidden talent, power, or usefulness from inactivity, redundancy, or lack of visible consequences.
Boundary: Ignore when the premises independently establish that the unused element actually has that specific beneficial capability.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims one cause for an outcome, then challenge it only with alternatives, counterexamples, or causal-comparison questions; do not treat background modifiers as direct refutations.
Error pattern: I overread a related-factor question as weakening, instead of separating true causal rivals from merely complementary variables.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask of each option: “Does this, if answered, directly test whether the claimed cause is not the real cause?” If no, discard it.
Use when: The stimulus is a causal explanation in everyday behavior, health, or social trends, and options ask different kinds of probing questions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic for definition, principle, arithmetic, or pure fact-recall questions with no causal claim.

Transfer rule: If a past loss is already unrecoverable, then ask whether the current choice is being changed to justify or recover that loss; if not, it is not a sunk-cost effect.
Error pattern: Mistaking any mention of an irreversible past cost for sunk-cost bias, instead of checking whether the present decision is distorted by that past cost.
Diagnostic check: Remove the past expenditure/loss from the story and see whether the chosen action would reasonably stay the same; if yes, mark “not sunk-cost effect.”
Use when: The scenario includes prior time, money, effort, or commitment and asks whether current behavior is irrationally driven by it.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about causation unrelated to current choice distortion or when the past cost is still avoidable/recoverable.

Transfer rule: If an argument concludes “only if” by eliminating one alternative, then add the assumption that the other alternative occurs whenever its enabling condition is met.
Error pattern: I focused on a tempting causal/background statement instead of the missing link needed to force the disjunction into a single remaining branch.
Diagnostic check: List each option in the either/or setup, mark each option’s stated prerequisite, then ask: “What extra premise guarantees one option whenever allowed, so the conclusion about the other follows only in the leftover case?”
Use when: Relevant for conditional-reasoning questions with an exclusive-looking choice set, gating conditions, and a conclusion narrowing one branch.
Boundary: Ignore when choices are not exhaustive, the conclusion is not produced by ruling out alternatives, or the needed assumption is about a definition rather than branch selection.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims a trait is the key cause of a shared ability, then check whether other members with that ability also have the trait.
Error pattern: I focused on an irrelevant side condition about where the subject can grow, instead of testing whether the proposed cause tracks the phenomenon across comparable cases.
Diagnostic check: Ask: among close comparators that also show the target outcome, is the alleged causal feature consistently present?
Use when: Relevant for causal explanations in biology or groups of similar entities where one observed trait is said to explain a distinctive tolerance or performance.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about this one case’s description, or when no meaningful comparison group exists.

Transfer rule: If a statement is used to make a proposed remedy irrelevant, then match it with a statement that blocks the remedy’s causal pathway at the needed step.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking argumentative function, not topic similarity; the right match neutralizes usefulness rather than adding support or background.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Does this statement independently show the proposed intervention cannot improve the target outcome, even if the intervention occurs?”
Use when: Relevant in boldface/function questions about plans, products, or causes where one claim is used to show no added benefit.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for factual equivalence, strengthening, or assumptions rather than the role a statement plays.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers causation from two groups differing on a target treatment, then check whether any other relevant conditions also differed.
Error pattern: Success pattern: weakening a causal claim by exposing uncontrolled confounders rather than adding background facts or partial alternatives.
Diagnostic check: List all variables that could affect the outcome; if any unequal variable besides the treatment exists, mark the causal conclusion as not established.
Use when: A comparison study claims one factor caused a result because one group had it and another did not.
Boundary: Ignore when groups are randomized or explicitly matched on all major outcome-related conditions.

Transfer rule: If a promise has the form “if condition, then action,” then “broke the promise” means the condition happened while the action did not.
Error pattern: Success pattern: treating a broken conditional commitment as requiring the trigger and denying the promised response, not inferring anything from cases where the trigger fails.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite it as condition → action; then test each choice for “condition true” and “action false” only.
Use when: Conditional promises, agreements, rules, or obligations where you must infer what follows from a violation or breach.
Boundary: Ignore when the statement is biconditional, causal, probabilistic, or asks about normal truth rather than specifically about breaking the commitment.

Transfer rule: If an argument says activity X should be permitted because riskier activity Y is permitted, then flag it as flawed unless X and Y are governed by the same kind of setting and authority.
Error pattern: Treats legality in one context as justification for legality in a different context by comparing relative danger only.
Diagnostic check: Identify the conclusion’s policy target, then ask whether the cited comparison case involves the same regulator, environment, and type of restriction; if not, reject the analogy.
Use when: The argument moves from “this other risky thing is allowed” to “therefore this restriction here is unjustified.”
Boundary: Ignore when the comparison case is under the same rules, purpose, and decision-maker.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “the current share is appropriate” to claims about future added funds, then test whether it illegitimately treats percentage fit as fixing dollar amounts.
Error pattern: I misread a proportion-versus-quantity flaw as a part-to-whole flaw.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each key claim in two forms—percent of total and absolute amount—and see whether the conclusion switches forms without support.
Use when: The stimulus discusses budgets, rates, shares, allocations, or “appropriate percentage” and then recommends spending choices after a total changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when every premise and conclusion stays in the same metric or when a true part-whole inference is explicitly made.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims a behavior is caused by missing parental social training, then prefer evidence that directly compares same-species subjects with and without that training and shows the predicted behavior change.
Error pattern: Strong reasoning links the proposed cause to the outcome while ruling out mere correlation or irrelevant aggression facts.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this option isolate parental socialization as the differing factor, compare similar groups, and measure aggression in a relevant context?
Use when: The stimulus gives a causal hypothesis about early upbringing shaping later behavior and asks for the strongest strengthening evidence.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for weakening, assumption, definition, or when options only describe prevalence, different behaviors, or unrelated contexts.

Transfer rule: If an argument excludes a category from one changed feature, then test whether stronger overall similarity still supports inclusion.
Error pattern: Overweighted a broad side fact about other categories and missed the premise-to-classification leap from one trait.
Diagnostic check: List the author’s defining criterion; ask, “Would the conclusion fail if the item still matches the target more than anything else overall?”
Use when: Classification, definition, or “ought not be classified as” arguments rely mainly on a historical trait or a single characteristic.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already proves that one feature is necessary or gives a complete, explicit definition.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires government regulation of firms’ market behavior to protect public welfare, then choose the option involving a regulable safety/health-related business activity, not private market choices.
Error pattern: Success comes from mapping every clause in the definition to the option and separating regulated objects from ordinary economic behavior.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is there a governmental oversight target here, involving entry, qualifications, pricing control, or safety/health compliance of a microeconomic actor?
Use when: Apply this on concept-definition multiple-choice items about public administration, regulation, market governance, or legal oversight of firms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem asks for voluntary decisions, market outcomes without state action, or macroeconomic policy rather than micro-level regulation.

Transfer rule: If a statement contrasts an activity seeming harmful in one context with experts using it therapeutically in another, then infer the broad property being tested from the expert-use context.
Error pattern: Success came from resolving an apparent contradiction by prioritizing the passage’s explicit medical conclusion over surface intuition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each context, mark which is appearance versus evidence-backed claim, and choose the option supported by the evidence-backed claim.
Use when: Relevant in reading questions with contrast words, expert findings, rehabilitation/therapy contexts, or seeming paradoxes about harm versus benefit.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices ask about unrelated facts, popularity, difficulty, or when no stronger evidence source is identified.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion applies a definition using a comparison term, then verify the term’s reference point matches the facts given.
Error pattern: Success pattern: I checked whether the argument’s evidence fit the definition rather than chasing side issues about degree, consequences, or other prices.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the definition as required conditions, mark any ambiguous term, and ask whether the stimulus fixes that term’s source or baseline.
Use when: Relevant for definition-based arguments, especially those involving comparisons across places, groups, times, or measurement standards.
Boundary: Ignore when the key term’s reference is explicitly specified or when the question asks for a causal assumption instead of definitional fit.

Transfer rule: If a definition contrasts “mere conduct completes the crime” with “completion requires a resulting harm,” then classify by asking whether the offense is complete upon the act alone.
Error pattern: I focused on vivid means or property-taking scenarios instead of testing whether the legal description requires a separate result.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each option as “complete when actor does X” versus “complete only when X causes Y”; choose only those fitting the first form.
Use when: This applies to criminal-law classification questions distinguishing conduct offenses from result-based offenses using statutory wording.
Boundary: Ignore this when the category depends on intent, victim status, thresholds, or special procedural elements rather than completion by conduct versus result.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a broad budget-driven trend and gives one project as an example, then choose the option summarizing the general trend, not the example’s research goal.
Error pattern: Mistaking a supporting example for the main point; narrowing from a broad policy/financial claim to one specific scientific question.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each sentence as claim or example, then verify the choice covers the central claim and would still fit if the example were removed.
Use when: The passage mentions funding limits, future approvals, cancellations, and then names a specific project as illustration.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference about the example itself, or the passage has only one concrete topic.

Transfer rule: If a claim is supported by benefits plus a duty phrase like “should” or “whenever possible,” then treat the recommendation as the main conclusion.
Error pattern: I chose a descriptive background statement instead of the author’s prescriptive takeaway.
Diagnostic check: Identify the sentence the other claims support; ask, “What is the author urging someone to do, not merely describing?”
Use when: The argument contains value language, feasibility qualifiers, and evidence about why a method or policy helps avoid errors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage is purely explanatory or causal and contains no recommendation, obligation, or endorsement.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “lucrative” from higher selling prices across markets, then check whether it assumes similar production costs, not just demand or baseline prices.
Error pattern: Mistaking a revenue comparison for a profit conclusion; focusing on price levels while ignoring cost comparability.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate profit as selling price minus cost and ask: “Could the conclusion fail if costs are much higher in the target market?”
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions comparing profitability, attractiveness, or margins between places, products, or business models using price evidence.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about price, demand, scarcity, or revenue rather than profit or lucrativeness.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims X causes Y from one civilization’s history, then test for another comparable civilization with X but not Y.  
Error pattern: Treating correlation within a single case as proof of causation without checking cross-case counterexamples.  
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Can I name a similar society where the alleged cause is present yet the predicted decline is absent?”  
Use when: The stimulus makes a broad causal claim from historical sequence, parallel trends, or one culture’s development.  
Boundary: Ignore when choices only discuss preferences, definitions, or side facts rather than a genuine comparable case bearing on the cause-effect link.

Transfer rule: If a scenario adds simple protective/handling steps during movement from producer to user, then classify it as circulation processing; if it changes freshness, creates a new product, or mainly prices/grades for sale, do not.
Error pattern: I overfocused on sorting/grading keywords and ignored the required stage and purpose of the operation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark two boxes: “occurs after production and before use” and “is only packaging/dividing/measuring/sorting/marking/assembly, not transformation or preservation”; choose only if both are checked.
Use when: Relevant for classification questions distinguishing logistics-handling activities from production, storage treatment, or retail merchandising.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition explicitly includes preservation, manufacturing, or sales/pricing activities.

Transfer rule: If a tax rate per unit is fixed and the taxed quantity steadily falls, then infer tax revenue steadily falls too.
Error pattern: Mistaking a decline in one category for required growth in an alternative category; ignoring direct quantity-to-revenue implications.
Diagnostic check: Identify the taxed base and rate; ask whether revenue equals rate × quantity and whether any other changing factor is stated.
Use when: The stimulus gives a constant per-unit charge, a trend in the taxed activity, and asks what must be true.
Boundary: Ignore this when the rate, exemptions, compliance, or tax base can change, or when only possible rather than necessary effects are discussed.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires a feedback loop, then choose the case missing confirmation, follow-up, or adjustment after sending/acting.
Error pattern: I overfocused on emotional tone or pressure and ignored whether the full feedback cycle actually closed.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark four steps: assignment/signal, acknowledgment, progress/status feedback, and receiver confirmation or adjustment; pick the one with a broken step.
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching questions about processes, communication loops, monitoring, or real-time correction.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is about effort, attitude, speed, or etiquette rather than process completion and feedback.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts current obstacles with proposed fixes, then choose the option summarizing both the problems and the response strategy.
Error pattern: I fixated on one mentioned remedy and missed the higher-level structure pairing challenges with countermeasures.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list in 3–5 words the passage’s main units; if you have at least one “problem” and one “solution,” prefer a synthesis option.
Use when: The prompt summarizes policy, management, or operational text with deficits, capacity gaps, reforms, and improvement measures.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a single detail, example, definition, or explicitly narrowed subpoint.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts levels of knowledge by saying one lacks grasp of essence/laws while another is logical and systematic, then infer a relative criticism of the weaker level, not inclusion or absolute certainty.
Error pattern: Mistaking a classificatory list for a part-whole or containment claim instead of extracting the evaluative contrast the author signals.
Diagnostic check: Underline adjectives about each category; ask, “Do these support hierarchy/credibility, composition, or certainty?” Choose only an option matching the stated relation.
Use when: Relevant in reading-comprehension items that define categories and compare their depth, rigor, or reliability.
Boundary: Ignore when the text explicitly states membership, equivalence, causation, or a universal claim beyond a comparison.

Transfer rule: If a claim says reducing one suspected cause still correlates with more of the outcome, then look for a replacement behavior that increases the outcome even more.
Error pattern: Success pattern: resolved an apparent contradiction by identifying a compensating substitution, not by attacking the trend or sample size.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What did the reducers switch to?” and test whether that substitute could outweigh the reduction in the original source.
Use when: Relevant in discrepancy questions comparing people who cut back on one item yet still show equal or higher totals of the measured effect.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only discuss motives, prices, or group proportions without changing the causal pathway for the outcome.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “no consistent causal link” from many apparent counterexamples, then require an assumption that a true consistent link would produce exception-free pairing in at least one direction.
Error pattern: Correctly spotted a necessary bridge from observed noncoincidence to denial of consistency, rather than chasing side explanations about missing records.
Diagnostic check: Identify the conclusion’s negation, ask what pattern a consistent link would predict, and verify the needed assumption makes the cited exceptions incompatible with that pattern.
Use when: Relevant in weaken/assumption items about causation, correlation, and claims denied because events often fail to coincide.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion allows probabilistic, partial, or one-way causation rather than strict consistency.

Transfer rule: If a claim says a mechanism causes an outcome, then favor evidence showing that blocking the mechanism prevents the outcome or enhancing it promotes the outcome.
Error pattern: Strong causal-support reasoning succeeds by testing intervention on the proposed cause, not by citing loose correlation or background facts.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Does this option change the alleged cause and predictably change the effect in the matching direction?”
Use when: Apply on strengthen questions about biological or physical mechanisms with a hypothesized cause, mediator, and observable result.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only mention exceptions, unrelated regions, residual baseline levels, or facts that do not manipulate the proposed mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which fact best undermines a stated excuse, then choose the option that directly negates that excuse under the same policy conditions.
Error pattern: I favored a related responsibility statement instead of targeting the merchant’s specific blocking rationale.
Diagnostic check: List each excuse given, then ask of each option: “Does this make that excuse invalid even when the merchant’s facts are true?”
Use when: Relevant in weaken/challenge questions about rule implementation, rights exceptions, refunds/returns, or policy-based justifications.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is to assign fault, describe consequences, or support the policy rather than rebut an excuse.

Transfer rule: If a safety claim is based on one narrow test group or endpoint, then look for evidence of harm in other affected populations or delayed/indirect outcomes.
Error pattern: Overgeneralizing from limited negative findings to a broad no-harm conclusion.
Diagnostic check: List the studied population, timeframe, and health measures; ask whether the conclusion extends beyond any of those limits.
Use when: An argument infers overall harmlessness from absence of detected effects in a specific sample, tissue type, or short observation period.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence already covers all relevant populations, mechanisms, and long-term outcomes matched to the conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a rule says “selected only when P and (Q or R)” and someone was not selected, then infer only “not(P and (Q or R)),” and test equivalent forms before choosing.
Error pattern: Treated failure of a sufficient condition as proof of one specific missing part instead of using the full negation logically.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the condition symbolically; negate it with De Morgan’s law; reject any option that adds unsupported facts or picks one missing component without necessity.
Use when: Needed for conditional statements with conjunctions/disjunctions and conclusions drawn from someone failing to meet an outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the premise states a biconditional, exclusivity, comparative ranking, or gives extra facts fixing which requirement failed.

Transfer rule: If a statement merely frames the topic and the conclusion could still stand whether that statement is true or false, then classify it as background compatible with both sides, not support or the issue resolved.
Error pattern: Mistaking a concessive opener/common-ground statement for the problem the argument aims to solve.
Diagnostic check: Remove the opening claim and ask: does the core inference still work, and would both agreement and disagreement with the conclusion still be possible?
Use when: The stimulus begins with “although/but/while” style concessions before presenting evidence and a narrower conclusion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the opening claim is later used as a premise, assumption, or explicit target.

Transfer rule: If a statement defines a causal chain, then choose the option that preserves the same chain without adding new outcomes or false equivalences.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracing permitted inferences only; failures come from overextending to stronger claims, interventions, or outcomes not stated.
Diagnostic check: Map links as cause → intermediate → result, then test each option for unsupported leaps, reversed causality, or extra claims.
Use when: Relevant for definition-based or logic MCQs describing mechanisms, especially with causes, mediators, and effects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for external knowledge, probability, value judgment, or when options depend on facts beyond the stated chain.

Transfer rule: If a passage centers on uncertainty, unknowns, or changing conditions, then prefer a theme about variability rather than mere difficulty or complexity.
Error pattern: I matched supporting details about many factors and implementation difficulty instead of the core framing concept introduced at the start.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the passage’s topic word and its governing property; if most sentences explain uncertainty/change, reject choices that only restate “hard” or “important.”
Use when: Apply this on main-idea questions where one option names a broad challenge and another names instability, uncertainty, or changeability.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly analyzes multiple components, procedures, or tradeoffs without emphasizing unknown or shifting conditions.

Transfer rule: If a stem asks for the argument’s “hypothesis,” then identify the unstated general principle needed to move from premise to conclusion.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting a hidden definitional assumption rather than paraphrasing the stated claim or choosing a side comment.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What universal rule must be true for this evidence to justify calling or not calling someone a member of a profession?”
Use when: Relevant in argument questions about classifications, titles, professions, or identity based on one criterion such as income, training, or behavior.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for the main conclusion, a directly stated premise, or an answer adding new factual claims instead of a bridging principle.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts harm because a group is excluded from a channel, then test whether that group’s needs are often met through another channel, weakening the harm claim.
Error pattern: I chose an adaptation/improvement fact instead of challenging the assumed link from exclusion to reduced well-being.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the chain “new trend → exclusion → less participation → worse life” and ask which option breaks the middle or final link most directly.
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions about social change, access barriers, and claimed quality-of-life impacts on a population.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for support, or when alternatives still depend on the blocked channel.

Transfer rule: If a causal claim rests on a framing manipulation, then test whether subjects actually accepted the framing.
Error pattern: I attacked the content of reported experiences instead of the link between the manipulation and the observed difference.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Does this fact show the treatment failed, was disbelieved, or differed only in wording rather than expectation?”
Use when: Relevant in experiments, surveys, or argument-weaken questions where conclusions generalize from different instructions, primes, or descriptions.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument does not depend on participants believing a prompt, or when an option directly breaks causation by another stronger mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion says an agency lacks power to curb a harm, then add the premise linking that missing power to an effective reduction of the harm.
Error pattern: I picked a tempting “weak supervision” statement instead of the necessary causal bridge from the uncontrollable factor to the outcome.
Diagnostic check: Remove the candidate premise and ask: does the argument still connect lack of authority over X to inability to reduce Y? If yes, reject it.
Use when: Relevant in necessary-premise questions where the argument moves from limited jurisdiction or control to practical ineffectiveness.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only compare institutions, restate authority facts, or discuss implementation details without affecting the harm-reduction link.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends by stressing harms or drawbacks after brief background, then choose the option capturing the author’s evaluative focus, not the setup details.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating context and features from the main thrust, then weighting the concluding judgment most heavily.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as background, description, or evaluation; if most emphasis or the final claim is evaluative, prefer the summary centered on that evaluation.
Use when: The passage gives history or characteristics first, then shifts to consequences, criticism, or concern about a system or policy.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage stays neutral, evenly balanced, or explicitly aims to explain origins, structure, or definitions.

Transfer rule: If an argument repeats a key word from premise to conclusion, then verify it keeps the same meaning in both places.
Error pattern: Equivocation success pattern: the right diagnosis is a semantic shift, not a causal, value, or scope issue.
Diagnostic check: Replace the repeated term with a short definition in each sentence; if the definitions differ or make the link invalid, flag ambiguity.
Use when: Apply this on verbal-reasoning questions where a conclusion relies heavily on one repeated abstract or figurative term.
Boundary: Ignore this when the term is clearly defined once and used consistently, and the flaw is instead about evidence, causation, or assumptions.

Transfer rule: If a prompt asks which option does not belong to stated characteristics, then keep only traits explicitly described in the passage’s category and exclude cultural significance if the passage lists physical features.
Error pattern: Success came from separating textual attributes from broader associative facts.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each choice as directly supported, inferable physical trait, or outside-category fact; choose the outside-category item.
Use when: Relevant for reading questions contrasting descriptive details with historical, cultural, moral, or symbolic statements.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage itself defines the broader significance as one of the characteristics or asks about overall importance.

Transfer rule: If an argument attacks a common explanation by noting missing support and then points to facts favoring another cause, then choose the structure matching “undercuts one explanation + supports an alternative.”
Error pattern: Success pattern: tracking argument method rather than topic details or truth of the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Mark each premise as either “absence of support for stated cause” or “positive support for rival cause”; if both appear, pick the choice describing that two-step move.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken or method questions where a passage contrasts a received view with evidence about what actually drives events.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument only states a rule, questions source reliability, or merely cites expert agreement.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a broad claim first and later gives effects or examples, then choose the option restating that lead claim most directly.
Error pattern: Mistook a consequence or emphasis detail for the main idea instead of the thesis sentence.
Diagnostic check: Mark the passage’s first complete claim, then ask of each option: thesis, cause, effect, or example; prefer the thesis match.
Use when: Short reading-comprehension items with one topic sentence followed by supporting descriptions, estimates, or consequences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly shifts focus later, contrasts viewpoints, or asks for an implication rather than main content.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires two neighboring powerful entities jointly radiating benefits outward, then choose the option with both dual-core cooperation and surrounding regional spillover.
Error pattern: Success came from matching all defining elements instead of fixating on any example of growth, integration, or having “two” internal components.
Diagnostic check: Underline four cues—two entities, both strong, neighboring/co-located, joint promotion of the surrounding area—and reject any choice missing one cue.
Use when: Apply this on concept-definition multiple choice where several options share surface similarities like coordination, development, or dual structure.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept does not require outward spillover or when “two” refers to sectors, districts, or city-suburb parts rather than two economies.

Transfer rule: If an argument defends a policy by citing efficiency or incentives, then question it with a deeper value or mission conflict that undercuts the policy’s legitimacy.
Error pattern: Success pattern: distinguishing a fundamental institutional objection from mere side effects, implementation flaws, or claims that the policy may be ineffective.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as principle-level, execution-level, psychological side effect, or outcome doubt; prefer the one that most directly challenges the policy’s underlying justification.
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions about reforms in schools, organizations, or professions where governance goals may conflict with core institutional roles.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem asks for practical harms, feasibility, evidence about results, or the strongest objection under stated operational goals.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires short-term market winning via flexible, personalized differentiation within an industry, then choose the option showing a firm changing non-price features to stand out from similar rivals now.
Error pattern: I overfocused on strong brand positioning and uniqueness, while missing the required competitive context, short-term aim, and adaptive differentiation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify all three boxes: same-industry rivalry present, distinguishing tactic beyond generic price war, and explicit near-term market gain.
Use when: Relevant for business-strategy definition questions contrasting positioning, promotion, price competition, and differentiation among multiple firms.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept is about long-term niche strategy, monopoly status, routine holiday promotions, or pure spending escalation.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a problem stems from a rule not being implemented, then weaken it by asserting that the rule actually is implemented, not by attacking side remedies.
Error pattern: I targeted a peripheral claim about possible solutions instead of the core causal premise linking nonimplementation to the harm.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, underline the main cause statement and ask which option most directly contradicts that exact premise.
Use when: Apply this on weaken questions with background facts, a stated cause of abuse/failure, and extra remarks about limited enforcement channels.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets a recommendation, comparison, or quantified prediction rather than a central causal premise.

Transfer rule: If a claim is supported by multiple reasons and a cue like “after all,” then treat that claim as the main conclusion.
Error pattern: Success came from separating the broad recommendation from narrower premises and examples.
Diagnostic check: Mark each statement as either support or supported; identify which sentence the others are trying to justify.
Use when: The argument includes background facts, an example industry, and policy commentary leading to one forward-looking recommendation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a subsidiary conclusion or when several claims are linked without clear support indicators.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires use of home-adjacent space/resources for intensive market-oriented production, then choose the option centered on backyard/courtyard-based planting, breeding, or processing.
Error pattern: Success came from matching all defining constraints instead of latching onto a single keyword like farming or household activity.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list required elements—location near home, use of surrounding idle space/resources, intensive production, and commercial output—and verify the candidate satisfies each.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions involving economic activities, land use, or household production models with multiple necessary conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is broad, noncommercial, or not tied to home-adjacent space and resource use.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires profit-driven social sharing, then exclude cases where sharing lacks any incentive, bargain, coupon, referral reward, or sales mechanism.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every required element and rejecting a tempting social-sharing example that missed the profit-driven trigger.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark three boxes: social interaction, product spread/sale, participant profit incentive; eliminate any option missing one box.
Use when: Apply this on definition questions with conjunctive criteria, especially business-model or classification items involving motives, mechanisms, and outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the definition allows optional traits, asks for best example rather than strict membership, or focuses on personal expression instead of a model.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires multiple distinct professional skills plus integration across knowledge, then choose the case showing two separate professions/disciplines actively combined in work.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every clause of a compound definition and rejecting distracting hobbies, volume of practice, or breadth within one field.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the required elements and verify evidence for each: skill one, skill two, and real cross-domain integration.
Use when: Apply this to classification questions built on strict definitions, especially where options mix professional abilities with leisure activities or subskills.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept asks only for excellence in one domain or does not require integration.

Transfer rule: If a rule says “A and not B imply C-or-D,” then test sufficiency for “not A” by assuming A and finding an option that makes the implication impossible.
Error pattern: Success came from using contradiction on a conditional rather than reversing it or confusing sufficient with necessary conditions.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as “A ∧ ¬B → (C ∨ D)”; for each candidate with ¬A as target, temporarily set A true and see whether the candidate forces ¬(C ∨ D) while keeping ¬B.
Use when: Apply to logic items with conditionals, conjunctions/disjunctions, and questions asking for a sufficient condition for a negated event.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for a necessary condition, probability judgment, or gives biconditional/equivalence rules instead.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires deliberate self-presentation to create a favorable impression, then reject examples lacking intent or lacking a positive-image goal.
Error pattern: Success came from separating purposeful impression-shaping behavior from merely noticeable, habitual, or misbehaving conduct.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is the person intentionally managing how others see them, and is the target impression favorable? If either answer is no, exclude it.
Use when: Apply this on definition-match questions about social behavior, motives, signaling, image control, or reputation management.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept does not require intention, does not require others’ perception, or includes negative-image management too.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus says only people with experience can truly understand and solve problems in a field, then infer any effective or creative solution there must come from someone with experience.
Error pattern: Success came from chaining necessary conditions carefully instead of choosing stronger comparative or frequency claims.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the argument as conditionals, link them, then reject any option adding “rarely,” “more,” field-invariance, or other unsupported strength.
Use when: Apply this on strengthen/support questions built from universal claims, necessity language, and experience/understanding/ability chains.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage gives statistics, exceptions, causal reversals, or asks for a weaken/explain answer.

Transfer rule: If an observed action could stem from a situational or relationship-based reason, then reduce any inference that it reflects the actor’s pure disposition or altruism.
Error pattern: Success comes from spotting attribution discounting: alternative plausible causes weaken the weight given to the most obvious cause.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, list the behavior, the initial inferred motive, and at least one credible alternative explanation; if the inference weakens, discount principle applies.
Use when: Relevant in social-judgment items where someone interprets another person’s behavior, motive, character, or intent from a single act.
Boundary: Ignore when the case is only admiration, evaluation, prediction, or advice without competing causal explanations for the behavior.

Transfer rule: If a concept describes being trapped by preference-shaped information exposure, then exclude options showing broad, goal-directed use rather than compulsive, self-reinforcing immersion.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the definition’s core mechanism, not surface keywords about internet use, posting, or platforms.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this behavior narrow inputs through personal preference and create habitual enclosure, or is it ordinary tool use across varied purposes?
Use when: Apply on questions contrasting a defined psychological/social phenomenon with examples that merely share the same medium or technology.
Boundary: Ignore when the definition targets physical accumulation, addiction generally, or non-information behaviors instead of selective exposure patterns.

Transfer rule: If rules mix “only if,” “if not X then not Y,” and a fixed outcome, then translate each into conditional/contrapositive form and test all remaining cases.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating what is forced from what stays underdetermined instead of overcommitting from chained conditionals.
Diagnostic check: Write each statement symbolically, apply the given fact first, propagate necessary consequences, then build two consistent scenarios for any target claim to see whether it varies.
Use when: Relevant for inference questions with several conditional constraints, exclusivity/necessity wording, and one final settled fact.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem requires probabilities, definitions, or outside knowledge rather than pure logical consistency.

Transfer rule: If a passage concedes a benefit then spends most space questioning outcomes, then choose the thesis combining convenience with hidden drawbacks, not a broad “weigh pros and cons” summary.
Error pattern: Mistaking a framing sentence or general setup for the author’s main claim instead of the specific evaluative conclusion developed afterward.
Diagnostic check: Mark the concession, the pivot words, and the final rhetorical question; if they all target one downside, prefer the narrower conclusion.
Use when: The text contrasts access/quantity/ease with learning, absorption, inheritance, or wisdom, especially through examples and rhetorical questioning.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage truly balances both sides equally or explicitly argues only for a neutral evaluation principle.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists examples of errors and ends with a broad evaluative takeaway, then choose the option stating the overarching call or theme, not a narrower remedy.
Error pattern: Mistaking illustrative symptoms or specific fixes for the author’s main point.
Diagnostic check: Summarize the passage in 8–12 words without examples; if your summary needs a specific error type, your choice is probably too narrow.
Use when: The passage opens with survey/findings, gives multiple examples, and closes with a general comment about a broader issue.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific measure, cause, or detail rather than the main idea.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion predicts eradication by replacing a harmful population, then prefer evidence showing the modified population can spread and outcompete across generations in the wild.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matching the answer to the argument’s bottleneck, not merely to local benefits or side details.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “What must remain true for long-term elimination?” Then verify the choice strengthens persistence, inheritance, and population-level dominance.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen questions about interventions that work by altering transmission routes, reproduction, or ecological replacement over time.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument hinges on immediate efficacy, safety, ethics, cost, or short-term individual outcomes rather than durable population takeover.

Transfer rule: If an argument concludes two options are equally safe from one safety metric plus a different risk metric, then test whether it illegitimately merges distinct dimensions into one overall judgment.
Error pattern: Chose an outside possibility instead of spotting a scope shift between harm severity and event frequency in the meaning of “safer.”
Diagnostic check: List each compared outcome, label whether it is frequency or severity, and ask whether the conclusion changes the evaluation standard mid-argument.
Use when: The stimulus compares overall safety, quality, or risk using statistics about different stages, outcomes, or types of harm.
Boundary: Ignore when all premises and the conclusion use the same metric and timeframe consistently.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a group cannot survive because it cannot afford a required change, then check whether it assumes that every member must actually make that change.
Error pattern: I focused on comparative cost differences instead of testing the hidden necessity link between regulation and forced conversion.
Diagnostic check: Negate the suspected assumption; if some affected members could already meet the new requirement without changing anything, the conclusion should collapse.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions involving new rules, compliance costs, business survival, or claims that all members of a group must upgrade.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion depends on relative advantage alone, not on whether a change is universally required.

Transfer rule: If an ad highlights a percentage or proportion, then convert it to absolute amount and compare it to the relevant recommended or needed total.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting denominator neglect—percentages can sound impressive while hiding trivial real-world quantity.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Per serving or use, how many units does this actually provide, and what fraction of the target requirement is that?”
Use when: Apply this to claims about concentration, purity, percentage content, or efficiency where usefulness depends on total delivered amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when the decision truly depends only on relative composition, not on meeting any external benchmark or practical intake level.

Transfer rule: If a category is defined by core functions, then test each option against every required function before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from function-based classification instead of relying on institutional familiarity or name cues.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it take deposits, make loans, and create deposit-like money; if any key function is missing, exclude it.
Use when: Apply this to finance, economics, or regulation questions that sort institutions by operational role within a system.
Boundary: Ignore this when the category is legal, ownership-based, historical, or uses a special textbook exception overriding functional traits.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts economic importance with moral/spiritual concerns and ends in a caution, then choose the option capturing the balanced main appeal, not a single supporting point.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions reward integrating the author’s full stance; over-focusing on one emphasized detail causes narrow choices.
Diagnostic check: Summarize the passage in one sentence containing both the positive context and the warning; reject any option missing either core element.
Use when: The text presents a trend, acknowledges its value, then criticizes neglected human consequences and implies a broader normative purpose.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, cause, example, or policy measure rather than overall intention.

Transfer rule: If a passage says a factor is usually helpful but an extreme case reverses the effect, then test whether the extreme removes a prerequisite for survival.
Error pattern: I overextended a growth-enhancing correlation and missed that threshold conditions can override trend-based benefits.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “In the extreme scenario, does the organism still have the minimum resource or habitat required to exist at all?”
Use when: Relevant in causal questions contrasting moderate improvement with collapse under extreme conditions, especially in ecology or resource-dependent systems.
Boundary: Ignore when the extreme case changes only the degree of a helpful factor, not the presence of a necessary condition.

Transfer rule: If a logic puzzle gives category totals plus equalities/inequalities, then convert each trait into binary slots and force the totals before choosing a candidate.
Error pattern: Success came from structured constraint propagation instead of guessing from a narrative description.
Diagnostic check: Make a 4×3 table, mark fixed same/different relations, apply the exact counts, and verify that only one person can have all three required traits.
Use when: Relevant in multiple-choice deduction problems with several people, several attributes, and statements about matching levels plus total counts.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on outside facts, probabilities, or meanings beyond explicit logical constraints.

Transfer rule: If one suspect cannot perform a required act and another never acts without a partner, then test every feasible culprit set against those constraints.
Error pattern: Success came from converting verbal dependencies into participation constraints and eliminating impossible individual/group combinations.
Diagnostic check: List all allowed culprit sets, remove any set lacking the needed capability or violating “never without” conditions, then see what member appears in every remaining set.
Use when: Relevant in suspect-selection logic problems with capability limits, dependency statements, and a closed set of possible culprits.
Boundary: Ignore when possibilities are not exhaustive or when statements are uncertain, probabilistic, or about motives rather than hard participation constraints.

Transfer rule: If a claim is defended by redefining any alleged counterexample so the claim stays true, then test for circular reasoning.
Error pattern: Treating the conclusion as guaranteed by the premise through a definition shift, instead of giving independent support.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would this argument still work if the disputed item kept its ordinary classification?” If not, it likely presupposes the point.
Use when: A principle is protected from objections by saying apparent exceptions cannot count under the key term.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument offers separate evidence for the reclassification rather than using it only to save the original claim.

Transfer rule: If a remedy targets one suspected cause but the problem persists, then look for an independent cause that still produces the same outcome.
Error pattern: Chose an option merely related to the setting or timeline, instead of one that causally explains persistence after the intervention.
Diagnostic check: Ask: after the recommended change is made, does this option still create the bad result on its own? If not, reject it.
Use when: Applicable to strengthen-explain questions about failed fixes, policy changes, or interventions that did not improve outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is to weaken the recommendation itself, predict side effects, or compare which cause was originally strongest.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives examples of setbacks but ends by urging continuation of one practice, then choose the option stating “continue despite risks,” not the broader background claim.
Error pattern: I focused on a supporting generalization instead of the author’s main prescriptive conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the thesis sentence, then ask: which option captures the recommendation/result that the examples are used to support?
Use when: Relevant for argument-main-idea questions with analogy, contrast, or examples of accidents/failures followed by a judgment about future action.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, an example’s purpose only, or a purely descriptive summary without any advocated stance.

Transfer rule: If an experiment’s conclusion claims true relief/cure, then prefer evidence showing the treatment only masks symptoms or changes reporting, not evidence that a small minority got worse.
Error pattern: I overweighted partial negative outcomes and missed a deeper attack on whether the observed improvement actually supports the claimed effect.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this choice challenge the meaning of the outcome measure, the causal interpretation, or only the net percentage improved?
Use when: The argument infers a broad therapeutic conclusion from symptom improvement in a treatment study.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about side effects, comparative safety, or overall benefit-harm balance rather than whether the stated conclusion is justified.

Transfer rule: If a claim says some ingredient is essential, then prefer evidence showing the outcome disappears when that ingredient’s source disappears and reappears when matched.
Error pattern: I favored a merely interesting difference instead of a causal necessity link tied to the hypothesis.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this choice connect the specific factor to both presence/absence of the result, rather than discussing novelty, quality, or tools?
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions testing whether one component is necessary for reproducing a historical product or process.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for sufficient causes, alternative explanations, or comparative performance rather than essentiality.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires fabricated facts plus intent to trigger criminal prosecution, then choose only cases with both a made-up criminal allegation and a report to authorities.
Error pattern: The key success pattern is separating harmful rumors or exaggerations from acts aimed at formal criminal charging.
Diagnostic check: For each option, verify three boxes: invented fact, accusation of a crime, and submission to police/prosecutors/courts; reject if any box fails.
Use when: Apply this on legal-definition multiple choice items about constitutive elements, especially where similar options involve gossip, civil harm, public shaming, or partial truth.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the offense does not require official reporting or when the question asks about morality, defamation, or noncriminal misconduct.

Transfer rule: If an argument opposes a limited legal/medical use because it will fuel wider illegal harm, then test whether that channel contributes meaningfully to the harmful supply.
Error pattern: Success came from targeting the causal bridge and scale assumption, not side facts about safety, addiction, or substitutes.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If this allowed use vanished, would the harmful downstream effect materially change?” Prefer evidence about volume, access, or diversion rates.
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions involving policy bans justified by leakage, diversion, black markets, or social harm from a permitted exception.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion rests on direct harm from the permitted use itself, or when choices attack a different premise than the supply-link claim.

Transfer rule: If a passage reports structural similarity across different complex networks, then infer only a shared pattern or law, not identity or universal sameness.
Error pattern: Success came from choosing the weakest supported generalization and avoiding metaphorical or absolute overreach.
Diagnostic check: Compare each option to the evidence and reject any that adds identity claims, all-encompassing scope, or causes not explicitly linked.
Use when: Apply this on inference questions built from analogies, simulations, network properties, or “similar to” statements across domains.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text directly states equivalence, mechanism, or universal applicability rather than limited resemblance.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists multiple defects and asks for the main meaning, then choose the option that abstracts and combines all defects at the same level.
Error pattern: Success comes from synthesizing parallel points; failure comes from selecting one detail, one cause, or one example as the whole.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each major point in 3–6 words and verify the option covers every point without adding a new emphasis.
Use when: Relevant for summary or main-idea questions built around “first, second,” parallel structure, or explicit enumeration of problems.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, strongest support, inferred cause, or the passage develops only one central claim.

Transfer rule: If a passage surveys one institution across several dynasties, then choose the option capturing its overall evolution, not a single subrule.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the text’s organizing thread across time and filtering out details that are merely examples.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the repeated subject and the time-sequence markers; if most sentences map changes to periods, prefer a broad developmental summary.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea questions with many historical periods, policy adjustments, and illustrative restrictions under one recurring system.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, cause, comparison, or one narrowly described regulation.

Transfer rule: If the stimulus contrasts reliable performance with inability to state the governing rules, then choose the analogy that keeps that same know-how vs explicit-rule gap.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the abstract relation, not the subject matter; avoid choices about different skills, stronger expertise, or unrelated abilities.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the core as “can usually classify/do X, cannot articulate the rules for X,” then verify both halves appear in the option.
Use when: Relevant in analogy/principle questions about tacit knowledge, intuitive judgment, competence without verbalized theory, or implicit rule-following.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus is about causal explanation, degree of skill, necessary training, or comparison between two distinct tasks.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires reducing environmental harm, then reject any option whose direct ecological impact outweighs secondary savings like less processing or packaging.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing core environmental effects over superficial “green” cues attached to cost-saving or “natural” language.
