Boundary: Ignore when the problem provides direct identity/overlap information or requires probabilistic, causal, or temporal reasoning instead of set inclusion.

Transfer rule: If a condition is one-way (“if X, then Y”), then do not infer “not X” from Y’s absence or “not Y” from X’s presence unless using the valid contrapositive.
Error pattern: I turned a one-directional constraint into an invalid reverse inference and pruned cases that were still allowed.
Diagnostic check: For each conditional, list only the direct implication and its contrapositive; then verify every elimination matches one of those two forms.
Use when: This applies to logic games with assignments under several conditional and difference constraints, especially after fixing some participants first.
Boundary: Ignore this when the rule is explicitly biconditional, exclusive, or states a full partition rather than a one-way trigger.

Transfer rule: If a puzzle gives category totals plus pairwise same/different constraints, then build a full assignment grid and eliminate options only after every count is satisfied.
Error pattern: You made unsupported attribute jumps from a local relation to a global identity, treating “same/different” clues as if they fixed exact categories.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list each person’s possible age/degree pairs, enforce totals row-by-row, and verify the chosen candidate is the only one consistent in every completed scenario.
Use when: Apply this to finite-people logic problems with two binary attributes, exact counts, and relational clues linking pairs.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on numerical calculation, probability, or direct factual recall rather than constraint satisfaction.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends by stressing why understanding a mechanism matters, then choose the option capturing that significance, not the broader background topic.
Error pattern: I focused on repeated context terms and selected the subject area instead of the author’s final communicative purpose.
Diagnostic check: Summarize each paragraph’s function in 5 words, then compare the last sentence’s purpose with each option and reject choices covering only setup facts.
Use when: The passage gives background, evidence, or examples, then closes with a claim about value, implications, or future application.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, definition, process description, or when no evaluative concluding pivot appears.

Transfer rule: If an argument links blocking a signal to a therapeutic effect, then check whether the missing premise connects that blocked signal to the body’s compensatory response that produces the effect.
Error pattern: I accepted a premise that merely restated relevance of a mediator, instead of identifying the needed causal bridge from inhibition to outcome.
Diagnostic check: Write the chain “drug → blocked mediator → physiological state → body response → claimed benefit” and locate the unproven link.
Use when: The stimulus is a causal medical or biological argument about messengers, set points, feedback loops, or homeostatic regulation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for evidence, definition, or correlation rather than a missing mechanism in a causal chain.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives a broad setup but repeatedly explains composition changes by a single causal factor across locations, then choose the theme centered on that governing factor.
Error pattern: I focused on what was described (distribution/results) instead of what organized the explanation (cause-and-effect driver).
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each paragraph’s main verb relation; if most sentences say the factor changes and materials follow, prefer the causal-factor title.
Use when: The text contrasts regions or stages and ties differences in makeup to changing conditions like heat, pressure, or distance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly catalogs categories or places without explaining them through one dominant mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts two risk types, then map each by probability, predictability, destructiveness, and preventability before choosing.
Error pattern: I accepted an option that matched only one contrasted trait and ignored the text’s causal framing about what often lies behind visible crises.
Diagnostic check: Make a two-column trait table from the passage, then eliminate any choice adding unsupported claims or reversing stated relationships.
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension items defining paired concepts, especially where one is said to evolve into or underlie broader outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on outside knowledge, calculations, or the passage gives no explicit comparative attributes.

Transfer rule: If a prediction claims a new tax will raise substantial revenue, then test whether the taxed activity will remain near current levels after the tax.
Error pattern: Chose a comparison-to-existing-revenue question instead of checking the causal assumption that demand and sales volume will persist.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What must stay true for the forecasted revenue to materialize?” then look for behavior or volume changes caused by the policy.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen/weaken or evaluation questions about forecasts, taxes, prices, regulation, or any policy whose payoff depends on continued transactions.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is purely definitional, historical, or arithmetic and does not hinge on post-change behavior.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers popularity or preference directly from sales totals, then test whether the metric is only a partial proxy for the claimed trait.
Error pattern: Confusing an observed indicator with the target concept; strong reasoning challenges the indicator-to-concept link rather than side facts.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could higher sales occur while true popularity is not higher?” If yes, prefer the option exposing that mismatch.
Use when: Relevant in questions where a survey, statistic, or market measure is used to conclude attitudes, popularity, quality, or demand.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is explicitly defined by that metric or the task asks about causes, not validity of the inference.

Transfer rule: If a passage names a situation and then gives explicit reasons, then choose the option expressing those reasons as the main idea, not the broader situation alone.
Error pattern: I selected an umbrella summary and missed that the passage centered on causal constraints behind the situation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark issue statements and because/reason statements; if reasons occupy most of the text, prefer the choice that captures the causes.
Use when: Apply this on main-idea questions where the text contrasts goals with deficiencies and discusses barriers, methods, or causes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for topic, title, purpose, or when causes are only brief examples, not the passage’s focus.

Transfer rule: If a passage sets a three-part framework and says to analyze a case within it, then infer only that the case involves all named parts, not any specific policy.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: map abstract categories to concrete actors and choose the option that preserves scope without adding extra claims.
Diagnostic check: List each category in the framework, translate each into real-world actors, and verify the option mentions all of them with no new prescription or causal claim.
Use when: Relevant for inference questions built from definitions, classifications, or analytical frameworks applied to a country, event, or issue.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage gives direct policy recommendations, value judgments, or narrower evidence supporting one specific action.

Transfer rule: If one speaker attacks a proposal by adding a plausible consequence the first argument never evaluated, then classify it as raising an unaddressed consideration.
Error pattern: Success pattern: distinguishing “new objection/constraint” from redefining terms, adding evidence, or supporting the original claim.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Does the reply introduce a separate effect or assumption that could weaken the proposal without disputing the stated facts? If yes, choose the objection role.
Use when: Apply on argument-role questions with two speakers, especially when the second focuses on indirect outcomes, side effects, or omitted costs/benefits.
Boundary: Ignore when the reply mainly changes definitions, offers stronger data for the same point, or directly supplies a missing premise for the first speaker.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a person is unaware of their own meaning from a theory about social context, then check for the missing link that the person lacks insight into their own context.
Error pattern: I accepted a tempting statement about intended meaning versus true meaning instead of supplying the assumption that connects the premise to the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map premise → intermediate claim → conclusion, and ask what must be true for the intermediate claim to imply the person’s self-unawareness.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/assumption questions involving self-reference, author meaning, and claims derived from background circumstances.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion does not depend on someone’s ignorance of their own relevant circumstances or when another premise already states that link.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires direct resident use in personal life, then select the option where households buy goods/services for their own consumption.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering by buyer identity and end use, excluding institutional, governmental, and production-related purchases.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: who pays, who directly uses it, and is it for living consumption rather than production or public operations?
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions that distinguish household activity from enterprise, school, or government spending.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept includes intermediate inputs, organizational procurement, or public expenditure as part of the definition.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects a harmful treatment, then check whether it compares those harms with the likely results of not treating.
Error pattern: Focused only on variation in side-effect severity, missing a required alternatives/consequences comparison.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does the conclusion need evidence about the no-action option or other options to be justified?”
Use when: Relevant in flaw questions about policies, medical interventions, or decisions justified solely by cited costs, risks, or side effects.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already evaluates the consequences of omission/alternatives or when the flaw concerns ambiguity, timing, or sampling instead.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts old and new governance aims yet says the new system still retains the old function, then reject choices claiming the two are completely separate.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking continuity within change rather than overreading contrast as total replacement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark whether the text says the prior function is abandoned, preserved, or subordinated; eliminate any option inconsistent with that status.
Use when: Apply to passages about policy transition, administrative reform, or shifts in emphasis where one function is reframed as serving another.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage explicitly states exclusivity, full replacement, or mutual opposition.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires manipulating a target through fear, guilt, or responsibility to force compliance, then choose the case where a personal threat is used to pressure another person’s choice.
Error pattern: I overfocused on ordinary punishment/penalty and ignored the interpersonal manipulation motive and emotional leverage required by the definition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option for all three: a target person, a coercive demand, and emotional pressure via threatened harm/suffering or withheld reward.
Use when: Relevant for classification questions distinguishing manipulation tactics from neutral rules, incentives, discipline, or unrelated violence.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the scenario lacks a demand for compliance or lacks emotion-based coercion aimed at a specific person.

Transfer rule: If a row puzzle says “the two on the left/right of X,” then first pin X to the only seat with two people on that side and propagate constraints positionally.
Error pattern: Misread side-count statements and treated nonexistent neighbors as possible, causing invalid seat placements and role assignments.
Diagnostic check: Draw three fixed seats; for each clue, mark which seat must host the referenced person because only that seat has two people on the required side, then verify every remaining clue against that layout.
Use when: Small linear-order logic problems with ages/jobs and clues about people sitting to one side of someone.
Boundary: Ignore when “left/right” is relative to facing direction, circular seating, or “side” means adjacent rather than all people on that side.

Transfer rule: If asked for the EXCEPT support choice, then test each option for a direct reason the actor would avoid the stated action and pick the one that does not strengthen it.
Error pattern: I treated a plausible contextual fact as non-support without checking whether it still gives the actor a motive to avoid cuts.
Diagnostic check: For each option, complete “This makes the actor less likely because ___”; eliminate any option where the blank is concrete and direct.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/EXCEPT questions about incentives, motives, or organizational behavior.
Boundary: Ignore when options are causal evidence about truth of a claim rather than reasons affecting the actor’s choice.

Transfer rule: If a passage links poverty reduction to attitudes, behavior, and “civilized quality,” then choose the option stating the practical importance of improving that quality in the poor group.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracing the author’s final purpose, not getting distracted by broad true statements or narrower causal fragments.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the thesis sentence and ask: does my choice match the passage’s target population, key intervention, and intended significance?
Use when: Apply this to purpose/main-idea questions that move from defining a problem to prescribing education, culture, or capacity-building.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific cause, example detail, or a purely factual restatement rather than authorial aim.

Transfer rule: If a claim uses “only X can Y,” then translate it as “everyone who Y is X,” not “every X did Y.”
Error pattern: Confusing a necessary condition with its converse, strengthening a one-way restriction into an all-members participation claim.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the statement in if-then form and test a silent member of X; if silence is allowed, reject any reading that says all X acted.
Use when: Relevant for quantified language like only, all, any, must, can, and disputes about what a statement logically implies.
Boundary: Ignore when the sentence explicitly states both directions or adds existence/totality information beyond the one-way condition.

Transfer rule: If an argument explains a lower trait by saying success is easier or attempts are fewer, then prefer evidence showing attempts are actually more frequent or success is not easier.
Error pattern: I focused on a broad fact about variation instead of testing the conjecture’s specific causal link between environment, encounter rate, and needed potency.
Diagnostic check: Restate the chain as cause→mechanism→outcome, then ask which option reverses or weakens the mechanism without merely adding unrelated variability.
Use when: Apply this on weaken questions involving causal speculation, adaptive explanations, or resource/effort claims tied to habitat or behavior.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices mainly test definitions, direct factual contradictions, or when the conclusion is purely descriptive rather than causal.

Transfer rule: If a fertilizer lists fewer than two of the three core nutrients, then reject it as a compound fertilizer.  
Error pattern: Success came from applying the definition by counting required nutrient categories rather than relying on familiar product names.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark whether each option contains nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium; verify at least two are present.  
Use when: This fits definition-matching questions about categories formed by combinations of named components or required feature counts.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the term is defined by source, manufacturing process, concentration, or includes nutrients outside the specified trio.

Transfer rule: If an item is claimed to be inheritable, then verify all three elements: the person is actually deceased, the item belongs entirely to that person, and the item is lawful property/right.
Error pattern: I accepted a superficially transferable claim without checking each legal-definition element one by one, especially ownership scope and legality.
Diagnostic check: For every option, mark three boxes—death occurred? wholly owned by decedent? legally inheritable? Reject any option with even one “no.”
Use when: Apply this to legal-definition multiple choice about estates, inheritance scope, marital/community property, debts/claims, compensation, or missing-person situations.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is not definition-driven or when a special statute expressly overrides the ordinary estate requirements.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion predicts a broad trend or disappearance, then test it with direct longitudinal population-level evidence, not subgroup anecdotes.
Error pattern: I overvalued a counterexample from a narrow subgroup instead of targeting the claim’s time-trend and generality.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this choice measure overall change across time in the relevant preference, and would it directly contradict the predicted decline?”
Use when: Relevant for arguments inferring social or cultural elimination from one group’s current tastes or preferences.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is only about a specific subgroup, mechanism, or present snapshot rather than an overall trend.

Transfer rule: If exactly-one statement must be true, then build a truth table and count truths for each candidate before choosing.
Error pattern: Misread or dropped an item inside a multi-option statement, causing an incorrect truth count.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each speaker’s claim as an explicit set/list, then for every answer choice mark T/F and verify the total equals exactly one.
Use when: Relevant for logic questions with several people making overlapping category or membership claims and a uniqueness condition.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are probabilistic, comparative, or depend on hidden assumptions rather than direct set membership.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires the body’s own fluid changing from liquid to gas on skin or mucosa, then choose only examples featuring that internal-to-external evaporation.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every necessary condition, not just the general idea of “cooling” or “liquid present.”
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the definition’s required mechanism, source, and location; reject any option missing one of those three.
Use when: Apply this to concept-classification questions where several choices seem related by outcome but differ in mechanism.
Boundary: Ignore this when the definition is broad, metaphorical, or asks for effects/results rather than the specific physical process.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers origin or category from a single fragmentary fossil, then test whether that fragment alone can reliably establish the relevant classification.
Error pattern: Strong reasoning spots when evidence is too incomplete to support a broad historical conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would this conclusion still follow if the specimen’s age were correct but its type could not be identified from the discovered part alone?”
Use when: The argument moves from one dated partial remain to claims about earliest instances, origins, or taxonomy.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence includes diagnostic features sufficient for identification or multiple independent lines of classification.

Transfer rule: If a passage says “as a result” a system can persist indefinitely, then infer the sustained sufficiency of the stated mechanism, not stricter necessary conditions.
Error pattern: Turned a supported sufficient process into an exclusive “only if” requirement by adding absolutes not stated.
Diagnostic check: Underline every universal or necessity cue in your choice; if the stimulus lacks matching words, reject that choice.
Use when: Applicable to strengthen/support questions where a causal chain explains how an organism, process, or system maintains itself over time.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus explicitly states exclusivity, necessary conditions, or complete elimination, or asks for a required assumption rather than support.

Transfer rule: If a claim is conceded early, then test whether it supports a rival policy while the conclusion still prefers another policy overall.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking argumentative role, not truth value; the risk is confusing “granted support for an alternative” with “main premise for the conclusion.”
Diagnostic check: Mark the conclusion, then ask of the target sentence: does the author ultimately rely on it, attack it, or concede it before giving a defeating consideration?
Use when: Relevant in role questions where an author compares two policies and admits one advantage of the rejected option.
Boundary: Ignore when the target sentence is itself the conclusion, a background definition, or evidence directly used to derive the final claim.

Transfer rule: If an argument denies category membership by citing failure of a necessary defining property, then choose the option with the same “if category, then property; not-property, so not-category” form.
Error pattern: Confusing a valid contrapositive structure with tempting surface stories about exclusion, causation, or typical traits.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each option as category → property; then test whether the conclusion is explicitly not-property → not-category, rather than affirming the consequent or using an unrelated contrast.
Use when: The stem classifies something using a necessary condition and rules membership out from absence of that condition.
Boundary: Ignore when the source uses sufficient-only conditions, probabilistic claims, biconditionals, or extra premises that change the inference form.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “serve people as they would want” to “serve their best interest,” then require an assumption linking what they would want with what benefits them.
Error pattern: Necessary-assumption success pattern: bridge a shift between a preference-based premise and a welfare-based conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Underline the key terms in premise and conclusion; if one side says “wanted” and the other says “best interest,” ask what statement makes those equivalent.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where the conclusion introduces a stronger or different standard than the premise.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion merely restates the premise or when a direct factual premise already connects the two standards.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires both specific parties and a legal/contractual basis, then verify every candidate matches both conditions.
Error pattern: Success came from using conjunctive filtering instead of matching on one surface feature like “dispute at work.”
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark two boxes: correct relationship pair and issue tied to law, regulation, or contract; choose only one with both.
Use when: Apply to definition-based multiple choice involving necessary elements, especially disputes, legal categories, or contract terms.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for best example, closest analogy, or causal explanation rather than strict category membership.

Transfer rule: If a passage says priorities have diversified but one factor remains the top concern, then choose the option preserving that stable priority.
Error pattern: Success came from separating “overall change” from “specific continuity” instead of assuming every aspect changed.
Diagnostic check: List each trend claim in the passage as changed, unchanged, ranked, or unsupported; accept only an option matching one listed status exactly.
Use when: Apply this to survey-summary or ranking passages contrasting shifting preferences with one enduring emphasis.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text gives causal explanations, time-series evidence for decline/growth, or options require inference beyond stated comparisons.

Transfer rule: If a grouping puzzle adds a temporary assignment, then treat it as a valid premise and propagate all constraints before questioning consistency.
Error pattern: I rejected the given scenario instead of integrating it, so I stopped search early and missed forced placements.
Diagnostic check: Build a full assignment grid, mark capacities, apply every conditional and “not together” rule, and verify each person is placed exactly once before choosing.
Use when: Use this on logic-distribution problems with fixed group sizes, conditional placements, and pairwise separation constraints.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is about detecting flawed premises or when conditions are explicitly optional, probabilistic, or inconsistent by design.

Transfer rule: If new evidence makes an existing category fail, then choose the case where the person revises the category or behavior, not merely applies prior knowledge.
Error pattern: Confusing assimilation/retrieval/skill transfer with true accommodation after disconfirming experience.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Was the old belief tested by reality, shown inadequate, and then changed?” If any step is missing, reject it.
Use when: Relevant for developmental or cognitive-psychology items contrasting learning from mismatch versus using warnings, memory, analogy, or prior training.
Boundary: Ignore when the scenario is only rule-following, recall of similar examples, habit formation without concept change, or straightforward transfer of an old skill.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends by contrasting earlier mystical views with modern concepts, then predict the next part will introduce the rational framework that replaced them.
Error pattern: I overextended a side topic from the body instead of following the closing transition and contrast structure.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the final sentence’s direction word or contrast, then choose the option that directly continues that unfinished comparison.
Use when: Relevant in “what comes next” questions where the passage surveys old theories and ends by pivoting toward modern understanding.
Boundary: Ignore this when the ending clearly broadens to examples, methods, or regional history rather than setting up a conceptual transition.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims a harmful transmission route causes deaths, then prefer evidence showing outcomes improve when that route is interrupted or removed.
Error pattern: I chose background/comparison evidence instead of a causal test tied directly to the proposed mechanism.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this choice create a before/after, exposed/unexposed, or interrupted-route contrast that would be expected only if the stated cause is true?
Use when: Relevant for strengthen questions built on a specific causal chain, especially involving transfer from one source to a vulnerable recipient.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is not causal strengthening or when a choice weakens comparability by adding unrelated traits or distant context.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a behavior is mainly caused by a price advantage, then require an implied link that buyers value the lower price as better overall value versus alternatives.
Error pattern: Success pattern: translating a causal claim about pricing into the necessary assumption connecting price differences to consumer choice.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If buyers did not see the cheaper option as better value, would the stated price advantage still explain the behavior?” If no, that link is required.
Use when: Relevant for assumption questions about market behavior, consumer switching, sales impact, and explanations centered on price.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already states buyer preferences or when the cause is about access, legality, supply, or enforcement instead of valuation.

Transfer rule: If asked what is not likely next, then continue only threads opened by the passage and reject options introducing a new comparison topic.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking discourse continuity rather than chasing prominent terms mentioned only as background.
Diagnostic check: List each option and mark whether its key subject was developed in the passage’s final focus; eliminate any option with no active setup.
Use when: Apply to passage-continuation, next-paragraph, or likely-content questions after a summary of a study, report, or announcement.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for broader context, contrastive analysis, or an author’s possible digression signaled by transition words.

Transfer rule: If a passage says earlier forms had only limited feeding methods and later anatomy newly enabled pursuing and seizing prey, then exclude predation by the earlier forms.
Error pattern: I inferred from missing skeletal information instead of chaining stated abilities, limitations, and later changes.
Diagnostic check: List each group’s explicitly stated capabilities; ask whether a choice is forced by those statements or merely not contradicted.
Use when: Relevant in must-be-true questions with timelines, “limited to” language, and contrasts between pre-change and post-change functions.
Boundary: Ignore when choices depend on outside biology knowledge or when the passage allows additional unstated behaviors despite listed examples.

Transfer rule: If a choice asks what can be true under linked conditionals, then build one full assignment for that choice and test every rule, instead of rejecting it from a partial implication chain.
Error pattern: Premature elimination from one-way/biconditional statements without checking contrapositives or whether the triggered condition actually occurs.
Diagnostic check: For the chosen option, place those people first, fill remaining event slots, then verify each conditional only when its antecedent is satisfied and confirm no capacity conflict appears.
Use when: Small scheduling or grouping problems with exact quotas, exclusivity, and several if/only-if constraints.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks what must be true or when independent numeric calculation, not feasibility construction, is central.

Transfer rule: If several wishes are conditional, then encode each as an implication and test option sets against all implications, including contrapositive-trigger interactions.
Error pattern: I mixed up sufficient and necessary conditions, treating a triggered clause as a guaranteed conclusion without checking consistency across all statements.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate set, mark each antecedent true/false; whenever true, verify its required destinations and exclusions all hold; reject any set with one violation.
Use when: Relevant in logic puzzles with family preferences, travel sets, and nested “if,” “if not,” conjunction, or exclusion conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are preferences without strict truth conditions, or when the task asks for probability, ranking, or explanation rather than logical entailment.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires thinking supported by direct bodily manipulation or imitation of concrete actions, then choose the option centered on performing or following actions, not verbal explanation or abstract inference.
Error pattern: I overvalued clever reasoning and ignored the requirement that the solution process itself be actual action tied to a concrete task.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would the person need to physically do or copy something step by step to think through it?” Keep only yes-answers.
Use when: Relevant for concept-definition questions contrasting motor/action-based thinking with image-based or abstract/conceptual thinking.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the stem asks about inference, representation, examples, or model-building mainly used for analysis rather than action execution.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires trauma-caused psychological sequelae, then exclude cases describing ordinary hardship, illness, or life stress without a clear traumatic trigger and response.
Error pattern: Success came from separating true trauma-linked symptoms from merely severe but non-traumatic adverse circumstances.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark (1) traumatic event, (2) later psychological reaction, and (3) causal link; reject any option missing one mark.
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching questions about disorders, syndromes, or categories that require both a qualifying cause and a resulting symptom pattern.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept is defined only by symptoms or only by exposure, without requiring both together.

Transfer rule: If a trial audience likes a program but official ratings are poor, then first test access/exposure factors like airtime, channel reach, or scheduling before judging content.
Error pattern: I overfocused on attitudes toward quality and ignored whether the target audience could realistically watch at the broadcast time.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the same target viewers be available and able to watch under real broadcast conditions?” If no, prefer a logistics explanation.
Use when: A scenario contrasts positive reception in a controlled test with weak real-world participation, ratings, turnout, or uptake.
Boundary: Ignore this when the contradiction already states equal access conditions and the issue is about preference, effectiveness, or content fit.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion claims decision freedom from autonomy, then prefer evidence showing external constraints on feasible choices over statements about duties or interests.  
Error pattern: I treated a normative caveat about considering others as stronger than a practical market constraint that directly limits what can be produced.  
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option reduce actual choice set or only add a general consideration?” Pick the one that makes some production choices unsellable or nonviable.  
Use when: The argument infers unrestricted business decisions from independence, autonomy, ownership, or freedom in an economic setting.  
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is about legal authority, moral obligation, or cooperation rather than real-world feasibility under demand conditions.

Transfer rule: If a term means “deficient/incomplete” rather than “absent,” then choose partial damage/impaired structure, not total loss.
Error pattern: I overcommitted to an absolute interpretation and ignored wording that allowed survival and later repair.
Diagnostic check: Replace the key term with graded alternatives—damaged, deficient, absent—and pick the strongest claim fully supported by the passage.
Use when: This applies to biology/medicine reading questions contrasting injury, deficiency, and complete removal of a structure.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text explicitly states total disappearance, complete loss, or an all-or-none process.

Transfer rule: If an argument ranks observed outcomes from a stated tendency, then check for unmentioned items that could fall between the ranked cases and disrupt the ordering.
Error pattern: Success pattern: spotting a hidden completeness assumption needed to move from known examples to an ordered overall conclusion.
Diagnostic check: List all categories the conclusion implicitly compares; ask, “Could any unmentioned member fit between two named members under the governing property?”
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where a conclusion gives an exhaustive ranking or sequence based on one causal or comparative variable.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about the mentioned items themselves, not the full set or overall abundance/order.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion infers one cause by ruling out others, then choose the option that makes the listed causes exhaustive.
Error pattern: I preferred a plausible cause-strengthener instead of the premise that validates elimination-based reasoning.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this option complete an only-these-causes set so the excluded causes force the remaining one?”
Use when: Arguments move from “not A and not B” to “therefore C” in causal, diagnostic, or multiple-choice support questions.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for a merely helpful clue, or when other possible causes are clearly left open.

Transfer rule: If a statement gives a one-way condition, then do not infer the opposite outcome when the condition fails.
Error pattern: Confusing a sufficient condition with a necessary one; treating “if P, then Q” as “only if P, then Q.”
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the claim as “P guarantees Q”; ask whether “not P” still leaves Q possible before eliminating any option.
Use when: Relevant for promises, plans, or causal claims phrased with “if,” especially when someone denies an action solely because the stated condition did not occur.
Boundary: Ignore when the wording explicitly makes the condition necessary, exclusive, biconditional, or states “if and only if.”

Transfer rule: If a definition targets legally protected intangible creations or distinctive commercial signs limited by law, then choose the option about rights to a created sign or invention, not physical assets or broad ownership.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating intangible intellectual results from tangible property and organizational property claims.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is it non-physical, created by intellect, used in production or market identification, and legally protectable for a defined term/territory?
Use when: Apply this to classification questions contrasting intellectual-property-type rights with equipment, land, buildings, or institutional assets.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition concerns tangible property, general corporate ownership, or rights without legal time/region limits.

Transfer rule: If a claim says a persuasion strategy will work better, then prefer evidence directly comparing responses to message framing, not just underlying preferences.
Error pattern: Strengthening succeeds when it closes the gap between what people value and what persuaders should emphasize.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this choice test the effect of presenting the same kind of thing in one framing versus another on willingness or uptake?”
Use when: Arguments move from facts about consumer motives or preferences to advice about how advocates, marketers, or experts should pitch something.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion is about what people actually choose absent messaging, or when options only compare products rather than framings.

Transfer rule: If a story shows people mechanically doing assigned steps while the purpose fails because a key role is missing, then choose the moral about responsibility/ownership over method.
Error pattern: I overfocused on procedural efficiency and missed the passage’s criticism of duty without accountability for the overall task.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is the main problem an ineffective method, or that workers continue without ensuring the job’s essential purpose is fulfilled?”
Use when: Short moral passages depict coordinated work, an absent participant, and pointless continuation of partial tasks.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly debates techniques, optimization, or alternative procedures rather than neglect of duty.

Transfer rule: If a category is defined by intrinsic material behavior, then reject examples whose conductivity comes from state, mixture, or impurities rather than the substance itself.
Error pattern: I over-applied a broad comparison definition and ignored whether the example matched the underlying physical class being described.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is the conductivity native to the pure material, and does it show hallmark semiconductor behavior beyond merely being intermediate?”
Use when: This fits classification questions about conductors, insulators, and semiconductors, especially when options use everyday materials or altered conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem explicitly defines categories only by raw conductivity range and says structure or mechanism does not matter.

Transfer rule: If a passage refutes a fear mainly to warn against hesitation, then choose the option about avoiding missed opportunities, not the refutation alone.
Error pattern: I fixated on a supporting denial and missed the author’s practical emphasis and intended takeaway.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What action or attitude does the author ultimately want readers to adopt?” Then match that, not just repeated claims.
Use when: Relevant in main-idea questions where the text counters an objection, mentions danger in practice, or highlights consequences of a mistaken view.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific claim, inference, or detail rather than the passage’s central emphasis.

Transfer rule: If asked for the choice that does not support a causal hypothesis, then test each option for whether it strengthens, weakens, or is irrelevant to the proposed cause.
Error pattern: Success came from checking temporal order and alternative exposure groups instead of treating all disease-related facts as supportive.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does the cause precede the effect, covary with exposure, and fit comparison groups without contradiction?
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/EXCEPT questions about causation, especially with pollution, disease, risk factors, or population comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is not causal or when the task asks for a sufficient assumption rather than evidential support.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion says a suspected cause actually reduces an effect, then choose evidence that provides a direct mechanism for reducing that effect.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the claim’s polarity and scope, favoring global causal support over local, mixed, or irrelevant effects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does this option explicitly explain how the factor lowers the target outcome, not merely cause another side effect?
Use when: Relevant for strengthen questions about causal reversals, especially when options mention mechanisms, intermediates, or geographically limited impacts.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for weaken, resolve, necessary assumption, or when evidence need only correlate rather than mechanistically support.

Transfer rule: If one place is between two others and adjacent to the eastern one, then those three must be consecutive in the order west→east, fixing the middle place immediately west of that neighbor.
Error pattern: Reversed directional relations and failed to enforce the adjacency constraint before placing the remaining pair.
Diagnostic check: Draw five slots; encode each clue as inequalities plus “distance = 1”; verify every claimed order by checking both direction and adjacency for each linked pair.
Use when: Linear ordering problems mix east/west relations with “adjacent” or “next to” constraints among several named items.
Boundary: Ignore when positions are not on one line, adjacency is undefined, or clues are probabilistic rather than exact.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers causation from a positive correlation, then first check for selection effects or reverse causality that could make the outcome determine the behavior.
Error pattern: I focused on a side effect of the behavior instead of attacking whether the compared groups were preselected by the outcome variable.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could higher-performing people be the ones allowed, chosen, or more likely to do this activity?” If yes, that option usually weakens best.
Use when: Correlational surveys compare participants vs nonparticipants and conclude the activity improves performance, ability, or health.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence already randomizes assignment or explicitly rules out preexisting differences and reverse direction.

Transfer rule: If a reply concedes a principle in clear cases but targets its usefulness in uncertain cases, then pick the choice limiting the criticism to that principle’s practical guidance in those cases.
Error pattern: Distinguish “this rule is inadequate for a common decision context” from broader attacks on the whole ethical system.
Diagnostic check: Mark concession, identify the challenged scenario, then eliminate any option that adds “no principle helps” or “the overall framework is false.”
Use when: A dialogue contrasts easy cases with ambiguous, typical cases and asks for the precise point of disagreement.
Boundary: Ignore this when the speaker explicitly generalizes to all principles or directly rejects the entire framework.

Transfer rule: If a claim says growth increases indirect manager-subordinate contact, then choose the option that states a direct likely consequence of reduced personal interaction.
Error pattern: I matched a broad social-structure idea instead of tracing the stated cause to its most immediate effect.
Diagnostic check: Restate the passage as cause → mechanism → outcome; reject choices that introduce new themes not explicitly linked by that chain.
Use when: The stem asks which option “supports the view” by explaining or extending a stated causal relationship in organizations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an analogy, value judgment, or outside knowledge rather than a consequence of the given mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a study’s conclusion is merely that some outcome is possible, then ignore representativeness attacks unless the claim generalizes prevalence or typicality.
Error pattern: Confusing possibility claims with population claims; treating selection bias as fatal even when only existence is being established.
Diagnostic check: Restate the conclusion using quantifiers—ask “some/can” or “most/usually”? If it is existential, test whether the criticism targets only representativeness.
Use when: Arguments cite examples, case studies, or selected successes to support a limited “can happen” or “is possible” conclusion.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the conclusion predicts average results, broad suitability, frequency, or policy for a wider group.

Transfer rule: If a claim treats a correlated behavior as health-improving, then look for evidence that healthier people were simply more likely to do that behavior.
Error pattern: Mistaking a side-effect objection about the behavior for a stronger alternative explanation based on selection bias or reverse causation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the observed difference remain if behavior had no effect because preexisting health influenced participation?” Prefer the option that says yes.
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions built from observational comparisons between users and nonusers, especially with health, productivity, or lifestyle outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus already establishes random assignment, temporal order, or controls that rule out preexisting-group differences.

Transfer rule: If people replace durable items well before failure while core needs remain met, then infer other motivations are driving replacement.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing a supported causal/motivational inference from stronger claims about design, technology, or history.
Diagnostic check: List the facts; ask which choice merely explains the early replacement without adding new trends, value judgments, or unsupported comparisons.
Use when: Relevant in conclusion questions contrasting actual behavior with stated adequacy or lifespan of a product or system.
Boundary: Ignore when evidence directly mentions breakdowns, explicit motives, changing capabilities over time, or normative recommendations.

Transfer rule: If a statement about audience/background conditions explains why a profession’s task is harder or different, then classify it as a condition transforming the task, not as evidence of results or intentions.
Error pattern: Confusing a premise that sets context for the main challenge with a premise offered as causal proof of success, purpose, or broader readership.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this statement explain what changed about the job itself, or does it support a later outcome claim?” Trace which sentence it directly modifies.
Use when: The argument compares past and present and includes audience knowledge, social conditions, or background trends affecting a creator’s burden.
Boundary: Ignore this when the statement is explicitly presented as an effect, an intended goal, or direct evidence for the conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a balance statement compares sums, then rewrite each as an inequality/equality and eliminate shared terms before ranking individual items.
Error pattern: Mixed sign interpretation and unsupported leap from pairwise sum relations to single-item weights.
Diagnostic check: Convert “left sinks/right sinks/balanced” into symbols, subtract common addends on both sides, then verify the resulting chain is consistent with the chosen order.
Use when: Weight/order puzzles give multiple balance conditions involving overlapping pairs or triples and ask for a full light-to-heavy ranking.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are not additive comparisons, the scale is unreliable/nonstandard, or extra constraints make cancellation invalid.

Transfer rule: If an argument judges a view’s accuracy or likely content from who produced it or their institutional role, then flag a source-based flaw.
Error pattern: Inferring the merit or substance of a claim from its origin rather than from direct evidence about the claim.
Diagnostic check: Underline each premise; ask, “Does any premise evaluate only the speaker/source?” If yes, see whether the conclusion still follows without source facts.
Use when: The stimulus contrasts classifications, theories, or beliefs and emphasizes authority, status, affiliation, motive, or establishment membership.
Boundary: Ignore when source facts are directly relevant evidence, such as expertise, bias affecting testimony, or causal claims about why a view was adopted.

Transfer rule: If an argument says sales rose because advertising rose, then test whether buyers were actually exposed to that advertising before choosing broader market explanations.
Error pattern: Mistaking an alternative cause for a stronger attack on the claimed causal link; overlooking missing contact between cause and affected group.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Did many purchasers notice the ads?” If exposure among buyers is low, the advertising-to-sales causation is sharply weakened.
Use when: A conclusion infers that promotion caused increased purchases from parallel increases in ads and sales.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence already establishes substantial buyer exposure or when the argument is about total market demand rather than ad effectiveness.

Transfer rule: If a condition fixes one item present/absent, then chain every rule and its contrapositive to list forced consequences before judging options.
Error pattern: Missed a disjunctive conclusion by reasoning toward one specific item instead of combining branches from the rule network.
Diagnostic check: Write all implications, add contrapositives, substitute the given fact, split on remaining unresolved cases, and note what is true in every branch.
Use when: Relevant for multiple conditional statements with negations, incompatibilities, and a question asking what must be true.
Boundary: Ignore when conditions are probabilistic, defeasible, or when the task asks for a possible rather than necessary conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a statement gives necessary conditions for an outcome, then infer only what must be absent or insufficient when one condition is missing; do not promote them to sufficient or “best” claims.
Error pattern: Confusing necessity with sufficiency and adding evaluative strength not stated by the passage.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the claim as “Outcome requires X and Y”; then test each option by contraposition and reject any option asserting guarantee, ideality, or extra comparison.
Use when: The passage uses cues like “basis,” “not enough,” “necessary,” “requires,” or lists multiple prerequisites for one result.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the text explicitly states sufficiency, probability, ranking, or causal superiority.

Transfer rule: If a passage builds to a prescriptive takeaway after background claims, then choose the option naming that final recommendation, not a supporting premise.
Error pattern: Mistaking an illustrative/supporting statement for the passage’s main idea; focusing on content details instead of the author’s ultimate point.
Diagnostic check: Summarize each paragraph/sentence role in five words; if one clause says what education/policy/action “must” do, test whether your option matches that directive.
Use when: The text moves from defining a concept to explaining implications, then ends with a claim about curriculum, emphasis, or educational practice.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, example, or implied fact rather than the central thesis.

Transfer rule: If a definition asks for a full production cycle, then choose the option that explicitly spans start-to-product stages within one agricultural activity.
Error pattern: I matched a superficially agricultural example but ignored whether it reached the defined endpoint of obtaining products.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark start, process, and product; reject any choice missing product output or mixing in later nonagricultural processing.
Use when: Relevant for definition questions about time-bounded cycles, especially in farming or livestock contexts with several sequential stages.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks about broad industry chains, repeated annual routines without endpoints, or nondefinition judgments.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus asks for the main conclusion, then identify the claim supported by the others, often the opening thesis followed by “to see this” evidence.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing the author’s ultimate explanatory claim from background facts and intermediate causal statements.
Diagnostic check: Mark each statement as premise or conclusion by asking, “Does this support another claim, or is it what the support is trying to establish?”
Use when: Relevant in argument-structure questions with an initial claim, explanatory language, and several tempting factual restatements.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for an inference, assumption, detail, or when multiple claims are jointly concluded without clear support direction.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires people traveling to another city to buy goods there, then choose the option showing actual cross-city shopping behavior, not just price comparison or relocation.
Error pattern: I matched on surface cues about price differences between cities while ignoring the required action and participants in the definition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each definitional element—actors, movement between cities, shopping act, and motive—and verify the option contains all of them explicitly.
Use when: Relevant for concept-definition multiple choice with necessary conditions, especially when distractors mention related prices, places, or economic effects.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept allows indirect comparison, online purchasing, migration, or other non-shopping behaviors as valid cases.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts a concept’s acceptable aspect with a criticized implementation, then choose the option targeting the criticized practice, not the broader definition.
Error pattern: I focused on a true but secondary clarification and missed the author’s main normative objection.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the sentence with strongest evaluation words; ask which option most directly matches that judgment and proposed constraint.
Use when: Apply this to main-point or viewpoint questions with contrast words, concessions, and a final explicit criticism.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a definition, detail recall, or an inference not centered on the author’s central criticism.

Transfer rule: If an argument states a reinforcing cycle, then treat each link as contextual/partial unless the text explicitly makes it the sole original cause.
Error pattern: Mistaking a feedback-loop description for a one-way causal claim and overstrengthening what the passage licenses.
Diagnostic check: List every causal arrow stated; mark whether it is direct, reciprocal, or exclusive; reject any choice adding exclusivity or reversing support level.
Use when: The stimulus describes economic or social chains, cycles, worsening spirals, or claims that one factor deepens another over time.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly says a factor is the primary, only, or root cause, or defines causes with necessary/sufficient language.

Transfer rule: If a definition lists environmental and sustainability criteria, then reject choices focused only on financial savings unless an ecological mechanism is explicit.
Error pattern: Success came from separating goal-aligned environmental means from merely business-oriented efficiency or cost reduction.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it directly reduce resource use, pollution, waste, land impact, or improve recyclability/clean production?
Use when: Apply to definition-based multiple choice where several options sound beneficial but only some match the stated purpose and mechanisms.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition explicitly includes profitability, affordability, or cost control as part of the concept.

Transfer rule: If a definition lists temporary cross-border purposes like visiting, exchange, trade, sports, or culture, then choose the option matching a short-term activity, not residence, official posting, or transport duty.
Error pattern: I overfocused on broad “foreign entrant” wording and ignored exclusion by purpose and role.
Diagnostic check: For each option, tag duration and purpose: temporary visit/exchange vs settlement/official service/crew transit; keep only temporary-purpose entrants.
Use when: A classification question defines a group by entry purpose, activity type, and implied temporary stay.
Boundary: Ignore this when the definition explicitly includes residents, diplomats, crew, or long-term migrants.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists benefits from several perspectives and ends with a trend/conclusion, then choose the option summarizing the motivating reasons, not the side effects or methods.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the author’s central purpose rather than grabbing the final sentence or any single detail.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Are most sentences answering why, what happens, or how?” Tally each sentence’s function before selecting.
Use when: Apply to main-idea questions where the text contrasts minor risks with major benefits and gives examples from different stakeholders.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly explains procedures, chronology, or consequences after a policy is implemented.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus says an unchosen factor can still affect evaluation, then reject any choice making choosability a necessary condition for that evaluation.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting a hidden universal principle in a tempting option that contradicted the stimulus’s explicit exception.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, ask: “Does this option forbid using any factor the stimulus already uses despite saying it is unchosen?”
Use when: Apply on EXCEPT/could-be-true questions with moral appraisal, causal or motivational factors, and contrasts between chosen actions and unchosen states.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus itself states that only voluntary or controllable factors count, or when the option merely allows rather than requires that restriction.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for complementary-demand behavior, then choose the pair used together where demand moves in the same direction.
Error pattern: Confusing complements with substitutes or unrelated goods instead of checking whether one item’s use increases the other’s usefulness.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Are these typically consumed jointly?” and “Would more or less of one naturally raise or lower demand for the other similarly?”
Use when: The prompt discusses interdependent demand, complements, joint consumption, bundled use, or positive demand linkage.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the relationship is substitution, independence, price effects only, or production inputs rather than consumer complements.

Transfer rule: If a counting problem mixes categories and one category is a subset of another, then model all statements as sets and enforce every containment before merging or separating people.
Error pattern: Undercounting/overcounting from treating linked descriptors as independent and from not checking whether a named subgroup already satisfies part of a broader count.
Diagnostic check: Draw category boxes, mark subset arrows, then test two extreme constructions: maximize overlap allowed and minimize overlap allowed without breaking any statement.
Use when: Apply this to “minimum/maximum possible people” questions with origins, memberships, or activities that can overlap across attributes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt gives exact identities, explicit disjointness, or fixed totals that remove freedom to choose overlaps.

Transfer rule: If the act’s legal effect can arise from one person’s expressed intent alone, then treat it as unilateral; if another party’s assent or matching offer/acceptance is needed, do not.
Error pattern: Mistaking a one-person physical operation within an existing service or transaction for a one-party juristic act.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Before this act has legal effect, must any counterparty agree, accept, or already stand in a contractual exchange?” If yes, reject unilateral classification.
Use when: Definitions contrast unilateral acts with contracts, purchases, leases, deposits, registrations, or other dealings involving institutions or counterparties.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is about factual performance steps, agency authority, or acts whose legal status depends on prior agreements.

Transfer rule: If an argument says action X would harm group Y and Y (or an agent tied to Y) never permits harmful actions, then infer rejection of X.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matching a two-step chain from predicted harm to a stated no-harm policy, then to refusal of the action.
Diagnostic check: Mark H = “X harms Y” and P = “decision-maker will not do/support anything harming Y”; confirm the conclusion is simply “not X/support.”
Use when: Relevant in analogy questions featuring policy decisions, protected interests, and a ban on actions with a specified negative effect.
Boundary: Ignore when the choice adds probability, reverses necessity/sufficiency, changes the actor, or argues for X rather than against it.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a tool’s core purpose and then gives a criterion for judging it, then choose the option combining function plus evaluation standard.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the author’s overall claim, not drifting to a narrower subpoint or a broader field-level description.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list in 3 words the passage’s object, purpose, and judging criterion; pick the option matching all three.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea questions where the text defines what something is for and how its quality is assessed.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an example, implication, detail, or a method rather than the passage’s central thesis.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from changed factual understanding about a work’s features to changed interpretive appropriateness, then require a principle linking those features to interpretation.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning identified the needed bridge assumption rather than attractive but irrelevant claims about authority, origin, or historical context.
Diagnostic check: State the premise change and conclusion change; ask, “What property changed, and must that property affect interpretive fit for the conclusion to follow?”
Use when: Apply this on principle-strengthen questions where new evidence about an object is said to undermine earlier readings of it.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion concerns value, expertise, authenticity, or timing instead of interpretive appropriateness.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires original material traces or objects that directly embody case facts, then choose the physical object itself, not a recording, photo, or expert-produced document about it.
Error pattern: Confusing derivative representations or testimonial records with tangible source evidence.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would this item still exist as case-related matter before any person documented, interpreted, or narrated it?”
Use when: Relevant in classification questions distinguishing real/object evidence from documentary, testimonial, or appraisal evidence.
Boundary: Ignore when the legal system explicitly defines copies, recordings, or reports as the same evidence category as the underlying object.

Transfer rule: If asked for what most directly supports a claim, then choose the option that restates the claim’s needed implication with the fewest added prescriptions.
Error pattern: I favored a stronger, more elaborate remedy instead of the closest support, adding assumptions beyond the argument.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark only ideas explicitly licensed by the passage; reject any choice that introduces extra duties, scope, or conditions not stated.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/support questions where several choices sound agreeable but differ in directness versus added content.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the best solution, broader principle, or a justified extension beyond the passage.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts examples showing opposite preferences, then infer preference-relativity, not denial of the underlying categories.
Error pattern: Mistook an argument about subjective evaluation for a claim about objective size concepts.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is the author challenging what counts as big/small, or only saying different people admire different forms?” Choose the latter if examples are taste-based.
Use when: The stimulus uses paired counterexamples, aesthetic judgments, or “some like X, others like Y” structure.
Boundary: Ignore when the text explicitly defines terms, denies category boundaries, or gives evidence about measurement rather than preference.

Transfer rule: If a question contrasts deductive certainty with creative possibility, then choose the option that extends a structured model to predict unseen cases, not one based only on analogy, reversal, or inspiration.
Error pattern: Mistaking vivid associative insight for the target type; overlooking disciplined creativity grounded in an established framework.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: does it use an existing system to generate a testable new possibility beyond known data? If yes, prefer it.
Use when: Relevant in definition-matching items about “horizontal/lateral” versus “vertical/logical” thinking, especially when several options look innovative.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for pure induction, deduction, causal inversion, or anecdotal discovery rather than model-based prediction.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires continuity at one stage in a workflow, then exclude cases with idle gaps or broken handoff between identical tasks.
Error pattern: Success came from checking every clause in the definition instead of matching by surface similarity like “same work” or “sequential movement.”
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option for stage/order continuity: same process step, timely transfer, and no interruption that disrupts ongoing production.
Use when: Apply this to definition questions about processes, operations, workflow sequencing, production stages, or uninterrupted handoffs across units/objects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept does not require continuity/order, or when pauses are explicitly allowed by the definition.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires behavior shifting toward a majority because of guidance or pressure, then reject options driven mainly by private preference, chance-seeking, or individual utility.
Error pattern: I focused on whether many people were involved, not on whether majority influence caused the behavior.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would this likely happen without observing or feeling pressure from the group?” If yes, exclude it from conformity.
Use when: Apply to social-psychology items contrasting crowd behavior, imitation, social norms, and individually motivated actions.
Boundary: Ignore this check when the concept includes any mass behavior regardless of motive, or when motives are explicitly mixed or undefined.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires home-based living plus community-supported professional/social services, then pick the option combining living at home with ongoing community services delivered at home or linked daily to home life.
Error pattern: I focused on one matching feature and ignored the full conjunction of required conditions.
Diagnostic check: List the definition’s necessary elements; reject any option missing even one, especially “lives at home” and “receives community-backed support/services.”
Use when: Definitions describe a category by multiple mandatory traits, especially in social service or policy examples.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the category is defined by examples, loose family resemblance, or “any one of” features.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends with policy verbs like “should,” “need,” or “must,” then choose the option that captures the advocated action, not earlier background comparisons.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions often hinge on mistaking supporting context or advantages for the author’s central recommendation; success comes from prioritizing the final directive.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as background, reason, or recommendation; if one sentence tells what ought to be done, test whether an option paraphrases that recommendation most directly.
Use when: Apply this to argumentative passages that compare methods, list favorable trends, then shift into a call for guidance, mobilization, or coordinated action.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage is purely descriptive, asks for a detail, or lacks any explicit normative or action-oriented claim.

Transfer rule: If an argument says event A is necessary for condition B and classifies B as downstream of A, then look for evidence that B can occur before A or without A.
Error pattern: Necessary-condition claims are best tested by counterexamples to temporal or logical dependence; direct exceptions strongly weaken causal reclassification.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the claim as “no B without prior A,” then scan choices for any case showing B preceding A or arising independently.
Use when: Apply to questions about causation, prerequisite conditions, disorder classification, or arguments built on “must,” “necessary,” or “therefore.”
Boundary: Ignore when choices only discuss correlation, prevalence, severity, duration, heredity, or recovery unless they directly bear on necessity.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why a metaphorical summary is used, then match the answer to the exact explanatory sentence supporting that metaphor.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing the author’s stated reason instead of choosing a broader, attractive paraphrase.
Diagnostic check: Underline the key metaphor phrase in the prompt, locate the sentence that explains it, and verify one option restates that sentence most directly.
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension items asking for the reason, basis, or meaning of a quoted label, image, or claim.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task requires inference beyond the passage, synthesis across paragraphs, or evaluation rather than text-grounded explanation.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires virtual content to be overlaid onto the current physical environment, then reject cases that merely display imported digital content to the user.
Error pattern: I matched “real-world involvement” too loosely and ignored the stricter overlay/integration condition.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Does the system sense the user’s present surroundings and align added virtual elements with that same scene, rather than just showing a separate feed?
Use when: Apply this on definition questions about mixed, virtual, or interactive technologies where multiple options mention devices, immersion, or user participation.
Boundary: Ignore this check when the definition does not require simultaneous real-scene integration or allows standalone digital display.

Transfer rule: If a concept means active, purposeful, timely switching between targets, then choose the case showing voluntary change after finishing or deciding, not simultaneous or stimulus-driven attention.
Error pattern: I confused intentional transfer with passive distraction by a sudden outside event.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is attention on one task/object first, then deliberately redirected to another, with no overlap and no external capture?
Use when: Apply this to items distinguishing transfer from distribution, stability, concentration, or involuntary orienting in psychology/logic definitions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is about multitasking, sustained focus, or reflexive attention caused by unexpected stimuli.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires proof about qualification plus legality/truth of ad content, then choose the document that directly certifies publishing eligibility under law.  
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every clause in the definition, not grabbing any legally issued business-related document.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it verify the actor named, the specific ad activity, and legal authorization to publish or support the ad claim?  
Use when: A multiple-choice item asks which document fits a formal legal/administrative definition of acceptable proof or certification.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question seeks penalties, general business status, production rights, or enforcement actions rather than admissible proof.

Transfer rule: If premises only show one class is contained in another or disjoint from a third, then do not infer the converse about the larger/result class.  
Error pattern: Illicit reversal of a one-way implication or subset chain; treating a necessary condition or superset as sufficient.  
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as sets/arrows, then ask whether the conclusion flips direction from X→Y into Y→X or from subset to converse.  
Use when: Two premises link categories by “all,” “if,” or exclusion, and the conclusion starts from the broader endpoint rather than the original starting class.  
Boundary: Ignore when a premise explicitly gives a biconditional, exact equivalence, or valid contraposition of the same conditional.

Transfer rule: If a passage introduces a new solution and ends with how it could work, then predict the next part will test or validate that solution.
Error pattern: Success came from following the author’s progression from background limits to proposal to likely evidence, not drifting into side explanations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each option as next-step, background, definition, or digression; prefer the one that advances the new proposal.
Use when: Apply this to continuation questions where the final sentences present a candidate method, mechanism, or proposal after setting up a need.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage signals a contrast, summary, historical aside, or explicit shift to causes, definitions, or comparisons.

Transfer rule: If a statement says some members of a former group now refuse to support a position publicly, then infer only that not all of that former group now publicly support it.
Error pattern: I treated “refusing to support publicly” as equivalent to “publicly opposing,” adding a stronger claim than the premise warrants.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the premise with set logic: “some A are not B”; then confirm the answer does not strengthen “not support” into “oppose” or introduce claims about outsiders.
Use when: Quantifier problems compare past and current stances and use weak negatives like refuse, fail, or do not support.
Boundary: Ignore this when the premise explicitly states opposition, exclusivity, or gives enough information about people outside the original group.

Transfer rule: If a passage builds a causal chain and ends with “only when” plus an outcome, then choose the option summarizing the prerequisite conditions for that outcome.
Error pattern: Mistook an upstream cause in the chain for the author’s main claim instead of the final conditional conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Mark premise links and the final trigger phrase; ask, “What must exist before the highlighted result can appear in large numbers?”
Use when: Relevant for argument-summary questions with multi-step causation, necessary-condition wording, and a concluding societal outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when options ask for a detail, comparison, attitude, or when no final conclusion is signaled.

Transfer rule: If an argument dismisses a claim mainly by citing the speaker’s self-interest or bias, then classify it as attacking motives, not analyzing the claim’s logic.
Error pattern: Mistaking an ad hominem motive attack for assumption identification and refutation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What specific premise is examined?” If none is evaluated and only the source’s incentives are highlighted, choose the motive-attack pattern.
Use when: A stimulus contrasts one side’s stated reasoning with comments about that side’s financial, political, or personal stake.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the argument actually tests a hidden premise or provides independent evidence against the claim itself.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers greater preference from fewer alternatives, then test whether opportunity or available time better explains the behavior.
