Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, tone, or a specific consequence rather than the passage’s central summary.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts old labor-based growth with large investments in advanced systems, then infer primary dependence on new technology, not merely on spending level.  
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from costly examples to a narrower economic category and missed the broader contrast stated in the premise.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the author’s main contrast in one sentence; then verify the option matches that contrast rather than just a supporting detail.  
Use when: Relevant for inference questions where examples with costs, projects, or infrastructure are used to illustrate a shift in what drives growth or competition.  
Boundary: Ignore when the passage explicitly asks about financing structure, investment type, or labor demand rather than the main driver.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers that improving one skill frees resources and boosts another, then prefer evidence showing changes in the first track changes in the second within the same period.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matching the answer to the argument’s proposed causal mechanism rather than to background facts or reverse-direction associations.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this choice show that greater gain in the proposed cause goes with greater gain in the proposed effect, instead of merely describing starting levels or sample representativeness?”
Use when: Strengthen questions involve training, improvement, and a causal claim from automatization/efficiency to performance in another task.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument needs external validity, rules out confounding directly, or asks for weaken, flaw, or resolve.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers quality from high spending, then ask whether high spending could instead signal an underlying deficiency or repair need.
Error pattern: I accepted a side fact about measurement/context instead of attacking the spending-to-adequacy link the conclusion depends on.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, state the core inference as “more spending therefore better condition” and test whether the opposite causal story also fits.
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions where evidence is budget, effort, frequency, or intensity used as proof of success, quality, or sufficiency.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already establishes spending efficiency, outcomes, or independent performance measures rather than using expenditure alone.

Transfer rule: If a rule says “required when P, unless incapable” and a person is not required, then test the contrapositive: if P applies to that person, infer incapacity.
Error pattern: I wrongly assumed another person must bear the duty instead of drawing the limited inference about the named person from the exception structure.
Diagnostic check: Symbolize as (P and capable) -> required; then derive not required -> (not P or incapable), and see whether any choice safely adds P to force incapacity.
Use when: Relevant for conditional statements with exceptions, legal obligations, and answer choices about one participant versus claims about others.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt gives separate reporting duties for others, or when incapacity is not an explicit exception to the obligation.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion assigns all remaining workdays to one employer because one day is spent elsewhere, then require an assumption that the employer actually has that many workdays available.
Error pattern: I focused on a background constraint about holidays instead of the hidden capacity/schedule constraint linking “other days” to the claimed workplace.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, count the days in the argument and ask: could the stated workplace legally or normally occupy all claimed remaining days without an extra assumption?
Use when: An argument infers a full weekly schedule from totals, exceptions, and “the other days” language across jobs or activities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the missing premise is about identity, causation, or definitions rather than schedule feasibility.

Transfer rule: If a passage traces a process to a final perception, then choose the option summarizing the overall endpoint, not one supporting component.
Error pattern: Narrow-detail fixation—elevating a mentioned subpart into the main idea instead of tracking the author’s central claim.
Diagnostic check: In 10 seconds, write the passage in 6–10 words; if your choice cannot match that sentence without extra specifics, reject it.
Use when: Expository texts describe stages, signal sequence words, and contrast sensing organs with later interpretation or integration.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, function of one structure, or explicitly requests a specific stage.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers a broad deficiency from one narrow preference indicator, then challenge whether the indicator validly represents the broader trait.
Error pattern: Arguments often overgeneralize from a single proxy to a multidimensional concept; strong weakening attacks the proxy-conclusion link, not side issues.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “If the measured preference changed, would the broad conclusion still be unsupported because the concepts differ?” If yes, target mismatch.
Use when: The stimulus uses survey percentages, tastes, or one behavior as evidence about overall knowledge, ability, or cultural attainment.
Boundary: Ignore when the cited indicator is explicitly defined as part of the broader concept or independently validated as a reliable measure.

Transfer rule: If a field definition links culture-level conditions to individual psychological traits or mechanisms, then choose the option explicitly connecting social/ecological context to character or mentality.
Error pattern: I focused on a literary or attitudinal example without checking for the required cross-level culture-to-psychology relationship.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark whether it includes both a macro cultural/social environment and a micro psychological outcome; keep only options with both.
Use when: Definitions emphasize interdisciplinary study, psychological mechanisms, and relations between individual variables and broader cultural, social, economic, ecological, or biological factors.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target field studies texts, values, or historical change without any individual-level psychological trait or mechanism.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects a criterion because it includes a certain subclass, then look for a principle that categorically excludes that subclass from the target category.
Error pattern: I chose a premise about improving theories instead of the hidden bridge linking “theoretically posited only” to “not real.”
Diagnostic check: Identify the author’s evidence and conclusion; ask, “What rule would make that evidence sufficient to deny the criterion?” Prefer a direct exclusion rule.
Use when: The stimulus attacks a proposal by noting that many members it accepts share a suspect feature.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a weakening detail, a methodological norm, or a rule about explanatory quality rather than category membership.

Transfer rule: If a passage uses a past case to support a prediction about a current belief, then identify the cited case’s function as an analogy or precedent, not just topic background.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking argumentative role; failure comes from choosing an option that merely restates subject matter instead of evidential function.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: remove the historical reference—does the conclusion lose support, context, or coherence? Match the option to that specific loss.
Use when: Relevant in role-of-a-statement questions featuring historical examples, comparisons across eras, or claims that one situation mirrors another.
Boundary: Ignore this when the cited material only defines terms, gives neutral background, or is rhetorically decorative without supporting an inference.

Transfer rule: If a statement says “all X cannot occur without Y,” then translate it as “every X requires Y,” and keep universal force intact.  
Error pattern: I weakened a universal claim into an existential/partial one and blurred “some may not” with a stronger or different necessity claim.  
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each premise in plain quantifiers: “all X -> Y” and “some X possibly not Z”; reject any option that downgrades “all” to “some” or changes modality.  
Use when: Relevant for verbal-logic items with all/some, cannot/without, may/not necessarily, and answer choices that differ only in quantifier strength.  
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on outside facts, causal mechanisms, or probabilistic interpretation beyond formal quantifier translation.

Transfer rule: If an argument says nonconfirming evidence disproves earlier evidence despite flawed observation conditions, then infer only that the disproof claim is unsupported, not broader claims about all possible observations.
Error pattern: Overextended from criticizing this evidence to asserting no evidence of that type could ever count.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Am I concluding merely that the stated inference fails, or am I adding a stronger counterfactual the speaker never licensed?”
Use when: Relevant in weaken/support questions contrasting bad data, nonconfirmation, and claims that prior results are false.
Boundary: Ignore when the speaker explicitly generalizes to all conditions or gives reasons excluding any better observations.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims one delivery route explains how key ingredients reached Earth, then look for evidence of an alternative route carrying the same ingredients.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning by attacking exclusivity/causal source rather than disputing background science or downstream effects.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does any choice show another plausible carrier or source for the same substance?” If yes, that choice likely weakens the conclusion most.
Use when: Relevant in weakening questions about origins, transmission paths, or “X brought Y” causal stories with multiple possible carriers.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is comparative, quantified, or already allows multiple contributing routes.

Transfer rule: If an argument applies a universal sufficient-condition rule to a specific case, then match it with an option using the same all→instance deduction.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking logical form instead of topic similarity, rhetoric, evidence strength, or modal wording.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite both stem and choice as “All/Any X are Y; this is X; therefore this is Y,” and reject any choice with probability, causation, necessity, or induction.
Use when: Relevant in analogy questions where one statement is a general class rule and the conclusion classifies a named case.
Boundary: Ignore when the original argument relies on statistics, trends, explanation, value judgment, or weakened/strengthened modal terms.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires missing a visible short-term surface change, then exclude cases about memory-source confusion or ownership of an experience.
Error pattern: Success came from separating perception failures during observation from later reconstruction or misattribution in memory.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Was there an observed object/person whose visible features changed over a brief interval, and was the miss due to not noticing that change then?
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching items involving attention, perception, scene continuity, interruptions, or identity/appearance shifts.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target concept concerns false memory, testimony distortion, imagination inflation, or long-delay recall errors.

Transfer rule: If a case features failure, insecurity, or blocked desire followed by a face-saving explanation, then choose it as rationalization.  
Error pattern: Mistaking deliberate deception or external factual analysis for a self-protective reinterpretation of one’s own motives.  
Diagnostic check: Ask: Did the person first face an ego threat, then give a socially acceptable reason that hides the real motive from self or others?  
Use when: Relevant in definition matching about defense mechanisms, excuses after not achieving a goal, or post hoc justifications of embarrassing behavior.  
Boundary: Ignore when the explanation is a genuine causal investigation, coercive lying for punishment avoidance, or action without a later justificatory story.

Transfer rule: If an argument attributes changed responses to a procedural change across time, then test whether it assumes no independent time-based cause explains the difference.
Error pattern: I focused on respondent memory, but missed a needed control-for-confounders assumption in a causal comparison.
Diagnostic check: List all differences between the two groups or occasions; if any unruled-out difference besides the claimed cause could change answers, the argument needs an assumption excluding it.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions comparing results from different times, samples, settings, or formats to infer an order or method effect.
Boundary: Ignore when the comparison is simultaneous or the argument already explicitly controls for temporal and contextual variation.

Transfer rule: If a definition says external reasons replace internal motives, then require evidence of an original internal motive being overridden by an external one.
Error pattern: I matched any incentive-driven behavior to the concept without checking whether the behavior initially came from internal control.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark (1) initial motive, (2) added external reason, (3) replacement of the initial motive, and reject any case missing step 1 or 3.
Use when: The concept hinges on a shift in motivation source, especially in psychology or behavior-definition multiple-choice questions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept concerns simple reinforcement, coercion, or outcomes without a before-and-after motive transition.

Transfer rule: If a plan guarantees success by concentrating on one historically best-performing option, then test whether concentration itself creates a single-point failure that defeats the guarantee.
Error pattern: Strong reasoning pattern: looked beyond past performance and checked whether the proposed strategy changes risk structure.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could following this proposal make the system less robust even if the chosen option performed best before?”
Use when: Arguments infer future assurance from historical survival, rankings, or averages and recommend putting most resources into one type.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only comparative preference, not a guarantee, or when diversification risk is irrelevant or impossible.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus redefines a familiar category by replacing the old basis with a new criterion, then choose the option stating that substitution most directly.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the author’s comparative structure instead of drifting to effects, preferences, predictions, or causes not asserted.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write “old basis → new basis” in 3–6 words and verify the choice preserves both terms and the direction of replacement.
Use when: Relevant for main-point or “most closely illustrates” questions contrasting traditional definitions with revised ones under new technology or conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for evidence, causal consequences, attitudes, or applications rather than the core redefinition.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives scandals, weak protection, and upcoming rules, then choose the option stating the broad need for oversight, not a side fact.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions reward synthesizing examples into the author’s purpose; supporting details about value, invisibility, or jurisdictions are distractors.
Diagnostic check: List each paragraph detail, then ask which option covers all of them as evidence for one claim rather than repeating only one detail.
Use when: The text mixes examples, causes, and policy responses around one social problem and asks what the passage is intended to explain.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, inference, tone, or the role of one sentence.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers one method is inefficient from producing fewer total gains, then compare gains per unit time before accepting it.
Error pattern: Mistook a tempting outside comparison for the real flaw: confusing absolute output with efficiency.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could this method yield fewer results only because it is used far less often?” If yes, look for time/exposure evidence.
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions about effectiveness, naturalness, productivity, or learning methods where one activity occurs much more frequently than another.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already controls for rate, equal exposure, or explicitly defines efficiency independently of time spent.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists an industry’s pain points, then presents one model as meeting those needs, infer the main point is that model’s significance to the industry.
Error pattern: Success came from matching problem-solution structure instead of overreading into exclusivity, prediction, or merger claims.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the text’s issue sentences and the remedy sentences; ask whether the author mainly argues “useful/important” versus “only way,” “future risk,” or “full integration.”
Use when: Apply on main-idea questions where a new concept is introduced, followed by reasons it helps a sector with many coordination problems.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage explicitly compares options, predicts outcomes, or argues adoption should be primary or exclusive.

Transfer rule: If an argument blames a minor code deviation for a bad outcome, then test whether an external factor exceeded the conditions the code was designed to handle.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning identified an alternative cause that breaks the claimed lesson from a single exception.
Diagnostic check: Ask: under full compliance, could the same outcome still occur because the event was outside the standard’s design assumptions?
Use when: A conclusion generalizes from one failure, especially in safety, engineering, policy, or causal-explanation questions.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus already rules out unusual external conditions or asks for a strengthener rather than a weakener.

Transfer rule: If a case shows a usual risk factor without the usual outcome, then favor an answer naming a local protective mechanism that breaks the causal path.
Error pattern: Success comes from explaining the exception directly rather than citing background factors that merely reduce risk in general.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this choice identify why the risk factor fails to produce the disease here, instead of mentioning unrelated habits or weaker contributors?
Use when: Relevant for weaken-exception or explain-the-discrepancy questions involving strong correlation, causal expectation, and an anomalous subgroup.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for the strongest cause, prevalence comparison, or when no anomaly between factor and outcome is presented.

Transfer rule: If an argument dismisses a cost increase because it is a small share of current retail price, then test for indirect supply effects that can raise price through reduced output.
Error pattern: Success pattern: looked beyond direct cost pass-through and checked whether producer exit or capacity cuts break the “small input share means small price effect” assumption.
Diagnostic check: Ask: could this higher input cost cause firms to reduce production, exit, or shrink future supply enough to raise prices independently of current cost share?
Use when: Relevant in weakening questions about prices, inputs, and claims that one cost cannot matter much because it is only a minor component.
Boundary: Ignore when supply is fixed or guaranteed, producer behavior is unchanged, or the argument already addresses supply-side responses.

Transfer rule: If asked whether a behavior is a reflex, then verify it is an animal/human response mediated by a central nervous system, not a plant movement or non-neural reaction.
Error pattern: I focused on voluntariness/instinct and overlooked the defining inclusion criterion: presence of a nervous system participating in the response.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: organism type? nervous system present? response triggered by stimulus through neural control? Eliminate any case failing these checks.
Use when: This applies to biology items contrasting reflexes, instincts, conditioned responses, and stimulus responses across different organisms.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question defines reflex broadly without requiring neural mediation or includes cellular/plant signaling as reflex-like.

Transfer rule: If a statement says all members of a group have a trait and some subgroup members are in that group, then infer those some also have the trait.
Error pattern: Mistook a one-way conditional for a biconditional by reversing or overextending “all X are Y” into “all Y are X.”
Diagnostic check: Rewrite claims as set links; test each choice by chasing arrows only forward from any guaranteed “some” example and reject anything needing reversal.
Use when: Relevant in quantifier problems mixing all/some/most, subgroup overlap, and a universal property attached to one category.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage explicitly gives equivalence, contraposition context, or no existential subgroup is guaranteed.

Transfer rule: If a prompt gives necessary negatives and positive boosters, then eliminate choices hitting strong negatives first and keep any option merely compatible with the boosters.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating “least likely” conditions from “more likely” enhancers instead of treating enhancers as mandatory requirements.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, mark N for forbidden/least-likely traits and B for bonus traits; reject any with clear N, then ask whether at least one remaining choice is still possible without B.
Use when: Apply to hiring, selection, or admission questions that mix exclusion signals with factors that only raise probability.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem states sufficient conditions, exact requirements, or a fully ranked comparison among all options.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a global trend from evidence about major regions plus one market, then check whether a premise extends coverage to the remaining significant regions.
Error pattern: I accepted a choice that echoed a cited detail instead of finding the missing assumption needed to generalize from partial evidence to the whole world.
Diagnostic check: List every scope word in the conclusion, list which groups the premises cover, and ask, “What uncovered group must be neutral or aligned for this inference to hold?”
Use when: The conclusion is broad and the premises discuss only some countries, sectors, or indicators.
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument is only about those named areas or when all major groups are already covered.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts two groups across several behaviors, then choose the option capturing the comparative overall theme, not one side’s detail or a moral slogan.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking contrast structure and selecting the broadest paraphrase supported by all listed differences.
Diagnostic check: List the groups, list each contrasted behavior, then ask whether the best option covers both groups and the shared dimension being compared.
Use when: Relevant in main-idea questions built around parallel descriptions, repeated "not only...but also" patterns, and explicit difference statements.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific inference, cause, evaluation, or a single subgroup’s characteristic.

Transfer rule: If a boldface sentence reports what others cite as support, then classify it as evidence-for-someone-else’s view, not the author’s conclusion.
Error pattern: Confusing background/supporting evidence for an endorsed conclusion, while missing that the author’s stance may be implied by a rebuttal.
Diagnostic check: Ask of each boldface: who believes this, what claim does it support, and does the author endorse it or challenge it?
Use when: Boldface-role questions include reported beliefs, contrasting groups, and a final statement giving a causal reason against an earlier expectation.
Boundary: Ignore this when both boldface parts are within one uninterrupted chain of the author’s own reasoning.

Transfer rule: If an argument cites an abundant raw material as money, then look for a hidden scarcity in the accepted monetary form, production process, or access.
Error pattern: I focused on continued use or coexistence instead of identifying the premise that directly reconciles abundance with value.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “What exact unit counts as money here, and is that unit limited by filtering, processing, skill, time, or control?”
Use when: Apply to resolve-apparent-conflict questions involving economics, value, scarcity, and examples where the underlying resource seems plentiful.
Boundary: Ignore when the dispute is about symbolism, legal status, or adoption over time rather than the source of value.

Transfer rule: If a group is stated to have a property and named people are members of that group, then assign that property to each named person; combine with any universal exclusion.
Error pattern: Successful chaining of set membership with a conditional prohibition to infer a necessary trait about specific individuals.
Diagnostic check: Write two links: named people → group property; group property → not excluded category. Verify the conclusion mentions only named people and only guaranteed consequences.
Use when: Relevant in must-be-true questions with universal statements, subgroup membership, and a rule excluding one category from another.
Boundary: Ignore when premises use possibility, typicality, converse assumptions, or ask for strongest support rather than certainty.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts current progress with a remaining gap and ends with a call to act, then choose the option stating the needed improvement, not a cause or side point.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions reward following the author’s final emphasis and overall purpose rather than latching onto background facts, comparisons, or inferred explanations.
Diagnostic check: Mark thesis cues like “but,” “still,” and “must”; summarize the last sentence in 8–12 words, then match the option closest to that summary.
Use when: Relevant for expository passages with trend description, contrast, international comparison, and a concluding policy or development recommendation.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a cause, detail, inference, or title, or when the conclusion merely restates an earlier claim without new emphasis.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers business feasibility from target-customer desirability, then test capacity and execution constraints before attacking uncertain quality claims.
Error pattern: I weakened a side assumption about effectiveness instead of the core link from promising demand to practical service delivery.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Even if students want this service, can the provider actually supply enough tailored support at the required scale?” If no, prefer that option.
Use when: Relevant in plan, marketing, or expansion questions that move from attractive customers/benefits to likely success.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about desirability or effectiveness itself, not about the provider’s ability to implement.

Transfer rule: If a claim links tiny everyday acts to shaping character, then infer practical guidance about starting from small acts, not stronger “must eliminate” or difficulty claims.
Error pattern: I overreached from a causal observation to a normative requirement about all bad habits instead of the nearest supported operational takeaway.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map each option to exact text support; reject any choice adding necessity, exclusivity, or evaluation not explicitly implied.
Use when: Apply this on inference questions where the stimulus contrasts small habits with inner qualities like mindset, character, or temperament.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly states broader necessity, compares alternatives, or asks for the author’s recommendation rather than strict implication.

Transfer rule: If an argument says blocking or reducing factor X will counter harm because mediator Y is necessary, then require a premise linking X to Y’s functioning.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the hidden causal bridge between the proposed intervention and the stated necessary mechanism, not from judging safety or availability.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “intervention → affected biological factor → required mechanism → outcome” and verify each arrow is explicitly supported or must be assumed.
Use when: Apply this to strengthen/assumption questions in biomedical or causal arguments proposing a treatment based on a discovered necessary condition.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices concern ethics, implementation, side effects, or background facts unless the argument’s conclusion depends on them.

Transfer rule: If premises say all members of a subgroup always dominate another subgroup, then use the contrapositive to infer subgroup status from any exception case.
Error pattern: Mistaking a one-way sufficient condition tied to subgroup membership for a broader causal rule based on correlated traits like size.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, rewrite each statement as if-then form and test its contrapositive; reject any option that adds a new determinant or generalizes beyond the stated groups.
Use when: Relevant in logic questions with universal claims, subgroup qualifiers, and tempting answers that extend a correlation into a rule.
Boundary: Ignore when the premises explicitly establish biconditionals, causal mechanisms, or direct rules covering the broader category.

Transfer rule: If a concept sequence is meant to show inverse connotation–extension, then each later term must add attributes while becoming a strict subset of the previous term.
Error pattern: I chose items linked by identity, part-whole, or overlapping categories instead of a genus-to-species narrowing chain.
Diagnostic check: For each adjacent pair, ask: “Does the later term equal all earlier attributes plus one new qualifier, and does every later instance belong to the earlier set?”
Use when: Options list chains of concepts and the task asks about connotation, extension, genus/species, narrowing, or classification hierarchy.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when relations are part-whole, location containment, role/person identity, or merely associated concepts without subclass inclusion.

Transfer rule: If a definition stresses bounded information, limited time/cost, and satisficing through partial-result comparison, then choose the option explicitly using a satisfactory-not-optimal standard under incomplete foresight.
Error pattern: I overweighted practicality and gradual improvement, while missing the core bounded-rationality mechanism required by the definition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the definition’s mandatory elements and verify the choice contains incomplete information, constrained resources, and satisfactory selection rather than optimal or emotional choice.
Use when: Relevant for concept-definition questions contrasting rational optimization, intuition/emotion, and bounded or incremental decision processes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition centers on long-term implementation, moral judgment, or outcomes rather than the decision rule itself.

Transfer rule: If a plan changes who makes decisions to boost productivity, then prefer evidence that the changed decision path directly frees more time for productive work.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning links the proposed mechanism to the stated goal, instead of focusing on attitudes, staffing side effects, or facts that leave the goal untouched.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Assuming the plan is adopted, does this fact make output per worker rise through the plan’s mechanism?” If not, reject it.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen questions about management restructuring, delegation, process redesign, or technology-enabled decentralization aimed at efficiency or productivity.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for weakening, necessary assumptions, or when answer choices concern feasibility, morale, or costs rather than productivity.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts strong aggregate achievements with weaker quality, impact, or autonomy indicators, then choose the option that preserves both sides and states the overall gap.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions reward balancing concessive structure; wrong choices usually overfocus on either praise or criticism, or narrow one detail into the thesis.
Diagnostic check: Mark positive evidence and negative evidence, then eliminate any option missing one side or turning a supporting point into the central claim.
Use when: The text uses transition cues like “however,” compares rankings with deeper capability measures, or contrasts scale with effectiveness.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage is purely descriptive, asks for a detail/inference, or presents no real contrast to integrate.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers hiring criteria from traits common among top performers, then check whether those traits are also common in the overall hired pool.
Error pattern: Mistaking a selected-group correlation for evidence of predictive superiority; ignoring base-rate/selection effects.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Would this pattern still look impressive if most hires already had that background?” If no, the support is weak.
Use when: Relevant in strengthening/weakening questions about recruiting, admissions, or success profiles drawn from “best,” “top,” or “most successful” members.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already compares success rates across applicant groups or provides controlled evidence beyond raw composition.

Transfer rule: If a passage defines an education by inner freedom, non-attachment, soul growth, and self-transcendence, then map it to the established philosophical education type those traits conventionally denote.
Error pattern: I chose a broad value-themed paraphrase instead of the category best matching the passage’s hallmark features.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list 3-4 core traits from the text and test which option uniquely covers all of them, not just one appealing theme.
Use when: The stem is definitional, abstract, and the options are overlapping educational concepts with one term of art.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text gives concrete scope, methods, or institutional aims that directly specify a different category.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires assessment after completion/use for learning and improvement, then exclude any option centered on ongoing monitoring during execution.
Error pattern: Success came from separating retrospective, summary evaluation from real-time supervision or audit of process compliance.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Did the evaluation begin only after the project was finished or operating, and is it summarizing past results rather than controlling current activity?
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions contrasting ex post review with construction-phase oversight, inspection, or routine management.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target concept explicitly includes formative, interim, or concurrent evaluation stages.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts how to address children versus adults, then select the factor tied to that contrast, not broader social traits.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the author’s explicit comparison and mapping it to the asked consideration.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each contrasted group in the passage and note the property distinguishing them; choose the option that matches that property directly.
Use when: The question asks what should be considered, and the passage gives examples of different wording for different kinds of people.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage emphasizes role, setting, relationship, or emotional tone more than category-based contrasts.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a policy affects few people, then check for ripple effects that force adjustments for related groups beyond the directly affected set.
Error pattern: I focused on a detail about current recipients instead of testing whether wage structures create indirect, broader impacts.
Diagnostic check: Ask: after the mandated increase, would employers need to raise pay for workers just above the floor to preserve rank, incentives, or training differentials?
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions about minimums, caps, thresholds, or regulations where the claim relies on “only a small group is directly affected.”
Boundary: Ignore when the policy has no spillover mechanism tying adjacent cases together or when external constraints block follow-on adjustments.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion treats “no detections yet” as “none exist,” then test whether observation limits could explain the missing evidence.
Error pattern: I ignored a hidden assumption equating absence of observed cases with absence of actual cases.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Could the target exist but remain undetected because current methods, tools, access, or signal conditions are inadequate?”
Use when: An argument infers falsity, nonexistence, or uniqueness from a failed search, no sightings, or no confirmed examples.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already establishes detection would be reliable if the thing existed, or when the issue is normative rather than evidential.

Transfer rule: If a rule is conditional, then check it only when its trigger occurs; if the trigger is absent, mark it irrelevant, not violated.  
Error pattern: Misread conditional constraints and day placements, treating inactive conditions as failures and mixing up which day a requirement targets.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, make a four-rule checklist; for every conditional, underline the trigger person/day, verify whether it occurs, and only then test the required consequence.  
Use when: Scheduling or logic-grid multiple-choice problems with grouped assignments, mutual exclusions, and “if...then...” constraints across different slots.  
Boundary: Ignore this when rules are biconditional, numerical optimization is required, or the task is not evaluating complete candidate schedules.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts workers will leave for higher pay, then require that no nonpay advantages plausibly offset the pay gap.
Error pattern: Mistaking a broad comparative claim about incentives for an absolute salary-ranking claim unsupported by the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: List all stated reasons to switch; then ask, “Could the lower-paid side still retain people because of benefits, conditions, prestige, or flexibility?” If yes, that missing negation is likely assumed.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions about attrition, recruitment, or choice between employers based mainly on compensation.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already addresses total compensation or when the conclusion depends on absolute levels rather than comparative motivation.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects a conclusion by attacking the speaker’s mood, motives, or psychology, then check whether it ever addresses the actual reasons offered for that conclusion.
Error pattern: Mistaking a criticism of the source for a refutation of the argument; choosing an alternative-state objection instead of a relevance-to-evidence flaw.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Could the conclusion still be supported even if the speaker is biased or anxious?” If yes, the reasoning likely ignores the argument’s support.
Use when: The stimulus cites tone, character, or mental state to wave away warnings, criticisms, or predictions.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument explicitly evaluates and rebuts the evidence or premises themselves.

Transfer rule: If a passage says a person’s specific works were “brought out” within a named genre, then infer the creator belongs to that genre, not that accusations are proven.
Error pattern: Mistaking allegations or lawsuits for established facts instead of separating reported claims from warranted inferences about category or role.
Diagnostic check: Mark each statement as fact, accusation, or evaluation; reject any option that turns an accusation into a confirmed event or outcome.
Use when: News-style prompts mention lawsuits, complaints, charges, acceptance of a case, or public controversy around works and ask what follows.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly states a court ruling, verified finding, or direct proof, rather than mere allegations or procedural acceptance.

Transfer rule: If an argument judges a protection measure by direct hit/success rate alone, then test whether comparative outcome data show it still reduces losses enough to justify cost.
Error pattern: Focused on a plausible indirect mechanism instead of the strongest evidence about overall effectiveness and cost-benefit.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Which option best compares protected versus unprotected cases on the final outcome the decision cares about?”
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions where a low performance statistic is used to claim a safety device, policy, or treatment is not worthwhile.
Boundary: Ignore when choices already provide full cost-benefit totals or when the conclusion is about mechanism rather than practical value.

Transfer rule: If a statement says “if condition, then obligation,” then the strongest inconsistency is a case accepting the condition while rejecting the obligation.
Error pattern: Confused a missing-premise converse/irrelevant statement with a direct contradiction of the original conditional claim.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the claim as “have X → should share”; test choices for one that matches “have X and not share/should not share.”
Use when: Relevant for conditional statements about duties, norms, or actions, especially in “most inconsistent” or contradiction questions.
Boundary: Ignore when the original claim is biconditional, quantified differently, or about causes/existence rather than obligation.

Transfer rule: If a choice adds a new causal claim, then verify the passage explicitly states that cause-and-effect link rather than merely neighboring facts.
Error pattern: I accepted a broad superlative paraphrase but missed that another option transformed description into unsupported causation.
Diagnostic check: For each option, label it as restatement, intensification, or causal inference; reject any option needing an unstated “because/therefore.”
Use when: Apply on reading-comprehension items asking which statement does not match the original meaning, especially with paraphrases about heritage, status, and threats.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage itself clearly states the causal mechanism or when the task asks for reasonable inference instead of strict textual consistency.

Transfer rule: If a stem says “could be true EXCEPT,” then test each option for strict compatibility with every comparative claim, especially words like “higher than any” or “greater than any.”
Error pattern: I treated an unsupported relationship as impossible and missed that an absolute superlative can rule out ties.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each premise in logic form; ask whether the option introduces equality, reversal, or mere coexistence, and reject only options that directly contradict a premise.
Use when: Comparative rankings, strongest/most/any, causal evidence, or scope-limited outcome claims appear in inference questions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for best explanation, weakening, or when source claims are explicitly probabilistic or approximate.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims one local practice caused better results, then prefer evidence comparing participants with nonparticipants under the same broader conditions.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning used a controlled comparison to isolate the proposed cause from rival explanations affecting everyone.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Which option creates a same-place, same-period contrast where the key difference is exposure to the alleged cause?”
Use when: Apply this on strengthen questions with competing explanations, especially causal claims about profits, performance, or trends.
Boundary: Ignore when choices instead provide only statewide trends, speculative mechanisms, or background correlations without isolating the target cause.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “no effect” from “no change during removal/absence,” then require that the observation window and interruption would have revealed any real effect.
Error pattern: I chose a statement about alternative evidence instead of the bridge linking the observed null result to the causal conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Negate the candidate assumption; if the argument can still move from “shortage/no change” to “no effect,” reject it.
Use when: Relevant in causal arguments using a temporary cessation, shortage, or pause to claim a treatment or factor does nothing.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about competing causes, historical trends, or when the argument does not rely on a null-result interruption test.

Transfer rule: If a statement gives a sufficient condition for receiving a benefit, then infer only “condition → benefit,” not the reverse.
Error pattern: Confusing one-way implication with its converse; treating possession of a benefit as proof the qualifying condition occurred.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the claim as an arrow and test each option’s direction: original, converse, inverse, or a separate consequence.
Use when: A prompt describes eligibility, rewards, policies, promotions, or guarantees tied to meeting a stated requirement.
Boundary: Ignore this when the wording explicitly says “if and only if,” “only if,” “all and only,” or otherwise states necessity too.

Transfer rule: If a passage stresses officials’ lawful-duty performance, dignity, and personal quality, then choose the option tying language use to institutional/legal consciousness, not broad social modeling.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from “set an example” rhetoric and missed the text’s duty-and-discipline core.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the passage’s stated reasons; if most are about official role, legality, professionalism, or required conduct, reject options centered on public influence or secondary effects.
Use when: The text discusses government or public-service staff, standardized language, and reasons framed as duty, image, professionalism, or compliance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly emphasizes communication efficiency, public education, cultural promotion, or humor/style effects.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives data as evidence and ends with a broad evaluative claim, then choose the option restating that final claim, not the example.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating supporting illustration from the author’s main emphasis and tracking the conclusion-level abstraction.
Diagnostic check: Mark the example sentence and the concluding judgment; ask, “Which option matches the judgment that the example is used to prove?”
Use when: Relevant in reading-comprehension questions with statistics, case examples, and a final sentence generalizing about status, level, or trend.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, purpose of a specific datum, or an inference beyond the stated conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a passage emphasizes the visitor’s sensory experience, symbolism, atmosphere, and emotional effect, then choose the option about artistic conception over physical layout.
Error pattern: I overweighted structural details and ignored that those details were used mainly to create a mood and sacred experiential scene.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Are most facts presented to map parts of the site, or to show what impression and realm the design makes people feel?”
Use when: The text mixes architecture with symbolic meanings, scenery, ritual elements, and descriptions of what viewers perceive or spiritually experience.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly explains spatial organization, construction features, or functional arrangement without sustained emphasis on mood or perception.

Transfer rule: If an argument links a stress-reducing intervention to better disease outcomes through immune effects, then require the missing causal bridge from stress to immune weakening.
Error pattern: Necessary-assumption questions often hinge on an unstated middle link in a causal chain rather than on extreme claims or details about how the intervention works.
Diagnostic check: Write the chain intervention → less stress → ? → relevant health effect; negate the missing link and see whether the conclusion loses support.
Use when: The stimulus argues that a psychological or social factor has medical value by connecting it indirectly to physiology.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the conclusion is only about stress reduction itself or when the bridge is explicitly stated.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts short-term unfair outcomes with long-term procedural value, then choose the option prioritizing procedure over case-specific justice.
Error pattern: Success comes from extracting the author’s main tradeoff, not overreading absolute claims or side comments.
Diagnostic check: Identify the concession, the justification, and the final value judgment; verify the answer matches the judgment, not merely a mentioned consequence.
Use when: Apply this to argument-interpretation questions about law, institutions, neutrality, due process, or long-term versus immediate outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage is descriptive only, rejects procedural priority, or asks for a detail rather than the main point.

Transfer rule: If two speakers both allow some value in a method but differ on whether it is best, then choose the claim about optimality, not total possibility.
Error pattern: Success came from separating “best assessment” from “ever adequate” and noticing one side proposed supplementation rather than rejection.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each speaker’s stance as best / acceptable / inadequate / unnecessary for the key method and pick the smallest claim both directly conflict on.
Use when: Relevant in dialogue questions asking what the speakers disagree about, especially with qualifiers like best, supplement, alternative, ever, or usually.
Boundary: Ignore this when a speaker explicitly denies all usefulness or when the disagreement turns on facts of timing, frequency, or definitions instead of evaluation strength.

Transfer rule: If an argument treats failure to praise as violating a ban on harm, then test whether it unjustifiably equates neutrality or omission with detriment.
Error pattern: Confusing “not beneficial” or “not complimentary” with “harmful,” by inserting an unsupported stronger condition.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the stated requirement and the evidence side by side; ask, “Does the evidence show actual damage, or only lack of positive mention?”
Use when: Relevant in flaw questions involving contracts, conditions, reputational claims, or shifts from a negative prohibition to a positive obligation.
Boundary: Ignore when the premises explicitly define omission as harmful or require affirmative praise, endorsement, or promotional content.

Transfer rule: If an option shows open information gathering and active encouragement of dissent, then treat it as the exception to groupthink-like patterns.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the definition’s core mechanism—pressure, conformity, or authority restricting expression—rather than surface mentions of groups or decisions.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this behavior narrow viewpoints or suppress disagreement? If no, mark it as the likely “not this concept” choice.
Use when: Apply this in concept-definition multiple choice items about flawed group decisions, conformity pressure, silence, or leader influence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is about individual bias, efficiency alone, or cases where disagreement is invited and genuinely protected.

Transfer rule: If a reply shows the evidence misses delayed or hidden cases, then classify it as weakening the support, not directly denying the conclusion.
Error pattern: Success pattern: distinguishing attacks on an argument’s evidentiary link from claims that the conclusion itself is false.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this response provide a reason the premise-to-conclusion inference is unreliable, even if the conclusion could still be true?”
Use when: Relevant in weaken/describe-role questions where evidence is time-limited, sampled early, or based on satisfaction, symptoms, or detection conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when the response supplies direct contrary evidence, restates the conclusion, or accuses the argument of circularity.

Transfer rule: If an example claims “lateral thinking,” then verify the idea was transferred from a different field or domain, not discovered within the same domain’s ongoing work.
Error pattern: Mistaking any inspiration or observation for cross-domain analogy; overlooking whether the source and target contexts are actually different.
Diagnostic check: For each option, name source domain and target domain; if they match or the source is merely an in-field observation, mark it as not lateral.
Use when: The definition hinges on borrowing ideas, methods, or phenomena from one field to solve a problem in another.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept allows within-field creativity, pattern spotting, or ordinary empirical discovery to count.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion rejects an argument by adding a necessary condition, then choose the option that directly links the argument’s stated premise to lacking that condition.
Error pattern: Mistook a converse/dependency statement for an undermining premise; picked a claim about what freedom requires instead of what freedom’s presence implies.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Assuming the original premise is true, does this option create a direct conflict or missing requirement that blocks the conclusion’s support?”
Use when: Relevant in weaken/infer questions with causal or prerequisite language, especially when the argument introduces an extra requirement midstream.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only restate benefits, give unrelated contrasts, or reverse the needed direction of implication.

Transfer rule: If a passage repeatedly links better governance to “professional response,” “professional counterparts,” and staffing across tasks, then choose the option about building professional talent, not broad cooperation or function expansion.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions hinge on the repeated causal driver; successful reasoning tracks the passage’s stated means, not merely the background context or listed participants.
Diagnostic check: Underline the recurring noun/adjective pair and ask, “What is presented as the needed solution across examples?” Pick the option matching that repeated solution.
Use when: The passage lists many duties or actors but keeps returning to one capacity requirement as the answer.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage compares alternatives, stresses outcomes only, or centers on institutional coordination rather than workforce capability.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects a current cause solely because it has existed a long time, then test whether it could have been causing the harm all along.
Error pattern: Mistaking “not new” or “less intense now” for “not causally contributing,” ignoring a persistent negative cause.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does the premise show absence of effect, or only historical continuity/degree?” If continuity still permits ongoing harm, the reasoning is weak.
Use when: Causal arguments compare present vs past conditions to dismiss criticism based on longevity, tradition, or reduced intensity.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument provides evidence the factor is harmless, offset, or causally irrelevant rather than merely longstanding.

Transfer rule: If a role must count as a civil servant, then verify all three: public-law duties, placement on the state’s official staffing roster, and state-funded pay/benefits.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the full definition instead of relying on workplace, seniority, or government affiliation alone.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, make a 3-box checklist—legal public function, formal establishment post, state compensation—and reject any case missing a box.
Use when: This applies to status-classification questions involving government agencies, public institutions, contract workers, service staff, or pending appointments.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question uses a different statutory definition or asks about broad public-sector employment rather than civil-service status.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires unlawful use of public authority causing harm to a private party and a payout by the state, then choose the option matching all three elements.
Error pattern: Success comes from element-by-element matching instead of picking any government payment or public-benefit spending.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: actor is a state organ/staff? act is illegal in official power? victim is a private rights-holder? payment is compensatory for that harm?
Use when: Relevant for legal-definition multiple choice with several government-related scenarios that can be confused with subsidies, honors, welfare, or private liability.
Boundary: Ignore when the concept does not hinge on illegality, official authority, causation of damage, and compensation to an injured non-state party.

Transfer rule: If a passage stresses information being filtered to match superiors’ expectations, then prefer the option explaining suppression because the superior would accept the earlier, convenient report.
Error pattern: I overfocused on factual awareness and ignored the motive created by organizational bias and expectation management.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this choice explain why forwarding the update would be unnecessary or undesirable given the boss’s likely reaction?”
Use when: The scenario involves bureaucracy, selective transmission, distorted reporting, replacement updates, or withheld corrections to prior reports.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question hinges on literal knowledge, chronology, or explicit statements rather than inferred motive for filtering.

Transfer rule: If a passage asks for the main point and gives reasons for a trend, then choose the option stating the broad causal claim those reasons support.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating supporting illustrations or explanations from the author’s central conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Summarize the passage in one cause→effect sentence; verify the chosen option matches that sentence and not just one supporting detail.
Use when: Relevant in main-point questions where the passage explains why something happened by citing audience preferences, reactions, or motives.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an example, an inference, or a specific supporting claim rather than the overall thesis.

Transfer rule: If premises identify a distraction mechanism and a target activity, then infer effects on anyone doing that activity while exposed to the distraction.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning from general causal claims to a narrower supported application without adding stronger outcomes or certainty.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map each choice to the stated cause, affected person, and effect; reject any choice adding inevitability, comparison, or a new causal step.
Use when: The stimulus gives behavioral or attentional effects and asks what is most strongly supported by them.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when choices require statistical strength, exclusivity, or facts about the speaker rather than the overhearer.

Transfer rule: If anecdotes show opposite outcomes from the same treatment, then first test whether a background factor could cause both without the treatment mattering.
Error pattern: I overpreferred a mechanism linking foods instead of considering a neutral explanation for conflicting experiences.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could normal fluctuation, regression to the mean, or timing alone produce each person’s observed change?” If yes, favor that explainer.
Use when: Relevant for causal-reasoning questions built on personal stories, especially when one case improves and another worsens after the same change.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt gives controlled comparisons, rules out spontaneous variation, or asks specifically for a biochemical mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a puzzle says exactly one statement is true, then formalize each statement precisely, including implications and quantifiers, and count truths for every option.
Error pattern: I used loose plausibility filtering and misread broad statements, failing to test all claims jointly against the “only one true” constraint.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, make a T/F table for all speakers; expand “or” as inclusive unless forced otherwise, and mark an implication false only when premise is true and conclusion false.
Use when: Apply this to logic multiple-choice items with rankings, conditional claims, exclusivity counts, or overlapping group-membership statements.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is probabilistic, asks for best explanation, or lacks a strict truth-count condition.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts a saying with a nuanced exception, then separate the author’s main claim from any mentioned proverb before picking the mismatch.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized a side comment into a contradiction and missed that one option merely restated the passage’s endorsed idea.
Diagnostic check: Mark each statement as endorsed, qualified, or rejected by the text; if an option adds modality shifts like “not necessarily” or “only,” test whether the passage explicitly supports that strength.
Use when: Relevant for verbal analogy or reading items with proverbs, concessions, contrast words, and options differing by quantifiers or necessity claims.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on outside facts, technical definitions, or a fully formal argument rather than author stance.

Transfer rule: If a scenario shows deliberate practice with a clear goal and attention-demanding effort, then classify it as explicit learning.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating intentional, rule-guided study from skill pickup through repeated exposure or immersion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark whether the person had a stated objective, consciously practiced, and invested focused mental effort; require all three.
Use when: Apply this on questions contrasting conscious learning versus automatic acquisition from environment, family background, or incidental repetition.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the example mixes both processes equally or lacks enough detail about intention and attention.

Transfer rule: If a legal definition requires negligence, then first exclude any option showing intentional harm or unavoidable mechanical failure before comparing outcomes.
Error pattern: I focused on severe consequences and ignored the required mental state and rule-violation causation structure.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark three boxes—traffic-rule breach, negligent rather than intentional mindset, and resulting serious harm/property loss; choose only one with all three.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about crimes, torts, or violations that hinge on specific subjective and objective elements.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept does not depend on mental state, or when multiple answers are allowed.

Transfer rule: If an argument equates the relevant cause in a high-risk system with ordinary human error that makes other harms nearly inevitable, then infer the same long-run near-inevitability for that system’s harm.
Error pattern: Successful causal analogical transfer from shared underlying human-error mechanisms to long-run outcome likelihood.
Diagnostic check: Map the chain: initial cause -> human error -> same kind as errors causing familiar recurrent events -> those events are nearly inevitable; then see whether the conclusion preserves scope and modality.
Use when: Arguments compare causes across domains and ask what conclusion is best supported, especially about probability over time.
Boundary: Ignore when options deny possibility, shift to management complexity or policy value, or overgeneralize beyond the stated causal link.

Transfer rule: If a question contrasts “structure” with “matter/items,” then map “structure” to arrangement/combination and “matter/items” to the constituent entities themselves.
Error pattern: I confused levels of description, replacing a definition contrast with examples of particles or subfields.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate each term as “pattern/relations among parts” versus “the parts themselves”; reject any option that treats both as the same kind.
Use when: Relevant in definition questions about composition, hierarchy, internal organization, or part–whole distinctions in science concepts.
Boundary: Ignore this when terms are explicitly defined as synonyms, or when the task asks for specific examples rather than conceptual roles.

Transfer rule: If asked which statement cannot support a conclusion, then eliminate choices that strengthen the claim and pick the one that is off-scope or not probative for that claim.
Error pattern: I favored a seeming drawback without checking whether it still provides net support; the real issue was relevance, not positivity vs negativity.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “If true, does this make the conclusion more likely, less likely, or neither?” Reject options about a different product, setting, or use case.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken EXCEPT questions where the conclusion is about replacing one technology with another in a specific domain.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the conclusion explicitly includes cross-domain adoption or when the option directly bears on the stated domain.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims two opposite climate shifts are equally serious, then choose evidence showing both produce comparable harm to the same affected system.
Error pattern: Success came from matching support to the precise comparative claim, not to background causes, timescales, or partial reversals.
Diagnostic check: Underline the conclusion, note the compared outcomes, and ask whether the option links each side to similarly severe consequences.
Use when: The stimulus ends with a balanced or “equally serious” judgment and the choices mix causal details with consequence evidence.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the conclusion is about mechanism, duration, likelihood, or policy rather than comparative severity of outcomes.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion generalizes from observed classroom behavior to an inner trait or broad interest, then require an assumption linking that behavior to the claimed trait.
Error pattern: Mistaking a cause/comparison statement for the needed bridge, instead of checking whether the evidence actually measures the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Write “evidence = ?” and “conclusion = ?”; ask, “What must make this evidence a valid indicator of that conclusion?”
Use when: The argument moves from attendance, participation, choices, or other observable actions to motivation, interest, belief, or awareness.
Boundary: Ignore when the premise already states the trait directly, or when the question asks for cause, explanation, or strengthening rather than a required assumption.

Transfer rule: If a passage identifies weak oversight as the cause of implementation failure, then infer a need to strengthen supervision/inspection, not broadly add institutions.
Error pattern: I matched a nearby noun phrase from the premise instead of the argument’s central causal lever.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state “What specific missing mechanism causes the bad outcome?” and choose the option that directly repairs that mechanism.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions where several choices sound reform-minded, but only one targets the named cause of noncompliance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage argues that organizational capacity itself, rather than oversight or enforcement, is the primary deficiency.

Transfer rule: If a choice shows a repeated, role-based or norm-governed practice shaped by customs, rules, rituals, or authority, then treat it as institutionalized; if it is merely private habit or preference, then do not.
Error pattern: Success came from separating social-role norms from ordinary repeated personal behavior.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Does this behavior persist because a group expects it, assigns roles, or enforces a script beyond the individuals involved?
Use when: Apply to sociology/definition items contrasting customs, rituals, regulations, assigned duties, and personal routines.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept concerns any repetition whatsoever, or when private habits are explicitly defined as institutional.

Transfer rule: If clues mix names and locations, then first map each person to a district uniquely and rewrite every comparison with actual person names before ordering ages.
Error pattern: I substituted identities prematurely and treated location-based references as if they already named a person, causing self-reference and invalid transitive comparisons.
Diagnostic check: Make a 3×3 person-location grid, eliminate each stated home district, assign the remaining matches, then translate each “sister in [district]” clue into person-vs-person inequalities and verify no one is compared to herself.
Use when: Relevant in logic puzzles where entities are fixed to categories and comparisons refer indirectly through those categories.
Boundary: Ignore when all comparisons are already direct between named people and no category assignment is needed.

Transfer rule: If an argument attacks a claim by comparing its evidence pattern to another obviously biased inference, then classify it as undermining by flawed analogy/example, not offering an alternative inference.
Error pattern: I mistook a critique via analogous bad reasoning for a proposal of a better conclusion from the same evidence.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is the speaker drawing a new conclusion from the evidence, or citing a parallel case with the same defect to discredit the original inference?”
Use when: The stimulus says “it would be like...” or otherwise compares one sampling/inference method to another to expose bias.
Boundary: Ignore this when the comparison is used to support, not attack, or when a genuinely new conclusion is drawn.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a treatment should be avoided because it adds a fatal risk, then ask whether that added risk changes overall outcomes versus deaths that would occur anyway.
Error pattern: I focused on broad outcome comparison and missed the needed net-effect/causal-substitution check.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, separate baseline death risk, treatment-caused risk, and overlap; ask, “Are these extra deaths, or mostly replacing deaths from the original condition?”
Use when: Relevant in causal arguments about interventions, side effects, malpractice, safety, or policies affecting already high-risk groups.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is purely about total outcome rates without asserting an added cause increases net risk.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts obsession with distant/public events against neglect of nearby relationships or duties, then infer the author urges attention back to immediate people and realities.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the contrast and implied value judgment, not fixating on surface topics like technology, information, or ambition.
Diagnostic check: List two praised or criticized behaviors in each side of the contrast; ask which option captures the passage’s evaluative shift rather than a literal detail.
Use when: Apply to intent/main-idea questions built on irony, contrast, or examples of distant concern versus local indifference.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage is neutral, mainly explanatory, or explicitly argues about tools/media rather than moral priorities.

Transfer rule: If a logic puzzle asks what must follow from a new assignment, then convert every conditional to its contrapositive and enforce one-to-one role exclusivity before testing options.
Error pattern: I stopped after a partial placement and treated unresolved branches as conclusions instead of eliminating all impossible cases.
Diagnostic check: Fix the given assignment, derive forced exclusions, then for each option try to build one full valid arrangement where the option is false; if none exist, it is inferable.
Use when: Use for constrained matching problems with unique assignments, conditionals, and a question asking what can be inferred or must be true.
Boundary: Ignore when multiple selections may share categories, clues are probabilistic, or the task asks for a possible rather than necessary outcome.

Transfer rule: If a passage moves from broad metaphors and setup to a final thesis about a later topic, then choose the option framing it as an introduction, not as the passage’s full standalone claim.
Error pattern: Mistaking illustrative supporting imagery for the main communicative purpose; overfocusing on repeated surface themes instead of discourse function.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does most of the text define/setup a concept, and does the ending point forward to a bigger subject?” If yes, prefer a framing-purpose summary.
Use when: The passage is abstract, thematic, and ends by naming a broader field, goal, or discussion it seems to prepare.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage directly argues one central claim with evidence and no sign of previewing later content.

Transfer rule: If a definition lists specific kinds of overreach, then test each option for actor, subject matter, hierarchy, and territory before choosing the non-example.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every choice to the definition’s dimensions instead of reacting to whether the act seemed harsh, unusual, or policy-related.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is this an administrative licensing act, and if so, does the actor exceed power by lacking authority, level, matter, or area?
Use when: Relevant for legal-definition multiple choice asking which case is excluded, especially with enumerated subtypes and tempting misconduct that may be a different legal issue.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about morality, effectiveness, criminality, or non-licensing conduct rather than jurisdictional scope.

Transfer rule: If a passage concedes severe harm yet still rejects prohibition, then infer it prioritizes some principle over maximizing safety.
Error pattern: Success came from weighing the author’s stated values against the evidence, not chasing extreme or unsupported policy claims.
Diagnostic check: List the harms cited, then mark the final recommendation; ask, “What value explains keeping freedom despite those harms?”
Use when: Relevant in argument questions where strong risk evidence is followed by appeals to liberty, markets, rights, or other principles.
Boundary: Ignore when the author never balances competing values, or when an option adds absolute claims, causal assumptions, or new policies.

Transfer rule: If cues point in opposite directions, then prefer the option expressing ambivalence or neutrality before assuming error, trickery, or hidden intent.
Error pattern: I overinterpreted inconsistent evidence as contradiction instead of considering mixed or noncommittal attitudes.
Diagnostic check: List each cue’s direct implication, then ask whether a single moderate stance can accommodate both without adding motives not stated.
Use when: A scenario contains behaviors or objects with opposing social signals and asks about underlying attitude or psychology.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt gives explicit intent, chronology, sarcasm, or a causal explanation resolving the conflict.

Transfer rule: If a creation is made by a member of an organization as an assigned or inherent job task, then classify it as duty work.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking both role-based affiliation and task-related purpose, not just authorship, skill, or workplace setting.
Diagnostic check: Verify two points: creator belongs to the organization, and the work was produced to fulfill assigned or normal duties.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions about employee-created works, organizational ownership, or works tied to official responsibilities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the category does not require organizational duty, or when the work is clearly personal, extracurricular, or outside assigned functions.

Transfer rule: If an argument says low representation means people are discouraged from entering, then test whether the trait could be lost after entry instead of before entry.
Error pattern: Mistaking an entry-stage explanation for the only cause; overlooking retention/attrition as an alternative causal path.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could this same distribution arise even if entry is normal?” If yes, look for evidence about quitting, promotion, reassignment, or survival rates.
Use when: The claim infers a barrier to joining from a mismatch between who is best/effective/selected and who is present in a profession or group.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already rules out post-entry differences or asks specifically about initial applicants only.

Transfer rule: If an argument says “only” one treatment works because a cause is biological, then check for the assumption that alternatives cannot fix that cause.
Error pattern: Assumption questions often hinge on excluding a rival explanation or rival treatment, not on comparing speed, prevalence, or side effects.
Diagnostic check: Negate the suspected assumption; if the conclusion could still stand when the alternative can address the stated cause, reject that choice.
Use when: Relevant when premises identify a specific causal mechanism and the conclusion limits effectiveness to one intervention.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is about best, fastest, or most common treatment rather than exclusive effectiveness.

Transfer rule: If an option includes systematic data collection plus organizing/analyzing results about a target group, then classify it as statistical work.
