Error pattern: Success came from matching the definition’s target—capacity or qualification—rather than focusing on severity, custody, or property loss.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “After this measure, does the person or entity lose authorization or legal ability to conduct a regulated activity?” If yes, select it.
Use when: Relevant when options mix status-based penalties with personal restraint, monetary/property penalties, or corrective measures.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the measure only punishes, detains, fines, confiscates, or educates without altering legal qualification or operating authority.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers failure from a rising percentage, then test whether the denominator or other categories changed instead of the target amount rising.
Error pattern: Mistaking a relative-share trend for direct evidence about the absolute level of the behavior being criticized.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Could this percentage increase even if the targeted disposal stayed flat or fell because non-target materials declined faster?”
Use when: Relevant in weakening questions that cite proportions, percentages, market share, or composition of a total as proof of success or failure.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence reports absolute quantities directly or when the total mix is shown to be stable.

Transfer rule: If a passage links two relationships causally or mutually, then reject any option that introduces an unsupported “more important than” ranking.
Error pattern: Success comes from distinguishing stated linkage or influence from stronger claims of priority, exclusivity, or evaluation.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, mark each option as paraphrase, necessary inference, or added comparison; eliminate any added comparison not explicitly stated.
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension items asking for the statement inconsistent with a passage that explains interdependence or conditional effects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the text itself clearly compares importance, gives a hierarchy, or uses explicit superlatives.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists reasons and then ends with a policy/should-do claim, then choose the option stating that final overarching recommendation.
Error pattern: Success pattern: distinguished supporting functions/examples from the author’s main argumentative conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as reason, description, or conclusion; if one claim is justified by all earlier points, prefer that as the gist.
Use when: The passage defines significance, gives multiple benefits, and closes by urging a national, institutional, or strategic action.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, theme of one paragraph only, or when no explicit recommendation/conclusion is present.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers origin from the oldest known evidence in one region, then prefer evidence showing an even older instance elsewhere over evidence about later spread.  
Error pattern: I attacked the migration path with a surprising location instead of targeting the premise that the earliest remains indicate the place of origin.  
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Which option most directly makes the claimed earliest-known evidence false or no longer unique?”  
Use when: Relevant for weakening questions where a conclusion depends on chronology, earliest occurrence, first appearance, or origin-from-oldest-find reasoning.  
Boundary: Ignore when the argument hinges on mechanism, definition, causation, or representativeness rather than comparative dates and locations.

Transfer rule: If a claim says most groups require abilities, then test each option against the minimum capability each available type combination can supply.
Error pattern: I matched a tempting quantifier statement without checking whether the listed members can jointly satisfy the stated majority requirement.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark whether every described group has at least one member for each required function; if any described group lacks a required function, reject it as impossible.
Use when: Apply this to logic questions about categories with missing abilities, combinations of types, and claims using most, half, only, or some.
Boundary: Ignore this when options concern external facts, future plans, or counts unrelated to functional coverage.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects a supposed conflict by citing a subgroup as having both traits, then check for a bridge linking that subgroup to the target class.
Error pattern: I accepted an internal mechanism assumption instead of testing whether the evidence set was relevant to the conclusion’s subject.
Diagnostic check: Identify the conclusion’s subject and the premise’s subject; ask, “What must connect these groups so evidence about one supports a claim about the other?”
Use when: The argument moves from facts about a successful subset, proxy measure, or indicator to a claim about a broader category or status.
Boundary: Ignore this when premises already explicitly define the subset as members of the target class.

Transfer rule: If a passage says “must do X or else Y” and also “if X, then Z,” then infer the contrapositive “not Z implies not X implies Y.”
Error pattern: Confusing a sufficient condition with a stronger requirement, and treating a derived effect as needing the same or greater threshold as its cause.
Diagnostic check: Translate each claim into arrows/logic symbols, take contrapositives, and verify the chosen option follows in every case without adding stronger quantities or new assumptions.
Use when: Necessary-condition, “otherwise,” “if…then,” and “must be true” questions with chained conditional statements.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are causal but nonexclusive, probabilistic, or use defeasible language rather than strict logical necessity.

Transfer rule: If a claim explains poor growth by calling land “raw soil,” then infer a hidden premise linking that soil state to inability to support plants.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the unstated causal bridge between a descriptive label and the observed outcome.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What assumption must be true for this new explanation to actually explain the missing vegetation?”
Use when: Apply this on weaken/strengthen or hypothesis questions where an expert introduces a new term as the reason for an observed phenomenon.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices merely compare regions, discuss human willingness, or shift from plant growth conditions to unrelated cultivation issues.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts expert data with public feeling in public affairs, then choose the option stating the priority relation, not an absolute rejection of data.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions reward extracting the author’s comparative thesis; traps overgeneralize examples or convert “more important” into “only important.”
Diagnostic check: Before answering, rewrite the passage as “In this domain, X matters more than Y because …” and verify the option preserves that exact comparison and scope.
Use when: The argument includes examples, evaluative language, and a contrast between subjective perception and quantitative indicators.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific example detail, causal mechanism, or an explicitly absolute claim by the author.

Transfer rule: If a conditional says one person requires another, then combine it with exclusivity rules to test whether the prerequisite pair is impossible.
Error pattern: I checked options for isolated contradiction instead of chaining all constraints to derive forced absences.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, build a mini implication graph and ask: assuming each option’s attendees are present, does any assumption force both a person and their forbidden counterpart?
Use when: Apply this on selection logic problems with XOR, at-least-one, exactly-two, all-or-none, and if-then attendance constraints.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices depend on probabilities, preferences, or counts without hard logical dependencies.

Transfer rule: If a logic puzzle says exactly one statement is false, then enumerate each candidate liar and test all statements under that single-false assumption.
Error pattern: Success came from checking global consistency rather than trusting an option that only looked locally compatible.
Diagnostic check: For each assumed liar, mark every person’s statement T/F from the proposed team, verify exactly one F, and reject any case with zero or multiple F’s.
Use when: Apply this to team/assignment problems with mutual same-group or different-group claims plus a fixed truth-count condition.
Boundary: Ignore this when statements are probabilistic, ambiguous, or the puzzle lacks an exact count of true/false statements.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion explains a before/after outcome gap, then choose the option that supplies the broadest causal change linking the periods.
Error pattern: Success came from preferring a systemic explanation over narrow, unmentioned fixes or one-sided details.
Diagnostic check: List the premise changes, then ask which option could plausibly account for the full difference across both periods without adding specific unsupported facts.
Use when: Relevant in causal inference questions comparing two eras, policies, or conditions and asking what follows best.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for a necessary assumption, a direct restatement, or evidence about a single event.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires buildup of persistent substances inside organisms and often along a food chain, then choose the option showing internal accumulation, not general pollution or digestive blockage.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every definitional element; failures come from latching onto environmental harm while ignoring organism uptake and concentration increase.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is there a hard-to-degrade substance? Does it enter organisms from the environment? Does concentration in organisms exceed surroundings or rise across trophic levels?
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about ecology, toxic substances, food chains, accumulation, or concentration changes in organisms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is about nutrient overloading, habitat litter, mechanical injury, or short-term indigestion without chemical accumulation.

Transfer rule: If a support question asks for the strongest backing, then choose the option that restates and strengthens the main evaluative claim, not one that merely repeats a premise.
Error pattern: Mistaking background or already-stated evidence for the best supporting conclusion-linked evidence.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, underline the passage’s main claim and ask of each option: does it add new support for that claim, or just paraphrase something already given?
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/support multiple-choice items with one central conclusion plus several descriptive premises.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is assumption, inference, or contradiction, rather than identifying the strongest support.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts a popular claim with “in fact” and gives examples, then choose the option restating that corrected claim most directly.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the author’s thesis-conclusion structure instead of drifting to stronger, broader, or merely related paraphrases.
Diagnostic check: Mark the common view, the pivot phrase, and the final judgment; verify your choice matches all three without adding causation, equivalence, or reversal.
Use when: Relevant in main-point questions built around rebuttal, qualification, and illustrative evidence about two similar concepts.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for an implication, detail, tone, or the best-supported inference rather than the central claim.

Transfer rule: If premises chain conditionals, then translate each into if→then form and link them before judging any option.
Error pattern: I accepted a plausible policy summary instead of testing whether it was logically forced by the stated conditions.
Diagnostic check: Write symbols for each claim, derive contrapositives, then ask of each option: “must follow, could follow, or unsupported?”
Use when: Apply this on verbal-logic items with necessity words like if, only if, must, cannot, and linked policy conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for best advice, attitude, or likely effect rather than strict entailment from premises.

Transfer rule: If eligibility is defined by a fixed statutory list, then match each scenario to a listed category and reject any hardship-only case outside it.
Error pattern: I over-weighted inability to pay and under-checked whether the claim type itself fit the enumerated legal-aid grounds.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each option by claim type, compare to the statute’s categories one by one, and eliminate any option lacking a direct category match.
Use when: A question gives a legal definition with explicit covered situations and asks which case is excluded or included.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the rule uses open-ended language, examples only, or a broad fairness standard instead of a closed list.

Transfer rule: If the definition requires the person to be the driver, then exclude cases where the angry actor is only a passenger or bystander.  
Error pattern: I matched on visible traffic anger but ignored a necessary role condition in the definition.  
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, list required elements; verify actor role, driving context, and aggression all fit, then eliminate any option missing one element.  
Use when: Relevant for definition-based multiple-choice items where several options share surface features like anger, conflict, or vehicles.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the category explicitly includes passengers, pedestrians, or any road user, not just the driver.

Transfer rule: If an argument dates an event from the age of the layer where an object is found, then test whether the object could have arrived in that layer later than the event.
Error pattern: I focused on matching the object’s own age to the target identification, instead of attacking the key assumption linking present location to original deposition time.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could movement, reburial, erosion, collapse, or delayed settling place this item here long after its first arrival?”
Use when: Relevant in archaeology, geology, forensics, or any question inferring timing from where something is currently embedded or discovered.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence establishes undisturbed context and rules out later displacement or redeposition.

Transfer rule: If an argument objects to deploying an untested safety device, then prefer evidence that its failure mode could increase overall danger despite intended benefits.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: compare net risk under use vs nonuse, not generic claims about accidents, testing, or mechanical failure.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: which choice most directly supports the objection by linking incomplete testing to misleading operation and worse outcomes?
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions featuring a pro-safety-benefit claim opposed by a reliability-based objection about untested equipment.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for weaken, assumption, principle, or when choices concern unrelated causes rather than the disputed mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a passage uses appeals, recommendations, or ideals, then do not infer that society already agrees or has achieved them.
Error pattern: Mistaking a normative statement (“should,” “appeal,” “allow”) for a descriptive fact already established.
Diagnostic check: Mark each option as claim about current reality vs advice/opinion; reject any option that upgrades a proposal into an existing consensus or condition.
Use when: Relevant in reading-comprehension items asking which statement is not true, especially with policy comments, criticism, or exhortation.
Boundary: Ignore when the text explicitly states surveys, agreements, official decisions, or other evidence that the reality already holds.

Transfer rule: If a legal definition specifies investor qualifications and liability, then test each option against every required element and disqualifying legal restriction.
Error pattern: I matched on a vivid clause about debt liability while ignoring whether the actor legally qualified to establish the entity.
Diagnostic check: For each option, make a checklist: eligible investor, lawful business purpose, proper ownership/liability structure, no incapacity or age bar; reject any failed item.
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching questions about legal entities, capacity, liability, and statutory prohibitions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks about policy, ethics, or facts outside formal legal-definition elements.

Transfer rule: If a passage praises progress but then shifts with “but/however” to risks and reflection, then choose the option capturing that balanced caution as the main idea.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions often hinge on contrast structure; success comes from weighting the author’s concluding emphasis over vivid examples.
Diagnostic check: Mark topic, contrast word, and final takeaway; ask which option includes both the domain discussed and the author’s evaluative stance.
Use when: The passage opens with achievements or examples, then pivots to consequences, responsibility, or broader impacts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, purpose of an example, or when no contrast/pivot changes the passage focus.

Transfer rule: If a passage rejects utilitarian metrics and gives deeper cultural or moral reasons, then choose the option capturing that higher-level purpose.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the author’s main argumentative pivot from practical objections to enduring spiritual value.
Diagnostic check: Underline the contrast and final claim; ask, “What broad takeaway remains after removing examples and rhetoric?”
Use when: Relevant for main-idea questions where the text contrasts exam, efficiency, or utility with culture, spirit, identity, or heritage.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, tone, inference, or a specifically narrower point than the overall thesis.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires admirers defending or downplaying flaws of a worshiped target, then choose the case showing excuse-making for that target’s wrongdoing.
Error pattern: I matched on strong admiration alone and ignored the key mechanism of filtering shortcomings while exaggerating advantages.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is there explicit negative evidence about the admired person, and do supporters reinterpret, minimize, or excuse it?”
Use when: Apply this to examples about idols, celebrities, leaders, or admired figures where reactions to faults are compared.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the case shows only preference, respect, idealization without faults, or popularity without any flaw-filtering response.

Transfer rule: If a missing-part question has mismatched topic/domain between stem and options, then first test which option restores a coherent argument structure rather than matching surface wording.
Error pattern: I chased a plausible premise by local association instead of checking whether the option fit the argument’s subject, role, and logical flow.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map stem topic + candidate role (premise/conclusion); eliminate any option whose content makes the argument incoherent or whose role breaks premise→conclusion progression.
Use when: Options mix premises and conclusions, include paraphrases, or seem drawn from a different scenario than the stem.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task is pure factual recall or all options clearly stay within one coherent topic.

Transfer rule: If asked which option does not weaken an argument, then test each choice only for whether it leaves the key causal link intact.
Error pattern: Mistaking a statement about imperfect correlation or asymmetry for neutrality when it can still undercut a causal argument.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this provide an alternative cause, attack a premise, or reduce the proposed cause’s plausibility? If yes, it weakens.
Use when: Relevant in causal-reasoning multiple choice questions, especially “except,” “does not challenge,” or “least weakens” formats.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task is to strengthen, explain, or infer directly rather than classify weakening effects.

Transfer rule: If a concept asks whether an effect persists after a stimulus ends, then choose the option where perception continues briefly after removal.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the defining temporal sequence rather than being distracted by vivid but unrelated sensory examples.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: did the stimulus stop first, and does the same sensation remain for a short time afterward?
Use when: Apply this to psychology or perception questions involving lingering sensations, visual traces, echoes, or similar post-stimulus experiences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the item is about weak detection, misinterpretation, poor cleaning, transparency, or any effect occurring while the stimulus is still present.

Transfer rule: If a passage traces a before/after process and names one historical change as the trigger for broad social growth, then choose the option capturing that overall process, not a supporting benefit.
Error pattern: I focused on a prominent detail cluster and mistook enabling conditions for the passage’s central thesis.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write a 7-word summary of each paragraph/sentence chain; if most parts point to one causal transition, match the option naming that transition.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea questions with chronology, cause-and-effect, and several examples of supporting mechanisms.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a specific detail, inference, author attitude, or definition rather than the passage’s overall focus.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists several dimensions of development and says a place differs by reaching “a higher form,” then choose the broad organizing category those dimensions instantiate, not a byproduct or result.
Error pattern: I fixated on an emphasized supporting phrase instead of identifying the abstraction that unifies all listed evidence.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map each clue to each option and ask which option can cover every listed dimension without leftover items.
Use when: The stem asks what fundamentally distinguishes something, and the passage provides multiple examples across social, spatial, and value-related aspects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specifically highlighted effect, image, or single detail rather than the overarching basis.

Transfer rule: If one observed trait is used to infer unrelated traits about the same person, then classify it as a halo effect.
Error pattern: I confused a broad positive worldview or stable leniency with trait-to-trait overgeneralization about one target person.
Diagnostic check: Underline the initial known trait, list each inferred trait, and ask whether those inferences come only from that first impression.
Use when: The options involve judging people and compare global optimism, fear, single incidents, or first-impression spillover from one characteristic.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the judgment comes from repeated evidence, situation-wide bias, or revising views from a specific contradictory behavior.

Transfer rule: If roles are linked by age comparisons, then first convert each statement into who cannot hold each role before testing options.
Error pattern: You treated “person and role are different ages” as blocking that person from that role; that confuses age inequality with identity assignment.
Diagnostic check: For each option, substitute roles into every clue and verify each age relation literally; reject only on a direct contradiction.
Use when: Apply this to one-to-one assignment puzzles where jobs or traits are constrained by relative comparisons like older, younger, or different ages.
Boundary: Ignore this when clues define roles directly without relational comparisons, or when age equality/identity is explicitly specified.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is not directly tied to preserving resources for future generations, then prefer the option about product development/marketing unless it clearly protects long-term resource stocks.
Error pattern: I overfocused on visible environmental harm and missed the distinction between direct resource preservation and broadly “green” or eco-friendly business activity.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this action directly conserve ecosystems, species, landscapes, or pollution loads over time? If not, mark it as the likely exception.
Use when: The prompt contrasts sustainable development, intergenerational equity, conservation, pollution control, habitat protection, and consumer-facing environmental claims.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the option explicitly links innovation or products to measurable long-term resource conservation.

Transfer rule: If an argument previews a judgment and later clauses give reasons for it, then treat that initial evaluative claim as the main conclusion.
Error pattern: Success pattern: distinguishing the author’s ultimate verdict from premises that quantify impact or list benefits.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, underline the claim supported by all others; ask whether each remaining statement functions as evidence for that claim.
Use when: Relevant in main-conclusion questions with contrast words like “nevertheless,” followed by several factual or value-based supporting statements.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for an assumption, inference, or when the repeated statement is merely background rather than supported.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects an analogy by highlighting a key difference, then choose the pattern “distinguish the cases to block the shared conclusion.”
Error pattern: Success came from identifying argument structure over topic language, especially contrast words signaling “similarity noted, conclusion denied.”
Diagnostic check: Ask: what are the two compared cases, what conclusion is drawn from their similarity, and what stated difference is used to stop that inference?
Use when: Relevant in method-of-argument questions involving analogies, ethical comparisons, or claims that one practice should be judged like another.
Boundary: Ignore when the speaker gives a new example, attacks a principle directly, or merely defines a term without using it to separate cases.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires irrational contamination fear plus anxiety-driven cleaning/avoidance, then reject choices showing mere preference or aesthetics without contamination logic.
Error pattern: I overfocused on ordinary hygiene vs excess and missed the requirement that the mismatch could be absence of contamination-related obsession entirely.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark evidence of perceived dirt/germs, anxiety, and compulsive cleaning/checking/avoidance; eliminate any option lacking that full contamination chain.
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching questions about disorders or syndromes with multiple necessary behavioral and motivational components.
Boundary: Ignore when the category is broad, metaphorical, or examples need only family resemblance rather than all core criteria.

Transfer rule: If a statement attributes a property to a group as a whole, then verify it is explicitly distributive before assigning it to one member.
Error pattern: Confusing collective claims about a class with member-level claims; treating a group predicate as if every individual must satisfy it.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the premise as “each member ...” and “the group/members collectively ...”; if only the first supports the conclusion, reject the inference.
Use when: A premise starts with a plural noun phrase about people or objects and the conclusion switches to a single named member.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the premise already quantifies individuals clearly or gives a definitional membership rule.

Transfer rule: If several speakers give propositional claims and exactly one is true, then encode each claim symbolically and test truth-counts under all outcome combinations.
Error pattern: Success came from exhaustive case analysis instead of choosing the statement that felt strongest or most direct.
Diagnostic check: Let each variable be binary, rewrite implications as equivalent forms, evaluate every possible assignment, and keep only assignments where the number of true statements equals one.
Use when: Use this for logic puzzles with conditionals, negations, conjunctions, and a fixed number of truthful speakers.
Boundary: Ignore this when claims are probabilistic, ambiguous in wording, or require outside facts rather than truth-table consistency.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires a computer-generated interactive 3D immersive environment with multi-sensory or all-round simulation, then choose only an option explicitly showing that setup.
Error pattern: I overvalued a vivid feeling of “being there” and ignored missing definitional elements like generated simulation and user interaction.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each required feature in the stem; reject any option lacking even one mandatory feature, especially interactivity or simulated 3D environment.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions about technologies, systems, or categories with several necessary conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the stem gives examples, typical cases, or sufficient indicators rather than strict necessary features.

Transfer rule: If a passage presents a benefit that depends on a stated prerequisite the country lacks, then choose the option highlighting that missing prerequisite as the obstacle.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing the author’s causal chain and locating the real bottleneck rather than selecting a broad, attractive background claim.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the chain claim→required condition→evidence; verify which option matches the condition supported as insufficient and blocks the outcome.
Use when: Relevant for argument-main-point questions with conditional reasoning, especially where advantages are described first but later limited by missing capacity or institutions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, assumption, tone, or when multiple prerequisites are compared without one being clearly singled out.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts several technologies, then choose the option matching the explicitly stated mechanism and output, not a nearby setting detail.
Error pattern: I latched onto a contextual condition and turned association into a claim of expansion or causation.
Diagnostic check: Underline nouns and verbs in the key sentence; verify the option preserves both the named device and its stated function/result.
Use when: Relevant for inference questions on short expository passages with multiple linked details, especially environment, infrastructure, and technology descriptions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for broader implication, opinion, or information that must be combined across multiple sentences.

Transfer rule: If an argument treats a cue found in many bad outcomes as a warning sign, then check how often that cue occurs in the full population, not just among bad outcomes.
Error pattern: Confusing P(cue | problem) with P(problem | cue); using one-way conditional evidence to justify prediction.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, ask: “Could this cue be common even when nothing bad happens?” If yes, base-rate information is missing.
Use when: Applies to causal or predictive arguments moving from accident cases, failures, or selected outcomes to advice about what to infer from a sign.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already gives comparison rates for the cue in normal cases or directly states risk given the cue.

Transfer rule: If one condition forbids both events together and each “not X” forces the other event’s negation or affirmation, then test all truth pairs and keep only the pair satisfying every statement.
Error pattern: Success came from integrating linked conditionals with a mutual-exclusion constraint instead of reading each rule in isolation.
Diagnostic check: Make a 2×2 table for both variables; eliminate pairs violating “not together” first, then each conditional; see whether exactly one pair remains.
Use when: Apply to two-variable logic questions with “if,” “only if,” negations, and a statement blocking simultaneous outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when choices depend on probabilities, timing beyond simple simultaneity, or more than two states per variable.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus rebuts someone’s evidence while defending a prior claim, then treat the conclusion as “that evidence does not justify the criticism,” not the defended claim itself.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating the author’s main point from supporting background that merely explains how the opposing evidence can be true.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: what is the writer ultimately trying to prove about the dispute—an evidential insufficiency or a factual population claim?
Use when: Apply this on main-conclusion questions with a quoted objection, counterevidence, and an alternative explanation that undercuts the objection.
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument directly argues for a factual state of the world rather than attacking another argument’s basis.

Transfer rule: If a plan’s direct step is only to increase attendance, then prefer support showing how higher attendance causally advances the ultimate goal.
Error pattern: Success came from matching an intermediate objective to a bridge premise, not from focusing on customer quality or background facts.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map goal → proposed action → needed missing link; choose the option that explicitly connects the action’s immediate effect to the final outcome.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions where an argument assumes that increasing exposure, traffic, or participation will improve sales or results.
Boundary: Ignore when an option directly strengthens the final outcome by another route, or when the argument is about necessity, explanation, or weakening.

Transfer rule: If an argument deems a costlier treatment unwarranted because short-term outcomes match, then check for omitted long-term benefits like relapse prevention or durability.
Error pattern: Cost-effectiveness claims often overgeneralize from immediate symptom change while ignoring later recurrence, maintenance, or total future burden.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the conclusion’s comparison metric and ask whether any choice introduces a different time horizon or outcome that could reverse the recommendation.
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions about treatments, policies, or programs compared mainly by short-run average results and expense.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already evaluates long-term outcomes, recurrence rates, and lifetime costs, or when choices discuss only irrelevant causes or pricing quirks.

Transfer rule: If testing complementarity, then check whether a price change in one good predictably changes demand for the other in the opposite direction, with other factors held constant.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the option to the formal cross-price-demand condition rather than relying on loose “used together” intuition.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each option as “price of X changes → demand for Y changes?” and verify the causal direction and the ceteris paribus clause.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about economic relationships between paired goods, especially with substitute/complement confusion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about purchasing bundles, quality replacement, or market events without a stated demand response linkage.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts varied methods but unifies them under one takeaway, then choose the broader thesis, not a supporting contrast.
Error pattern: I focused on a prominently repeated detail and missed the author’s final interpretive claim.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase the last two sentences into one sentence; if one option matches that summary better than the earlier details, prefer it.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea questions where examples, differences, or evidence lead to a concluding generalization about principle or meaning.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, comparison, or directly stated subsidiary point rather than the central message.

Transfer rule: If asked for a statement’s role, then map the conclusion, then identify which intermediate claim that statement directly supports.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing premise → subclaim → conclusion instead of matching keywords or picking the most familiar paraphrase.
Diagnostic check: Paraphrase the argument into boxes and arrows; verify the statement is evidence for a claim about legal standards, not for the moral principle or a mere example.
Use when: Apply on role/function questions with mixed descriptive evidence, normative claims, and an explicit conclusion signaled by words like “therefore.”
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks whether a claim is true, assumes hidden premises, or requires strengthening/weaken­ing rather than role identification.

Transfer rule: If a passage says many/some people claim a moral principle, then infer only that some appeal to that noneconomic justification.
Error pattern: Success came from converting “many claim” into the weakest guaranteed existential statement and avoiding stronger quantifiers or truth claims.
Diagnostic check: List each quantifier and modality; rewrite them minimally: many → some, claim → appeal/assert, do not upgrade to only, most, or sound.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions with reported beliefs, mixed economic vs moral reasons, and tempting answers that strengthen scope or certainty.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus endorses the principle itself or gives universal/majority evidence supporting stronger conclusions.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “not in category” from absence of a feature every member of that category has, then match it to a choice with the same universal-feature contrapositive form.
Error pattern: Confusing a category-membership test with a direct rule application or with statements about only some members.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite stimulus as “All X have Y; this lacks Y; therefore not X,” then require the option to preserve both the membership claim and the negated-feature conclusion.
Use when: The stimulus classifies an item by citing a defining trait said to belong to all members of a group.
Boundary: Ignore when the premise is causal, temporal, probabilistic, or uses “some/most/no” in a different quantifier pattern.

Transfer rule: If an offense asks for obstruction of public service, then verify there is intentional interference with lawful official duties by force, threats, organized crowds, or comparable coercive means causing disruption.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every statutory element instead of being distracted by family disputes, private criticism, or retaliation unrelated to duty performance.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list actor, target official role, lawful duty in progress, obstructive conduct, and coercive element; reject any option missing one item.
Use when: Apply this to criminal-law questions defining official-duty obstruction with multiple scenarios mixing personal conflict, abuse history, and workplace interference.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the issue is official misconduct, revenge after the event, or noncoercive persuasion without duty obstruction.

Transfer rule: If two views differ on whether empathic behavior alone counts as moral, then choose the option that tests necessity by pairing empathy with no moral-reasoning capacity.
Error pattern: I chased a correlation claim instead of the core definitional disagreement about what qualifies as moral behavior.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would the empathy-sufficient view accept this, and would the reasoning-required view reject it, solely because reasoning is absent?”
Use when: Apply this on strengthen/consistency questions contrasting sufficient-vs-necessary conditions, especially empathy versus principled reasoning.
Boundary: Ignore this when options compare degrees, causes, or consequences without directly probing whether reasoning is required for moral status.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a move matters only by escaping a harmful old strategy, then choose support that makes success depend on a profitable alternative.
Error pattern: Strengthening works by reinforcing the author’s necessary condition, not by praising resources, motives, or general market reactions.
Diagnostic check: Identify the conclusion, underline any “only if/unless/if continues” condition, then test each option for whether it directly increases that condition’s necessity.
Use when: Apply to strengthen questions about mergers, strategy shifts, profitability, or arguments contrasting sustainable models with cash-burning competition.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for weaken, explain, resolve, or when options provide direct evidence about factual outcomes instead of strategic necessity.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts higher profit margins from lower costs, then test whether selling prices might also change, since margin depends on both cost and price.
Error pattern: Success pattern: focusing on the unstated variable in a profit claim rather than on background facts already held equal.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the conclusion as “margin = price − cost” and ask which answer could alter price or otherwise directly break that equation.
Use when: Relevant in business or economics arguments comparing future profitability, margins, or earnings across groups after a cost change.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about costs, or when prices are fixed by the prompt, law, or contract.

Transfer rule: If a claim says removing a requirement improves ability, then prefer evidence that the old requirement directly distorted learning or training.
Error pattern: Chose a fact showing outcomes might still occur without the rule, instead of a fact explaining why abolishing the rule helps.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this option compare the training process with vs. without the requirement and show a mechanism for improvement?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions about policy cancellation, educational incentives, or whether a rule helps or harms core goals.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks what preserves compliance/popularity only, or when no causal policy-effect claim is being evaluated.

Transfer rule: If one option in an “either/or” pair is excluded, then force the other option and propagate every incompatibility it creates through the remaining pairs.
Error pattern: Success came from chaining conditional constraints instead of checking choices independently.
Diagnostic check: Write each rule as pair/exclusion logic; assume the stated absence, mark forced picks, eliminate forbidden partners, and see which selections become unavoidable.
Use when: Use for selection puzzles with fixed quotas, either-or requirements, and “cannot both be chosen” restrictions.
Boundary: Ignore when conditions are probabilistic, preference-based, or not strict logical constraints on a small finite set.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts two modes and reports their effects, then choose the option that restates the comparative causal claim without adding stronger interpretations.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching scope and wording; failures come from replacing reported effects with loaded abstractions or turning examples into exhaustive definitions.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark whether every key relation in the passage is preserved: two modes, differing effects, same target judgment, no extra universals.
Use when: Apply on reading-comprehension items that summarize experimental findings, contrasts, or cause-and-effect statements across conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for inference beyond the text, evaluation of methodology, or outside knowledge.

Transfer rule: If a passage explicitly states an effect and a related change, then choose the option that restates only those stated effects without adding broader claims.
Error pattern: Success came from preferring a close paraphrase over options that introduced causation, universality, or evaluative outcomes not directly mentioned.
Diagnostic check: Underline each noun and verb in the passage’s main claim; reject any option containing a new mechanism, stronger judgment, or wider scope than those underlined.
Use when: The question asks what is directly supported, and the passage gives a concrete policy change plus stated consequences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for inference, author's implication, or best explanation beyond explicit statements.

Transfer rule: If a passage asks what it is intended to describe, then choose the core thesis stated as cause or claim, not the later remedy list.
Error pattern: I over-weighted detailed policy measures and mistook supporting solutions for the main idea.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark one sentence as the problem/claim and others as evidence, causes, or responses; pick the option matching that marked thesis.
Use when: Relevant in expository passages that first explain why a condition occurs and then propose many interventions or examples.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly asks for measures, recommendations, or the passage is mainly procedural.

Transfer rule: If asked which statement cannot explain an outcome, then keep only choices that provide a causal reason for the outcome and reject statements that merely praise the opposite behavior.
Error pattern: I confused supportive evidence for a recommended action with an explanation for why people fail to follow it.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this make the low observed rate more likely, or does it only describe benefits if the action is taken?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken or explain/not-explain questions about a gap between expert advice and actual behavior.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for justification of the recommendation itself, not causes of noncompliance or low adoption.

Transfer rule: If a statement forbids one direction (“if not wanted, then don’t impose”), then test contraposition and avoid inventing the unsupported positive reverse.
Error pattern: Treated a one-way necessary-condition claim as if its converse or affirmative counterpart also followed.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as “not P -> not Q,” derive only “Q -> P,” then compare each option to see whether it matches original/contrapositive versus converse/inverse.
Use when: Relevant for conditional, moral, or sufficient/necessary wording with negatives like “do not,” “unless,” “only if,” or “should.”
Boundary: Ignore when the source is explicitly biconditional, definitional, or gives both directions independently.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion says a system is impossible without a perfect prerequisite, then test whether that prerequisite can itself develop through building the system.
Error pattern: I reinforced a supporting premise instead of attacking the necessity claim or exposing a two-way dependence.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does any option show the alleged prerequisite is imperfect at first yet can improve alongside the target system?”
Use when: Arguments move from “needs regulation/law” to “therefore impossible unless the legal framework is already complete.”
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only that the prerequisite helps, speeds, or strengthens success, not that it is strictly necessary beforehand.

Transfer rule: If a statement says “P only if Q,” then rewrite it as P → Q; do not infer Q → P.
Error pattern: Direction-of-implication confusion led to adding unsupported facts from a necessary condition.
Diagnostic check: Convert every conditional to arrows/contrapositive, mark any forced facts, then verify each claimed conclusion is derivable without using the converse.
Use when: Relevant in logic questions with nested conditionals, “only if,” contrapositives, and a mix of mandatory and optional selections.
Boundary: Ignore this when the wording is biconditional (“if and only if”), explicitly symmetric, or the task is numeric rather than implication-based.

Transfer rule: If a statement says something would be inconceivable without X, then choose the option framing X as a prerequisite or necessary condition.
Error pattern: Success came from translating strong necessity wording into a support statement rather than chasing examples, details, or related developments.
Diagnostic check: Replace the core claim with “Without X, not Y”; then test each option for exact necessity direction: X enables Y, not merely X and Y both changed.
Use when: Relevant for inference/support questions built on conditional, causal, or necessity language such as without, requires, depends on, or prerequisite.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for sufficient causes, examples, chronology, or a broader summary beyond the claim’s logical structure.

Transfer rule: If asked which fact cannot weaken a causal inference, then test each option for whether it offers an alternative cause, a counterexample, or only shows the cause is not sufficient/curative.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating attacks on causation from facts merely compatible with a contributing-factor claim.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: does this make the proposed factor less likely to be relevant, or can both still be true without conflict?
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken questions built on correlations, timing changes, or improved conditions followed by fewer cases.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is absolute necessity/sufficiency or the option directly targets the exact wording of that stronger claim.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts labor with capital and stresses social/collective production, then choose the option about appropriation of others’ surplus, not a definition of capital.
Error pattern: I matched a familiar theory term instead of tracing which claim the passage actually supports.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, paraphrase the author’s final inferential step in one sentence and verify the option restates that consequence, not just a related concept.
Use when: Relevant in theory-heavy reading questions where several options are doctrinally true but only one is directly entailed by the passage.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a definition, historical fact, or a principle established outside the given text.

Transfer rule: If a definition centers on expressing inner thoughts or spiritual/intellectual activity to others, then choose the option involving communicative expression through words, writing, art, or gesture.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the core function of the act to the definition, not being distracted by legal, workplace, compensation, or permit contexts.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this act primarily communicate a person’s ideas or inner life to an audience?” If yes, it likely fits; if it mainly requests, compels, trains, or remedies, reject it.
Use when: Relevant for concept-classification questions distinguishing expressive rights from administrative, contractual, training, or tort-related actions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition targets economic, property, procedural, or duty-based rights rather than communication or expression.

Transfer rule: If a weakening question targets a causal adaptation hypothesis, then prefer an alternative trait shift that explains the same decline without the proposed mechanism.
Error pattern: I supported the hypothesis by picking evidence that makes inherited resistance plausible instead of asking what best reduces its explanatory power.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the hypothesis’s core link, then test each choice: does it break that link, offer another cause, or strengthen it?
Use when: Relevant in arguments about reduced effectiveness over time, selection across generations, or behavior versus physiological resistance.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for support, or when choices only describe background facts unrelated to the causal decline.

Transfer rule: If an argument says small deviations in either direction cause a bad outcome, then infer it claims the current setting was chosen to avoid that outcome.
Error pattern: Successful recognition of a two-sided “too much/too little” structure supporting a design-or-purpose conclusion from an optimal middle point.
Diagnostic check: Identify (1) one variable, (2) harms from increasing it, (3) harms from decreasing it, and (4) a conclusion that the present level serves the target purpose.
Use when: Relevant in parallel-reasoning questions featuring balance, calibration, timing, dosage, or recipe-style optimization.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is merely predictive, normative, or causal without claiming intentional setup for a beneficial result.

Transfer rule: If a claim says impacts were organized rather than random, then prefer evidence showing a mechanism that directs incoming objects into patterned trajectories before impact.
Error pattern: I favored downstream effects of repeated strikes over a causal process that explains the nonrandom spatial pattern itself.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this choice explain how objects become patterned before impact, rather than what impacts might later change or merely redescribe the pattern?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions contrasting random distribution with coordinated placement and citing unusual clustering as evidence.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for consequences, timing, alternative explanations of aftermath, or simple uniqueness without a generating mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts an old excuse with newer evidence, then choose the option rejecting that excuse, not a downstream policy detail.
Error pattern: I overfocused on a supporting example and missed the author’s main argumentative target.
Diagnostic check: State the passage as “People said X, but actually Y; therefore not-X as justification.” Then match the choice to that template.
Use when: Relevant in gist/main-point questions with rebuttal structure, especially when examples illustrate feasibility rather than prescribe priorities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific recommendation, detail, or best-supported implication instead of the overall thesis.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires workers to blend genuine emotion into in-person service interactions, then choose the option showing a human employee expressing warmth during direct customer contact.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every defining element instead of fixating on only one cue like friendliness, technology, or job title.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify four boxes: human worker, service context, face-to-face interaction, and displayed emotion integrated into the task.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions where the target concept has several necessary conditions, especially about workplace behavior.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept allows remote interaction, nonhuman agents, or merely describes occupation without behavioral evidence.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a stated factor is the only reason for an outcome, then look for evidence of an independent causal reason for that same outcome.
Error pattern: I weakened with an exception/detail about market participants instead of attacking the exclusivity of the claimed cause.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this choice provide another plausible cause of the outcome, rather than merely qualify scope, frequency, or who is involved?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken questions involving causal claims, especially “only reason,” “solely because,” or similar exclusivity language.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is not making an exclusive-cause claim or when choices only dispute quantity without offering a rival cause.

Transfer rule: If a passage names causes, traits, and remedies, then choose the option covering the broad governing idea, not one listed remedy.
Error pattern: I overfocused on the longest, most concrete proposal and missed the text’s higher-level summary of what constrains the issue.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each sentence as cause, characteristic, or response; pick the choice that best spans the dominant categories across the whole passage.
Use when: The question asks for main content/main idea and the passage mixes diagnosis of a problem with policy or solution details.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a specific measure, purpose, or implied recommendation rather than the overall gist.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a treatment caused an outcome by comparing two groups, then check that the groups were comparable before the treatment.
Error pattern: Causal-comparison questions hinge on hidden baseline-equality assumptions, not on broader benefits, outside populations, or external confirmation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If the groups differed in an important preexisting trait, could that alone explain the outcome gap?” If yes, look for an assumption eliminating that difference.
Use when: One study splits subjects into groups, gives different conditions, and concludes one condition improved performance or memory.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is only descriptive/correlational or when randomization/control of key preexisting differences is already established.

Transfer rule: If costs rise yet profits also rise, then look for a profit-preserving offset such as higher selling prices, subsidies, or demand shifts.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning identifies a mechanism that directly links the adverse change to a compensating revenue or support increase.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Does this option explain how profit can stay up despite higher input costs, rather than merely restating or slightly changing costs?”
Use when: Apply to paradox/explain questions involving profits, costs, prices, margins, or policy effects on firms.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is not to reconcile conflicting facts or when an option lacks a direct path to profit impact.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “has a right/permission” to “must/ought/obligation,” then flag a missing premise equating permission with duty.
Error pattern: Confusing what is allowed with what is required; treating a sufficient legal or moral entitlement as an obligatory action.
Diagnostic check: Underline every modal term, then test whether the conclusion strengthens the claim from may/can/right to should/must/obligated without support.
Use when: Relevant in flaw questions featuring rights, permissions, legality, or authority in the premises and obligation language in the conclusion.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the argument explicitly states a bridge principle connecting rights or permission to obligation.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts ideal limits with a new tool’s practical effect, then choose the option stating that tool’s core enabling role.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the author’s central claim instead of drifting to prerequisites, side benefits, or downstream outcomes.
Diagnostic check: Summarize each paragraph in five words, then ask which option matches the repeated subject-verb focus across most sentences.
Use when: The text explains how one mechanism improves a system, especially after noting older systems’ flaws and later consequences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for implication, attitude, detail, or best support rather than the main idea.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires organizing and combining multiple resources, then exclude cases that merely use a single contact to complete one task.
Error pattern: I overfocused on whether an example felt strategic or rich, instead of checking for actual selection, coordination, and integration of diverse resources.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark the resource sources, the coordinating actor, and the integration step; if any are missing, do not treat it as resource integration.
Use when: Apply this on management-definition questions involving combining people, channels, assets, relationships, or information into an organized whole.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target concept includes simple referral, procurement, or one-off assistance without broader configuration.

Transfer rule: If a statement introduced as “obvious/evident” gives a needed condition linking the topic to an intermediate premise, then treat it as support, not as a view to rebut.
Error pattern: Misread an asserted premise as an opposing objection rather than as part of the author’s evidence chain.
Diagnostic check: Map each claim as premise/intermediate conclusion/final conclusion; ask whether the statement is asserted by the author and whether later reasoning depends on it.
Use when: Role-in-argument questions with conditional language, especially “only if,” “unless,” and cue words presenting claims as accepted.
Boundary: Ignore this when the statement is explicitly attributed to critics, marked as a challenge, or presented for rejection.

Transfer rule: If a prompt defines a style by contrasting what is avoided with how meaning is conveyed, then choose the option that preserves both the method and intended effect.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching explicit defining features instead of drifting to broader praise, inferred goals, or extra claims not stated.
Diagnostic check: Underline the source’s two core elements—delivery style and audience impact—and verify the option includes both without adding new themes.
Use when: Relevant for “according to the definition/statement” questions asking which paraphrase or understanding best fits a descriptive passage.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task requires external knowledge, causal explanation, or evaluation beyond restating the described characteristics.

Transfer rule: If a passage warns that hidden issues will accumulate and explode without early action, then choose the option stressing preventive measures.
Error pattern: Success pattern: prioritize the author’s prescription and causal warning over broad background statements or narrower side topics.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the problem, consequence, and recommended response; select the choice matching the response, not merely the setting.
Use when: Relevant in main-idea or emphasis questions where the text contrasts “not yet visible” issues with severe later fallout.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a supporting detail, an example, or a specific subgroup rather than the central takeaway.

Transfer rule: If evidence could come from natural causes or deliberate action, then choose the option that challenges whether the evidence supports the claimed cause.
Error pattern: I favored a tempting but irrelevant possibility instead of testing the link between the new evidence and the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If this evidence were produced by a non-target cause, would the conclusion still follow?” If yes, the argument is unsupported.
Use when: An argument infers historical behavior or causation from physical traces, deposits, damage, or artifacts.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence is already established as intentional or when the question asks for a strengthening implication, not a flaw.

Transfer rule: If two actors are from the same species and the conflict is mainly for status, mates, or rank, then do not classify it as resource/space competition.
Error pattern: Success came from separating ecological competition from social or reproductive conflict within a species.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: are they different species sharing limiting food, habitat, light, or water, and does each reduce the other's access?
Use when: Apply this on biology items contrasting organism pairs, habitats, feeding overlap, weeds/crops, or animals using the same niche.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question explicitly includes intraspecific competition or defines competition broadly to include social dominance contests.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a treatment causes better outcomes from a group average difference, then require an assumption that treated and untreated groups were comparable before treatment.
Error pattern: Confusing correlation with causation by ignoring selection effects and baseline differences; success comes from spotting the needed no-preexisting-advantage assumption.
Diagnostic check: Remove the treatment mentally and ask whether the same outcome gap could still arise from who was selected; if yes, the causal claim lacks support.
Use when: The stimulus compares participants versus nonparticipants and concludes the activity itself improved performance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the evidence includes random assignment, before-and-after data, or an explicit control for initial differences.

Transfer rule: If a choice is forced between two actions and one action is impossible because a necessary precondition failed, then infer the other action occurred and use conditionals on that action.
Error pattern: Treated a one-way conditional as reversible, concluding “not first action” from information that only blocks the second action.
Diagnostic check: Translate to symbols; mark “only if” as visit → agreement; apply contrapositive no agreement → no visit; then from either/or infer the other action; only then test any remaining conditional.
Use when: Statements mix an exclusive-looking alternative with “if,” “only if,” and a denied prerequisite.
Boundary: Ignore when the alternative is not exhaustive, multiple actions can occur, or the conditional is biconditional/equivalence.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims a technology can help solve a broad problem, then prefer support that links the problem’s scale or urgency to the need for that technology.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching evidence to the conclusion’s real target, not to attractive details about mechanism, composition, or hype.
Diagnostic check: Underline the conclusion, name its target in five words, then reject any choice that only explains how it works or praises side benefits.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions where a new invention is said to address a societal need or future challenge.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is specifically about feasibility, safety, nutritional quality, or environmental impact.

Transfer rule: If a chain of sufficient conditions for an action ends in a prerequisite explicitly denied, then conclude the original action cannot occur.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing contraposition through linked conditionals instead of chasing destination details.
Diagnostic check: Translate each statement into arrows, mark the impossible fact, propagate backward with “if P then Q” and its contrapositive “not Q then not P.”
Use when: Relevant in logic questions with nested prerequisites, “only if,” “must,” and a stated real-world constraint blocking one link.
Boundary: Ignore when links are disjunctive, probabilistic, defeasible, or when the blocked fact is not actually required for the target action.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends with why people keep investigating, then choose the option capturing that main motivation, not a background comparison.
Error pattern: Mistook contextual contrast for the author’s primary point; overweighted setup details instead of the concluding emphasis.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as background, contrast, or claim; if one sentence states what people seek or do, prefer the option paraphrasing that action/reason.
Use when: The paragraph contrasts time scales, gives brief context, then finishes with a statement about curiosity, inquiry, or continued research.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a supporting detail, chronology fact, or a purely descriptive comparison rather than the main point.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a higher selling price does not increase per-unit profit because costs rose, then require an assumption that the price increase is no greater than the cost increase.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matched the conclusion’s profit claim to the needed relationship between revenue change and cost change, not to side facts about logistics.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate profit as selling price minus cost and ask whether the conclusion fails if price rose more than cost.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions about pricing, margins, markups, or claims that increased prices are not exploitative because expenses increased.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument concerns total profit, supply volume, fairness, or legal duty rather than per-unit profit.

Transfer rule: If asked which option does not undermine a causal/ability conclusion, then keep the choice that leaves the key link intact and reject choices offering alternative causes or attacking the measure.
Error pattern: I treated a fact supporting one side detail as preservation of the conclusion, instead of testing whether it still changes the inference structure.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “If this were true, would the conclusion become less well supported?” If yes, it undermines; if no, it is the target.
Use when: Arguments infer improved skill, quality, or ability from better outcomes over time despite changing population or context.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for strengthening evidence, explanation, or a directly true statement rather than non-undermining.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires a status “while still married” plus a new marriage/de facto union, then verify the original marriage had not legally ended at the time of the new union.
Error pattern: I focused on relationship outcome after divorce instead of checking the timing and knowledge conditions against each element of the definition.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark three boxes: existing spouse at that moment, new marriage/cohabitation formed, required knowledge present; accept only if all required boxes are yes.
Use when: Apply this to legal-definition multiple choice questions with necessary conditions, timing words, and knowledge/intention elements.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is graded by degree, causation, or best explanation rather than strict element matching.

Transfer rule: If several speakers are each “half right,” then encode each atomic claim as true/false and enforce exactly one true claim per speaker plus all-different outcomes.
Error pattern: Treating partially correct compound statements as globally compatible instead of testing mutual exclusivity and uniqueness across all assignments.
Diagnostic check: Build a grid of people × positions; for each speaker mark their two claims, require one T and one F, and eliminate any assignment that gives duplicate positions or both/neither true.
Use when: Relevant in ranking or placement puzzles with multiple paired claims, “half right” wording, and distinct final results.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are not separable into atomic claims or when “half right” refers to something other than exactly one true component.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives a causal chain ending in social or moral consequences, then choose the option that preserves that chain rather than a broader theme or side point.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions are solved well by tracking the author’s central cause-and-effect claim, not by reacting to abstract contrasts or background framing.
Diagnostic check: Underline the driver, the mechanism, and the outcome; reject any option missing one link or replacing the conclusion with context.
Use when: The passage is argumentative, uses causal language, and includes background conditions plus a stated harmful result.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for tone, implication, title, or a detail rather than the overall thesis.

Transfer rule: If a reply says “not cause X but cause Y,” then classify it as offering an alternative explanation, not denying the observed effect.
Error pattern: Success came from separating disagreement about cause from disagreement about facts, premises, or severity.
Diagnostic check: Identify the shared phenomenon both speakers accept; then ask whether the response rejects that phenomenon or only replaces its cause.
Use when: Relevant in argument-role questions where two speakers discuss the same trend, decline, or event and one answers with a competing cause.
Boundary: Ignore when the response attacks evidence, definitions, assumptions, or consequences rather than supplying a new causal account.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a marriage-market imbalance from signup ratios, then prefer the option describing asymmetric filtering within that market over one adding general preferences without linking to participation outcomes.
Error pattern: I chose a plausible attitude-based story instead of the cause that directly explains the observed skewed composition.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this option create the exact direction of surplus/shortage by changing who gets screened out, rather than merely describing standards or background facts?”
Use when: Relevant for causal-explanation MCQs about disproportions, selection effects, matchmaking pools, or observed ratios.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for value judgments, predictions, or mechanisms unrelated to the measured imbalance.

Transfer rule: If an argument credits one factor for a better outcome, then test whether a prior-stage advantage or borrowed learning could instead explain it.
Error pattern: Mistook a merely compatible statement for a weakening one; failed to compare alternative causes against the cited cause.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this choice show the outcome came from inherited experience, external support, or shifted costs rather than the claimed driver?”
Use when: Relevant in causal weaken questions comparing early and late developers, adopters vs pioneers, or efficiency gains across groups and time.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only say others can also improve, restate trends, or discuss costs without linking them to the compared outcome.

Transfer rule: If a paragraph contrasts one example with another to judge artistic value, then choose the option stating the author’s evaluative conclusion about the criticized side.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the main claim rather than getting distracted by setup about audience change or illustrative examples.
Diagnostic check: Mark the thesis sentence and the contrast marker; ask which option matches the final judgment, not a supporting reason or background trend.
Use when: The passage includes contrast words, examples, and a concluding assessment about realism, value, or artistic effect.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, cause, or example-specific point instead of the passage’s emphasis.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists data collection plus examples of how stores adapt decisions from it, then choose the option capturing the higher-level purpose, not just the data function.
Error pattern: I fixated on a prominent mechanism/detail and missed the author’s main evaluative summary about what the system ultimately enables.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, separate each sentence into means, examples, and stated end goal; choose the option matching the end goal/theme sentence.
Use when: The passage explains a technology, gives several examples, and ends with language like “ultimate goal,” “thus,” or “it can be seen.”
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific function, process step, or explicitly requests a detail rather than the main introduction.

Transfer rule: If an argument says an outcome will occur unless a condition changes because people will assign blame, then look for an assumption linking that blamed belief to the predicted outcome.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing the causal chain and choosing the missing bridge, not a stronger claim, reversal, or unnecessary comparison.
Diagnostic check: List premise facts and conclusion; ask, “What must be true for blamed perception to actually produce the forecasted result?” Negate each candidate and see which breaks the argument.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions with forecasts about elections, behavior, or decisions driven by public belief, blame, or perception.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already states the perception-to-outcome link or when choices mainly quantify weights, preferences, or sufficient conditions beyond necessity.

Transfer rule: If a passage uses comparative trend words like “renaissance,” “modest,” or “again,” then infer only the minimal past-versus-present claim those words entail.
Error pattern: I overreached from a stated benefit to an unstated mechanism instead of extracting what the wording directly guarantees.
Diagnostic check: Underline every comparative or temporal term, restate its weakest implication, and reject any option adding causes, scale, or quality details not explicitly said.
Use when: Relevant for inference questions built on nuanced wording about trends, profitability, and advantages where one choice paraphrases a single loaded term.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for best explanation, assumption, or strengthened conclusion rather than information explicitly provided.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a new expense will boost results, then test whether it displaces a more effective use of the same budget or effort.
Error pattern: I focused on a flaw inside the proposed tactic instead of comparing its effectiveness against the strongest relevant alternative.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does any choice show the recommendation causes loss of a better-performing method, making the net effect doubtful?”
Use when: Apply this to weaken questions about business advice, plans, investments, or strategies that assume added spending will improve outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when options do not involve tradeoffs, limited resources, or comparative effectiveness among competing actions.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives background facts but culminates in an evaluative point, then choose the option capturing that main implication, not a supporting detail.
Error pattern: Success comes from distinguishing central takeaway from restated premises and selecting the statement that integrates the passage’s logic.
Diagnostic check: Underline contrast/turn words and the final claim; ask which option would still summarize the passage if earlier factual clauses were removed.
Use when: Apply this to main-idea questions with several true detail options and one broader statement about significance, consequence, or opportunity.
