Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a directly stated fact, specific inference, or definition rather than overall meaning.

Transfer rule: If a concept asks for its elements, then match each option to the standard component set and reject choices describing an external action or consequence rather than a component.
Error pattern: Success came from structural classification—separating internal parts of an attitude from behaviors that change the world.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the canonical components from memory, then tag each option as cognition, feeling, behavioral tendency, or outcome/action; pick the nonmember.
Use when: Relevant for psychology or theory questions asking which item is not part of a definition, model, or multi-part construct.
Boundary: Ignore this when the field uses a different framework, or when actions/results are explicitly defined as elements in that source.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives several supporting reasons but repeats a priority claim, then choose the option stating that priority, not a single reason.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions reward identifying the author’s central conclusion over collecting vivid descriptive details.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the thesis in 5–10 words and mark each sentence as conclusion or support; pick the choice matching the conclusion.
Use when: The passage contrasts two actions, uses priority language, and offers multiple justifications for one stance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, or the options paraphrase only a specific supporting point.

Transfer rule: If an introduction highlights a research gap after brief background, then choose the option that directly states the understudied topic and likely next focus.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the passage’s shift from broad context to a specific unresolved area rather than picking a general background theme.
Diagnostic check: Mark the final contrast/gap sentence, extract its subject plus missing knowledge, and verify the option matches both parts.
Use when: Apply to article-opening questions with background, significance, limits of prior work, and a narrowed unanswered target.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for the main idea of the excerpt itself, or when later-paragraph clues override the introduction’s gap signal.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “people do not feel constrained” from their voluntary acceptance of extra limits, then strengthen it with a principle linking willingness to add limits to not already feeling heavily limited.
Error pattern: I favored a comparison fact instead of a bridge assumption connecting the cited behavior to the claimed mental state.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this choice explain why the observed behavior would indicate the conclusion, rather than merely showing the behavior occurs elsewhere too?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions where evidence is voluntary action and the conclusion is about perception, freedom, or feeling controlled.
Boundary: Ignore when the best support attacks alternatives, gives causal history, or the conclusion is not about what the behavior signifies.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion claims a trait may be genetic, then prefer evidence showing the parent-child link persists after controlling for environmental or behavioral factors.
Error pattern: Strong reasoning isolates heredity from shared environment; weak reasoning cites triggers, interventions, or nonbiological family influence without separating causes.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Does this option reduce lifestyle/shared-environment explanations while keeping the biological-parent association strong?”
Use when: Apply to arguments inferring genetic causation from higher rates among people with affected biological relatives.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is about treatment, immediate triggers, social transmission, or when heredity is already directly established.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a treatment should be allowed because it is safe and might help, then test for harms caused by replacing better available care.
Error pattern: I focused on whether the treatment works intrinsically, missing an indirect-harm weakness based on opportunity costs and treatment substitution.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Could choosing this option delay, crowd out, or discourage a more effective intervention, creating net harm despite low direct risk?”
Use when: Apply this to policy or recommendation arguments about harmless remedies, permissive standards, or “might help and won’t hurt” reasoning.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already compares against alternatives or when no realistic better option could be forgone.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims certain examples will satisfy all needs, then require an assumption that the examples exhaust the relevant possibilities.
Error pattern: I accepted a choice about whether the product is needed at all, instead of the missing link between cited cases and an “all needs” conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Replace “all needs” with “all relevant cases”; ask, “What unmentioned categories could still matter, and does any option rule them out?”
Use when: The stimulus moves from coverage of some situations to a universal sufficiency claim using words like all, sufficient, only, or most.
Boundary: Ignore this when the gap is causal, comparative, definitional, or about necessity rather than completeness of covered cases.

Transfer rule: If a passage names a process but emphasizes “only when,” required terrain, timing, and concentration, then choose the option about necessary conditions/main prerequisites.
Error pattern: Success came from weighting the author’s emphasis and constraints over background setup or brief mechanism description.
Diagnostic check: Underline repeated necessity cues and list each requirement; if most sentences supply prerequisites rather than status, distribution, or obstacles, pick the conditions-focused summary.
Use when: The question asks for the main idea of an explanatory paragraph mixing context, method, and limiting factors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly compares categories, reports current development, or centers on engineering difficulties rather than prerequisites.

Transfer rule: If a choice directly compares the same goal metric under the same timeframe/resource conditions and shows the rejected option performs better, then pick it as the strongest weakener.
Error pattern: Strength comes from matching the decision’s stated objective and attacking the core comparative inference, not from offering side effects or different outcomes.
Diagnostic check: Ask: what exact metric is the decision trying to maximize, and which option gives a head-to-head result on that metric for the alternative?
Use when: An argument chooses one strategy based on limited observed results and seeks to maximize a named objective.
Boundary: Ignore this when options change the objective, alter resources/timeframe, or only discuss indirect preferences without comparative performance evidence.

Transfer rule: If an argument turns average outcome data into a universal pay-for-better policy choice, then check whether it assumes no cheap way to target the better option only to cases needing it.
Error pattern: Success pattern: I identified a hidden assumption linking population-level cost-effectiveness to all-individual treatment policy.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the policy framing collapse if clinicians could quickly identify who uniquely benefits from the pricier option?” If yes, that assumption is required.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions involving cost-per-life, average trial benefits, and a forced either/or policy recommendation.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already states individual prediction is impossible or when it compares only aggregate budgeting without prescribing uniform use.

Transfer rule: If a choice asks “most unlikely/possible,” then build a full assignment grid and test each option against all constraints plus capacity limits.
Error pattern: I used local implication chasing and vague plausibility instead of exhaustive feasibility checking across the whole matching.
Diagnostic check: For each option, assign those two together first, propagate every conditional, enforce “exactly two per accompanist,” and see whether any singer becomes impossible or overfilled.
Use when: Apply this to distribution or scheduling puzzles with pairings, conditional rules, mutual exclusions, and fixed quotas per category.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is purely definitional, probabilistic without fixed feasibility constraints, or solvable by a direct stated rule alone.

Transfer rule: If a statement has form P → (Q ∨ R), then the guaranteed contrapositive is (¬Q ∧ ¬R) → ¬P, not either single negation alone.
Error pattern: Treated a disjunction in the consequent as if each part separately followed under contraposition.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the statement symbolically; negate the whole consequent with De Morgan’s law, then test any candidate by truth table or counterexample assignment.
Use when: Conditional reasoning problems involve “or,” contraposition, necessity, or translating everyday language into logic.
Boundary: Ignore when the connective is “and,” exclusive-or, or when extra premises change what follows.

Transfer rule: If an argument condemns a policy because it creates a bad motive, then check whether it assumes that motive will sometimes influence behavior.
Error pattern: Necessary-assumption questions often hinge on a hidden bridge from “has reason/incentive” to “will at least occasionally act.”
Diagnostic check: Negate the bridge claim; if the argument survives when actors never act on the motive, the bridge is not required.
Use when: The reasoning moves from incentives, interests, or temptations to incompatibility with duties, harms, or practical consequences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion is only about motives themselves being objectionable, not about resulting suppression or conduct.

Transfer rule: If advice is meant to achieve a specific outcome, then assume the targeted behavior must materially affect that outcome.
Error pattern: I chose a consequence/urgency premise instead of the premise linking the recommendation to the stated goal.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Without this option, could the recommendation still fail to influence the desired result?” Reject choices about causes, credentials, or downstream harms.
Use when: A question asks for a necessary assumption behind a recommendation, intervention, or prohibition aimed at improving some condition.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for sufficient support, best explanation, or a broader causal background rather than a required link.

Transfer rule: If a concept includes only agency actions taken to form, approve, or carry out a decision, then exclude mere background events or calendar interruptions not performed as implementation acts.
Error pattern: Success came from separating intentional administrative conduct from incidental circumstances occurring during the same period.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Is this a deliberate step by the agency or staff that advances, prepares, reviews, communicates, or executes the decision?”
Use when: Apply this on definition-and-exception questions about process terms, especially when one choice is just a contextual event.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the term explicitly includes external conditions, delays, or environmental factors as part of implementation.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists causes and mechanisms, then choose the option that states the final overall effect, not an intermediate step.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing the argument chain from system creation to value conflict to the concluding harm.
Diagnostic check: Mark the passage’s last evaluative claim, then verify the choice covers both main consequence domains rather than one supporting detail.
Use when: Apply this on gist/main-point questions with causal buildup, abstract social critique, and several options echoing isolated sentences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, example, definition, or directly stated subordinate cause.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives a normal mechanism and explains how one factor disrupts it, then infer only the directly stated function of that mechanism.
Error pattern: Success came from choosing a conservative restatement and avoiding broader health claims or unsupported comparisons.
Diagnostic check: Mark each candidate as stated, necessary paraphrase, causal extension, or outside-scope generalization; select only stated/necessary paraphrase.
Use when: The stimulus describes body processes, signaling, cause-and-effect, and asks what can be concluded from limited premises.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for best explanation, strongest support, or outside knowledge is explicitly required.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts one side’s strategy with its impact on another side, then title it by the central consequence emphasized, not the opening background.
Error pattern: Overweighted the introductory topic and missed the paragraph’s main thrust toward threat/implication for the other party.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark who acts, what tools/trend are highlighted, and who is portrayed as needing to respond; choose the option covering that pressure.
Use when: Relevant for title questions where an opening context is followed by a shift to consequences, warning, or strategic challenge.
Boundary: Ignore this when the whole passage stays descriptive about one subject without a clear pivot to effects on another.

Transfer rule: If asked for a passage’s subject, then choose the option that captures the central vehicle/event tying all sentences together, not the final rhetorical takeaway.
Error pattern: I over-weighted the concluding abstract statement and under-weighted the repeatedly framed main event driving the paragraph.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write a 5-word gist naming the paragraph’s anchor topic; reject any option that sounds like a consequence, detail, or commentary on that anchor.
Use when: Relevant for main-subject/title questions in short passages mixing background, vivid details, and a concluding opinion.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for the author’s view, implication, purpose, or a specific detail rather than the overall subject.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers causation from a correlation, then support it with evidence that experimentally changes the factor and shifts the outcome accordingly.
Error pattern: Success pattern: prioritizing intervention-based evidence over mere presence, similarity, or descriptive facts.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Which choice manipulates the proposed cause and shows the predicted change in the effect?”
Use when: Relevant for strengthen questions where an observed association is used to argue that one variable produces another.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is about definition, mechanism only, or statistical prediction without any causal conclusion.

Transfer rule: If an objection cites higher upfront cost, then support the proposal by showing offsetting lifecycle savings or avoided costs tied to the current alternative.
Error pattern: Strong reasoning links a new fact directly to the stated objection; weak reasoning offers side benefits, broader applications, or facts about the problem’s importance without improving the cost comparison.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this choice reduce total long-run cost versus the status quo despite higher initial expense?” If not, discard it.
Use when: Cost-benefit arguments, especially proposals challenged for being too expensive initially.
Boundary: Ignore when the objection is about safety, legality, feasibility, or effectiveness rather than economic justification.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers a program caused an outcome from lower rates among participants, then test whether participants also differ in other outcome-affecting behaviors.
Error pattern: Mistaking sample representativeness or scope issues for the more central confound of self-selection and alternative causes.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the people who opted in also be doing another protective action that would lower the outcome even without the program?”
Use when: The evidence compares volunteers, adopters, or labeled participants with usual rates or nonparticipants to argue causal impact.
Boundary: Ignore when assignment is randomized or the argument already controls for participants’ other relevant preventive behaviors.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers more underlying problems from more reported cases, then test whether access, reporting, or service availability changed.
Error pattern: I focused on a conflicting trend elsewhere instead of attacking the link between observed counts and the hidden cause.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the increase occur even if the true problem rate stayed constant because previously affected people were not counted or did not seek help?”
Use when: Relevant for causal claims drawn from time-series counts of consultations, diagnoses, complaints, arrests, or other observed service-use data.
Boundary: Ignore when the measure is population-based prevalence with stable detection rules and unchanged incentives or access.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers one group’s attitude from higher sales, then verify where the sales occur before treating them as evidence about that group.
Error pattern: Mistaking a per-capita/population alternative for the stronger flaw that the measured purchases may come from a different group entirely.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could most of the counted units be bought or used outside the target population?” If yes, prioritize that over size-based comparisons.
Use when: The argument uses circulation, purchases, views, or counts to infer preferences, awareness, or concern of a specific population.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence is explicitly restricted to the same group whose trait is being inferred and external consumption is ruled out.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects a causal explanation because other groups lacked the same effect under the same condition, then test whether the cause could still operate in one group only.
Error pattern: Faulty cross-group comparison—assuming no causal role for one case from absence of similar outcomes elsewhere.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the argument still fail if this condition can trigger change only in this specific kind of subject?”
Use when: The stimulus compares different species, populations, or categories to dismiss a proposed cause for one target case.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion concerns a universal claim requiring the same effect across all compared groups.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion denies category membership, then link the category’s necessary property to the target’s lack of that property.
Error pattern: I treated “paid” as the key test, ignoring that the argument’s usable bridge was the measurable-by-money condition.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the argument as conditional chains and ask: which missing premise lets me validly derive “not work” from the stated intermediate property?
Use when: The stimulus gives universal statements, a negative conclusion, and one premise introduces a secondary property of the main category.
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument already has a complete contrapositive path or when answer choices merely restate a subset relation.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives similarity evidence and asks what is consistent, then choose the option that restates the supported relation, not one that adds a new place, scope, or “first time” claim.
Error pattern: I overextended a local discovery statement into a broader factual claim not directly stated.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, underline every noun and qualifier, and verify each appears or is entailed by the passage; reject any choice with added entities, quantities, or chronology.
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension items contrasting observed details with answer choices paraphrasing them.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly asks for inference beyond the text or background knowledge.

Transfer rule: If an argument applies a definition using a comparison term, then verify that the term’s reference standard matches the evidence given.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting a definitional gap between stated criteria and the data used to claim the label.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What exact benchmark does the definition require, and does the premise measure that same benchmark rather than a nearby one?”
Use when: Relevant in definition-based questions, especially with cross-group comparisons, legal/economic terms, or ambiguous baselines.
Boundary: Ignore when the standard is explicitly fixed in the prompt or when the claim does not depend on interpreting a comparative criterion.

Transfer rule: If groups are assigned by different criteria at different times, then combine only what the rules guarantee and allow overlap or nonparticipation unless exclusivity is stated.
Error pattern: Mistaking a one-way schedule description for stronger claims about all members, exclusivity, or impossibility across time periods.
Diagnostic check: List each rule as condition→activity, mark the sorting criterion for each time block, then ask whether any option adds “all,” “none,” or cross-period restrictions not explicitly given.
Use when: Statements classify people by one attribute in one period and another attribute in another period.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly states participation is exhaustive, exclusive, or links the periods.

Transfer rule: If a statement links an earlier premise to the final prediction, then classify it as supporting the main conclusion, not as an intermediate conclusion, unless later premises support it.
Error pattern: Mistaking a premise in a causal chain for a subconclusion because it sounds inferential or general.
Diagnostic check: Mark the final claim, then ask of the target sentence: does anything later support it, or does it only help derive the final claim?
Use when: Arguments stack causal or conditional steps from background facts to a forecast or overall thesis.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target claim is explicitly restated as something the author sets out to prove.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists several harms of one trait and ends with a recommendation, then choose the option capturing that overall warning, not one isolated effect.
Error pattern: Narrow focus on an early supporting detail instead of the passage’s central thesis and concluding takeaway.
Diagnostic check: Summarize the text in 8–12 words; if your choice omits the main subject or the final recommendation, reject it.
Use when: A reading question asks for main content, and the passage uses multiple examples to support one broad claim.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, cause-effect link, or an explicitly limited subpoint.

Transfer rule: If an argument states a claim first and the rest gives a causal chain supporting it, then treat the opening claim as the main conclusion.
Error pattern: Mistook an intermediate premise in the support chain for the author’s ultimate conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What is this speaker trying to prove overall?” then remove each sentence; the conclusion is the one best supported by all remaining statements.
Use when: A stimulus contains an initial assertion plus later mechanism/explanation sentences signaled by words like since, thus, because, or thereby.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an intermediate conclusion, role of a statement, or the argument is purely conditional.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims a stimulus strengthens organisms against that same stressor, then prefer evidence showing real-world exposure fails to improve—or worsens—the target outcome.
Error pattern: I matched a shared mechanism term instead of testing whether the new fact weakens the causal chain from trigger to claimed benefit.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this option compare exposed vs unexposed cases on the final performance outcome, and does it move opposite the conclusion?
Use when: Relevant for causal weaken questions with a proposed biological or behavioral mechanism linking stimulus, internal change, and improved resilience.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for support, mechanism illustration only, or when options discuss unrelated traits, side effects, or different outcomes.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which items could occupy one slot under sequencing rules, then test each candidate by constructing at least one full valid schedule.
Error pattern: Prematurely fixed unspecified positions and treated one feasible arrangement as the only arrangement, missing other possibilities.
Diagnostic check: For every candidate in the target slot, place all forced positions first, then search remaining slots for a contradiction-free completion; reject only if every completion fails.
Use when: Ordering games feature fixed placements, adjacency/nonadjacency rules, precedence rules, and a “could be” or “which are possible” prompt.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for a necessary outcome, proves uniqueness already, or candidates are eliminated by a direct rule without full-case testing.

Transfer rule: If a passage defines a quality and then explains how to realize it, then choose the option that captures the central prescription, not a side condition or broader slogan.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the repeated core actions and filtering out peripheral themes not developed as the main point.
Diagnostic check: Underline repeated verbs or requirements; if one option compresses most of them into a single actionable thesis, prefer it.
Use when: Apply to main-idea questions with definitional opening lines followed by practical conditions, traits, or methods.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for an inference, purpose, example function, or a narrowly stated supporting detail.

Transfer rule: If a trait is defined as fact-based confidence in one’s abilities, then choose the case grounded in specific self-assessment and controllable improvement.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating realistic self-belief from arrogance, stereotyping, wishful thinking, or conclusions drawn from irrelevant comparisons.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is the person using concrete evidence about their own performance, identifying a changeable cause, and making a proportionate judgment?
Use when: Apply this to character-definition questions about confidence, self-esteem, rational belief, or healthy personality traits.
Boundary: Ignore this when the target concept rewards overclaiming, social dominance, optimism alone, or judgments based on external labels rather than evidence.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers that a behavior causes an outcome from a correlation, then test whether the outcome could instead be a precondition for the behavior.
Error pattern: Mistook a weak counterexample/comparison for a causal refutation; failed to check reverse causation and selection effects.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Could people already possessing the outcome be the ones able or likely to do the behavior?” If yes, prefer that over mere exceptions.
Use when: An argument moves from “people who do X tend to have Y” to “doing X helps produce Y.”
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence is experimental, time-ordered, or explicitly controls for prior differences.

Transfer rule: If asked which fact does not weaken a causal claim, then prefer a fact that would, if anything, make the effect harder despite the proposed cause.
Error pattern: I treated “same as others” as neutral, but comparative parity on the supposed key factor usually undercuts claims that it explains a special outcome.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this provide an alternative cause, deny uniqueness/effectiveness of the proposed cause, or instead strengthen the puzzle the cause helps explain?
Use when: Relevant for weaken/except questions about causal explanations supported by a distinctive trait and an unusually good outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is not causal, or when choices concern definitions, scope, or pure sufficiency/necessity logic.

Transfer rule: If a trend in living arrangements is used to infer difficulty of independent living, then require an assumption linking ability to live independently with actually choosing to do so.
Error pattern: Causal/ability claims are inferred from preference-sensitive behavior without checking whether behavior tracks capability rather than taste or norms.
Diagnostic check: Ask: if independence became easier, would at least some people switch away from living with parents; if not, the inference fails.
Use when: Relevant for assumption questions that move from higher co-residence, enrollment, purchases, or similar choices to stronger claims about affordability or feasibility.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already gives direct evidence about capability or states preferences are unchanged and behavior reliably reflects ability.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what most supports a prediction about an intervention raising sales, then choose the fact that directly links the intervention to more purchases.
Error pattern: Success comes from preferring causal bridge evidence over background trends, company motives, or facts about interested audiences.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Assuming this statement is true, does the intervention itself create a clear path from the current problem to increased buying?”
Use when: Relevant for strengthen questions about forecasts, plans, or policy changes where several choices are merely descriptive or indirectly related.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task is weaken, resolve, or identify an assumption rather than add direct supporting evidence.

Transfer rule: If a passage says the same facts can be connected in multiple discipline-acceptable ways, then choose the option allowing multiple valid descriptions.
Error pattern: Success pattern: distinguishing variability in narrative arrangement from changes in factual truth or permission to invent.
Diagnostic check: Underline claims about facts, then claims about how facts are organized; ask whether the answer changes the facts or only the presentation built from them.
Use when: Relevant in questions contrasting evidence, interpretation, narrative construction, and historiography or social-science description.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage explicitly says evidence is false, indeterminate, or includes invented content rather than alternative organization.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion says recovery fixes feelings but not performance, then choose evidence showing post-recovery subjective improvement alongside persistent objective impairment.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning matched support to the exact causal gap instead of background conditions, averages, or pretest health facts.
Diagnostic check: List conclusion parts, then verify the option directly measures the disputed outcome after the intervention, not before or during setup.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions about experiments, especially where behavior/performance must be distinguished from reported state or temporary treatment effects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for assumptions, flaws, or when options only compare groups without measuring the claimed residual effect.

Transfer rule: If a grouping puzzle asks whether a pair can coexist, then instantiate all linked conditions and try to complete a full valid roster around that pair before deciding.
Error pattern: I treated one-way implications and exclusivity rules as if they worked in reverse, creating unsupported bans and overlooking hidden conflicts.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate pair, force both in, propagate every rule forward only, count required/forbidden members, and see whether any quota or either-or constraint is violated.
Use when: Apply this to fixed-size selection problems with exclusive pairs, conditional participation, and “only if/unless” statements.
Boundary: Ignore this when constraints are probabilistic, preferences rather than hard rules, or the task is not about joint feasibility.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a specific cause from a marker, then test whether the marker also has a plausible alternative source.
Error pattern: Causal attribution from a correlated indicator is strong only when exclusivity of the indicator is established.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Could the cited substance, pattern, or signal be produced by another mechanism in the same system?” If yes, that weakens the inference.
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions where evidence is a material trace, anomaly, or signature used to support a historical event or causal hypothesis.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already rules out alternative origins or when the evidence is direct observation of the cause itself.

Transfer rule: If options list imported items under conditional rules, then convert every statement into import-set implications/forbidden pairings and test each option against all of them.
Error pattern: Success came from reducing the rules to a key incompatibility and a mandatory-addition rule, then eliminating options that violated either.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write each rule as “selected X ⇒ must include Y” or “selected X ⇒ cannot include Y,” then scan every option for any triggered violation.
Use when: Apply this on selection/logic questions with import, scheduling, membership, or eligibility conditions linked by if/then language.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when choices are numerical computations, probability estimates, or when conditions describe causes rather than constraints on allowed sets.

Transfer rule: If a paradox contrasts higher nutrient intake with worse outcomes, then test whether the source differs in bioavailability or contains something that blocks absorption.
Error pattern: I matched overlapping consumption patterns instead of checking whether the proposed fact explains why the supposedly richer source is less effective.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this choice change how much of the key substance the body actually uses, and does it explain both sides of the contrast?”
Use when: Relevant for resolve-the-discrepancy questions involving diet, medicine, mechanisms, or any case where intake and effect diverge.
Boundary: Ignore when the gap is about measurement, timing, population differences, or when absorption/utilization is not part of the causal chain.

Transfer rule: If a relation is claimed transitive, then test whether chaining two valid links always forces the same link between the first and third items.
Error pattern: Success came from checking structural logic of the relation, not relying on familiar real-world examples.
Diagnostic check: Build a three-item chain xRy and yRz; ask whether xRz must hold in every possible case, and reject it if any counterexample exists.
Use when: The prompt defines a relation by how it behaves across A-B-C links and asks which everyday or mathematical relation fits.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the relation is symmetric, role-based, or causal without guaranteed inheritance across chains.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires rules plus monitoring or sanctions to constrain behavior for implementing orders or maintaining order, then choose the option with explicit compliance procedures.
Error pattern: Success came from matching all core elements instead of picking choices showing only encouragement, training, or general improvement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list required elements from the definition and verify the candidate includes each one with a concrete behavior-control mechanism.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions about management, institutions, regulation, discipline, incentives, or enforcement.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept is mainly about outcomes, culture, ability-building, or voluntary support without mandatory restrictions.

Transfer rule: If an argument treats average absenteeism as removable staffing, then ask whether absences would still occur after headcount is reduced.
Error pattern: I focused on special-role workers instead of the hidden assumption that the same amount of absence can coexist with fewer employees.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, subtract the proposed cut from staffing and test whether the stated average or exact absences would now reduce available workers below the level tied to normal output.
Use when: Staffing, capacity, scheduling, or productivity arguments infer permanent cuts from recurring absences or unused slack.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument explicitly shows post-cut attendance, replacement coverage, or output under the reduced staffing level.

Transfer rule: If an argument uses survey preference as proof of a specific product quality, then check whether the preference could be explained by a different factor.
Error pattern: I accepted a denominator/sample-framing criticism when the deeper flaw was a causal leap from popularity to the advertised attribute.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the survey result still occur if buyers chose mainly for price, availability, packaging, or habit rather than the claimed quality?”
Use when: Relevant for ads or arguments that cite consumer preferences, rankings, or votes as evidence for why something is better.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence directly measures the claimed trait or when alternative drivers are ruled out by the survey design.

Transfer rule: If a theory says higher levels barely affect lower ones, then prefer evidence where changing predators triggers major herbivore and plant changes.
Error pattern: Success pattern—tested answer choices against the theory’s core causal claim rather than picking any choice about food webs.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the theory’s predicted direction of influence and ask which option shows a strong violation of that prediction.
Use when: Relevant for weaken/evidence questions about causal ecosystem models, trophic levels, or claims of one-way bottom-up control.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for supporting evidence, definitions, or when a choice only restates lower-level resource limits without cross-level reversal.

Transfer rule: If a passage says one factor has outpaced another and the slower factor is the bottleneck, then mark statements blaming the faster factor as inconsistent.
Error pattern: I reversed the direction of the bottleneck, misattributing the application limit to the leading variable instead of the lagging one.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “What is ahead? What is behind? What causes the limit?” and verify each option preserves that causal direction.
Use when: Apply this to compare/contrast passages about bottlenecks, constraints, rates, capacities, or “cannot improve because” reasoning.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question hinges on definitions, timeline claims, or evidence absent from a speed/causality comparison.

Transfer rule: If a passage states problems, then gives development requirements, methods, and expected effects, identify the central issue those methods aim to address, not the setup details.
Error pattern: Overweighted introductory background/problems and missed the author’s main emphasis signaled by purpose-and-effect language.
Diagnostic check: Underline the final goal clause; ask, “What single issue are the proposed abilities and improvements meant to alleviate or solve?”
Use when: Main-idea questions where the passage moves from context/problems to prescriptions and ends with intended outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for supporting details, lists multiple coequal themes, or the passage is purely descriptive without a remedy/result structure.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a likely occurrence in the remaining segment because the usual total has not yet appeared, then match it to the same “overdue remainder” structure.
Error pattern: Mistaking an average or usual total over a whole period for evidence that the unobserved tail is now probably where the missing instances must occur.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is the conclusion shifting from whole-period frequency to probability concentrated in the remaining part solely because earlier parts lacked the event?”
Use when: The stimulus compares observed-so-far absence with a customary total and predicts the event in the short time or portion left.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only possible, or when independent causal evidence specifically raises the remaining segment’s likelihood.

Transfer rule: If a claim about an overall average is supported by a few vivid examples, then test whether the examples are a representative sample of the whole set.
Error pattern: Mistaking salient anecdotes or selected categories for sufficient evidence about a population-level statistic.
Diagnostic check: List the cited cases, ask whether they were systematically chosen, and ask what omitted categories could offset them.
Use when: The argument disputes a broad quantitative estimate by citing several specific items or personal experiences.
Boundary: Ignore this when the evidence is shown to be randomly sampled or otherwise demonstrably representative of the full population.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a vague rule could be applied unfairly by decision-makers, then look for a principle granting those decision-makers control over interpretation.
Error pattern: I favored a choice matching the bad outcome instead of the missing assumption that links vagueness to that outcome.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Who has authority to interpret the vague standard, and does an option explicitly give that authority to the actor alleged to misuse it?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/justify questions about ambiguous policies, discretionary enforcement, and claims that bias could drive sanctions.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already states interpretive authority or when the needed support concerns degree, frequency, or consequences rather than control.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a tool or method is being developed or used for a task, then infer only that capability, not broader superiority or exclusivity claims.
Error pattern: Strong performance came from choosing the directly supported, least overstated inference rather than adding assumptions about effectiveness, dependence, or human inability.
Diagnostic check: For each option, underline its key claim and match it to an explicit sentence; reject any option needing words like “often,” “cannot,” “rely on,” or comparative leaps.
Use when: Apply this on inference questions built from short expository passages about technologies, studies, or projects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for main idea, evaluation, or outside-world plausibility instead of strict textual inference.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts failure from projected demand exceeding stated limits, then identify the hidden link connecting over-limit conditions to the predicted failure.
Error pattern: Strength in assumption questions comes from testing whether the conclusion collapses without a specific bridge from quantitative pressure to the claimed outcome.
Diagnostic check: Negate the candidate assumption; if the system could exceed the cited threshold yet the predicted bad result need not occur, that candidate is required.
Use when: Relevant for capacity, threshold, overload, forecast, or infrastructure arguments that move from rising usage to breakdown or inability.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is only about likelihood, cost, timing, or causes unrelated to crossing a stated maximum.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers that combining individually successful elements makes the combined whole successful, then flag a part-to-whole composition flaw.
Error pattern: I treated a structural fallacy as a causal-oversight issue by focusing on missing explanations instead of the invalid aggregation step.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is the evidence only that separate components had a trait, while the conclusion assigns that trait to their combination?”
Use when: Relevant in arguments about products, plans, teams, or ideas built by merging features that each worked well alone.
Boundary: Ignore when there is evidence the combination itself was tested or a mechanism shows the trait transfers jointly.

Transfer rule: If two subgroups partition a larger population and one subgroup is much larger, then use worst-case allocation to test whether a cross-subgroup comparison must hold.
Error pattern: Treated a plausible statement as deducible without checking adversarial distributions consistent with the totals.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate claim, assign as many relevant people as possible to the competing subgroup; if the claim still holds, it is guaranteed.
Use when: A problem gives only totals, ratios, and subgroup sizes, while answer choices compare nested or crossed categories.
Boundary: Ignore this when exact subgroup breakdowns, independence assumptions, or direct category-specific counts are provided.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion says a motive was solely X from behavior plus favorable facts, then assume a principle linking that behavior under those facts directly to sole motive X.
Error pattern: Sufficient-assumption success pattern: choose the rule that makes the cited facts guarantee the author’s psychological conclusion, not one about possibility or partial support.
Diagnostic check: Abstract the premises as behavior + no cost + customer benefit; ask which option, if added, yields “therefore sole motive” by valid substitution.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions involving motive, intent, or cause inferred from a company’s or person’s choice.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for weaken/strengthen, or when the conclusion is comparative, probabilistic, or not about exclusive motive.

Transfer rule: If a prompt asks what a passage “means by” a concept, then classify the passage by its function in the definition—method, process, cause, or value—not by appealing wording.
Error pattern: I matched broad positive language to an abstract benefit category instead of identifying the passage’s definitional role.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, paraphrase the passage in five words: “This describes how to ___”; if it lists channels, tools, or implementation actions, choose the method/function category.
Use when: Relevant for verbal classification items where a concept is followed by examples, media, procedures, or implementation details.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage focuses on why it matters, whether it is required, or its timing/context rather than how it is carried out.

Transfer rule: If a passage frames new conditions and resulting social/normative problems, then choose the option naming that broader issue pair, not a detail mentioned in support.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the author’s main setup-to-theme move and resisting tempting concrete examples or background facts.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the passage’s repeated abstract nouns and causal links; pick the option that covers both the context and the problem introduced.
Use when: The stem asks what an introduction will discuss next after describing changes, consequences, and weakened old constraints.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, example, definition, or explicitly limits the next section’s scope.

Transfer rule: If a passage states permission or possibility, then reject answers that upgrade it to frequency, universality, or a stronger specific method.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting scope/intensity distortion between what is allowed or occasional and what is claimed as common or absolute.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark every quantifier/modality term and compare it to the passage; flag any shift like may→often, some→all, discipline→specific act.
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension items that paraphrase rules, attitudes, legal allowances, or parenting/behavior claims.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for inference beyond wording or when the passage itself gives explicit frequency, universality, or named methods.

Transfer rule: If asked which option does not support a harm-based conclusion, then separate choices that directly increase harm from those that describe unrelated or potentially offsetting benefits.
Error pattern: Strengthen/weaken support questions are solved by matching each option’s causal direction to the conclusion, not by picking any true statement about the topic.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “If this were added, would belief in the conclusion become stronger, weaker, or unchanged?” Eliminate any choice that strengthens.
Use when: The argument predicts reduced survival, ability, safety, or performance and options provide mixed causal facts about the same environment.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for the strongest support only, or when an indirect ecological chain clearly links the fact to the conclusion.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a unique source from matching composition, then look for another source that would share the same signature.
Error pattern: I overvalued a timing detail and missed a stronger alternative-explanation attack on uniqueness.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could these observations arise from a different route, reservoir, or process linked to the cited source?” If yes, that weakens more.
Use when: Provenance questions rely on chemical, statistical, or fingerprint similarity to identify origin.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim already rules out shared-origin alternatives or when chronology directly determines possibility.

Transfer rule: If a passage opens with a policy goal and later criticizes a practice, then infer the main point is that the practice violates that stated goal.
Error pattern: I fixated on a supporting reason about one group’s capability instead of the author’s overall evaluative claim.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What is the thesis sentence?” Then separate background, reasons, and consequences from the central judgment.
Use when: Relevant in main-idea questions where the text names a reform, principle, or standard first and then argues a behavior undermines it.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific supporting reason, role of a detail, or a directly quoted subclaim.

Transfer rule: If a principle contrasts expected emotion only toward reality with actual emotion toward known fiction, then choose the case showing a real feeling despite awareness it is fictional.  
Error pattern: I matched mere false belief causing emotion instead of the paradoxical success case: emotion surviving acknowledged unreality.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does the person know the trigger is fictional, and do they still genuinely feel the target emotion?  
Use when: Relevant for analogy questions built around paradoxes, especially belief-versus-emotion and fiction-versus-reality distinctions.  
Boundary: Ignore when options concern simple factual error, doubtful testimony, or nonemotional judgments rather than felt responses.

Transfer rule: If an argument says better labeling would greatly improve prevention, then prefer evidence that current labels are being misunderstood in a way explicit labels would fix.
Error pattern: I chose data about who is harmed most, but the key issue was whether the proposed change would change parent behavior.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this option show a mechanism linking the new information format to fewer mistakes, rather than just describing injury frequency or hazard severity?
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions about warnings, instructions, disclosures, or labels intended to guide decisions.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument turns on product danger itself, legal feasibility, or enforcement rather than user interpretation of information.

Transfer rule: If a passage explains a chain of relations with metaphors and an example, then choose the option summarizing that causal hierarchy, not a definition or side claim.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the author’s main thesis across supporting images and anecdote instead of fixating on one sentence.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write a 6–12 word thesis using the passage’s linked concepts; eliminate choices that define terms, reverse dependence, or narrow scope.
Use when: Apply for rhetorical or abstract reading-comprehension items with metaphors, quotations, and a concluding evaluative sentence.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a detail, example function, vocabulary meaning, or the author’s attitude rather than the main idea.

Transfer rule: If a proposal depends on biometric identification, then prefer evidence that the trait is sufficiently unique and stable across people.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning matched the claim’s key mechanism instead of drifting to side issues like vendors, unrelated services, or generic comparisons.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the needed causal link in one sentence and verify the choice directly strengthens that link.
Use when: Apply this on strengthen questions about plans, products, or policies whose benefit relies on a specific technology working as intended.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for a weakness, assumption, or when the options concern costs, ethics, or implementation barriers rather than mechanism validity.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers one subgroup has no difficulty from an overall vacancy surplus, then test whether the surplus comes from jobs mismatched to that subgroup’s qualifications.  
Error pattern: Confusing aggregate market balance with subgroup outcomes; overlooking segmentation and fit between seekers and openings.  
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Are the excess vacancies in roles this subgroup can and will fill?” If not established, the conclusion is unsupported.  
Use when: A claim moves from broad labor statistics or averages to conclusions about a specific population’s prospects.  
Boundary: Ignore when evidence directly matches openings to the subgroup’s skills, preferences, and realistic access.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires government departments cooperating with non-governmental/non-profit groups or the public for public-interest management, then choose the option showing both sides jointly performing the task.
Error pattern: I matched on “public welfare/community service” but ignored the required cross-sector government-plus-society collaboration structure.
Diagnostic check: Underline actors and verify three elements: government involvement, non-government/public participation, and a shared management function—not merely one side acting alone or only internal coordination.
Use when: The stem gives a formal definition of a governance/management model and options vary by participating actors and organizational relationships.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept is about volunteerism, charity, or ordinary interdepartmental cooperation without an explicit government-society partnership requirement.

Transfer rule: If a passage mainly details how an animal gets, swallows, and chooses food, then classify it by feeding/predation behavior, not broad life traits.
Error pattern: Chose an overly general category instead of the dominant theme created by repeated actions around obtaining and consuming prey.
Diagnostic check: List the main sentence topics; if most are about prey capture, prey types, swallowing, fasting, overeating, or cannibalism, select the feeding-behavior category.
Use when: The text is an animal profile with several concrete details about hunting method, diet, meal size, and responses to food scarcity.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage centers on habitat, reproduction, appearance, lifespan, or nonfeeding physiology.

Transfer rule: If a definition is criticized for lacking strictness, then test whether it overincludes cases that fit the wording but should be excluded.
Error pattern: I focused on vagueness or missing detail instead of checking the definition’s extension against clear counterexamples.
Diagnostic check: Invent one borderline case satisfying the stated definition; if experts would reject calling it that, prefer the choice exposing overbreadth.
Use when: The prompt asks about definitional rigor, strictness, precision, or which example best shows a definition is too broad.
Boundary: Ignore this when the flaw is instead ambiguity, missing procedures, unclear authority, or absent evaluation criteria.

Transfer rule: If a question fixes one variable, then convert every rule into direct implications/contrapositives from that fact and eliminate options against all rules.
Error pattern: Success came from chaining conditionals correctly and not treating one-way statements as biconditionals.
Diagnostic check: Write the forced truth values from the given assumption, then test each choice by substituting it into every rule, especially contrapositives and “unless/only if” rewrites.
Use when: Apply this to logic puzzles with several named entities, conditional statements, and a prompt that asks which scenario is consistent under an added assumption.
Boundary: Ignore when rules are probabilistic, causal, or defeasible rather than strict logical constraints.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a benefit from comparing group outcomes, then test whether the difference could instead be caused by the comparison group being harmed.
Error pattern: Mistook an unnecessary study-design detail about group coverage/exclusivity for the needed causal assumption blocking an alternative explanation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If the other group’s condition worsened outcomes, would the conclusion about this factor’s benefit collapse?” If yes, that possibility must be ruled out.
Use when: Relevant in causal claims drawn from contrasts between two groups, especially when one group lacks the target factor and has a different exposure.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is purely descriptive or the argument already experimentally eliminates reverse or alternative causal effects.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives a claim, then a limiting condition, then an analogy, identify the final causal takeaway as the main idea.
Error pattern: I selected an unsupported side implication instead of the author’s concluding explanation built from the whole passage.
Diagnostic check: Underline the thesis sentence and the last explanatory sentence; ask which option combines both without adding new relationships or narrower contexts.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea questions where evidence lists traits, then notes constraints, and ends by explaining a phenomenon.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, tone, or when the ending is merely an example, not the conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a case includes an initial impression but later judgment is revised by substantial new performance evidence, then do not classify it as anchoring.
Error pattern: Mistaking any first-impression scenario for anchoring, instead of requiring that the first information continues to dominate the final judgment.
Diagnostic check: Ask: after later contrary evidence appears, does the evaluator still stick near the initial view, or clearly update away from it?
Use when: The options describe sequences with early cues, later information, interviews, classes, pricing, branding, or other staged judgments.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when no time-order exists, no later evidence appears, or the concept tested is framing, signaling, halo effect, or contrast rather than persistence of the first cue.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims a side effect harms a population, then ask how often the affected subgroup is actually exposed to that side effect.
Error pattern: Strong evaluation focuses on impact frequency/size, not on background details or harms to irrelevant things.
Diagnostic check: Identify the causal chain, then test whether the key event rate linking the intervention to population-level harm is known.
Use when: The conclusion says a policy or protective action is itself dangerous because it harms a condition needed only in a specific circumstance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the missing issue is not exposure frequency but whether the causal link or comparison baseline is true.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts market replacement from material advantages, then test for omitted switching/adoption costs that could block the shift.
Error pattern: Success pattern: looked beyond product features to implementation barriers affecting whether builders can realistically change methods.
Diagnostic check: List the claimed advantages, then ask: what extra cost, retraining, equipment, code, or supply hurdle must users overcome to adopt the alternative?
Use when: Relevant in prediction, causal, or comparative arguments about one technology/material replacing another.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about inherent superiority, not about likely adoption or market share.

Transfer rule: If an argument says X is the root cause of Y because X accompanies Y, then test whether a prior factor causes both X and Y.
Error pattern: I favored an alternative additional cause over a stronger common-cause explanation that undercuts causal primacy.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map causes as X→Y, Z→Y, or Z→X and Z→Y; prefer the option that makes the claimed cause downstream rather than merely not unique.
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions about causal claims using words like root cause, therefore, leads to, accompanied by, or because.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is to strengthen, compare frequencies, or when the option only restates coexistence without a causal structure.

Transfer rule: If harm is imposed on an uninvolved third party’s lawful interests to avert an immediate danger protecting broader interests, then classify it as emergency avoidance.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking the harmed party’s role; this category requires third-party loss, not self-harm, fighting an aggressor, or accidental injury.
Diagnostic check: Mark three boxes: immediate danger exists; action is taken to prevent greater harm; the loss falls on someone other than the actor or wrongdoer.
Use when: Apply for scenarios mixing rescue, self-defense, accidents, and property-sacrifice choices where legal categories can be confused.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when no third party is harmed, the threat is not imminent, or the act mainly targets the source of danger.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion compares safety after removing a concentrated harmful part, then assume the remaining total harmful amount is no greater than the comparison case.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning matched the conclusion’s comparison to the exact missing quantity relation, instead of chasing side facts about size, other toxins, or severity.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, restate the claim as an inequality; ask, “What precise amount must be less than or equal to what other amount?”
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions involving concentration in one part, a treatment or removal step, and a comparative safety claim between two cases.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument turns on causation, definitions, or population frequency rather than a direct quantitative comparison.

Transfer rule: If an objection says a proposal removes a benefit, then check whether non-targeted alternatives could preserve that same benefit.
Error pattern: Confusing criticism of one means with criticism of the underlying function; treating a current method as uniquely necessary.
Diagnostic check: List the claimed function, then ask, “Could another material, process, or design deliver this function under the proposal?”
Use when: Relevant in arguments about bans, replacements, regulations, or policy changes where opponents cite lost benefits of the current approach.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already rules out substitutes with evidence, or when the issue is direct feasibility rather than interchangeable means.

Transfer rule: If a puzzle says exactly one of several statements is true, then test extreme world-states first and count truths under each.
Error pattern: I treated each option in isolation and never enforced the global “exactly one true” constraint across all speakers.
Diagnostic check: Build a truth-count table for the key cases—none, all, or mixed membership—and verify which case makes the speaker truth total equal one.
Use when: Apply this to logic questions with quantified claims like “some,” “none,” “all,” plus a specific individual claim.
Boundary: Ignore this when statements are probabilistic, vague, or not jointly about the same underlying classification.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires active public participation in policy formulation, implementation, evaluation, or supervision, then choose the case where ordinary stakeholders directly give input to policymakers on the policy itself.
Error pattern: Mistaking managed publicity, quota-based representation, or indirect channels for genuine broad public participation.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Who participates, at what policy stage, and do they directly express their interests to shape the policy rather than merely promote, relay, or formally represent?
Use when: The stem defines a governance concept by participation process, actor role, and policy stage.
Boundary: Ignore this when the target concept centers on formal office duties, advocacy campaigns, or implementation-only behavior rather than participatory policymaking.

Transfer rule: If an analogy says persuasion works by identifying existing desires, then choose the completion linking the target option to fulfilling those desires, not changing them.
Error pattern: Success pattern: preserving the source mechanism and mapping it directly to the new case.
Diagnostic check: State the source process in one sentence, map each role to the new scenario, and verify the choice keeps the same causal structure.
Use when: Relevant in analogy, parallel-reasoning, or sentence-completion items where one domain’s persuasion strategy is transferred to another.
Boundary: Ignore when choices depend on extra facts, moral evaluation, or when the analogy is explicitly challenged or limited.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion infers a new category from a juvenile specimen’s current size limits, then check whether normal development later changes the relevant anatomy.
Error pattern: Successful weakening targets a hidden assumption that present juvenile features must persist into adulthood.
Diagnostic check: Ask: could growth, tooth replacement, bone remodeling, or stage-specific structures create space or alter fit later without implying a different species?
Use when: Relevant in arguments from fossils, juveniles, incomplete remains, or any age-stage evidence used to classify species or types.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim already accounts for developmental change or when the classification is based on stable adult-defining traits.

Transfer rule: If a defamation question requires deliberate fabrication/spreading and serious harm, then select conduct that publicizes an unverified specific accusation as fact and causes grave consequences.
Error pattern: I overvalued mere suspicion or workplace accusation and underchecked whether the speaker invented/embellished facts and spread them broadly.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark yes/no for each option: specific factual claim, no reliable verification, repeated dissemination to others, reputational harm, seriousness threshold; choose only if all core boxes fit.
Use when: Apply this on criminal-law items distinguishing rumor-based reputational offenses from insults, opinions, superstition, private disputes, or cautious internal suspicion.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the offense definition does not require fabrication/rumor-spreading plus serious consequences, or when civil liability standards are being tested.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires a literary work grounded in firsthand factual experience and honesty, then choose the option describing a concrete literary creation built from direct investigation.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every defining element instead of latching onto only “real events” or “fieldwork.”
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the required traits and verify the candidate explicitly has all three: factual basis, firsthand/on-site inquiry, and resulting literary writing.
Use when: Relevant for “which fits the definition” questions where several options share surface keywords like history, truth, research, or writing.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target category is academic, theoretical, adapted, or only source-material-based rather than an actual literary nonfiction work.

Transfer rule: If two findings conflict because one variable tracks a hidden risk factor, then prefer the choice that identifies a confounder making the “healthier-looking” group die sooner for another reason.
Error pattern: I evaluated options for direct causal support instead of seeking a third-variable explanation that reconciles both results.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could one group differ in another life-span driver correlated with body size?” Eliminate choices that only restate harms or benefits of gain/loss.
Use when: A question asks to resolve apparently inconsistent study results about correlation, health, or longevity.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for strongest cause, mechanism, or intervention effect rather than reconciliation of two datasets.

Transfer rule: If asked to spot noun-to-verb usage, then test whether a noun is being used as an action meaning “treat/regard someone or something as that noun.”
Error pattern: I matched vivid wording instead of checking whether the key word shifts lexical category from noun to verb.
Diagnostic check: In each option, replace the candidate word with “regard as X” or “befriend/make into X”; if the sentence still works, it fits noun-derived verbal meaning.
Use when: Relevant in grammar or rhetoric questions about flexible word class usage, especially classical or literary phrasing.
Boundary: Ignore when the highlighted word is plainly adjectival, locational, or literal naming rather than expressing treatment, transformation, or role assignment.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a general rule plus an explicit exception, then choose the option that restates only what is directly asserted, with the exception preserved.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching literal entailment; failure usually comes from overgeneralizing the rule or ignoring stated carve-outs.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the passage as “eligible unless exception”; test each option for exact support and reject any that adds universality, new causes, or broader claims.
Use when: Apply this to legal, policy, or logic questions defining eligibility, rights, or duties with qualifying conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for implication beyond the text, evaluation, or outside legal knowledge.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims X causes congestion, then favor evidence showing congestion is driven by a broader background factor independent of X.  
Error pattern: I chose a cause-explaining detail instead of an alternative-cause fact that directly reduces the claimed causal impact.  
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option show the jam would be heavy even without the target behavior, or only explain why the behavior happens?”  
Use when: Causal weakening questions about traffic, pollution, delays, or crowding where several options discuss reasons, correlations, or context.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for a strengthen answer, a policy solution, or evidence about removing the behavior’s actual effect.

Transfer rule: If a role question includes an opponent’s proposal plus the author’s recommendation, then map each bold claim to whose view it describes and whether it supports an intermediate or final conclusion.
Error pattern: Mistaking a supporting sub-conclusion for the main conclusion by ignoring the argument’s final policy claim.
Diagnostic check: Identify the ultimate recommendation, then tag each bold statement as opponent-description, evidence, intermediate conclusion, or main conclusion; verify every “that/therefore/only through” link.
Use when: Arguments contrast rival policies, criticize one option’s effects, and then present a causal chain for the preferred option.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage is purely descriptive or lacks a clear recommendation or hierarchical support structure.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives examples only to support a broader normative claim, then choose the option stating that claim, not the descriptive background contrast.
Error pattern: I overfocused on repeated comparison details and missed the author’s main takeaway signaled by evaluative wording and summary sentences.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the thesis sentence and ask, “Do later examples justify this exact claim, or merely illustrate context?”
Use when: The passage contrasts two traditions, then uses examples to argue for a principle about how qualities should relate or be balanced.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for a specific fact, comparison detail, or directly stated descriptive distinction.

Transfer rule: If a claim says “better to accept criticism for doing X than for not doing X,” then compare the criticism attached to both actions and choose evidence showing the alternative is criticized more.
Error pattern: I picked a generally pro-openness statement instead of evidence that directly reverses the speaker’s cost-benefit comparison.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the argument as “X is preferable because criticism of X is less bad than criticism of not-X”; then test whether the option compares those two criticism levels.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken or refute questions featuring “better than,” tradeoffs, or criticism/risk comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore when options instead hinge on legality, definitions, causes, or broad benefits unrelated to the compared costs.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a brand’s demand depends on aspirational status created by advertising, then prefer the choice linking ad audience changes to loss of that status among future buyers.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing the hidden causal chain from advertising exposure to social prestige to purchase behavior, rather than focusing on cost or irrelevant readership claims.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map premise → mechanism → conclusion; ask, “Who must see the ads for the stated motive to keep working?”
Use when: Apply on strengthen/weaken/completion questions involving luxury, signaling, prestige, aspiration, or indirect effects of marketing.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument turns on direct product information, price sensitivity, or audience overlap without any status-driven motive.

Transfer rule: If premises say an action is wasteful and avoiding waste is required, then infer that action cannot be part of any no-waste plan.
Error pattern: I chose a stronger comparative claim not supported by the text, instead of a necessary-condition inference directly licensed by the premises.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each choice as absolute, comparative, or necessary; reject any choice introducing “most effective,” “entirely,” or new causal reach absent from the stimulus.
Use when: Apply on inference questions with normative claims, stated harms, and links from one practice to increased or decreased waste.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus provides rankings, sufficiency for total elimination, or explicit exceptions that justify stronger claims.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers causation from a before/after drop following a policy change, then test for exposure changes that could independently reduce the outcome.
Error pattern: Mistaking a side-rate detail for a true alternative cause; overlooking denominator/confounding variables that change how often the risk situation occurs.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Did the number of opportunities for the event change across periods?” If yes, prefer that evidence over facts merely about severity mix or enforcement constancy.
Use when: Temporal causal claims compare counts before and after an intervention, especially for accidents, crime, disease, or usage-dependent events.
Boundary: Ignore when rates are already normalized for exposure or the argument explicitly rules out major background changes.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers reality from sincere eyewitness reports, then test whether the reports are independently corroborated rather than whether an alternative cause was documented.
Error pattern: I treated missing explanatory evidence as strong disproof, instead of attacking the reliability of the premise actually carrying the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “What must be true for these reports to justify action?” Then look for facts about witness conditions, corroboration, repeatability, or misperception.
Use when: A claim relies mainly on anecdotal sightings, testimony, or observations and explicitly dismisses lying as the only credibility issue.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument hinges on physical evidence, statistical trends, or causation mechanisms rather than witness reliability.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “X and Y share property A” to “therefore X and Y also share property B,” then classify it as analogy by shared attribute.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting structure over surface wording in an advertisement’s persuasive leap.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the core claim as “because both are ___, what helps one will help the other”; if that fits, test for an analogical inference.
Use when: The stimulus compares two categories or organs and uses one accepted effect to recommend a product, action, or belief about the other.
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument gives direct evidence, defines terms, or reports measured results instead of transferring a property across similar things.

Transfer rule: If a claim is one-way (“steady growth implies broad price rises”), then use contrapositive for valid inference, not converse or stronger causal additions.
Error pattern: Mistaking a sufficient-condition statement for permission to infer reverse direction or extra thresholds not stated.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as If G then P; test choices by asking whether they equal “not P, therefore not G” rather than “P, therefore G” or new claims.
Use when: Relevant for conditional-reasoning questions with words like if, as long as, inevitably, only if, unless.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage gives biconditional evidence, explicit reverse causation, or independent premises supporting added effects.

Transfer rule: If several statements quantify the same group, then rewrite each as a logical form and compare negations/implications before testing answer choices.
Error pattern: I treated related statements independently and did not enforce global consistency among universal, existential, and negated-universal claims.
