Error pattern: Success came from separating decision quality and definitional fit from outcome, and checking each required element rather than being swayed by benefits or losses.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the core elements—state organ/staff, public administrative problem, according-to-law decision, sufficient information, systematic demonstration—and verify each explicitly.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about official acts, especially when options differ by actor, procedure, purpose, or implementation outcome.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for best policy, legality alone, effectiveness, or causal success instead of definitional classification.

Transfer rule: If a falling bad outcome is said not to prove better underlying health, then prefer an explanation showing improved survival after birth rather than healthier births.
Error pattern: Chose a scope/aggregation criticism instead of a causal mechanism that disconnects the trend from the claimed average condition.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this option explain lower mortality while leaving newborn baseline health unchanged?” Reject choices that only note uneven data or unrelated harms.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions about statistics, trends, or indicators being challenged as measures of an underlying trait.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for the best measure itself, or when an option directly addresses birth health rather than post-birth intervention.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires both breadth and depth, then verify independent evidence for each dimension before judging membership.
Error pattern: I treated multidisciplinary labels as sufficient breadth and overlooked that some profiles show depth concentrated in one integrated field only.
Diagnostic check: Mark one item for broad, cross-domain general knowledge/experience and a separate item for deep, distinctive expertise; if either mark is weak or merged, reject it.
Use when: Applying category definitions built from two structural components, especially “broad plus deep” talent or profile classifications.
Boundary: Ignore this when the category can be satisfied by excellence in a single specialty or when breadth/depth are explicitly redefined as overlapping.

Transfer rule: If an argument gives a universal “no reason for anyone” policy claim, then check whether earlier evidence still supports the action for some subgroup.
Error pattern: Overgeneralizing from limits of one causal factor to dismiss all benefit from an intervention despite acknowledged partial benefit elsewhere.
Diagnostic check: List each stated causal route and mark whether the proposed action affects it; if at least one route remains affected, reject any blanket dismissal.
Use when: Conclusions move from “this does not affect one cause” to “therefore nobody should do it” in causal or health-policy arguments.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument actually rules out every relevant pathway or explicitly restricts its conclusion to unaffected cases.

Transfer rule: If a law’s purpose is broad but its wording explicitly excludes a setting, then reject claims that protection extends to workers whose workplace is that excluded setting.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from a workplace-only law to all nonworkplace exposure, instead of testing how legal scope affects special cases.
Diagnostic check: List the law’s covered locations and excluded locations; then map each claimant group to where they work or are exposed.
Use when: Relevant for legal-scope questions involving stated purpose, statutory wording, and groups whose cases blur ordinary category boundaries.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about beliefs, motives, or likely effects not determined by the law’s literal coverage.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion asserts existence of overlap between a derived group and a trait, then add an assumption linking the source majority group to that trait strongly enough to force at least one overlap.
Error pattern: Chose a tempting converse/restatement instead of the missing bridge that guarantees existence.
Diagnostic check: Translate statements into set relations; ask “What group already feeds into the conclusion’s subject, and what extra premise ensures at least one member also has the conclusion’s predicate?”
Use when: Arguments mix all/most/not all claims and conclude “some” about a downstream category.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is universal, causal, or already supported without needing an existence bridge.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from lower per-person likelihood to fewer businesses, then test whether total population growth could keep or raise total demand.
Error pattern: Mistaking a trend in averages or proportions for a trend in absolute counts; ignoring base-rate and scale effects.
Diagnostic check: Ask: even if each person is less likely to buy, could more people overall still produce the same or greater number of customers?
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions linking demographic change, percentages, or per-capita behavior to market size, totals, or business counts.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is explicitly about rates/proportions only, or when total population is fixed or otherwise accounted for.

Transfer rule: If a condition is stated as necessary via “must A or B,” then do not infer “not B” from knowing the person has the outcome and has A.
Error pattern: Mistaking an inclusive necessary disjunction for an exclusive either/or; denying one route just because another route is present.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as outcome → (A ∨ B); then ask, “Could both A and B be true?” If yes, any conclusion of not-A or not-B is unsupported.
Use when: Arguments use requirements, prerequisites, or “in order to” language with an “or,” then conclude one option is absent.
Boundary: Ignore when the statement explicitly says exactly one option holds, excludes overlap, or gives additional facts ruling one out.

Transfer rule: If an argument cites safety for one organ or dimension, then check whether the conclusion broadens to overall health or all harms.
Error pattern: Scope shift from a limited premise to a broader conclusion; I accepted side-correlation instead of matching the exact expansion.
Diagnostic check: Underline the premise’s target and the conclusion’s target; if the conclusion covers more body systems, outcomes, or populations, flag a flaw.
Use when: Relevant in flaw questions where evidence is about one specific effect, but the claim says “safe,” “healthy,” or “nothing to worry about” more generally.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is explicitly limited to the same effect, organ, and population as the supporting evidence.

Transfer rule: If an argument explains a trend as entirely due to one belief or factor, then test whether it unjustifiably rules out other plausible causes.
Error pattern: Overexclusive causal reasoning—treating one supported cause as the only cause without evidence eliminating alternatives.
Diagnostic check: Highlight absolute terms like “entirely,” “only,” or “must”; ask, “What other independent causes could produce the same outcome, and were they addressed?”
Use when: A stimulus links attitudes or beliefs to behavior and then makes a total causal claim about a social pattern.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument actually compares alternatives, provides evidence excluding rivals, or makes only a partial-cause claim.

Transfer rule: If a definition excludes profit-making as the primary purpose, then eliminate any option centered on earning fees or commercial compensation.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every option against the definition’s core criterion instead of being distracted by social or collective-sounding labels.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: What is its primary purpose, who benefits, and does money earned function as the central goal?
Use when: Apply this on definition-based multiple-choice items contrasting public-interest groups, service bodies, associations, and paid representative or commercial activities.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition allows revenue-seeking entities or asks about legality, effectiveness, or morality rather than category membership.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers audience indifference from a single case, then prefer evidence showing similar cases did affect audience judgments.
Error pattern: Chose relevance to plot exposure instead of directly testing the claim about viewers’ reactions and broader authenticity assessments.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Which option gives observed audience or critic response to a comparable mistake, rather than production context or narrative importance?”
Use when: The conclusion is about what mistakes do or do not affect for audiences, critics, or evaluators of authenticity, quality, or credibility.
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument hinges on causation, timeline, definitions, or internal mechanics rather than audience response generalization.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts old exclusivity with people entering homes, sharing, and common ownership, then choose the option centered on public accessibility, not just the delivery medium.
Error pattern: I overfocused on a vivid tool/example and missed the broader theme that multiple examples supported.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Is this option the umbrella idea tying all examples together, or only one mechanism mentioned?” Reject options covering only a single channel.
Use when: The text lists several methods, platforms, or reforms and asks for the main meaning, opening, or essence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly asks for a specific method, platform, or directly named mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a concept stresses generating alternative approaches or reframing the path to a goal, then choose the option that changes strategy or means, not one that narrows to a diagnosis or follows a preset plan.
Error pattern: Mistaking broad consideration within standard convergent evaluation for genuine divergence; confusing differential diagnosis or orderly planning with creative reframing.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it produce multiple possible routes or a novel route by redefining how to achieve the same end, rather than selecting among established explanations?
Use when: Definitions contrast creative, multi-angle, many-answer thinking with deduction, diagnosis, classification, or planned execution.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for formal logic, evidence-based elimination, or routine expert assessment instead of thinking style.

Transfer rule: If a concept says the overall outcome is limited by the weakest part, then choose the case where one poor element harms the larger whole.
Error pattern: I matched surface wording literally and ignored the relational structure between an individual component and a collective result.
Diagnostic check: Ask: what is the “container,” what are its “boards,” and does one weakest board determine the whole system’s performance or reputation?
Use when: Relevant for analogy, management, reputation, team, system-capacity, or chain-effect questions about partial strengths and one decisive weakness.
Boundary: Ignore when the example is only about personal reward, legal liability, or standout strength without affecting the whole.

Transfer rule: If two conditionals share the same trigger’s alternatives, then rewrite them symbolically and test contrapositives or linked implications for any statement that must follow.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping messy prose into conditional logic instead of relying on topic-based plausibility.
Diagnostic check: Define variables for each outcome, write both “if” statements, derive valid contrapositives, and accept only choices matching a direct implication chain.
Use when: A stimulus gives multiple conditional claims about strategic choices, consequences, threats, or temporary suspensions and asks what must be true.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the argument depends on causation, intentions, probabilities, or outside facts rather than formal conditional structure.

Transfer rule: If a verbal-logic item mixes subset and implication facts, then translate each statement into set links and test each option for contradiction versus mere possibility.
Error pattern: Success came from checking compatibility by chaining constraints instead of guessing from everyday associations or location wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each category pair as “must,” “cannot,” or “unknown,” then verify whether an option asserts a forbidden overlap or only an unproven one.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice statements about properties, places, and housing types connected by qualifiers like all, some, only, and not.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on arithmetic, definitions outside the prompt, or probabilistic/common-sense assumptions rather than formal relations.

Transfer rule: If a passage says the “key lies in people” for achieving goals, then choose the theme emphasizing human agency in practice, not broad claims about controlling nature or history.
Error pattern: Overgeneralized from a practical leadership point to a sweeping philosophical thesis.
Diagnostic check: Replace the author’s wording with each option; reject any option that adds stronger scope, metaphysics, or domains not explicitly mentioned.
Use when: The question asks for the main idea of a short abstract passage contrasting outcomes with the role of people.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly argues a grand historical law or compares humans with nature.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts similar cultures with different outcomes and different cultures with similar outcomes, then reject culture as the main cause and choose the claim attacking cultural explanation.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the author’s target claim and using cross-case comparison to identify which explanation is being undermined.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the compared groups and ask: do the examples vary independently of culture but align with another factor named by the author?
Use when: Apply to main-point or meaning questions built on examples, contrasts, and causal explanations in social or historical arguments.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage supports multiple causes equally or asks for a detail rather than the author’s central conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a logic puzzle says exactly one statement is true, then test each candidate answer against every statement and count truths explicitly.
Error pattern: I relied on partial elimination after misparsing the premises instead of doing a complete consistency table.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each claim as a set of allowed/excluded winners; for each option, mark each claim true/false and verify the total is exactly one true.
Use when: Statements overlap by inclusion/exclusion, involve finalists/champions, or there is a fixed truth-count condition like “only one”.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is probabilistic, ambiguous in wording, or asks for best explanation rather than strict logical consistency.

Transfer rule: If two explanations pit age against time-in-field, then prefer evidence that separates those variables by holding one atypical while observing the outcome.
Error pattern: Success came from targeting a discriminating fact, not a merely relevant background factor or another possible cause.
Diagnostic check: Ask of each choice, “If this were yes or no, would it shift support differently between the two explanations?” Reject choices that affect both similarly.
Use when: Relevant for weaken/strengthen or useful-to-investigate questions with competing causal explanations built from correlated variables.
Boundary: Ignore when an option directly measures the claimed outcome itself, or when the hypotheses are not competing causal accounts.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires honesty plus keeping promises, then prefer actions allowed by the contract’s reciprocity rules over any involving concealment, collusion, or secret disclosure.
Error pattern: I overfocused on one surface phrase and ignored the full definition, especially the reciprocity/performance condition that can justify nonperformance.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, mark H (deception?), C (collusion/confidentiality breach?), and R (response to the other side’s breach permitted by reciprocity?); pick the only option with no violation marks.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions about good faith, contract performance, mutual obligations, exceptions, or justified refusal after breach.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the rule is strict liability, morality-only, or does not include reciprocal obligations or defenses.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims a new survey method will better reflect overall opinion, then test whether the new method could itself create participation bias between opposing groups.
Error pattern: I focused on whether respondents are qualified to judge, instead of whether the sample remains representative under the new collection process.
Diagnostic check: Compare who is more likely to respond under old versus new methods; if one sentiment group may be newly overrepresented, the conclusion is unsupported.
Use when: Relevant in arguments about polling, evaluations, feedback systems, or any change in access, timing, or submission method.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is about response quality or competence rather than representativeness of opinions.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires coordinated improvement on major corridors via infrastructure, public service, or transit management, then choose the option that directly changes corridor travel conditions for all travelers.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every definitional element and rejecting choices that are only enforcement, financing, or isolated regulation changes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the required components and verify the option affects a main corridor, uses one listed intervention type, and plausibly improves speed, reliability, or safety.
Use when: Apply this on concept-definition multiple choice with several necessary conditions and transportation-policy examples.
Boundary: Ignore this when the definition allows partial matches, targets a single user group only, or asks for exceptions rather than instances.

Transfer rule: If a behavior is followed by an added aversive consequence that makes that behavior less likely later, then classify it as positive punishment.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating “adding something unpleasant” from “removing something pleasant” and from mere warning, correlation, or reward.
Diagnostic check: Ask three questions: Did the behavior happen first? Was a new unpleasant consequence imposed afterward? Did the behavior decrease afterward?
Use when: Apply this on behavior-learning questions contrasting reinforcement vs punishment or positive vs negative consequences.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the case only states prohibition, natural coincidence, preference, or lacks evidence that consequences changed future behavior.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a policy goal is desirable but one approach is infeasible while the target has mixed effects, then infer a workable alternative policy, not merely criticize the infeasible one.
Error pattern: I stopped at rejecting one option instead of combining all premises to select the most supported comparative policy conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each premise’s role; ask which choice uses feasibility plus mixed-benefit/harm facts together and goes beyond a weaker restatement.
Use when: Relevant in conclusion questions about public policy, especially when premises discuss impracticality, demand, benefits, and harms.
Boundary: Ignore when choices are only descriptive, when no alternative policy is mentioned or implied, or when feasibility evidence is absent.

Transfer rule: If a plan reallocates a helpful resource from one group to another, then require that taking it away will not undo the gain elsewhere.
Error pattern: Strong assumption reasoning succeeds by checking for harmful side effects in the source group, not by chasing comparisons, counts, or outside examples.
Diagnostic check: Remove the chosen assumption and ask whether the proposal could still fail because the donor group becomes worse enough to offset benefits.
Use when: A policy shifts resources between subgroups and cites evidence only about benefits where resources are added.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is about creating new resources, or already gives evidence that losses in donor groups are negligible.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends by saying a goal requires “a lot of hard and meticulous work,” then predict the next part will explain implementation or organization, not restate earlier background.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking discourse movement from problem description to proposed action.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as setup, difficulty, or transition; if the last sentence signals necessity of work, choose the option describing how that work is carried out.
Use when: This applies to continuation questions where several options merely echo earlier points but one advances from challenges to response.
Boundary: Ignore this when the final sentence introduces a new specific topic, contrast, example, or quantitative detail.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires prioritizing positive value while accepting manageable negatives, then choose the option showing calm pursuit of the good despite adversity.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the full structure of the definition, not just picking any upbeat or hopeful wording.
Diagnostic check: Underline three elements—positive focus, explicit tolerance of negative effects, and behavior guided by maximizing the positive; reject choices missing any one.
Use when: Apply to concept-definition questions about attitudes, traits, or decision criteria embedded in poetic, figurative, or emotional language.
Boundary: Ignore this when options differ mainly by factual content, chronology, or when the definition does not involve tradeoffs with harm or risk.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus shows a deeply held view staying fixed after contrary testimony, then choose the principle about distrusting the source rather than revising the belief.
Error pattern: Successful abstraction from a specific vignette to a general belief-preservation principle under source conflict.
Diagnostic check: Identify the prior commitment, the conflicting message, and what changed; if only the speaker’s credibility drops while the original belief stays, match that pattern.
Use when: Relevant in principle-strengthen/match questions featuring testimony, authority, endorsement, or criticism against an entrenched opinion.
Boundary: Ignore when the person actually updates the original belief, or when the answer choices add normative advice, scope limits, or domain-specific requirements absent from the stimulus.

Transfer rule: If an argument says adding an omitted category makes an alleged deficit less credible, then infer the omitted category favors the side claimed to be disadvantaged.
Error pattern: I reversed direction, treating a weakening factor as if it intensified the original imbalance.
Diagnostic check: Ask: after including the missing component, would the net balance move toward zero or away from zero; choose only an assumption that moves it toward zero.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions about balances, totals, omissions, or claims that fuller accounting undermines an apparent gap.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion does not depend on adding the omitted category changing the direction or size of a measured difference.

Transfer rule: If a passage opens by contrasting a minor dispute with a larger enduring contribution, then choose the option naming that dominant contribution, not one listed effect.
Error pattern: I focused on vivid downstream reactions of readers/viewers instead of the passage’s central evaluative claim about the work itself.
Diagnostic check: Mark the thesis sentence, then separate core claim from examples/results; if several emotions or identities are presented after the main assertion, treat them as support.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea questions where the text lists impacts, feelings, or social functions after an initial judgment.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific effect, audience response, or supporting detail rather than overall emphasis.

Transfer rule: If evidence links a condition to an abnormality dated earlier than birth in some cases, then infer only that a possible prenatal cause exists.
Error pattern: Strong reasoning succeeds by making the weakest warranted claim and avoiding reversals, quantifier shifts, or genetic/causal overreach.
Diagnostic check: List the exact supports, mark whether each is correlation or timing evidence, and choose the option that adds no stronger certainty than that list allows.
Use when: Apply this on “most strongly supported” questions with group comparisons, percentages, and developmental timing facts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stimulus gives experimental causation, explicit necessity/sufficiency, or asks for explanation rather than supported inference.

Transfer rule: If a defective product causes personal injury or direct damage to other property, then treat product-liability compensation as available; if loss is only the product itself or indirect economic loss, then do not.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every required element of the legal definition instead of reacting to any quality problem.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark four boxes: defect, safety hazard, victim beyond the product itself, and direct bodily/other-property damage; choose only options checking all four.
Use when: Apply on legal-definition multiple choice about defective products, tort liability, and who may claim damages.
Boundary: Ignore when the rule covers contract remedies, warranties, labeling-only disputes, normal aging/misuse, or purely consequential business loss.

Transfer rule: If a term is defined by several alternative signs, then test each option against the exact definition and pick the one lacking any listed feature.
Error pattern: Success came from strict definition-matching instead of being distracted by related but non-definitional symptoms or lifestyle details.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark whether it shows disorderly eating, preference for stimulating intake, or abdominal discomfort after excess intake; choose the only option with no match.
Use when: Apply this on definition-based multiple-choice questions with examples containing extra narrative, causes, or consequences mixed with core criteria.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for causes, treatments, severity, or when common-sense associations matter more than a formal definition.

Transfer rule: If a statement says an outcome cannot occur without a condition, then infer the condition is necessary for that outcome.
Error pattern: Success came from translating necessity language correctly and resisting unsupported reversals or extra causal claims.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each key sentence as if outcome, then required condition; accept only choices matching that direction exactly.
Use when: Apply on inference questions with cues like “no…without,” “only by,” “only if,” or “must rely on.”
Boundary: Ignore when the passage gives definitions, probabilities, or sufficient-condition claims not framed as necessity.

Transfer rule: If a puzzle says exactly two statements are false, then truth-table each speaker and eliminate any case with not-exactly-two mismatches before choosing.
Error pattern: I jumped from a tempting local implication to a global conclusion without enforcing the fixed false-statement count across all claims.
Diagnostic check: List each statement as T/F under a candidate scenario; count falsities, and verify every conditional with its antecedent status, not just its consequent.
Use when: Apply this to multi-speaker logic problems mixing conditionals, direct claims, and an exact number of incorrect statements.
Boundary: Ignore this for single-fact questions or when the number of false statements is unspecified or irrelevant.

Transfer rule: If an argument treats “not shown false” as support for truth, then flag a proof-from-ignorance flaw.
Error pattern: Confusing lack of disconfirming evidence with positive justification for a claim.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the support as “No one proved not-X; therefore X” and ask whether X could still be false.
Use when: The reasoning relies on absence of proof, failed refutation, or missing evidence against a claim.
Boundary: Ignore when the setting legitimately shifts burden of proof or when exhaustive checking would guarantee the claim.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts more deficiency from reduced synthesis/absorption, then look for a compensating increase in intake or an alternative source that breaks the net-shortage claim.
Error pattern: Strong weakening often comes from offsetting the alleged causal loss, not from evidence that repeats, treats, or merely correlates with the outcome.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this choice increase the missing nutrient/factor or provide another route, enough to undercut the predicted deficiency?” If not, reject it.
Use when: Relevant for causal arguments about health risks built from reduced exposure, reduced production, or one impaired step in a biological chain.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about one mechanism itself, or when no compensating source could affect the stated outcome.

Transfer rule: If asked for the EXCEPT choice in a discrepancy question, then eliminate options that could make both facts true and choose the one that fails to explain or worsens the mismatch.
Error pattern: Mistaking a factor that can reduce actual intake or nutrient absorption for a non-explanation; overlooking whether demand differs from effective consumption.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Assuming this is true, can the trend and the deficiency rise both occur together?” Reject any option that clearly can.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen-weaken paradox items involving demand, sales, popularity, availability, preparation, or subgroup distribution.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is to find the best explanation rather than the exception, or when options are not causal.

Transfer rule: If asked for the exception to evidence for a hypothesis, then test whether each choice bears on the claimed mechanism, not just whether it is geologically interesting.
Error pattern: I accepted a fact that seemed surprising as irrelevant, instead of checking whether it actually supports movement/rearrangement over time.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “If true, would this specifically strengthen past connection, matching structures, shared life, or climate-position change?” Reject the one that does not.
Use when: Relevant in “which does not support” questions about scientific theories with multiple evidence types and one out-of-scope statement.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for direct truth, chronology, or definitions rather than evidential relevance to a hypothesis.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts current harmful trends with what buildings should connect to, then choose the option stating that positive guiding principle.
Error pattern: Overweighting the final negative consequence instead of the author’s central normative claim.
Diagnostic check: Mark “problem,” “cause,” and “should”; if one choice captures the “should” and others restate harms, pick the “should.”
Use when: Main-idea questions in argumentative paragraphs that criticize fashion-driven change and discuss preserving historical or cultural context.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a result, specific effect, or implied consequence rather than the paragraph’s intended emphasis.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts science with superstition and explains why superstition misleads, then choose the conclusion that follows the stated remedy or purpose, not an extreme side claim.
Error pattern: Strength in causal-summary reasoning; success came from tracking the author’s main claim instead of attractive but unsupported examples or exaggerations.
Diagnostic check: Underline premise verbs about purpose, cause, and effect; ask, “Which option restates the central takeaway using only supported scope and strength?”
Use when: Relevant for argument-completion or inference questions defining concepts, contrasting them, and implying how to address a harmful belief.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for a specific example, data-based detail, or an exception rather than the passage’s overall conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts many examples with one dominant use or quantity, then choose the option matching the stated main emphasis, not a narrower location claim.
Error pattern: Overweighted a memorable statistic and turned it into exclusivity or concentration without textual support.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark whether every key modifier is supported by the text; reject any answer adding “mainly,” “pillar,” “almost all,” or regional scope not directly stated.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension items summarizing descriptive passages with lists, quantities, and regional examples.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for an inference beyond the text or when the passage explicitly states exclusivity or priority.

Transfer rule: If a weakening question claims a policy harms X, then test whether stopping the problem would indirectly help X enough to undercut the claimed harm.
Error pattern: Success came from looking for a net-effect consideration on the same endangered group, not just facts about feasibility or past effectiveness.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does any option show the threatened group is already being harmed by the status quo the policy targets?”
Use when: Relevant in policy arguments balancing one population’s interests against another’s, especially with ecological or causal tradeoffs.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is only about immediate direct risk, legality, or implementation rather than overall comparative impact.

Transfer rule: If an argument says all X are A-or-B and all B are also A, then infer all X are A; match that inclusion pattern.
Error pattern: I chased subject-matter similarity and missed the exact quantifier/conditional structure of a valid subsumption chain.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite in symbols: X→(A∨B), B→A; test whether this yields X→A, and pick the option with the same form.
Use when: Relevant for analogy questions featuring categories, either/or predicates, and a second premise making one branch a subset of the other.
Boundary: Ignore when choices hinge on “most/some,” on negation/contraposition, or on affirming a property to conclude category membership.

Transfer rule: If a statement is conditional, then also test its contrapositive by reversing and negating both sides before choosing.
Error pattern: Missed a valid contrapositive and instead preferred an unsupported weak real-world claim.
Diagnostic check: For each “if P, then Q,” write “if not Q, then not P,” and verify the choice matches a premise or a chained result.
Use when: Relevant in logic questions built from one-way implications, especially when options paraphrase reversals, contrapositives, or chained conditionals.
Boundary: Ignore when the stem gives probabilistic, causal, or defeasible claims rather than strict conditionals.

Transfer rule: If funds were publicly solicited for a stated specific purpose, then any leftover or unusable portion requires following donors’ expressed wishes before redirection.
Error pattern: I favored a broad trust-in-directors principle instead of matching the argument’s need for a narrow rule that justifies permission while minimizing extra limits.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: does this principle both support the claimed need for donor permission and avoid banning ordinary reallocations outside specifically solicited-purpose cases?
Use when: An argument hinges on a principle question about earmarked donations, surplus funds, and the least restrictive justification.
Boundary: Ignore when money was not purpose-specific, donors already granted discretion, or the issue is legal authority rather than principle fit.

Transfer rule: If a statement raises a factual difference between cases and immediately explains why it does not matter, then treat it as acknowledging and defusing a possible objection, not as core support.
Error pattern: Mistaking a concession/rebuttal move for a premise that directly advances the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If I remove this sentence, does the conclusion lose support, or does the argument merely lose its reply to a challenge?”
Use when: The stimulus compares cases and includes “it is true,” “however,” “but,” or similar wording before dismissing a difference.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the statement is actually the rule, evidence, or causal basis the conclusion depends on.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a specific motive from slowed behavior under social pressure, then test whether a general performance-impairment effect could explain the slowdown instead.
Error pattern: Mistook an irrelevant comparison for a weakener and missed a broader alternative cause that explains the observed pattern without the claimed motive.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does any choice provide a generic mechanism that would produce the same timing differences even if the proposed mental state were absent?”
Use when: Relevant for causal/explanatory questions that interpret behavior as evidence of emotion, ownership, or intention from response-time changes.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only discuss other contexts, unrelated tasks, or frequency/representativeness rather than the measured behavior itself.

Transfer rule: If a recommendation ranks sites by an outcome rate, then test whether differences in case mix or selection effects make that rate noncomparable across sites.
Error pattern: I chased a tempting side effect about costs and patient redistribution instead of challenging whether the cited metric validly measures harm.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Could this site’s worse rate result from treating systematically riskier cases?” If yes, the rate alone is weak evidence.
Use when: The argument chooses, rewards, or blames a provider, school, team, or policy based on raw performance statistics.
Boundary: Ignore when the choices are shown to handle comparable populations or the metric is already risk-adjusted.

Transfer rule: If a passage moves from broad background to a final specific claim, then choose the option matching that last narrowed claim.
Error pattern: Success came from following the argument’s narrowing structure instead of stopping at an earlier, more general statement.
Diagnostic check: Mark each clause as background, intermediate support, or endpoint; answer with the claim that the earlier clauses are used to justify.
Use when: Apply this to main-focus questions where the text starts broadly, then shifts to one domain and ends with an era-, group-, or outcome-level statement.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, purpose, or when the final sentence is only an example rather than the thesis.

Transfer rule: If a price-gap question asks about the same commodity, then choose only an example where one good differs solely by circulation, region, season, or quality.
Error pattern: I matched any price comparison instead of verifying the “same commodity under allowed causes” requirement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: same product? same use category? price difference caused by link/area/season/quality rather than different goods, brands, or intrinsic value?
Use when: Relevant in concept-definition multiple-choice items about economic price differences, especially when distractors compare different products or editions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is about value differences, product substitution, branding effects, or asks for any price comparison broadly.

Transfer rule: If both treatment and control improve equally at first and then worsen together, then look for a shared situational cause, not the treatment itself.
Error pattern: Mistook a group-wide parallel pattern for a placebo or belief effect instead of identifying a common environmental explanation.
Diagnostic check: List what differs between groups and what is identical; if the timing and rates match across groups, test whether a common condition explains both phases.
Use when: Comparative studies show similar outcomes in all arms, especially with changes tied to study setting or time in the setting.
Boundary: Ignore when groups diverge meaningfully, or when evidence directly links beliefs or the intervention to different outcomes.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers more people are receiving a penalty from a rising population stock, then test whether longer duration of that penalty could explain the rise instead.
Error pattern: Mistook a downstream flow factor for a stock-versus-duration issue; failed to separate entries into a population from time spent in it.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: could the total grow even with unchanged intake because occupants remain longer? Look for sentence-length, release, or minimum-term changes.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/weaken questions involving prison, hospital, unemployment, backlog, or any accumulated population measured over years.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim already controls for duration/release rates or concerns only new admissions rather than total population.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires equal-authority units deciding a shared issue through consultation, then choose the option showing peer departments jointly deliberating and reaching a resolution.
Error pattern: I focused on consultation/approval language but missed the equal-status, cross-unit, common-problem requirement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark three boxes—peer entities, shared issue, joint consultative resolution; reject any option missing one box.
Use when: Relevant for organizational-decision definition questions involving approval, meetings, signing, consultation, or multiple departments.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept allows hierarchical approval, unilateral sign-off, or decisions within a single chain of command.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion claims a specific causal benefit from a short-term treatment, then prefer evidence comparing that short-term treatment against a baseline on the same outcome.
Error pattern: I chose a broad plausibility statement instead of an option that directly strengthens the claimed cause-and-effect relationship.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this option mention the intervention duration, a comparison group, and the exact measured effect? If any are missing, reject it.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions about experiments, causal conclusions, and claims from animal studies or treatment timing.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for general background knowledge, definitions, policy advice, or the weakest/irrelevant option.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “cannot be politically significant” from “cannot produce a specific effect,” then test whether significance is being assumed to require that effect.
Error pattern: Conditional-gap check: the reasoning succeeds only if the conclusion’s broad status depends on the cited necessary condition.
Diagnostic check: Negate the suspected assumption; if something could still have the broad status despite lacking the effect, the argument collapses.
Use when: A conclusion classifies something as impossible, worthless, or insignificant because it lacks one pathway, mechanism, or outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion merely predicts reduced likelihood or gives one sufficient route rather than a required basis.

Transfer rule: If a statement combines “everyone who helped X was helped by Y” with “if anyone didn’t help X, then Z helped X,” then test each named person against both conditions.
Error pattern: Failed by treating one person’s nonparticipation as directly implying another specific non-help relation, instead of chaining the quantified rules.
Diagnostic check: List each named person, mark whether they helped the target, then derive who must have helped whom from each conditional before choosing an option.
Use when: Relevant in logic questions with universal/conditional statements about helping, exceptions, and a named person who helped nobody.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on probabilities, ordinary language plausibility, or missing links between individuals.

Transfer rule: If a passage says a formal institution disappeared but its influence or evolved customs remain, then choose the option preserving that distinction.
Error pattern: Strength in separating the survival of effects from the survival of the original system and rejecting unsupported causal extensions.
Diagnostic check: Mark each option as directly stated, inferred, or added; reject any option that upgrades “influence/customs remain” into “the whole institution remains.”
Use when: Relevant for reading questions contrasting past systems with present-day residues, continuities, or transformed practices.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage explicitly says the institution itself continues unchanged or asks for causes beyond stated text.

Transfer rule: If a case shows intrusive self-recognized thoughts causing repeated checking despite prior certainty and no practical need, then classify it as obsessive-compulsive.
Error pattern: Success came from matching all defining features, not just noticing repetition or anxiety alone.
Diagnostic check: Verify four points: intrusion is repetitive, content is unnecessary/redundant, the person knows it is their own and unreasonable, and resists but cannot stop.
Use when: Apply this to behavior-disorder classification items involving repeated acts, reassurance seeking, checking, or ritual-like actions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when repetition is practical, goal-directed, externally justified, delusional, or not experienced as unwanted.

Transfer rule: If a causal argument predicts a group-level rise from reduced exposure to a factor, then test whether affected and unaffected people actually differ on that exposure.
Error pattern: I overvalued a compensating possibility and ignored a stronger attack on the argument’s assumed correlation between cause and outcome.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does any option show the predicted-risk group has no lower exposure than others?” If yes, prefer it over mere mitigation.
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions built on a chain like condition → mechanism → disease/risk increase.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices directly break necessity/sufficiency definitions or provide stronger evidence about measurement, timing, or reversed causation.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires therapeutic improvement for disabled or recovering people, then reject choices showing only ordinary companionship without a treatment or rehabilitation function.
Error pattern: I matched an unusual mechanism instead of checking whether every required element of the definition was explicitly satisfied.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark subject status, animal-human contact, and stated therapeutic outcome; eliminate any option missing one required element.
Use when: This applies to definition-matching multiple-choice questions where several options sound beneficial but differ in whether they meet all criteria.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the best example, common usage, or implied benefit rather than strict definitional membership.

Transfer rule: If a passage defines a condition and lists high-risk occupations, then infer only effects that can plausibly explain behavior in those groups, not broad future trends or rankings.
Error pattern: Chose an amplified societal conclusion instead of the most directly supported occupation-specific implication.
Diagnostic check: For each option, trace a two-step support chain from the stated definition and group list; reject any choice needing extra assumptions like prediction, comparison, or prevalence growth.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions built from definitions, symptoms/effects, and examples or high-risk populations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly gives trend data, severity comparisons, or policy-level claims.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from a subject’s properties to the required method for studying it, then test whether it unjustifiably assumes the method must share those same properties.
Error pattern: Mistaking resemblance as necessity—projecting features of the object onto the reasoning process.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could a different kind of method still explain this subject well, even if it lacks the subject’s features?” If yes, the inference is weak.
Use when: The conclusion prescribes how to reason, investigate, or explain based mainly on what the target phenomenon is like.
Boundary: Ignore when independent evidence links method effectiveness to those features, rather than mere similarity.

Transfer rule: If someone voluntarily handles another person’s specific affair without a prior duty or authorization and aims to protect that person’s interests, then treat it as management without cause.
Error pattern: I confused ordinary care, rescue based on special duties, or contractual/property-management obligations with voluntary intervention.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: Who owns the affair, what legal/contractual/family duty exists, and did the actor intervene unasked mainly to preserve the other person’s interests?
Use when: This applies to civil-law scenarios about unsolicited help, emergency preservation, property repair, or temporary handling of another’s matters.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the actor has a statutory, contractual, employment, guardianship, or preexisting caregiving duty.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts broad reforms with one foundational condition, then choose the option naming that central condition, not side effects or methods.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the thesis sentence and treating later examples, consequences, and elaborations as support rather than the main claim.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write a 5-word summary of the first claim, then verify each paragraph part either defines it, supports it, or results from it.
Use when: Apply this on main-point questions with abstract policy arguments, especially when the text lists harms solved by one key institutional change.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for detail, inference, tone, or the author’s proposed process rather than the overall thesis.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts adoption after commercialization, then test the key economic feasibility condition that links technical promise to real-world uptake.
Error pattern: I focused on external enforcement instead of the hidden assumption that actors will adopt only if implementation is financially attractive.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What must be true for users to switch voluntarily?” Then check cost, payback, installation, and operating burden before considering secondary factors.
Use when: Relevant for claims that a new technology will change organizational behavior, incentives, or pollution outcomes because it is more efficient or profitable.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion is about technical performance alone, or when adoption is mandated regardless of cost.

Transfer rule: If an EXCEPT question asks what cannot explain a reported decrease, then eliminate choices that would instead raise the measured count or leave the decrease unsupported.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating changes in the population from changes in observation, location, or pressure, and checking the direction of each effect.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would this make fewer target animals be caught there, more be caught there, or neither?” Reject any option pointing the wrong way.
Use when: Apply this on causal multiple-choice items about declines, increases, or trends in catches, sightings, sales, or totals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for best support, strengthens a claim, or allows multiple causes without a directional mismatch test.

Transfer rule: If asked for the choice that does NOT explain a surprising result, then test each option for direct relevance to that result and eliminate any statement about a different phenomenon.
Error pattern: I accepted a superficially plausible distractor instead of checking whether it actually addressed the specific discrepancy described.
Diagnostic check: For each option, write “explains by ___”; if the blank cannot connect causally to the observed subgroup outcome, mark it as the exception.
Use when: Relevant in EXCEPT/weaken-support questions where several answers sound scientific or related but only some address the exact observation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for any related fact, background detail, or a full explanation rather than the non-explaining choice.

Transfer rule: If a passage explains meaning by decomposing character shapes/components into a rhetorical effect, then choose the option about rhetoric based on graphic form.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matched the author’s focus on structural character analysis, not sound, general semantics, or broad logic.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the passage’s operations—split/combine parts, interpret resulting characters, identify the linguistic domain named by that operation.
Use when: The text discusses Chinese characters’ visible components, strokes, radicals, or recombination to create expressive effects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage centers on pronunciation, etymology without expressive purpose, syntax, or formal reasoning instead of shape-based expression.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus gives a threshold or nonlinear relationship, then reject proportional extrapolations and choose the statement preserving “not necessarily linear” effects across ranges.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking curve shape and domain limits instead of assuming a constant rate from one intake level to another.
Diagnostic check: Sketch low-range proportional growth, mark the threshold, then compare whether each choice assumes one slope everywhere or introduces unsupported causes/absolutes.
Use when: Apply this on strengthen/inference questions with saturation, diminishing returns, thresholds, plateaus, or “until X, then Y” quantitative descriptions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stimulus explicitly states a single constant proportional relationship across all values or asks about unrelated mechanisms.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts market enthusiasm or prices with neglected intrinsic worth, then choose the option about price–value mismatch, not a broad cause list.
Error pattern: I overfocused on background reasons and ignored the author’s main evaluative contrast in the ending.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as background, evidence, or thesis; if the final judgment compares what is chased versus what is overlooked, center the summary on that comparison.
Use when: The passage includes historical context plus a present-day critique of collectors, markets, or valuation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for causes only, or when no contrast between external price and inherent value is stated.

Transfer rule: If premises give only one-way conditionals, then infer contrapositives only for each link separately and do not combine them into reverse or conjunctive claims.
Error pattern: Treated valid contraposition as if it also justified reversing direction and bundling multiple consequences into a stronger statement.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each statement as P→Q; list allowed moves as P→Q and ¬Q→¬P only, then test whether the option needs Q→P or joins unrelated consequents.
Use when: Relevant in verbal-logic questions with chained “if,” “only if,” negations, and several parallel traits or outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the source explicitly states biconditionals, equivalence, definitions, or independent premises that directly support the conjunction.

Transfer rule: If two similar inputs produce opposite outcomes, then prefer an answer naming a mechanism present only in the harmful case that directly disrupts the stated causal chain.
Error pattern: I chose an added-benefit detail for the good case instead of explaining why the bad case reverses the expected effect.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this option explain both sides by preserving the benefit in one case and blocking it in the other, rather than merely strengthening one side?
Use when: Relevant in contrast questions about fresh vs. processed states, timing differences, or opposite results from closely related treatments.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks only for a contributor to one outcome, not a reconciler of contrasting outcomes.

Transfer rule: If an argument goes from “all known/so-far discovered X are in place P” plus “someone uses only X,” then match it with “probably/unlikely only from P,” not certainty.
Error pattern: Successful analogical matching by preserving a weak evidence base (“known/discovered”) and a probabilistic conclusion from restricted consumption.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the core form as “only known X are in P; agent uses only X; therefore agent probably not outside P” and verify both qualifiers survive.
Use when: Relevant in parallel-reasoning questions involving location-limited known instances, exclusive use/eating/collecting, and a hedged conclusion.
Boundary: Ignore when choices strengthen to universal claims, change the direction of restriction, or shift from “known/discovered” to “all/every.”

Transfer rule: If an argument claims one ingredient makes a product healthy despite a harmful ingredient, then attack whether the touted ingredient actually supports that health claim in this product/context.
Error pattern: I chose a generic “cast doubt on the conclusion” move instead of targeting the premise that carries the producer’s positive inference.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map conclusion → supporting premise → rebuttal; ask, “Does this option weaken the exact premise that makes the product seem beneficial?”
Use when: Competing arguments cite different ingredients or effects, and the task asks what best counters a marketing-style health conclusion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the strongest rebuttal is direct evidence about net overall effects, dosage, or causation rather than premise-specific support.

Transfer rule: If a passage presents methods or examples, then choose the option naming the author’s ultimate purpose/theme, not a supporting means.
Error pattern: I over-weighted the concluding implementation detail and missed the higher-level thesis the details were meant to serve.
Diagnostic check: State the passage in one sentence using “The author uses X to achieve/emphasize Y”; answer with Y, unless X is repeated as the central claim.
Use when: Relevant in main-idea questions where metaphors, examples, and research suggestions appear alongside a broader evaluative claim.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a specific proposal, evidence, or directly highlighted practical recommendation.

Transfer rule: If promotion uses public media/events or sponsorship paid by a seller to indirectly or directly boost goods/services, then treat it as advertising.  
Error pattern: I focused on broad publicity or campaigning and ignored the requirement that the message serve a commercial seller or service provider.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify all three: payer is a business/provider, exposure is public through a media/event vehicle, and the aim is market promotion rather than private influence or noncommercial compliance.  
Use when: The options mix political activity, gifts/bribes, sponsorships, internal rules, or other public-facing actions under a definition of advertising.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition does not require a commercial promoter or when publicity is purely personal, governmental, or internal.

Transfer rule: If two comparisons use different denominators for the same yield ratio, then convert them into a ratio about denominator composition before choosing.
Error pattern: Mistook an absolute-land conclusion for a proportional-land inference; compared totals instead of how changing the base alters relative rates.
Diagnostic check: Define output, cultivated area, and total area symbols; write both average formulas; divide the formulas to isolate cultivated/total shares and see what must be larger.
Use when: Relevant in word problems comparing averages under alternate bases, especially with cultivated vs total, active vs inactive, or included vs excluded subsets.
Boundary: Ignore when the compared quantities are not the same numerator, or when extra assumptions about absolute amounts are required.

Transfer rule: If asked which statement cannot support a causal conclusion, then keep only claims that specifically increase the target outcome and reject ones that stop at broad or adjacent effects.
Error pattern: I treated any negative consequence as support, failing to distinguish the exact claimed outcome from merely related harm.
Diagnostic check: For each option, rewrite it as “more exposure → ___”; if the blank is not the precise endpoint in the conclusion, mark it as non-support.
Use when: Apply this on weaken/support-except questions involving causal arguments, correlations, and answer choices with similar-sounding psychological or health effects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion itself is broad, explicitly includes intermediate states, or asks about plausibility rather than logical support.

Transfer rule: If a definition includes symptom type, minimum frequency, minimum duration, and daytime impact, then verify all criteria explicitly before choosing.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every diagnostic element and rejecting choices that fit only one symptom or a different sleep issue.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark four boxes—sleep initiation/maintenance problem, daytime fatigue, frequent recurrence, long enough duration—and pick only one with all boxes checked.
Use when: Apply this to medical or psychological classification questions that give threshold-based definitions with multiple required conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for causes, treatments, exceptions, or the “most likely” case without strict definitional criteria.

Transfer rule: If a definition lists core elements and asks for the inaccurate statement, then map each option directly to an explicit phrase and reject the one that negates a stated element.
Error pattern: Success comes from strict definition-to-option matching; failure comes from relying on plausibility or broad policy knowledge instead of textual entailment.
Diagnostic check: Underline the definition’s required components, then mark each option as supported, unsupported, or contradictory; choose only a contradiction, not a merely extra detail.
Use when: Apply this to definition-based multiple choice, especially with “according to the above” and one statement that may reverse a key feature.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for best policy judgment, inference beyond the text, or multiple statements can be partially true.

Transfer rule: If an argument says one difference must explain an outcome, then look for another difference that could block or alter the supposed causal factor.
Error pattern: I attacked missing mechanism instead of challenging the exclusivity of the proposed cause with a concrete alternative explanation.
Diagnostic check: List all relevant differences between the compared treatments; ask whether any nonhighlighted difference could change potency, delivery, or interference.
Use when: Comparative causal arguments infer that superior results come from location, format, or route because one ingredient seems held constant.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only add uncertainty or background facts and do not introduce a plausible competing cause.

Transfer rule: If a principle gives necessary and sufficient conditions, then test each judgment only against those stated conditions, not likely effects or side facts.
Error pattern: I replaced the rule’s criteria with an irrelevant proxy, treating cost-to-giver or outcome as decisive instead of intent and customary value.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the rule’s explicit triggers for each category and verify the option’s stated facts match them word-for-word.
Use when: Apply this on principle-conformity questions using terms like unless, if, only if, or disjunctions about motives, expectations, or thresholds.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for real-world plausibility, hidden assumptions, or unstated moral standards beyond the given rule.

Transfer rule: If a passage ends by promising “the following key points” will improve outcomes, then predict the next part gives practical reference points or tips, not earlier background categories.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking forward-looking discourse markers and choosing the option that matches the announced upcoming content.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, underline any preview phrase like “the following,” restate what content type it signals, and eliminate options that merely repeat setup context.
Use when: Apply this in reading-inference questions about what will be discussed next after an introductory paragraph.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the main idea, cause, summary, or when no explicit preview cue appears.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts a method by one defining property, then infer only exclusions implied by that definition, not uniqueness or converse claims.
Error pattern: Mistook a stated feature of one method for “only this method has it,” confusing sufficient description with necessary exclusivity.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each claim as direct restatement, valid contrapositive/exclusion, converse, or unsupported quantifier leap; reject converse and “only” upgrades unless stated.
Use when: Relevant in deduction questions built from comparisons, definitions, and qualifiers like non-contact, mechanical, all, almost all, or because.
Boundary: Ignore when the source explicitly gives biconditionals, uniqueness language, or independent evidence establishing exclusivity.

Transfer rule: If a passage praises a theory and then states its consequences, then infer the author endorses those stated consequences, not broader unrelated claims.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking the author’s attitude and the downstream implication chain instead of overextending to absolute philosophical claims.
Diagnostic check: Mark evaluative words and link each “because/therefore” step; choose only an option that matches the author’s endorsed consequence verbatim in meaning.
Use when: Apply this on inference questions with quoted views, author commentary, and argument flow from a definition to a claimed result.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the quoted person’s own view, external truth, or a stronger generalization than the passage states.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “greater responsibility” to “therefore one must accept criticism/attacks,” then test whether that extra burden logically follows from the stated duty.
Error pattern: Confusing a higher standard of obligation with entitlement for others to impose unrelated costs is a common unsupported leap.
Diagnostic check: Separate the claim into premise and conclusion; ask, “Does the conclusion add a new kind of burden not contained in the premise?”
Use when: Relevant in weaken/challenge questions where a normative argument links status, power, or duty to permission for blame, attack, or mistreatment.
Boundary: Ignore this when the premise explicitly states that accepting criticism is itself part of the role or duty.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives background pressures and then presents a “therefore/urgently requires” shift, then choose the option naming that required transformation, not a side effect.
Error pattern: Mistaking a supporting condition or trend for the author’s main emphasized thesis.
Diagnostic check: Mark problem, cause, required response, and example; if one statement links cause to required response, prefer that over evidence or implementation details.
Use when: The text contrasts old and new roles, argues duties should be reassigned, and ends with a policy example supporting a broader shift.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a factual detail, a direct consequence, or the specific mechanism rather than the central claim.

Transfer rule: If judging a division, then verify one basis only, full coverage of the parent, mutual exclusivity, and same-level children.
Error pattern: Chose a tempting conceptual split that was relevant but not jointly exhaustive or not parallel under one standard.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: one criterion? any overlap? any omitted members? can every child be described as “a kind/part of” the parent at the same level?
Use when: The task asks whether a classification, partition, or taxonomy is logically proper.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt allows overlapping attributes, causal factors, perspectives, or partial decompositions rather than strict division.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives mechanism evidence for harm but avoids absolute or broadest claims, then choose the option that matches the supported scope and certainty.
Error pattern: Success comes from preferring a cautiously worded summary over exaggerations about total prevention, survival collapse, or unrelated damage.
Diagnostic check: Compare each option against the text for strength and target: mark any choice adding absolute terms, unsupported outcomes, or shifted objects.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions built from partial studies, causal chains, and qualifiers like limited data, greater impact, or reduced ability.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage explicitly states a universal, total, or directly measured outcome matching a stronger option.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus changes only how information is presented and reports a change in decisions, then select the principle that presentation method influences outcomes.
Error pattern: Success came from abstracting the manipulated variable and observed effect instead of chasing broader status, precision, or setting claims.
Diagnostic check: Identify the intervention, hold other facts fixed, and ask, “What changed, and what behavior shifted as a result?”
Use when: Relevant in principle/example questions featuring an experiment or comparison between two communication styles, framings, or procedures.
Boundary: Ignore when the choices require causation unsupported by the comparison or focus on unrelated traits not directly manipulated.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a missing protective factor makes an outcome unlikely, then test whether the underlying threat is common enough to matter.
Error pattern: I focused on an appealing side condition instead of the causal assumption linking absence of protection to actual risk.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Even without the protector, would the bad event frequently occur?” If that rate is unknown, prioritize information about the threat’s prevalence.
Use when: Relevant in causal/necessary-condition arguments about safeguards, buffers, or preventers reducing harm and conclusions about likelihood.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument hinges on direct production, definitions, or comparisons rather than on preventing a background danger.

Transfer rule: If a study reports a measurable marker changing before illness, then choose the option about predictive monitoring or early prevention, not a stronger causal claim.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized correlation into mechanism and degree, ignoring the practical significance emphasized by the study.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does the evidence show prediction, causation, reversal of prior belief, or timing of disease onset? Eliminate any option adding unsupported causality.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension questions summarizing study significance from observed associations, biomarkers, warning signs, or pre-symptom changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage directly tests a mechanism experimentally or explicitly states a causal conclusion.

Transfer rule: If an argument dismisses one objection but still keeps the same recommendation for a new stated reason, then choose the principle that elevates that new reason into a decisive criterion.
Error pattern: Mistaking a contrasted-but-rejected issue for the basis of support; following salient fairness/objectivity language instead of the premise that actually does the work.
Diagnostic check: List each premise, mark which concern is neutralized, then ask: “What remaining premise alone must justify the conclusion?” Match the answer choice to that premise.
Use when: A stimulus presents multiple possible judge-selection criteria and explicitly undercuts one before affirming the conclusion anyway.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion balances criteria, compares degrees, or relies on combining factors rather than one surviving prerequisite.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a delay/cost is necessary because a named process is the only safeguard, then test whether that safeguard could occur by another route without the delay.  
Error pattern: I treated an exaggerated support claim about public incompetence as required, instead of checking for a hidden exclusivity link between the institution and the safeguard.  
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the protective process happen before release even if the stated gatekeeper were bypassed?” If yes, the conclusion is weakened and that missing negation is likely assumed.  
Use when: The conclusion justifies a burden by claiming “only way,” “must,” or “price to pay” to obtain protection or quality control.  
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already explicitly rules out all alternative mechanisms or routes.

Transfer rule: If a claim is introduced, then supported by examples and followed by “so/thus/therefore,” treat that claim as the main conclusion, not an assumption.
Error pattern: Mistaking an explicitly stated, supported thesis for a hidden premise required by the argument.
Diagnostic check: Remove the opening claim and ask: do the later sentences function as evidence for it, and does the final inferential phrase restate it more generally?
Use when: A role question asks about argument structure and the passage contains a broad statement plus illustrative comparison or anecdotal support.
Boundary: Ignore when the statement is merely background, contradicted later, or needed for the evidence to make sense rather than supported by it.

Transfer rule: If a statement reports one method actually producing an extreme result, then infer only that this method can achieve that result in this case, not that other factors caused it.
Error pattern: I generalized from a publicity outcome to broad claims about consumers, quality, or market strategy beyond the stated evidence.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, underline the exact cause-result link and reject any option adding new variables, comparisons, or universal claims not explicitly licensed.
Use when: Relevant for inference questions built from a single anecdote about marketing, popularity, causation, or “greatest/maximum” outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt provides comparative data, multiple causes, or asks for the best explanation rather than a strict inference.

Transfer rule: If an argument dismisses a credibility objection because no one has proved the evidence false, then flag a flaw: undermining need not equal disproving.
Error pattern: I confused criticism of the objector’s assumption with the responder’s stronger assumption that only demonstrated falsity can weaken evidence.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Is the speaker requiring conclusive proof of deception/error before allowing any doubt about the evidence’s reliability?”
Use when: A claim relies on survey, testimony, or reports, and the reply rejects possible bias, dishonesty, or unreliability for lack of proof.
Boundary: Ignore when the speaker gives independent reasons the source is reliable or when the objection itself claims certainty rather than mere possible undermining.

Transfer rule: If a payment is written as security between the contracting parties, then require forfeiture by payer on breach and double return by receiver on breach.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every legal element instead of choosing an option with only a similar label or purpose.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, make a 4-point checklist: parties to contract, written agreement, security for performance, symmetric breach consequences (lose vs double repay).
Use when: Apply this on legal-definition multiple-choice items involving payments, guarantees, earnest money, reservations, or prepayments with breach terms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the rule being tested lacks a writing requirement, involves a third-party holder, or the payment is merely a loan, discount, or refundable intent fee.

Transfer rule: If a memory task involves deliberately trying to bring learned information to mind, then classify it as explicit; if it shows automatic skill, fluency, or priming, then do not.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating conscious retrieval of facts/events from unconscious influence on performance or perception.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the person need intentional recall to answer or perform, or would it happen automatically without trying?”
Use when: Relevant for questions contrasting recall/recognition of studied material with habits, procedural skills, language fluency, or perceptual familiarity.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when choices hinge on other distinctions, such as short-term vs long-term or semantic vs episodic memory.

Transfer rule: If a claim says an activity broadly benefits development, then prefer evidence showing the activity creates a direct harmful effect on the same developmental domains.
Error pattern: Success came from targeting the core causal conclusion rather than choosing a merely inconvenient, unrelated, or conditional detail.
Diagnostic check: List the claim’s outcomes, then ask of each option: does it directly show the activity undermines one outcome, or only describe context, preference, or a separate trait?
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions about broad educational, psychological, or social benefits attributed to one practice.
Boundary: Ignore when options attack study design, sample validity, or comparison groups instead of the claimed effects themselves.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects a reply by splitting into two cases where that reply fails either way, then choose the option with the same either-way conditional structure and same role for the rebuttal.
