Error pattern: Valid contraposition of a necessary-conjunction claim; success comes from preserving the conjunctive structure.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as “Success only if A and B”; then test whether the conclusion is exactly “No success, so not (A and B).”
Use when: The stimulus uses requirements, necessities, prerequisites, or “must have both” language tied to an outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the premise gives sufficiency, uses “or,” or the conclusion singles out one condition instead of denying the pair.

Transfer rule: If a passage states “at all times at least one of two conditions holds,” then infer the contrapositive-style result: if one is absent, the other must be present.
Error pattern: Mistaking a one-way sufficient clue or a special-case month fact for a biconditional/exhaustive condition.
Diagnostic check: List the universal rule and each one-way trigger separately, then test each choice by asking whether it follows from coverage alone or improperly reverses a trigger.
Use when: Relevant in conditional-logic questions with “either/or/both,” time-based policies, and extra facts about one specific case.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the statement is exclusive, probabilistic, or explicitly gives a two-way equivalence.

Transfer rule: If a speaker’s identity is inferred first, then test each candidate statement against that person’s truthfulness status and pick the one whose truth value matches.
Error pattern: Chose the option that merely mentions the inferred person instead of checking whether the statement would be true or false under that inference.
Diagnostic check: Substitute the inferred actor into every option, mark each proposition true/false, then eliminate any option inconsistent with the actor’s always-true or always-false behavior.
Use when: A logic problem links fixed truthfulness types to possible speakers/authors and asks which statement could appear or be asserted.
Boundary: Ignore when truthfulness is probabilistic, context-dependent, or multiple statements can be jointly made without exclusive authorship.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers one checker is better from fewer observed errors, then require an assumption that both groups had errors available to catch.
Error pattern: I compared workforce quality with outcomes and imported a stronger causal explanation instead of identifying the necessary hidden precondition.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the conclusion fail because one side had nothing to correct?” If yes, look for an assumption ensuring comparable opportunities for detection.
Use when: Relevant in arguments comparing efficiency, vigilance, or skill using defect rates, mistakes found, or clean final outputs.
Boundary: Ignore when the premise already states equal initial error opportunities or the conclusion concerns standards, staffing, or definitions rather than detection performance.

Transfer rule: If a passage says remedies are lacking, ineffective, or not feasible, then infer absence/insufficiency of protection mechanisms, not new normative proposals.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating descriptive claims about current conditions from prescriptive or broader claims not directly stated.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as fact, cause, or opinion; choose the option restating the factual condition with the least added scope.
Use when: Apply on inference questions where the text discusses rights protection, compensation, channels of relief, or institutional safeguards.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the passage explicitly argues what should be enacted, predicts outcomes, or compares multiple institutions.

Transfer rule: If an argument says one kind of advocacy should be treated like another despite possible harm, then choose a principle banning suppression solely because dissemination may be harmful.
Error pattern: Success pattern: abstract the shared feature between the example and target case instead of focusing on subject matter differences.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state both cases generically as “group advocates view; view may harm some people”; accept only a principle that covers both.
Use when: Relevant in principle-justify questions using analogy, parity, or “the same should be true” reasoning about speech or advocacy.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument depends on extra differences between cases or on outcomes beyond mere harmful dissemination.

Transfer rule: If a boldface statement describes a trend/innovation and the argument later forecasts what will happen because of it, then treat the first as the development and the forecast as the main claim unless another sentence clearly gives the prediction.
Error pattern: Mistaking a conceded obstacle or cost-based objection for the conclusion instead of seeing it as a counterconsideration within a larger predictive argument.
Diagnostic check: Mark each sentence as premise, concession, or conclusion by signal words; then ask which claim the final support is trying to make probable.
Use when: Boldface-role questions feature contrast terms, economic drawbacks, and a later “however/therefore/likely” prediction.
Boundary: Ignore this when both boldface parts are straightforward premises or when no future-oriented claim is being defended.

Transfer rule: If a category is defined by how value transfers, then sort each listed item by transfer pattern and choose only items consumed or fully transferred within one production cycle.
Error pattern: Misclassified mixed lists by focusing on industry context instead of testing each item against the defining criterion.
Diagnostic check: For every item, ask: “Is its value used up entirely in one cycle, or does it transfer gradually over many cycles?” Reject any option containing the second type.
Use when: Relevant for classification questions contrasting one-time transfer/consumption with gradual, repeated transfer across production.
Boundary: Ignore when the classification is based on ownership, legality, purpose, or social role rather than transfer timing in production.

Transfer rule: If an argument classifies a fossil or trait as proving a category member, then test whether it assumes only that category could possess that trait at that time.
Error pattern: I chose an attractive alternative scenario instead of identifying the exclusivity assumption required for the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could some other kind of creature also have had this feature without making the conclusion true?” If yes, the needed assumption blocks that possibility.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where evidence is a physical feature, imprint, or marker used to infer taxonomic identity or earliest occurrence.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion does not depend on unique ownership of a trait or when multiple categories are already allowed.

Transfer rule: If an argument says “avoid policy X because X causes harm,” then test whether not doing X would cause equal or greater harm.
Error pattern: I focused on a loosely related trend instead of comparing the policy with its main alternative and its direct consequences.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “What happens if the recommendation is followed?” If that outcome worsens the target problem more than the criticized policy, it weakens the argument most.
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions with causal chains, feedback loops, and policy recommendations about whether to act or refrain.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only give distant background, broad forecasts, or facts that do not compare the recommendation against its practical alternative.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers comparative influence from comparative connection development, then require an assumption linking development level to influence strength.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting the missing bridge between a physical or structural comparison and the claimed causal or functional comparison.
Diagnostic check: Identify premise metric and conclusion metric; ask, “What principle converts more-developed pathways into more influence?” If none is stated, choose the option that supplies it.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where premises discuss anatomy, quantity, or structure but conclusions compare power, effect, control, or causation.
Boundary: Ignore when the premises already state that structural differences determine influence, or when the conclusion concerns only structure itself.

Transfer rule: If a claim says changing consumption would not reduce a shortage, then look for evidence that the alternative use of the same resources would feed many more people.
Error pattern: Success came from targeting the causal efficiency assumption, not getting distracted by other independent causes of the shortage.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this choice compare input-to-output efficiency between current production and the proposed alternative, and thereby show meaningful net availability gains?”
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions about food supply, resource allocation, production efficiency, or whether a behavioral shift would affect aggregate scarcity.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument hinges on distribution, access, politics, timing, or non-resource bottlenecks rather than production efficiency.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires the actor to adopt another person’s perspective, then choose the case where no one is actually perspective-taking, only transmitting experiences or advice.
Error pattern: I overfocused on usefulness for communication and ignored the core mechanism: temporary shift into the other party’s standpoint, feelings, or values.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Who is the actor, whose viewpoint is entered, and is there an active attempt to imagine from that viewpoint?
Use when: Apply this to definition questions involving empathy, role-taking, viewpoint adoption, or perspective-based communication abilities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is about sharing information, persuasion, teaching outcomes, or relationship effects without required perspective shift.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts conditions before widespread use with outcomes under normal use, then infer only a conditional trend about spread, not absolute biological claims.
Error pattern: Success came from preferring the weakest supported inference and rejecting choices that overstate causation, mechanism, or impossibility.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark words like “root cause,” “will not,” or mechanism claims; eliminate any option stronger than the passage’s evidence.
Use when: Apply this on inference questions about selection, resistance, treatment pressure, or changing prevalence across environments.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage directly provides a mechanism, universal claim, or explicit causal proof.

Transfer rule: If several conditional statements must be jointly satisfied except one, then test each answer choice by counting how many statements become false under that scenario.
Error pattern: Success came from consistency checking across a nearly-all-true set, but the prior reasoning risked treating conditionals as “not applicable” without a full truth-count.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate outcome, mark every statement true/false using implication rules; accept only a case with exactly one false statement.
Use when: Relevant in logic puzzles with rankings plus conditional claims and a constraint like “all but one expert were correct.”
Boundary: Ignore when statements are not truth-evaluable from the given data or when multiple exceptions are explicitly allowed.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a valued liberty may be limited because competing harms outweigh the loss, then choose the principle allowing that liberty to be overridden in some cases.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the principle to the exact logical bridge, not to broader policy methods or stronger-than-needed standards.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the gap as “supporting X is still consistent if X can sometimes yield to Y”; reject choices adding utilitarian tests, automatic restriction, or mere side considerations.
Use when: Relevant in principle-strengthen questions about apparent inconsistency between endorsing a right and endorsing a specific restriction.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument needs empirical evidence, causal support, or a decision rule about implementation details.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts rapid popularity driven by imitation with little attention to intrinsic quality, then choose the option separating popularity from usefulness/value.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: abstract the central contrast and ignore options that turn it into advice, broader criticism, or unrelated consequences.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the text’s driver, the neglected factor, and the implied takeaway; accept only a choice matching all three.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea questions about herd behavior, social proof, diffusion, or popularity metrics versus inherent merit.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly argues for a recommendation, reports concrete outcomes only, or defines usefulness directly.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a core problem, explains mutual reinforcement, and ends with a broad takeaway, then choose the option expressing the overall advocated principle, not a restated supporting relation.
Error pattern: I elevated a descriptive mechanism into the main point instead of identifying the author’s central recommendation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each sentence as problem, evidence/process, or conclusion; pick the choice that matches the conclusion spanning all prior parts.
Use when: Relevant for “main meaning,” “best summary,” or “central idea” questions with causal chains and a final evaluative or prescriptive sentence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, inference, or the role of one sentence rather than the whole passage.

Transfer rule: If a contract seems break-even, then look for downstream revenue the contract creates, especially captive follow-on sales.
Error pattern: Focused on why the bid won instead of what fact would make the executives’ profit claim true.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option create additional profit beyond the initial deal, or only describe selection, logistics, or neutral details?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions with an apparent contradiction between low margins now and claims of profitability later.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim concerns only the original transaction’s margin or when no repeat purchases/ancillary sales are plausible.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a factor does not hinder progress because progress still occurred, then test whether the factor could impede growth without stopping it.
Error pattern: Treated “still increasing” as proof of “not being impeded,” overlooking partial hindrance amid overall advancement.
Diagnostic check: Ask: compared with a no-factor baseline, could the outcome have risen less, more slowly, or from stronger counterforces despite rising overall?
Use when: Relevant in causal arguments about trends over time where one side cites continued improvement to dismiss a claimed obstacle.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is total prevention, or when evidence directly compares rates with and without the factor.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires both individual freedom and a shared whole beyond the individual, then choose the option that explicitly combines private interests with pursuit of common interests.
Error pattern: Success came from matching all necessary conditions instead of picking choices that express only morality, social mood, or group identity.
Diagnostic check: Underline each required component in the definition and verify the candidate contains every one; reject any option missing one component.
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching questions with multi-part criteria, especially abstract civic, ethical, or social concepts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for examples, causes, or best policy rather than strict satisfaction of a definition.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires all listed conditions, then test each option against every condition and reject any single-condition failure.
Error pattern: Success comes from conjunctive definition matching rather than choosing an option with only economic benefit or partial environmental improvement.
Diagnostic check: Make a three-part checklist from the definition; for each option, mark satisfies/violates/unknown, and select only one with all satisfies and no violations.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice items that define a category using several necessary environmental or resource criteria.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stem asks for the best improvement, primary goal, or comparative advantage instead of strict membership by definition.

Transfer rule: If a passage names one case, then gives several because-clauses for that case, choose the option stating that case’s reasons.
Error pattern: Mistaking a brief comparison or setup example for the main idea, instead of the author’s explanatory target.
Diagnostic check: Mark topic sentence, contrast/setup sentence, and all causal phrases; if most support one subject, pick the option centered on that subject.
Use when: Expository questions compare countries, categories, or examples, then spend more space explaining one selection or policy.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage distributes equal explanation across multiple cases or asks for a contrast rather than a main point.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires power over a relevant market, then verify broad market share plus actual ability to control terms or block entry, not mere local uniqueness or popularity.
Error pattern: Correct pattern is matching every definition element; common failure is equating being the only seller, one of several strong firms, or being famous with dominance.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: what is the relevant market, is power shown across it, and is there evidence of controlling price/quantity/terms or restricting entry?
Use when: Apply on legal/economic definition questions about market power, monopoly, competition, or relevant-market scope.
Boundary: Ignore when the question concerns simple popularity, product preference, or facts lacking evidence about market-wide control.

Transfer rule: If an argument presents pros/cons but then says a recommendation is “premature,” then choose the option stating overall caution about adopting the practice.
Error pattern: Correctly distinguished the author’s main point from supporting possibilities and from background concessions.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What claim would the author most want accepted even if the speculative harms proved false?”; prefer the broad evaluative stance over any single cited risk.
Use when: Relevant in main-conclusion questions with a concession, speculative downside examples, and language questioning readiness to act.
Boundary: Ignore when the stimulus directly endorses a specific factual prediction or policy, rather than cautioning against moving too quickly.

Transfer rule: If a claim predicts a short-term price drop despite long-term supply exit, then look for a temporary surge in current market supply.
Error pattern: I focused on reduced demand instead of reconciling the timing mismatch between immediate and later effects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map each option to near-term supply, near-term demand, long-term supply, or long-term demand, and prefer the one affecting the named time horizon.
Use when: Apply this on market/economics questions with opposite short-run and long-run predictions or transitional effects from firms exiting.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is not about timing, inventory release, or temporary supply shifts.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion compares two people linked through separate premises, then add only premises that create a transitive chain from the first to the second.
Error pattern: I treated “supports” or “doesn’t contradict” as sufficient, instead of testing whether the added premise guarantees the target comparison.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite all statements as >, =, <; combine them stepwise and ask whether the target relation follows in every allowed ordering.
Use when: Relevant in ordering/ranking syllogisms with comparative words like better, worse, equal, and a missing bridge between two endpoints.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on causation, probability, definitions, or nontransitive relations rather than strict ordering.

Transfer rule: If an argument goes from “most members of group G have trait T” to “this thing has T, so it is probably in G,” then flag it as reversing a one-way statistical claim.
Error pattern: Confusing a common feature of a group with evidence that possessing the feature makes membership likely.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the logic as “Most G are T; X is T; therefore X is probably G” and ask whether the statistic given is about G→T rather than T→G.
Use when: The stimulus uses “most,” “generally,” or “usually” and concludes group membership from a described trait.
Boundary: Ignore when the premise instead states “most things with T are G” or gives bidirectional/conditional equivalence.

Transfer rule: If a passage defines a concept, then separate descriptive components from the stated purpose/function and answer with the purpose.
Error pattern: I focused on what the concept includes or explains, instead of the effect it is said to achieve.
Diagnostic check: Mark phrases as definition, means, and end-goal; choose the option matching the end-goal clause, not the background description.
Use when: Relevant in reading questions asking for “main function,” “purpose,” or “role” after a concept is unpacked in several linked clauses.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for content, features, origins, or examples rather than the concept’s practical function.

Transfer rule: If an argument treats a trait linked to harm as the cause of harm, then check for a confounding factor that influences both the trait and the outcome.
Error pattern: Mistaking correlation for causation by ignoring selection effects or third-variable explanations.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could a different characteristic make people both more likely to have this trait and more likely to produce the outcome?” If yes, weaken the causal claim.
Use when: A policy conclusion targets a visible category because that category shows a higher rate of some bad result.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already rules out major confounders or provides direct causal evidence.

Transfer rule: If a passage states a broad problem and immediately proposes systemic reform, then infer it is pointing to the underlying/root cause, not a specific contributing factor or degree.
Error pattern: Mistaking a general, policy-level inference for a narrow causal detail about one mechanism.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as root cause, partial cause, measurement, or effect; choose only the one matching the passage’s level of generality.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions where the argument moves from a social problem to a call for reform or structural change.
Boundary: Ignore when the text explicitly quantifies one factor, names a mechanism, or asks for direct factual support rather than implied scope.

Transfer rule: If a forecast says current scarcity will not raise price much, then look for a nearby offsetting supply source that can enter this year’s market.
Error pattern: I used a historical-comparison fact that weakened analogy support instead of identifying the mechanism that directly neutralizes the stated scarcity.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “What specific stock, carryover, or substitute supply could keep availability high despite a poor current harvest?”
Use when: Relevant for market, price, supply-demand, storage, inventory, or forecasting arguments where current production seems to imply higher prices.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument turns on demand shifts, regulation, quality differences, or when no delayed/extra supply channel is mentioned or plausible.

Transfer rule: If a category requires human-made or historically preserved remains, then exclude natural landforms or phenomena.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the definition’s source criterion instead of being distracted by fame or tourism value.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: was it created, modified, or intentionally preserved by human historical activity rather than by nature alone?
Use when: This fits definition-based multiple choice with mixed examples of monuments, ruins, artifacts, sites, and natural places.
Boundary: Ignore this when the category explicitly includes natural heritage, cultural landscapes, or combined human-nature sites.

Transfer rule: If an argument mentions others’ claim and then gives reasons leading to the opposite evaluation, then treat that claim as a position the argument disputes, not as support.
Error pattern: Mistaking a cited opposing viewpoint for a premise or counterargument-supporting premise instead of recognizing its dialectical role.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each statement as author-endorsed, opponent-view, or intermediate conclusion; then see whether the final conclusion affirms or rejects the cited claim.
Use when: Relevant in role/function questions where the stimulus quotes what some group says before presenting the author’s reasoning.
Boundary: Ignore when the cited statement is later used as evidence toward the same final conclusion rather than being undermined.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists recurring market abuses despite improved order, then choose the conclusion calling for stronger supervision/enforcement mechanisms, not broader structural reform or direct control.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the remedy to the named problem level; avoid jumping from specific oversight failures to sweeping governance changes.
Diagnostic check: Underline each problem cited, classify it as rule-breaking/monitoring failure vs system-design issue, and pick the option addressing the dominant class.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions where the stem asks what the author will most likely conclude after examples of disorder, fraud, or quality violations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage explicitly shifts to institutional restructuring, ideology, or macro-control rather than enforcement gaps.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts medium/form with content/depth, then choose the option preserving the author’s stated core criterion rather than side comments.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating the thesis from concessive or illustrative remarks and not over-weighting emotionally charged examples.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the sentence naming “the key/core,” paraphrase it in neutral terms, and eliminate choices about convenience, superiority, or unrelated examples.
Use when: Apply this to main-idea or “most accurate understanding” questions with contrasts, concessions, and examples about reading, media, or method.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, attitude, or when no explicit central criterion is stated.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers a genetic cause from people thriving despite risk factors, then prefer evidence showing the trait clusters in close relatives.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: strengthen by adding heritability evidence that links outcomes across family members, not by restating mixed lifestyle details.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this new fact make an inherited explanation more likely than lifestyle luck or exceptions?” If yes, it strongly strengthens.
Use when: Relevant for causal-strengthen questions involving nature-versus-environment, unusual resilience, or claims about innate predisposition from survival patterns.
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is not about inheritance, relatives are irrelevant, or stronger evidence directly isolates a non-genetic cause.

Transfer rule: If an argument touts accuracy on times it predicted an event, then ask whether it made that prediction often enough; prefer facts showing substantial prediction frequency.
Error pattern: I accepted overlap on non-event forecasts, which is irrelevant because it neither increases the speaker’s tested sample nor compares reliability on the key question.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, identify the claimed metric, then test each option for whether it strengthens that exact metric by affecting base rate, sample size, or direct comparison.
Use when: Relevant in strengthening questions involving conditional success claims, forecast accuracy, or arguments built from “most times when we predicted X, X occurred.”
Boundary: Ignore when the argument’s weakness is not representativeness or comparison, but instead causation, definition, or missing alternative explanations.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a policy is unfair because it makes a subgroup fund harms beyond its own offense type, then choose the principle forbidding cross-severity cost shifting.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the conclusion’s fairness complaint to a principle that directly blocks the disputed payment requirement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the conclusion as a normative rule and ask which option, if assumed valid, makes that rule immediately follow.
Use when: Relevant for principle-strengthen questions about fairness, penalties, and whether one class may be charged for benefits tied to another class’s more serious conduct.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument turns on deterrence, administrative use of funds, proportional amount, or factual effectiveness rather than fairness linkage.

Transfer rule: If an argument claims X raises Y and therefore improves Z, then test whether the Y increase is durable and actually persists long enough to affect Z.
Error pattern: Success pattern: weakening a causal chain by attacking the stability or duration of the intermediate effect, rather than discussing side benefits or irrelevant comparisons.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Does the evidence show only a brief bump in the mediator, or a lasting change that could plausibly produce the claimed downstream outcome?
Use when: Relevant for cause-effect arguments with a stated mechanism, especially “temporary improvement leads to meaningful learning/performance gains.”
Boundary: Ignore when the claim is only about immediate short-term effects, not lasting outcomes or broader learning.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives conditional claims, then translate them into formal if/only-if relations and derive contrapositives before using any statistics.
Error pattern: I treated a tempting arithmetic statement as derivable, ignoring that the question hinged on logical necessity from stated conditions.
Diagnostic check: List each claim as fact, cause, necessity, sufficiency, or prediction; then ask whether my choice is directly stated or follows by valid contrapositive, not by extra assumptions.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension items mixing data with conditionals, causal language, and policy requirements.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task explicitly asks for estimation, approximation, or outside domain knowledge rather than strict textual entailment.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus justifies an evaluation by citing what feature made an action appropriate, then choose the principle that elevates that cited feature to the main criterion.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the speaker’s stated basis of judgment, not importing broader social norms or recipient-focused assumptions.
Diagnostic check: Underline the exact property offered as the reason; ask, “Which option makes this property sufficient or primary?”
Use when: Relevant in principle-justify questions where a person gives an example and explains why it was fitting, acceptable, or appropriate.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a flaw, assumption, or outcome prediction rather than the governing evaluative principle.

Transfer rule: If an argument says all members share features but some are not used for the usual function because those features serve other functions, then pick the analogy with the same feature/function exception structure.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching abstract roles—category, common parts, usual function, and exceptions—not surface topic or wording.
Diagnostic check: Map both arguments into four slots: class, shared attributes, standard use, counterexamples with alternative use; accept only a choice matching all four.
Use when: Relevant in analogy or parallel-reasoning questions involving shared anatomy/components and a denied default purpose for some members.
Boundary: Ignore when choices depend on causal claims, quantities, chronology, or value judgments rather than a parts-to-function analogy.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires an internal cause under otherwise normal conditions, then eliminate cases driven by pollution, illness, or other external triggers.  
Error pattern: I overfocused on visible whitening and ignored the causation clause that distinguishes intrinsic traits from externally induced changes.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would this whitening still occur without the cited outside exposure or disease?” Keep only those with hereditary/internal origin.  
Use when: This applies to definition-matching questions where the key discriminator is cause, especially internal-versus-external mechanism under normal environment.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the term is defined only by appearance or outcome, or when external causes are explicitly included in the definition.

Transfer rule: If a claim says media effects are uniform, irresistible, and audience differences negligible, then favor evidence of active audience reaction or social resistance.
Error pattern: I overvalued a generic stimulus-response statement that can support the claim instead of testing whether an option directly challenges passivity or uniformity.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: does this show variation, filtering, pushback, or limits on media influence? Eliminate choices that merely restate causation or discuss policy without effect on reception.
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions about communication theories, audience agency, persuasion models, or one-way effects on recipients.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument is about business incentives, regulation outcomes, or exposure counts rather than how recipients process messages.

Transfer rule: If a statement says “whenever P, should Q,” then only infer its contrapositive “if not Q, then not P,” not exceptions or causal details.
Error pattern: Confusing a one-way conditional with unsupported reversals, negations, or added premises about hidden causes.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the claim as P → Q, then test each option by matching it to P → Q, ¬Q → ¬P, Q → P, or ¬P → ¬Q; accept only licensed forms.
Use when: Apply this on verbal-logic items with triggers like “as long as,” “if,” “whenever,” “must,” or recommendation rules.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt adds biconditional language, explicit exceptions, probabilistic wording, or independent factual evidence beyond the conditional.

Transfer rule: If an argument links removing something to rising levels of a harmful substance, then check whether it assumes that thing normally reduces or absorbs that substance.
Error pattern: Necessary-assumption questions often hinge on an unstated causal bridge connecting the cited change to the predicted outcome.
Diagnostic check: Negate the suspected bridge; if the argument’s prediction no longer follows or becomes unsupported, treat that bridge as required.
Use when: The stimulus mixes environmental or system changes, causal claims, and a forecast based on eliminating a prior stabilizing factor.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion can stand from stated facts alone or when the missing claim is merely evaluative, not causal.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus seems harmful yet low doses produce benefits, then prefer an explanation where the small harm triggers a compensating protective response with net gain.
Error pattern: Success came from seeking a causal mechanism that reconciles the paradox, not choices that merely restate degree, frequency, or variation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option show how the same factor can cause minor damage yet activate broader repair or defense that outweighs it?”
Use when: Apply to paradox/explanation questions involving dose-dependent reversals, adaptation, hormesis-like effects, or beneficial outcomes from mild stress.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is not explanatory, or when evidence points to selection, measurement artifacts, or direct benefits unrelated to induced repair.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires a holiday-based sales method, then verify both a holiday/time-off trigger and a promotion aimed at boosting sales during that period.
Error pattern: Success came from checking all defining elements instead of matching on any single sales tactic like discounts, ads, or events.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark two boxes: holiday-linked timing and promotional purpose tied to that timing; reject any option missing either box.
Use when: Apply this to definition questions where examples may look similar but differ in cause, timing, or purpose.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the category is defined by outcomes only, not by a specific trigger plus intent.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists multiple harms from one unmet condition, then infer the author’s intended point is the necessity of fixing that root condition, not any single intermediate effect.
Error pattern: I focused on a repeated mechanism/result inside the paragraph instead of the broader normative takeaway tying all consequences together.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What change would remove most listed problems?” Then choose the option expressing that necessary condition or overall purpose.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea or intended-meaning questions where the paragraph gives several consequences, social harms, and a concluding stability/welfare concern.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a directly stated detail, a sole causal step, or one explicitly emphasized subproblem rather than the overall message.

Transfer rule: If two speakers offer rival causes for the same outcome, then identify whether they disagree about causation, not about background facts in either story.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating accepted premises from the disputed causal link between an action and a result.
Diagnostic check: List each speaker’s claimed cause, then ask: do both accept the outcome but reject the same cause? If yes, choose the causation disagreement.
Use when: Apply this on dialogue questions asking what speakers disagree about, especially when one cites policy effects and the other cites outside influences.
Boundary: Ignore this when a speaker directly denies a factual premise or when the dispute is about timing, degree, or definitions.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts a choice from one stated advantage, then require evidence that this advantage is the main decision driver.
Error pattern: I favored an option about future side effects instead of linking the conclusion to the criterion actually used by decision-makers.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What hidden assumption connects the cited benefit to the predicted action?” Then pick the option that makes that factor primary or decisive.
Use when: Applicable to strengthen questions where two actions are compared and the argument infers which action agents will choose.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is weaken, flaw, or resolve, or when the conclusion does not depend on a specific preference criterion.

Transfer rule: If several headcounts describe overlapping categories, then compute totals with set bounds: minimum by maximizing allowed overlap, maximum by minimizing overlap under any exclusivity constraints.
Error pattern: Treated category counts as disjoint and ignored that people can belong to multiple attribute groups while some job-role groups are explicitly non-overlapping.
Diagnostic check: Partition categories into independent dimensions; mark which pairs can overlap or cannot; then calculate lower bound via largest feasible overlaps and upper bound via smallest feasible overlaps.
Use when: A counting question gives multiple group sizes across traits, origins, or duties and asks what total population could be.
Boundary: Ignore when categories are stated mutually exclusive/exhaustive in one dimension or when exact intersections are directly provided.

Transfer rule: If a statement says “not present implies either not invited or no time,” then infer only possibilities for absences, not guaranteed attendance or extra negatives.
Error pattern: Success comes from reading a one-way conditional carefully and avoiding converse, inverse, and stronger universal claims.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as P(absent) -> (not invited OR no time); test each option by asking whether it merely allows one listed absence-cause or instead asserts the reverse/stronger claim.
Use when: Apply this on verbal-logic items with “either/or,” attendance/presence conditions, and inference choices about who may or must be absent.
Boundary: Ignore this when “either/or” is explicitly exclusive, biconditional, or supported by additional premises linking invitation, time, and presence.

Transfer rule: If a passage argues about who composes, operates, and controls a system, then choose the option naming its management/governance characteristics.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the conclusion’s main focus, not being distracted by broader context or opening praise.
Diagnostic check: Underline the conclusion and list its repeated nouns/verbs; verify the chosen option captures most of those terms directly.
Use when: The prompt asks what the author is most likely explaining, and the passage contrasts governance structures, participants, or control.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets causes, effects, examples, or a narrower detail rather than the passage’s central explanatory focus.

Transfer rule: If people make chained accusations about who lied, then assign each speaker a truth value and enforce every statement as a consistency condition.
Error pattern: Success came from systematic case-checking instead of choosing the most intuitive accusation pair.
Diagnostic check: Let each speaker be truthful or lying; derive consequences from all three statements and reject any assignment that makes one statement mismatched.
Use when: Apply to logic puzzles with interdependent claims about truthfulness, especially cycles where one speaker comments on another’s honesty.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are probabilistic, ambiguous, or not strictly about whether earlier statements are true or false.

Transfer rule: If an argument says different conviction rates are due to lawyer quality, then prefer support showing underlying guilt rates do not already favor the higher-conviction group.
Error pattern: Causal-support questions are strongest when they rule out a natural alternative explanation, especially base-rate differences between compared groups.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “If both groups had similar or less actual culpability in the higher-conviction group, would the stated cause better explain the outcome?”
Use when: Two populations are compared on an outcome, and the claim explains the gap by one factor such as resources, representation, or procedure.
Boundary: Ignore when choices mainly restate legal ideals, add irrelevant size facts, or introduce unrelated mechanisms instead of comparing true underlying rates.

Transfer rule: If an argument says one ought to take a step only because the default outcome is bad, then check for an assumption that the person actually cares about avoiding that outcome.
Error pattern: Practical-necessity arguments often hinge on an unstated motivation premise linking the consequence to a reason for action.
Diagnostic check: Remove the “cares about the result” premise; if the conclusion about what one ought to do loses force, that premise is required.
Use when: The claim recommends planning, prevention, or paperwork based on what happens otherwise under rules or default arrangements.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already states the agent’s preferences or relies instead on legal, moral, or factual impossibility.

Transfer rule: If statements combine implication, conjunction, and a known fact, then formalize each claim and test which single speaker can be false without contradiction.
Error pattern: I treated one report as directly false from the observed event, instead of checking global consistency across all statements and the “exactly one false” condition.
Diagnostic check: Assign symbols, derive consequences from the known fact, then make a mini truth table for each speaker being the lone false one; eliminate cases that force multiple falsehoods.
Use when: Apply this to logic questions with several people’s claims, conditionals, and a constraint like “only one is wrong” or “exactly one lies.”
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on real-world causation, probability, or ambiguous language rather than strict propositional relations.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a factor is the key to an outcome, then translate it as a necessary-condition claim for that outcome, not automatically as a causal effect of a proposed measure.
Error pattern: Mistaking a policy recommendation derived from a premise for something directly proved by the premise, instead of tracking necessity vs means.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “Outcome requires ___; recommendation uses ___ to improve it”; accept only choices matching the first blank unless the second link is explicitly stated.
Use when: Apply this on strengthenable arguments with “key,” “basis,” “premise,” or “therefore” linking a condition to a policy step.
Boundary: Ignore this when the stimulus explicitly states empirical causation between the measure and the condition, or asks for a practical recommendation rather than an implication.

Transfer rule: If asked for a statement “not necessary,” then remove each option and ask whether the conclusion could still stand without it.  
Error pattern: I treated a background link in the causal chain as optional while overlooking that a performance claim added by an option may exceed what the conclusion requires.  
Diagnostic check: Build a minimum support map: evidence sign → event link → usefulness claim; mark any option that only strengthens scale, precision, percentage, or combination details as nonessential.  
Use when: Relevant in premise-necessity questions with scientific findings, predictive models, or arguments moving from detection to practical forecasting value.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a sufficient assumption, strongest support, or the option restates an explicit conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a passage states several premises and then gives a causal/concluding sentence, then choose the option matching that final claim, not an earlier supporting statement.
Error pattern: I selected a repeated premise instead of the author’s main conclusion signaled by summative wording.
Diagnostic check: Underline conclusion markers and ask, “Which option expresses what the earlier sentences are used to prove?”
Use when: Relevant for main-point questions where multiple sentences restate background ideas before a final inferential claim.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a stated fact, example, or premise rather than the passage’s central point.

Transfer rule: If a claim says a behavior has no advantage, then prefer evidence showing the behavior produces a concrete survival or deterrence benefit.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning focused on weakening the core assumption by supplying an alternative adaptive function, not side facts about labels or incomplete observation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this choice identify a mechanism by which the odd behavior helps against the relevant threat?” If yes, prioritize it.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen/weaken questions about animal behavior, intention, play, function, or adaptation under predator-prey conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only question terminology, researcher confidence, frequency in other contexts, or missing environmental knowledge without linking to benefit.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives parallel reasons for two different sides, then choose the option that captures the shared significance to both, not one side’s detail.
Error pattern: Main-idea success comes from integrating multiple supporting claims instead of fixating on the opening sentence or a single consequence.
Diagnostic check: List each stakeholder mentioned, write their stated interest in the subject, and verify the answer covers all of them at the same level.
Use when: Apply this on central-idea questions with contrast words, two perspectives, and several facts all pointing to one broader importance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, author attitude, or when only one party is actually discussed.

Transfer rule: If a stain is protein-based, then avoid heat and rinse or wash promptly with cold water first.
Error pattern: I reversed the causal effect of heat, treating warmth as helpful instead of recognizing it can set protein soils.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does heat denature this material and make it bind more tightly?” If yes, reject warm or hot treatments.
Use when: The prompt involves cleaning, biological residues, cooking-like coagulation, or any context where proteins lose structure under heat.
Boundary: Ignore this when the substance is not protein-based or when guidance depends on dissolving fats, sanitizing, or fabric-specific constraints.

Transfer rule: If a claim says an early exposure reduces a later risk, then prefer evidence directly comparing exposed individuals with later outcomes for that same item.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the conclusion’s full causal chain; distractors often switch item, authority, or durability instead of showing the claimed effect.
Diagnostic check: Underline exposure, timing, target condition, and outcome; accept only an option that explicitly links all four in one statement.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen questions about prevention, causation, or risk reduction from an intervention or habit.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for weaken, principle, analogy, or when indirect mechanism evidence is explicitly sufficient.

Transfer rule: If choices mix moral duties with business goals or capabilities, then select the option expressing an ethical obligation to stakeholders or society.
Error pattern: Success came from separating normative principles from strategic aims, technical means, and routine operational activities.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would this still matter as a right-or-wrong duty even if it reduced profit or speed?”
Use when: The question asks for ethics, social responsibility, proper conduct, or moral norms in business or organizations.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the prompt asks for competitive strategy, management functions, innovation methods, or performance objectives rather than moral standards.

Transfer rule: If an argument shifts a key term to a different category or scope midstream, then flag it as “name-confuses-reality.”
Error pattern: I focused on a provocative claim instead of checking whether the same word kept the same real-world referent throughout.
Diagnostic check: Underline the repeated term, define its intended class in each sentence, and test whether one use is literal while another is only nominal or broader/narrower.
Use when: Relevant in verbal-logic items about definitions, category mistakes, equivocation, scope shifts, or misleading labels.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the issue is ownership, part-whole inference, value judgment, or ordinary exception handling without a term-meaning shift.

Transfer rule: If a selection puzzle asks what is required after fixing one member out, then enumerate all remaining valid rosters and intersect them to find what appears every time.
Error pattern: I reasoned locally about each option instead of doing an exhaustive necessity check under the added condition.
Diagnostic check: After adding the temporary condition, list all legal 4-member sets; mark forced xor choices and one-way implications, then take the common members across every valid set.
Use when: This applies to small conditional lineup problems with exact team size, exclusive-or constraints, and one-directional dependency rules.
Boundary: Ignore this when the set is too large to enumerate quickly or the question asks for possibility rather than necessity.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “repeat offenders eventually get caught” to “most offenders eventually get caught,” then check whether it assumes most offenders are repeat offenders.
Error pattern: Scope-shift between a subset with a stated tendency and the whole group named in the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: List the subject in each premise and the conclusion; if the conclusion covers a broader population, ask what bridge assumption makes that expansion valid.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where probability over repeated acts is used to conclude something about most members of a class.
Boundary: Ignore when the premises already quantify the whole population or when the conclusion stays within the repeat-offender subset.

Transfer rule: If a group has stable goals, repeated tasks, fixed procedures, and defined roles over time, then classify it as an institutional organization.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking structural continuity and routinized operations rather than focusing on temporary cooperation or social closeness.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option for four traits: ongoing existence, clear role division, recurring work, and standardized procedures; reject any failing two or more.
Use when: Apply this on questions contrasting formal organizations with ad hoc groups, families, crowds, or one-off cooperative arrangements.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept concerns informal networks, kinship units, spontaneous collective behavior, or short-lived teams.

Transfer rule: If an argument favors one view mainly by exposing why a rival view seems implausible, then classify it as supporting by undermining the alternative.
Error pattern: Success pattern—identify the function of the reasoning, not the topic details or truth of either view.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Does the speaker present new facts or attack methods, or just pose considerations that make the competing explanation less believable?
Use when: Relevant in argument-strategy questions with two interpretations and rhetorical questions about the rival’s fit with the evidence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage chiefly offers direct proof for one view, critiques research procedure, or dismisses contrary evidence without engagement.

Transfer rule: If an argument says anonymity guarantees no bias, then check whether it assumes the decision-maker cannot identify the source by other cues.
Error pattern: Success pattern: spotting a hidden bridge from “no explicit identifier” to “no possible recognition,” an unstated necessary condition.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the person still know whose work it is without the missing label?” If yes, the fairness defense needs that assumption.
Use when: Apply to assumption questions involving blind review, anonymous processes, or claims that lack of labels eliminates favoritism or retaliation.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already rules out alternative recognition methods or when the issue is unrelated to identity-based bias.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts audience attitudes from current live performance quality, then test whether the audience mainly forms those attitudes through a different channel.
Error pattern: I weakened a premise-link locally but missed a broader dependency on where the claimed effect actually comes from.
Diagnostic check: Map the causal chain and ask, for each step, “What is the primary source of this outcome?”; prefer answers that sever the chain upstream.
Use when: Relevant in weaken questions with multi-step causal arguments about popularity, appreciation, learning, or perception.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already establishes the audience’s main exposure route or when choices only compare degrees within the same route.

Transfer rule: If an argument explains lower observed counts by lower activity rather than lower population, then prefer evidence that reduced activity directly lowers detectability.
Error pattern: I chose a fact about causes of movement instead of a fact linking movement levels to whether observers can see individuals.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would this fact make equal population size produce very different counts under different activity levels?” If not, reject it.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen questions involving sightings, counts, surveys, camouflage, motionlessness, or observation conditions versus true abundance.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion concerns actual population change supported by breeding, mortality, migration, or capture data rather than visibility.

Transfer rule: If categories split along two dimensions, then build a full 2×2 table and use complements/intersections before inferring any subgroup.
Error pattern: Mixed incompatible groups and treated one subgroup as belonging to the opposite category, causing invalid subtraction and contradiction blindness.
Diagnostic check: List each set’s dimension, verify every subtraction uses a true subset, then sum all table cells to the total and check each count is nonnegative.
Use when: Totals are partitioned by traits like subject/sex/status, and answer choices compare derived subgroup sizes or inequalities.
Boundary: Ignore when data already gives the target subgroup directly or categories are not mutually exclusive/exhaustive.

Transfer rule: If a passage explains a proposed mechanism for how something originated, then choose the option naming that hypothesis, not a broader evolution topic.
Error pattern: I generalized from an origin account to an overall development theme and picked a scope that was too broad.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is the text mainly stating how this thing first came into being, step by step, rather than discussing later change or required conditions?”
Use when: Apply this on main-idea questions where the passage describes components, roles, and assembly into a first stable unit.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage emphasizes evidence, comparisons, later adaptation, or a list of prerequisites instead of an origin mechanism.

Transfer rule: If premises create subset chains and a restriction applies only to one major, then map each person through the chain and test whether the restriction actually reaches them.
Error pattern: Confusing one person’s guaranteed attributes with another person’s possible attributes, and overextending a ban from one category to a broader one.
Diagnostic check: Draw arrows for every “all” statement, mark each person’s starting category, then ask for each option: guaranteed, impossible, or still possible?
Use when: Relevant in categorical-logic multiple choice with people, majors, institutions, and words like all, none, may, and is.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on arithmetic, causation, or extra real-world knowledge rather than formal inclusion/exclusion relations.

Transfer rule: If a passage repeatedly contrasts two media on recall, comparison, reflection, and question-asking, then choose the option stating which medium better supports thinking.
Error pattern: I picked a broad effects-on-behavior summary instead of the passage’s central evaluative comparison about cognition.
Diagnostic check: List each contrast and mark whether it concerns memory/thought quality or general habits; if most points are cognitive advantages for one medium, prefer that thesis.
Use when: The prompt asks for the main content of an argument built from repeated side-by-side comparisons of information formats.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly explains social consequences, preferences, morality, or gives no clear better-versus-worse comparison.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires continuous imbalance or severe dysfunction, then exclude brief, situational stress reactions that remain within ordinary functioning.
Error pattern: Success came from separating transient emotions from sustained disorder-level states that disrupt behavior or indicate breakdown.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is the reaction prolonged, hard to resolve, and impairing normal behavior beyond the triggering event, rather than a short-lived nervous response?
Use when: Apply this to definition-matching items contrasting clinical or crisis states with common emotional reactions to loss, withdrawal, attachment, or performance pressure.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition explicitly includes normal temporary stress, mild anxiety, or any reaction regardless of duration or impairment.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers learning from improved repeat performance, then look for a non-learning causal factor that also changes with repeated attempts.
Error pattern: I weakened with an irrelevant background fact instead of targeting the claimed cause behind the observed improvement.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option explain the performance gain without relying on experience or the stated mechanism?” If not, discard it.
Use when: The stimulus compares first-time versus later outcomes and concludes practice, learning, or experience caused the difference.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already rules out alternative changing traits or when choices address only unrelated population facts.

Transfer rule: If an argument shifts a term from an explicit category label to a hidden attribute within another phrase, then match it with choices showing the same lexical reinterpretation.
Error pattern: I focused on surface dialogue or stubbornness instead of tracking whether the key word changes grammatical role or semantic function across statements.
Diagnostic check: Underline the repeated key term, state its role in the first sentence, then test each option for the same role-preserving or role-shifting pattern.
Use when: Relevant in analogy questions involving quoted speech, repeated words, ambiguity, ellipsis, or category-versus-property confusion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the core flaw is causal reasoning, quantifiers, analogy by structure only, or pure factual inconsistency without term reuse.

Transfer rule: If asked which fact best supports a broad prevalence conclusion, then choose the option that adds direct, large-scale evidence linking many cases to the target trait.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the claim’s scope and direction, favoring population-level confirmation over local caveats, definitions, or attacks on premises.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it increase the estimated number of relevant cases across the whole domain more directly than the others?
Use when: Relevant for strengthen questions moving from sample findings to “common/almost everywhere” conclusions about frequency or distribution.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is weaken, explain, or when an option’s broad statistic is irrelevant to the specific target trait.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts overcrowding will self-correct because a destination becomes less attractive, then test whether its unique benefits remain unavailable elsewhere.
Error pattern: Success pattern: weakening by attacking the mechanism linking rising costs/problems to reduced inflow, not by merely describing harms or proposing policies.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Even if conditions worsen, do people still have strong reasons to keep choosing this place because substitutes lack key functions?”
Use when: Relevant for causal claims about migration, demand decline, market correction, or balancing effects driven by reduced attractiveness.
Boundary: Ignore when choices are already easily substitutable, or when the question asks for support, policy preference, or current severity rather than mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a choice adds comparison, extremity, or a new attribute not stated, then treat it as the likely unsupported/incorrect option.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing paraphrases of the passage from an option that introduced extra claims beyond the text.
Diagnostic check: For each option, underline every claim and match each to a specific phrase in the passage; if any part lacks direct support, flag it.
Use when: Apply this on reading-comprehension questions asking which statement is incorrect, unsupported, or inconsistent with a descriptive passage.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task requires inference beyond explicit wording or when the passage itself makes broad comparisons or evaluative rankings.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “there isn’t enough evidence for claim X” to “therefore not-X,” then flag a sufficiency-to-falsity error.
Error pattern: Treating failure to prove a position as proof of its opposite instead of recognizing uncertainty or suspension of judgment.
Diagnostic check: Rephrase the key step as “insufficient support for X, therefore opposite of X”; if that paraphrase matches, the inference is invalid.
Use when: The stimulus contrasts disputed explanations, new scholarship, or weak support, then draws a definite contrary conclusion.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument also supplies independent evidence against X, not merely criticism of the evidence for X.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “more acceptance/positive response” to “more learning/other outcome,” then require an assumption linking that intermediate state to the final outcome.
Error pattern: Strength in spotting missing bridge assumptions between a stated prerequisite and the conclusion’s stronger comparative claim.
Diagnostic check: List premises and conclusion in abstract form; if the conclusion adds a new outcome term, ask “What principle makes more of the premise-condition imply more of that outcome?”
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where the author shifts from attitude, behavior, or necessary condition language to claims about effectiveness, success, or results.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion merely restates the premise-condition or when the bridge principle is explicitly given.

Transfer rule: If premises form a one-way chain with converse traps, then infer only what is explicitly licensed and weaken conclusions to possibility unless necessity is stated.
Error pattern: Success comes from following conditional direction carefully and avoiding reversal, contraposition errors, or overstrong universal claims.
Diagnostic check: List each statement as an arrow or negation; test the candidate by deriving it stepwise, and reject any choice needing a flipped arrow or extra assumption.
Use when: Apply this to verbal-logic questions built from linked conditions about causes, requirements, or implications.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on definitions, probabilities, or outside facts rather than formal entailment from stated conditionals.

Transfer rule: If a passage presents alarming impacts first and a brief remedy second, then choose the option stating the overall call for attention/action, not the specific remedy.
Error pattern: Main-idea questions reward identifying the author’s purpose across all sentences rather than fixating on a supporting detail or proposed measure.
Diagnostic check: Summarize each sentence’s role in 3–5 words; if most roles build urgency and only one gives a solution, pick the broader purpose.
Use when: The text mixes statistics, harms, causes, and a short recommendation, and asks for the paragraph’s main idea.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, inference, title nuance, or when multiple paragraphs develop a concrete plan.

Transfer rule: If an argument’s strategy depends on performing a physical step first, then assume that step remains feasible in the real target case.
Error pattern: I matched a broad, relevant-sounding statement instead of the necessary condition that keeps the mechanism from failing.
Diagnostic check: Remove the suspected assumption and ask: would the feeding method become impossible rather than merely less common or less explained?
Use when: The conclusion says a behavior succeeds because of a sequence, tool, or organism trait that must function before later effects occur.
Boundary: Ignore when the answer choices concern only background prevalence, comparison groups, or consequences after the key enabling step.

Transfer rule: If a passage explains waste via mismatched authority and cost-bearing, then infer the principle of symmetry between decision power and payment responsibility.
Error pattern: I overfocused on surface contrast between public and private consumption instead of extracting the deeper causal criterion stated in the explanation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the author’s reason in one sentence using “because”; choose the option that preserves that because-clause, not just the direction of criticism.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension items contrasting examples, systems, or groups while justifying a judgment with an abstract reason.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a policy preference, definition, or explicit conclusion rather than the underlying evaluative principle.

Transfer rule: If a broad prediction is challenged by one recovery example, then ask whether unusual interventions created that recovery.
Error pattern: Success pattern: testing whether the cited case is representative rather than accepting it as a natural trend.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the example still support the conclusion if targeted rescue policies, protections, or habitat management were removed?”
Use when: An argument generalizes from a subgroup, region, or time period to dismiss a wider forecast or causal claim.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence already compares typical cases across the whole population and rules out special treatment.

Transfer rule: If a crime category lists specific methods, then match each option to those methods and exclude acts that are only a different predicate offense plus later use.
Error pattern: I overfocused on surface similarity and missed the legal-method boundary between unauthorized use by finding and use following a separate theft.
Diagnostic check: For each option, label the acquisition method and compare it to the definition’s enumerated methods; ask whether the taking itself changes the offense classification.
Use when: A multiple-choice item asks which case does not fit a legal or policy definition built from listed qualifying acts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the category is based on outcomes, harm level, or broad intent rather than enumerated means.

Transfer rule: If an argument answers a different issue than the accusation, then flag irrelevance rather than judging the truth of its side claims.
Error pattern: I focused on a missing alternative explanation instead of checking whether the premises actually addressed the stated claim.
Diagnostic check: Underline the conclusion and each premise; ask, “Does each premise bear directly on this exact allegation, not on safety, intent, or some nearby topic?”
Use when: Apply this on flaw questions where a speaker denies blame by citing harmlessness, good intentions, or precautions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the disputed claim itself is about safety, intent, or due care rather than whether the event occurred.

Transfer rule: If a prompt presents two seemingly opposed views as both partly supported, then choose the option that integrates them rather than one that rejects a side or overgeneralizes.
Error pattern: I collapsed a nuanced synthesis into an absolute slogan, favoring a broad negation instead of the conclusion that preserves both object-side and observer-side elements.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each option as reject, deny, or reconcile the stated viewpoints; pick the one that explicitly keeps compatible parts of both.
Use when: Relevant in verbal-logic questions comparing objectivity versus subjectivity, especially when examples support each side.
Boundary: Ignore when the stem asks for a contradiction, exclusive choice, definition recall, or evidence clearly eliminates one side.

Transfer rule: If a response argues a proposal will trigger downstream effects that reduce demand for the proposer’s own product, then classify it as self-undermining.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing indirect economic feedback instead of judging only the proposal’s stated goal.
Diagnostic check: Map the causal chain proposal → input prices/costs → buyer competitiveness → buyer demand → original industry demand; ask whether the last link harms the proposer.
Use when: Relevant in policy or market arguments involving supplier-buyer dependencies, pricing restrictions, tariffs, or protectionist measures.
Boundary: Ignore when the reply attacks premises, changes topics, or lacks a clear chain back to the original actor’s outcome.

Transfer rule: If a concept is defined by generating many possible ideas, then choose the option that emphasizes open-ended exploration rather than selecting, deducing, or applying one fixed method.
Error pattern: I confused broad idea generation with narrow decision-making and treated evaluation/selection as if it were creative expansion.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Could several qualitatively different responses all fit?”; reject any option whose task naturally aims at one determinate result.
Use when: Apply this on concept-identification questions contrasting creative, expansive cognition with analytic, convergent, or procedural problem solving.
Boundary: Ignore this check when the term is redefined by the course, domain jargon overrides common psychology usage, or the prompt asks for the source’s stated convention.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why in-person interaction is necessary, then prefer the option naming a unique channel only in-person provides over general benefits of meetings.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing indispensable mechanisms from broad, secondary, or value-judgment claims.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask, “Could this still happen reasonably well by email, chat, or video?” Eliminate any that can.
Use when: Relevant in communication-method, policy-justification, or “best illustrates necessity” questions comparing face-to-face with remote work.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for overall advantages, morale effects, implementation goals, or organization-wide consequences rather than necessity.

Transfer rule: If a choice intentionally restricts available quantity to simulate scarcity and support premium pricing or brand value, then classify it as hunger marketing.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the full mechanism, not just noticing high prices, discounts, or any generic limit.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify all three: deliberate seller-controlled restriction, perceived short supply, and a marketing/profit or brand-building purpose.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about sales tactics, pricing strategy, supply control, scarcity, exclusivity, or launch methods.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when scarcity is natural, limits are for safety/service capacity, or price changes occur without an intentional scarcity signal.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from “old rationale no longer applies” to “therefore eliminate the practice,” then require an assumption that the alternative better serves the stated current goal.
Error pattern: Strong assumption reasoning succeeds by spotting a gap between rejecting the original justification and proving the recommended replacement is preferable.
Diagnostic check: Negate the suspected assumption; if the conclusion can still stand after the negation, it is not required.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where a policy is defended only by saying its historical basis has disappeared and a new beneficiary is invoked.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already provides independent evidence that the proposed change improves the target outcome.

Transfer rule: If a passage defines a concept and then lists what the process includes, then choose the option capturing the full definition, not an opening descriptor.
Error pattern: I fixated on the first sentence’s broad characterization and missed the later scope-expanding details that carried the author’s main point.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the thesis sentence, then verify which option covers every major component mentioned after “include,” “also,” or equivalent expansion signals.
Use when: Relevant for definition, main-idea, or summary questions where the passage contrasts a general description with a more complete elaboration.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, tone, or only the first claim rather than the overall thesis.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers a broad category trait from observing only some instances, then match it with another statement that generalizes from limited cases, not from all cases or class-to-subclass inheritance.
Error pattern: I confused inductive sample-to-population reasoning with applying a property from a general class to a specific member.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each option’s logic form: some→all, all→summary, class→member, or factual assertion; choose only the same form.
Use when: The prompt asks for “same way of reasoning” and the original argument is based on surveyed examples or observed cases.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the original argument is deductive, exhaustive, definitional, or purely factual rather than inferential.

Transfer rule: If a claim says no excuse is allowed even when duty harms self-interest, then infer the argument presupposes possible conflict between duty and self-interest.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning by extracting a necessary presupposition from a definition, not by choosing a stronger moral, social, or factual claim.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What must be true for this ‘cannot be excused because it hurts oneself’ statement to make sense?” and select only that minimal assumption.
Use when: Relevant in completion questions built from definitions, especially when language contrasts obligation with personal benefit.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion requires causal, evaluative, or universal claims beyond what the definition strictly entails.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires harmful light from an environmental excess source, then exclude cases of ordinary sunlight exposure during normal outdoor work.
Error pattern: I overfocused on whether reflected glare looked artificial and missed the source/intensity condition in the definition.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is the light unusually enhanced by the environment, beyond normal exposure, and causing adverse effects?
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions about pollution, hazard, or pathology where both source and threshold matter.
