Use when: Apply this on logic puzzles with quantified claims, conditionals, and a stated count of liars or truth-tellers.
Boundary: Ignore this when statements are not about the same group/time, are not true negations, or multiple-liar counts are unknown.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “not necessarily low-fat” from a successful higher-fat diet, then prefer evidence showing that the specific fats themselves produce the benefit.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning links the study result to the conclusion’s causal gap instead of choosing facts that are merely compatible, tangential, or about compliance.
Diagnostic check: State the conclusion’s missing bridge in one sentence, then test each option by asking whether it directly supplies that bridge.
Use when: Apply on strengthen questions involving comparative studies, causal claims, and a conclusion that generalizes from observed outcomes to a property of a component.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is not causal strengthening or when an option only affects feasibility, popularity, or unrelated co-treatments.

Transfer rule: If a theory requires a standout advantage developed through sustained effort, then choose the case showing both a distinctive personal edge and deliberate cultivation of it.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching every clause of a definition, not from picking a merely positive or career-related example.
Diagnostic check: Underline required elements, then verify the option explicitly has uniqueness, effort over time, and achievement flowing from that advantage.
Use when: A multiple-choice item asks which example fits a defined theory, principle, or classification with several necessary conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the prompt asks for a counterexample, partial fit, weakest support, or a causal claim beyond definitional matching.

Transfer rule: If coverage depends on “third party” status, then classify each injured person/property by their relationship to the vehicle at the accident moment.
Error pattern: Success came from applying exclusions first, then checking whether status changes after leaving the vehicle.
Diagnostic check: Make a two-column list: excluded while in/on/owning/operating the vehicle versus potentially covered once outside it; place every claimant there.
Use when: Relevant for insurance-definition questions with shifting roles of driver, passenger, owner, cargo, onboard property, and people who exit the vehicle.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the rule is about fault, policy limits, causation, or damages rather than category-based insured-versus-third-party status.

Transfer rule: If an argument explains broad outcomes through one claimed survival motive, then attack whether that motive is actually the key driver of human cognition or behavior.
Error pattern: I weakened a side claim with a tempting factual comparison instead of targeting the mechanism linking cause to conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, underline the causal chain and ask: “Which choice directly breaks the stated why, not just a correlated assumption?”
Use when: Relevant for causal explanations that infer development, ability, or social outcomes from environmental pressure and a single behavioral premise.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for evidence, analogy, or a challenge to data accuracy rather than the explanatory mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts a new phenomenon with a traditional standard using a final “however/nevertheless,” then choose the option capturing that concluding contrast, not the earlier background.
Error pattern: Success came from weighting the author’s evaluative conclusion over descriptive setup about benefits or context.
Diagnostic check: Mark the text’s pivot word, split pre-pivot vs post-pivot claims, and ask which option matches the post-pivot judgment in broader wording.
Use when: Relevant in main-idea questions where the passage praises something first, then limits, qualifies, or rejects an equivalence afterward.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, purpose, tone, or when no real contrast pivot structures the passage.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives a sequence of recommended foods/actions, then choose the option about specific recommendations, not a broader caution theme.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from warning language and selected a summary topic instead of the passage’s primary instructional focus.
Diagnostic check: List the passage’s main function in one phrase—warning, explanation, or recommendation—and count which content occupies more of the text.
Use when: Applicable to inference/main-idea questions where both “precautions/dangers” and “what to eat/do” answers seem plausible.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly defines a concept, compares items, or gives only harms without a concrete recommended plan.

Transfer rule: If a stimulus says pairing a target with already-liked things via images changes attitudes, then infer advertisers will include images of audience-liked things, not merely reduce text.
Error pattern: I jumped from “pictorial help works” to “use less prose,” confusing a helpful method with the specific mechanism that drives the effect.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the causal chain as target + image-linked liked object -> improved attitude; choose the option that preserves every link in that chain.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/inference items about advertising, conditioning, association, or recommendations based on what causes persuasion.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion concerns costs, medium choice alone, or comparisons unsupported by any stated attitudinal-link mechanism.

Transfer rule: If an argument rebuts a causal claim by citing lifespan differences, then choose the option that links the disease’s incidence strongly to older age.
Error pattern: I favored a superficially relevant healthcare-comparison fact instead of the evidence that directly connects the rebuttal’s stated variable to the outcome.
Diagnostic check: Identify the rebuttal’s pivot variable, then ask: which option most directly makes that variable a plausible explanation for the observed rate gap?
Use when: The stimulus explains group differences by exposure time, age structure, or survival rather than by the proposed cause.
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument is about detection, reporting, or treatment effects rather than who lives long enough to develop the condition.

Transfer rule: If a definition first sets scope by excluding broad categories, then filter choices by what the stated concept is not before matching examples.
Error pattern: I matched a tempting within-year pattern while ignoring the passage’s framing about generalized vs narrowed scope and variable type.
Diagnostic check: List the allowed time scales and excluded phenomena from the definition, then verify each option fits both the time scale and the named subject.
Use when: A concept is defined by nested categories, exclusions, and examples, especially in classification or “which belongs” multiple-choice items.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for causal explanation, quantitative comparison, or when options are direct paraphrases of a single sentence.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts reduced hiring from higher labor costs, then test whether firms can offset costs through prices or other margins instead of cutting jobs.
Error pattern: I chose a background trend that does not address the stated causal link; I missed a premise-undermining alternative mechanism.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option directly weaken the step from increased cost to fewer employees, or does it merely discuss conditions around the issue?”
Use when: Apply on weaken questions involving causal economic arguments about costs, affordability, employment, or profit effects.
Boundary: Ignore when choices attack definitions, scope, or evidence quality rather than the cost-to-outcome mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a claim asks for the unsupported option, then separate stated facts from policy-value conclusions and reject any option not implied by the passage.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting an overreach: turning import facts into a claim about harm to a stakeholder without textual support.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark whether it is directly stated, necessary for the conclusion, merely plausible, or introduces a new causal effect; choose the new causal effect.
Use when: Apply to reading questions that present statistics plus a concluding policy message and ask which statement is not supported.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage explicitly discusses stakeholder impacts, tradeoffs, or causal harms/benefits.

Transfer rule: If a passage emphasizes that a text awaits capable readers to be revived and enriched by their lives, then choose the option about reader-driven renewal, not a broader side benefit.
Error pattern: I fixated on an early general statement and missed the paragraph’s controlling emphasis in its later sentences.
Diagnostic check: Identify the main verb/theme repeated near the end; ask whether the best option captures that central mechanism rather than a background purpose or partial detail.
Use when: The paragraph starts broad, then shifts to how interpretation, reception, or re-reading gives works continuing vitality.
Boundary: Ignore this when the passage mainly argues for preservation, value, or differences without stressing readers’ active role.

Transfer rule: If asked for the choice that does NOT weaken, then test each option for whether it offers an alternative cause, reverse causation, or instability; pick the one that instead supports or is neutral to the claim.
Error pattern: I treated any new causal fact linked to the same variables as a weakener, instead of checking its direction and whether it undermines the inference from correlation to causation.
Diagnostic check: For each option, write “weakens because ___” in six words; if you cannot state a clear undermining mechanism, do not mark it as a weakener.
Use when: Relevant in correlation-to-causation arguments, especially EXCEPT questions with choices about causes, effects, interventions, or trait stability.
Boundary: Ignore when the stem asks for strengthen, assumption, or inference, or when the argument is not making a causal leap.

Transfer rule: If an example shows an initially negative or discounted message becoming more accepted later as source influence fades, then treat it as the target effect.
Error pattern: I overfocused on early impact and later decline, missing the required delayed increase in evaluation after source discounting weakens.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify three parts: low-credibility source at first, content retained over time, and later attitude shift upward toward that content.
Use when: Apply this to scenarios about persuasion, memory over time, source credibility, and changing evaluations after a delay.
Boundary: Ignore this when change comes from mere repetition, boredom, new evidence, relationship changes, or any immediate credibility advantage.

Transfer rule: If a statement mixes “better than” and “not as good as,” then rewrite each clause into a single inequality direction before combining them.  
Error pattern: Comparative-order questions often fail when one phrase is converted with the wrong direction or merged into a chain too quickly.  
Diagnostic check: For every sentence, make two pairwise comparisons on paper, then verify each proposed ranking edge appears explicitly and does not reverse any original clause.  
Use when: This applies to ranking, ordering, seating, or performance problems built from chained comparative statements about several entities.  
Boundary: Ignore this when relations are numeric, conditional, or involve ties/intervals rather than strict pairwise ordering.

Transfer rule: If a treatment claim is based on removing a correlated substance, then require that substance to be causally responsible, not merely associated or downstream.
Error pattern: Causal-assumption evaluation in weaken/assumption questions; success comes from separating correlation, cause, and effect direction before considering practical details.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “If the substance were only a symptom or byproduct, would the treatment logic still hold?” If no, that causal link is required.
Use when: A stimulus cites studies showing co-occurrence plus a mechanism that can alter one factor, then concludes it will cure or treat the condition.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already establishes causation experimentally or the conclusion is only about changing a marker, not curing the condition.

Transfer rule: If a theory says domains should stay separate, then pick the option that explicitly blocks advantages in one domain from being converted into power or gain in another.
Error pattern: I focused on domain specialization instead of boundary-crossing restrictions between domains.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does this choice contain a rule preventing status, office, wealth, or skill from transferring across social spheres?
Use when: Definitions stress separate fields, anti-monopoly, limits on spillover, or preventing one advantage from dominating society.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept is about excellence within one field, role competence, or general inequality without cross-domain conversion.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers broad public opinion from survey data, then verify the surveyed group matches the target population on relevant traits.
Error pattern: Mistaking a specialized or unusually exposed subgroup for a representative sample of everyone.
Diagnostic check: Ask: who was surveyed, how do they differ from the general public, and could that difference systematically change the reported attitudes?
Use when: Polls, percentages, or study results are used to rebut or support claims about society at large.
Boundary: Ignore this when the sample is randomly drawn from the target population or representativeness is independently established.

Transfer rule: If a passage condemns how debate is framed, then choose the option targeting that framing’s harm, not the triggering incident or media attention.
Error pattern: I fixated on surface talk about public uproar and reporting instead of the author’s evaluative thesis about symbolic generalization.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state in one sentence what the author says is wrong and with what consequence; match both parts to an option.
Use when: The passage opens with a vivid anecdote, then shifts to commentary about labels, stereotypes, simplification, or broader social discussion.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for a factual detail, the anecdote’s direct cause, or a plainly stated group trait.

Transfer rule: If asked for a passage title, then choose the option that best captures the author’s central claim and emphasis across the whole text, not just one example or theme word.
Error pattern: Success comes from identifying the repeated value judgment and purpose statement rather than focusing on descriptive background details.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, summarize the passage in 8–12 words naming topic + stance; select only the title that matches both.
Use when: Apply this to main-title questions where the passage mixes context, examples, and a concluding appeal or evaluation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, inference, tone, or a heading for only one paragraph.

Transfer rule: If a policy’s goal depends on current suppliers continuing the activity, then test whether the policy removes their incentive to produce the thing being redirected.
Error pattern: Success came from checking total supply effects, not just whether distribution changes toward the target institutions.
Diagnostic check: Ask: after the rule, will the amount found or available likely rise, stay flat, or fall because key actors stop participating?
Use when: The argument proposes a restriction meant to increase access, availability, or research use by changing who may receive goods.
Boundary: Ignore when the policy’s success does not rely on voluntary supplier participation or when supply is fixed regardless of incentives.

Transfer rule: If a claim says overreliance on a tool weakens an ability, then prefer evidence showing lighter users perform that ability better in similar tasks.
Error pattern: Strengthen questions are best answered by direct comparative evidence, not by neutral facts, partial exceptions, or points that also support the opposing side.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it increase the gap between high-use and low-use groups on the target ability without introducing a rival explanation?
Use when: Relevant for causal or comparative arguments about technology, habits, dependence, and skill development across groups.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task asks for weakening, assumption, explanation, or when options address only definition or feasibility rather than comparative performance.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires awareness or regulation of one’s own thinking/attention/learning, then choose the option showing deliberate self-monitoring or control of cognition.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the definition’s core mechanism rather than surface references to mind, belief, or judgment.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is the person explicitly noticing, evaluating, or adjusting their own mental process?” If yes, it fits; if only discussing objects, others, or outcomes, reject it.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching items about self-regulation, learning strategies, attention control, reflection, or monitoring one’s cognition.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target concept concerns general behavior, physiological aids, or reasoning about external states without self-directed cognitive control.

Transfer rule: If a court upholds an agency’s assignment despite a proximity policy, then prefer the option affirming the assignment’s legality under the governing zoning scheme.
Error pattern: Success comes from choosing the basis that directly justifies the judgment, not abstract statements about policy, geography, or parental preference.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Which option, if accepted as true, by itself makes rejecting the lawsuit legally coherent?”
Use when: Apply this on legal-reasoning MCQs asking for the most likely basis for a ruling after an administrative allocation or districting decision.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for general principles, policy critique, or facts undermining the legality of the administrative act.

Transfer rule: If a claim about the public relies on a subgroup survey, then test whether that subgroup is representative before accepting the conclusion.
Error pattern: Treating an experienced or specialized sample as a stand-in for the general population.
Diagnostic check: Ask: who was surveyed, how do they differ from the target population, and could those differences affect the opinion being measured?
Use when: An argument infers broad public attitudes from responses of industry members, enthusiasts, experts, or other unusually exposed groups.
Boundary: Ignore this when the sample is shown to be representative through valid sampling methods or the conclusion is only about that subgroup.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires work done for an employer or using its resources to fulfill assigned duties, then choose the option explicitly tied to commissioned tasks or unit conditions.
Error pattern: I focused on who invented something, not whether the invention arose from assigned work or organizational resources.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each option for employer assignment, task connection, and use of organizational materials; reject any missing these core conditions.
Use when: Apply this to definitions distinguishing personal creations from employment-related, institutional, or duty-based outputs.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the category is defined by novelty, usefulness, ownership transfer, or patent status rather than work relationship.

Transfer rule: If an argument explains policy outcomes by elected officials tracking voters, then choose a completion linking those officials’ positions or reelection incentives to voters’ preferences.
Error pattern: Success came from preserving the argument’s causal chain rather than jumping to side claims about the issue itself.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map subject → motive → outcome, and reject any option that introduces a new topic, norm, or unsupported cause.
Use when: Relevant for strengthen/completion items about democratic decision-making, accountability, public opinion, elections, or policy responsiveness.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for moral evaluation, factual prediction, or contains evidence that actors are insulated from voter pressure.

Transfer rule: If asked which option is outside a passage’s scope, then map each option to an explicit statement or necessary paraphrase and eliminate only the one introducing new content.
Error pattern: I accepted a directly stated sentence as out-of-scope and failed to distinguish explicit support from an unsupported elaboration.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark E (explicit), P (clear paraphrase), I (reasonable inference), or N (new claim); choose only N as the answer.
Use when: Relevant in reading-comprehension items asking “not included,” “not supported,” or “outside the discussion” among closely related statements.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for the best inference, main idea, attitude, or a conclusion beyond the passage.

Transfer rule: If one group suffers more from the same harmful condition, then prefer an option giving that group fewer unaffected alternatives or the others extra protected access to the needed resource.
Error pattern: Success pattern: explained a comparative outcome by identifying a mechanism that differentiates groups under the same cause, rather than restating exposure or severity.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this choice create an asymmetry in access, resilience, or compensation that directly links the shared cause to the unequal effect?”
Use when: Comparative weaken/explain questions where all groups face the same stressor but one declines more.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for causation of the base effect only, or when options do not introduce any group-differentiating mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a term requires a centered, interconnected multi-city region, then choose the option naming a functional regional cluster, not a broad administrative area.
Error pattern: Success came from matching every definitional element instead of relying on familiar geography or scale alone.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify four boxes: multiple cities, differing city levels, one or two core metros, and strengthening transport/economic links forming an integrated whole.
Use when: Apply this to definition-match questions about regional systems, especially where some choices are provinces, macro-regions, or politically grouped territories.
Boundary: Ignore this when the concept is purely administrative, legal, or cultural and does not require networked city integration.

Transfer rule: If two speakers argue opposite policies from different causal claims, then infer only a shared background assumption required by both arguments, not either speaker’s disputed rule.
Error pattern: I overcommitted to one speaker’s conditional and treated it as common ground instead of extracting the minimal overlap between both positions.
Diagnostic check: List each argument’s premise-conclusion chain; mark claims used by both, and reject any candidate that appears in only one chain or depends on a subgroup.
Use when: Two viewpoints contrast on effects, audiences, or policy, and the question asks what they agree on or what the dialogue supports.
Boundary: Ignore this when one speaker explicitly endorses the other’s principle or the prompt asks for the stronger, speaker-specific commitment.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion says “if everyone did X when feasible, a large bad effect would drop,” then check that people currently fail to do X in feasible cases.
Error pattern: This is an assumption-of-impact question; the key is spotting a needed gap between current behavior and the proposed changed behavior.
Diagnostic check: Negate the candidate assumption and ask whether the argument’s reduction claim loses support because no behavior would actually change.
Use when: Relevant for conditional policy arguments comparing “would be otherwise” outcomes and proposing widespread feasible substitution.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already states current noncompliance or relies instead on a different causal link.

Transfer rule: If a claim says “no one succeeds who does X,” then infer only “successful → not X,” and combine it with any existence claims.
Error pattern: Treated a necessary condition as a graded causal relationship instead of making a strict conditional plus existence-based deduction.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each sentence into arrows/quantifiers, note at least one existing subgroup member, then test which option is forced in every case.
Use when: Arguments mix universals, negatives, and existential claims about subgroups, especially with “no,” “all,” “some,” or “significant number.”
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic for questions requiring outside facts, probabilities, or comparative/causal strength not stated in the premises.

Transfer rule: If influence comes from peers comparing with one another and it pushes someone to conform in attitudes, values, or behavior, then classify it as peer pressure.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matched every required element of the definition instead of choosing any social influence or conflict.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Are the actors peers, is there comparison within the group, and does that comparison create pressure to conform? Require all three.
Use when: Relevant for definition-matching items about social influence, conformity, group norms, or interpersonal pressure.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when influence comes from authority, negotiation, cooperation, or competition without conformity pressure among equals.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists several negative reading trends across places/groups, then choose the broad option summarizing the overall condition, not a single cause or subgroup.
Error pattern: Success comes from synthesizing multiple details into one umbrella claim and resisting answers that zoom in on one example.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each sentence as scope, evidence, or example; pick the choice covering all evidence without adding a new focus.
Use when: The question asks for the most accurate summary or main idea of an informational passage with several supporting findings.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for a specific detail, cause-effect relation, or the passage centers on one clearly dominant point only.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers causation from a correlation, then first test whether a third factor could explain both the behavior and the outcome.
Error pattern: I favored a direct countereffect within the proposed cause instead of checking for a stronger confounder behind the observed group difference.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Could one characteristic disproportionately shared by the treatment group independently raise the measured outcome?” If yes, prefer that weakening move.
Use when: Relevant in observational comparisons, especially when researchers compare users vs nonusers and infer prevention or health benefits.
Boundary: Ignore when the study is randomized or when the candidate alternative factor is already controlled for or unrelated to the outcome.

Transfer rule: If a definition requires support to a product’s own producers that increases competitive advantage, then select any policy help meeting that effect, not only direct cash or price payments.
Error pattern: I matched a familiar subsidy form too narrowly and ignored broader policy assistance explicitly included by the definition.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark recipient, government support, agricultural producer/product link, and whether it improves domestic or international competitiveness; reject any option missing one.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions with inclusive phrases like “including” or “other preferential policies.”
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition restricts support to explicit payment mechanisms or excludes indirect policy assistance.

Transfer rule: If a category is defined as normal and unavoidable within the economy, then exclude unemployment caused by one-off external disasters or accidents.
Error pattern: I overfocused on voluntary quitting and ignored whether the cause was internal, recurring labor-market frictions versus abnormal shocks.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: would this unemployment still arise in a stable economy without extraordinary events? If no, reject it as natural.
Use when: Apply this on classification questions contrasting structural/frictional/job-discipline cases with disaster-driven, war-driven, or sudden exogenous destruction cases.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the definition explicitly includes temporary disaster effects or uses a broader nonstandard meaning of natural.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives a forward causal chain and one later effect is stated as necessary, then infer from an earlier trigger to that necessary effect.
Error pattern: I treated a possible outcome as guaranteed and used an invalid contrapositive on a one-way causal statement.
Diagnostic check: Trace the chain step by step; mark each link as certain or probable, and reject any choice that flips direction or negates a non-biconditional.
Use when: Relevant in conditional/causal arguments with mixed certainty terms like “will,” “probably,” “might,” and multiple intermediate consequences.
Boundary: Ignore when the answer depends on reversing a causal link, denying a sufficient condition, or asserting certainty from a merely possible result.

Transfer rule: If a passage says evidence “indicated,” “suggested,” or “may be,” then choose the option that matches the directly observed trait, not the broader hypothesis.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating reported findings from speculative interpretations and from avoiding claims strengthened beyond the text.
Diagnostic check: Mark each answer as observation, inference, or extrapolation; reject any choice that adds certainty, causation, exclusivity, or methods/results not explicitly stated.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension questions summarizing research reports, fossils, scans, or scientific claims with hedging language.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the author’s implication, strongest supported inference, or knowledge beyond the passage.

Transfer rule: If a behavior is voluntary, outside formal duties, and helps coworkers or the organization, then classify it as organizational citizenship behavior.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating discretionary, prosocial extras from required performance, coercion, or harmful conduct.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is it required by the job? Is it freely chosen? Does it improve team or organizational functioning?
Use when: Apply this to workplace-behavior questions contrasting formal obligations, compliance, conflict, and helpful voluntary acts.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept asked is task performance, counterproductive behavior, or anything defined by formal role requirements.

Transfer rule: If clues compare sums before/after swapping people, then convert each statement into inequalities and subtract shared terms instead of inferring pairwise order directly.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from group comparisons, treating sum relations as immediate individual rankings and not checking consistency across all constraints.
Diagnostic check: Write symbolic weights, derive all pairwise inequalities by cancellation, then verify the final full ordering satisfies every original statement simultaneously.
Use when: Apply this on ranking problems with multiple entities, swap/exchange wording, and comparisons involving pair totals or combined weights.
Boundary: Ignore this when each clue already gives direct individual comparisons only, with no grouped sums, swaps, or near-equality conditions.

Transfer rule: If a passage states achievements plus a warning and a must-do response, then choose the option expressing the required future action, not the background fact.
Error pattern: I focused on a literal detail explicitly mentioned and missed the author’s main prescriptive conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Mark clauses as fact, contrast, and imperative; before answering, ask which option matches the final “must/should/need” claim.
Use when: Relevant for main-idea or “described in words” questions with praise-then-gap structure and a closing policy or action statement.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a directly stated detail, a specific example, or a purely factual summary without recommendation language.

Transfer rule: If a claim says “only if condition, then result,” and the argument gives the result, then infer the condition by mapping it as result → required condition.
Error pattern: Success pattern: correctly recognizing a necessary-condition structure and using affirmation of the consequent only when the statement explicitly makes the condition necessary.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the premise into “result only if condition” or “if result, then condition”; verify the conclusion states the condition from an observed result-role.
Use when: Relevant in analogy questions featuring “only,” “only if,” “can...only when,” licenses, qualifications, prerequisites, or required background conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when the premise is “if condition, then result” without exclusivity, or when the argument instead denies the result, denies the condition, or mixes causal language.

Transfer rule: If a statement says learning X is necessary to achieve Y under condition Z, then infer the contrapositive: without X, not Y when Z occurs.
Error pattern: Mistook a recommendation/causal rationale for the strongest logical consequence, instead of testing necessity and contraposition.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the claim as “If want Y under Z, must have X”; then ask, “If not X, does Y fail under Z?”
Use when: Arguments use “must,” “have to,” “only if,” or advice linking preparation/ability to success in a future condition.
Boundary: Ignore when the statement is merely motivational, probabilistic, or about preferences rather than a necessary condition.

Transfer rule: If an argument prefers a mediocre option over one with higher upside and downside, then look for a principle privileging avoiding the worst case over pursuing the best case.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the argument’s decision criterion, not surface topic overlap or broad political ideals.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, state the premise contrast as “steady middle vs extreme high/low,” then ask which principle converts that contrast into a preference.
Use when: Relevant in strengthen/principle questions involving tradeoffs, risk asymmetry, or comparisons between consistent mediocrity and volatile extremes.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument hinges on popularity, fairness, causal effects, or likely average outcomes rather than worst-case avoidance.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from a whole class to one member, then first verify the class term keeps the same meaning and level throughout.
Error pattern: Equivocation or identity shift between the category itself and a representative member makes a seemingly valid inheritance step invalid.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the premise and conclusion with explicit subjects; ask whether the exact same term refers to the same object/class in both statements.
Use when: Apply this to categorical arguments using class membership, subclass examples, or property transfer from groups to individuals.
Boundary: Ignore this when terms are explicitly fixed, levels are matched, and the only issue is factual truth rather than term identity.

Transfer rule: If an authority uses nonbinding encouragement plus supportive measures to influence people within its jurisdiction toward a policy goal, then classify it as administrative guidance.
Error pattern: I overfocused on official public announcements and missed the required combination of administrative主体, soft means, local counterpart consent, and policy purpose.
Diagnostic check: Verify four boxes: within jurisdiction; actor is an administrative organ; method is advice/call/consultation/information rather than order/contract; target cooperates voluntarily, often with incentives.
Use when: The choices mix warnings, contracts, diplomatic initiatives, and local policy encouragement by government bodies.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the act is mandatory enforcement, a commercial agreement, or foreign/intergovernmental conduct outside ordinary domestic administration.

Transfer rule: If one speaker reframes a stated reason as merely a sign of a broader concern, then look for disagreement about whether the stated reason is the only reason.
Error pattern: Mistaking a dispute about underlying purpose or motivation for a dispute about effectiveness, scale, legality, or factual impact.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What explicit reason does each speaker give, and does the reply broaden, narrow, or reject that reason rather than assess outcomes?”
Use when: Dialogue contrasts “for the sake of X” with “you’re missing the point” and introduces a deeper rationale behind the same action.
Boundary: Ignore when the reply directly challenges predictions, quantities, legality, or causal sufficiency instead of reframing the action’s purpose.

Transfer rule: If an argument recommends a choice from an early average advantage, then test whether later or distributional outcomes could reverse that advantage for the stated goal.
Error pattern: Confusing short-term group averages with long-term or target-specific success; good reasoning spots timeframe and metric mismatch.
Diagnostic check: Compare the conclusion’s goal/time horizon with the premise’s measure; ask whether another measure later, or at the high end, could favor the alternative.
Use when: The claim moves from “initial earnings/statistics” to advice about what people should choose to maximize future income.
Boundary: Ignore when premise and conclusion use the same population, metric, and time period, with no broader future goal implied.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives a cautious causal claim plus a mechanism, then choose the option that restates that claim at the same strength without adding effects.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the author’s main conclusion and avoiding choices that exaggerated, narrowed, or introduced unsupported side claims.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, underline the conclusion phrase and compare each option for scope, certainty, and whether every key idea appears in the passage.
Use when: Apply this on argument-meaning questions where one sentence states a thesis and another sentence merely explains how it could happen.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for flaw analysis, inference beyond the text, or evaluation of evidence quality.

Transfer rule: If a premise fixes one variable’s value, then substitute it into every conditional and use the contrapositive to find which remaining assignment would force a contradiction.
Error pattern: Success came from reducing chained conditionals after applying the given fact, instead of checking choices in isolation.
Diagnostic check: Translate each statement into if-then form, mark any antecedents made impossible by the fixed fact, then test whether a choice activates a rule whose conclusion clashes with that fact.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice logic problems with several conditional predictions plus one observed outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when statements are probabilistic, comparative, or not strict conditionals, or when the task is not contradiction detection.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists concrete mechanisms and outcomes, then choose the option that restates only those supported effects without adding stronger claims.
Error pattern: Success comes from evidence-matching and paraphrase alignment rather than picking the most positive or broad summary.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark every claim as stated, implied, or added; reject any option containing even one unsupported addition.
Use when: Relevant for reading-comprehension questions comparing a new method with an old one through multiple stated benefits and predicted impacts.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the task requires outside knowledge, causal evaluation beyond the text, or selecting a partially true statement.

Transfer rule: If several proposals each claim an exclusive “only choice,” then test pairwise compatibility first and prefer combinations without mutual exclusivity.
Error pattern: I treated individually plausible plans as jointly feasible, ignoring that multiple “only/ no other choice” statements cannot both hold.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each claim in logic form; mark any statement asserting uniqueness, then see whether accepting two statements makes either deny the other.
Use when: Relevant in feasibility/selection questions with several proposals, especially where wording includes either-or, only, necessary, or no other choice.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when options ask for independent truth, multiple plans can coexist by design, or exclusivity language is clearly rhetorical rather than logical.

Transfer rule: If an argument cites a source’s two inconsistent beliefs, then check whether it gives a reason to treat one belief as false rather than the other.
Error pattern: Mistaking a conflict in someone’s commitments for a refutation, instead of noticing the unsupported choice between them.
Diagnostic check: Identify the two claims attributed to the same party; ask, “What independent premise selects which claim to reject?”
Use when: Relevant in flaw questions where a conclusion is drawn from inconsistency, hypocrisy, or self-undermining statements by one speaker or group.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument actually supplies a principle, evidence, or hierarchy that clearly resolves the inconsistency.

Transfer rule: If an argument recommends a treatment from symptom matching alone, then prefer an option showing that treatment directly impedes recovery or worsens the target condition.
Error pattern: Strong weakening succeeds by attacking the recommendation’s causal assumption, not by giving alternatives, background facts, or partial support.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does this choice make the proposed remedy less effective or harmful for the same case, rather than merely mentioning another remedy or benefit?
Use when: Relevant in “directly weaken” questions about advice, interventions, or prescriptions justified by observed symptoms.
Boundary: Ignore when choices only broaden context, describe unrelated stages, or compare treatments without showing a direct conflict with the recommendation.

Transfer rule: If a public-finance question defines an activity as borrowing/lending with later repayment, then choose the option showing the government raising or providing funds through a debt instrument.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the formal mechanism, not the surface topic of “government money.”
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is there a debtor-creditor relationship, a principal amount, and a repayment/interest obligation? If any element is missing, reject it.
Use when: Relevant for distinguishing credit financing from taxes, fines, fees, subsidies, or ordinary enterprise transactions in public-sector contexts.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the concept asked is general revenue collection, punishment, ownership change, or non-repayable fiscal transfers.

Transfer rule: If a logic option question gives conditional constraints, then test each candidate against every rule, treating implications only in the stated direction.
Error pattern: I accepted choices by checking only whether triggers were absent, and I failed to verify the full consequence chain for each listed condition.
Diagnostic check: For each option, write T/F for every rule as “trigger present?” and, if yes, “required result present?”; reject on the first violated rule.
Use when: Apply this to sequencing or arrangement problems with adjacency limits plus several “if...then...” statements and answer choices as complete assignments.
Boundary: Ignore this when rules are biconditionals, quantified, or open-ended construction tasks instead of fixed-option validation.

Transfer rule: If a concept requires collected, sorted, and aggregated expressions from the public, then exclude examples that are merely administrative practices or policy procedures without a public-expression component.
Error pattern: Confusing governance mechanisms influenced by society with the summarized public sentiment itself.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: where are the public voices, how are they gathered, and is the result an opinion climate rather than an institutional measure?
Use when: The stem defines a social-science term by necessary elements and asks for the non-example.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target concept includes official actions, procedures, or outcomes even without public participation.

Transfer rule: If an argument concludes “no harm” from normal operation traits, then check for inherent byproducts or long-term effects under normal operation, not just accident scenarios.
Error pattern: I focused on dramatic exceptional events instead of attacking the conclusion with a routine, built-in source of harm.
Diagnostic check: List whether each choice describes accident risk, social cost, economic burden, or unavoidable normal-output harm; prefer the one that directly contradicts “no harm” during standard functioning.
Use when: Relevant for weaken questions where a broad safety claim is inferred from limited benefits or clean operation premises.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion is only about accident risk, cost, noise, or public acceptance rather than overall harm.

Transfer rule: If a conclusion says an exposure is harmless because one measured marker shows no damage, then look for other health outcomes in the exposed group that the study did not test.
Error pattern: Arguments overgeneralize from limited negative findings to a broad safety claim.
Diagnostic check: List the exact evidence measured, then ask whether any unmeasured but relevant harms could still occur despite those results.
Use when: A study-based claim moves from “no effect found on this indicator/sample/timeframe” to “no health effect overall.”
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is explicitly limited to the tested outcome, population, and period, or alternatives are merely concern, effort, or unrelated background rates.

Transfer rule: If an argument dismisses objections solely because the objectors are interested parties, then test whether it assumes interested parties’ reasons are automatically invalid.
Error pattern: Confusing source bias with argument quality; treating who said it as enough to reject what was said.
Diagnostic check: Restate the argument with “these critics may be self-interested, but their reasons could still be sound”; if the conclusion weakens, that assumption is required.
Use when: A stimulus moves from opponents’ motives, incentives, or affiliations to “there are no good objections” or “the proposal should proceed.”
Boundary: Ignore when the reasoning independently evaluates the objections’ content rather than disqualifying them by source.

Transfer rule: If a passage highlights current uses plus calls for further improvement to meet future mission needs, then prefer the option stating a future development direction over one stating only a present limitation.
Error pattern: I fixated on a mentioned drawback and treated it as the main takeaway instead of weighing the author’s overall thrust and forward-looking claim.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each sentence as benefit, limitation, or forecast; choose the option matching the dominant concluding category.
Use when: Apply this to expository passages that mix advantages, constraints, ongoing research, and explicit future-oriented language.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a narrow factual detail, exception, or strongest immediate limitation rather than the passage’s overall conclusion.

Transfer rule: If a choice states fluid amount per unit time in volume units, then mark it as volume flow; if it gives distance, area, storage, or totals without time-normalized volume, reject it.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the formal definition to units instead of being distracted by impressive water facts.
Diagnostic check: Underline the measured quantity and denominator; accept only forms like cubic measure per second/day/year, not speed, area, length, or static capacity.
Use when: The question asks you to classify physical descriptions by a definition involving quantity passing a surface over time.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the target concept is mass-based flow or when the passage is not about through-surface rate.

Transfer rule: If a boldface claim is an unsupported forecast used as evidence and a later boldface is what “clearly can be concluded,” then treat the first as support and the second as the main conclusion.
Error pattern: Mistaking a premise-level subclaim for an intermediate conclusion because it sounds inferential or summarizes evidence.
Diagnostic check: For each boldface, ask: “Is this offered without support here?” and “Does any later sentence depend on it, or does the argument stop with it?”
Use when: Boldface-role questions with forecasts, causal estimates, or quantified components feeding a final overall judgment.
Boundary: Ignore when the first boldface is explicitly derived from prior premises or when the second is used to justify a further claim.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from an overall group average to a claim about one subgroup or species, then test whether that subgroup could break the broader pattern.
Error pattern: Illicitly applying a population-level trend to a specific case without evidence that the subset tracks the whole set.
Diagnostic check: Identify the comparison class, then ask: “Does the stated average include many categories, and is there any direct data for the named subset alone?”
Use when: Relevant in arguments about averages, rates, or tendencies for broad groups that infer a result for one identified subtype.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument provides subgroup-specific evidence or a rule explicitly linking the subgroup to the overall pattern.

Transfer rule: If an argument predicts a new technology will be an effective alternative, then prefer a choice adding another adoption-relevant advantage over the current standard.
Error pattern: Success came from matching support to the conclusion’s scope instead of fixating only on the stated efficiency premises.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option strengthen overall substitutability or desirability without introducing a major limitation, comparison reversal, or narrower use case?”
Use when: Relevant in strengthen questions comparing an emerging product with an incumbent and concluding it will be a practical alternative.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for weakening, explaining a mechanism, or selecting a statement about constraints rather than support.

Transfer rule: If a claim infers causation from a correlation, then look for a third variable that differs between groups and directly explains the outcome.
Error pattern: I focused on a side effect of the proposed cause instead of testing whether the observed link could be spurious due to confounding.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does any option identify another group difference tied to the outcome that could account for the correlation without the claimed cause?”
Use when: Relevant in survey, observational, or non-randomized comparison problems where one group shows lower risk or better performance.
Boundary: Ignore when the evidence is randomized/controlled or when choices only discuss irrelevant side effects, mechanisms, or preferences unrelated to the outcome.

Transfer rule: If an argument says a feature does not establish category membership because a further capacity is unproven, then infer it assumes that capacity is required for the category.
Error pattern: Correct pattern: identifying the hidden necessary condition linking missing evidence to rejection of the stronger claim.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “If the item lacked this specific capacity but had all stated evidence, could it still count?” If yes, the argument fails; if no, that requirement is assumed.
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where the conclusion denies classification and the premise only shows an insufficient indicator.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument attacks evidence quality, causation, or scope rather than requiring a missing definitional criterion.

Transfer rule: If one bold claim is introduced as what others argue and later evidence is said to suggest the opposite, then treat the first as an opposed position and the second as the author’s conclusion.
Error pattern: Confusing a reported viewpoint with evidence, instead of tracking who endorses each statement.
Diagnostic check: For each boldface claim, ask: who says this, does the author endorse it, and is later support aimed for or against it?
Use when: Boldface-role questions with attributed claims, contrast words, and study/results language.
Boundary: Ignore when both bold statements are plainly premises or both are endorsed conclusions in a chain.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “ineffective” from “does not produce X,” then look for an assumption linking effectiveness to requiring X.
Error pattern: I chose a statement about what is needed for X instead of what is needed for effectiveness; I matched a nearby concept, not the conclusion’s key term.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the argument as premises → conclusion and ask, “What bridge makes these premises sufficient for that exact conclusion term?”
Use when: Relevant in assumption questions where the conclusion introduces an evaluative term like effective, justified, valid, or good.
Boundary: Ignore when the missing link is causal, definitional, or about comparing alternatives rather than connecting a premise property to the conclusion standard.

Transfer rule: If a motive question asks which statement is wrong, then match each option to explicit text support and reject any option adding a new motive not stated.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from nearby themes and treated a plausible implication as unsupported while missing the truly invented motive.
Diagnostic check: For each option, label it explicit, reasonable paraphrase, or new addition; if it introduces vanity, legacy, or intent absent from the passage, flag it.
Use when: Apply on reading-comprehension items about character intention, attitude, or psychology where several choices restate similar sentiments.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on outside literary context, irony, or earlier plot details not contained in the quoted passage.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives background causes and ends with a clear consequence, then choose the option stating that final consequence as the main idea.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating supporting context from the author’s central claim and following the argument to its endpoint.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the topic sentence or concluding claim, list which sentences are evidence, and verify the option matches the claim, not the background.
Use when: Apply this on main-idea questions with cause-effect chains, forecasts, and several industries or domains mentioned.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a title, detail, purpose, attitude, or when the passage is balanced without a single dominant conclusion.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers profitability from adoption and income growth, then test whether outside support or selection effects could explain both without true profitability.
Error pattern: I accepted a broad comparative downside instead of attacking the causal link from “they grow it” to “it benefits them financially.”
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could growers adopt it and report higher income even while losing money on it?” Look for subsidies, mandates, bundled contracts, or offsetting payments.
Use when: A claim uses observed participation or revenue increase as evidence that a practice is beneficial to the participant.
Boundary: Ignore when the argument already controls for external incentives and directly measures net profit or welfare.

Transfer rule: If efficiency should lower use but data show no drop, then look for a concurrent change that creates new demand and offsets savings.
Error pattern: Success came from applying a reconcile-the-paradox strategy: find a hidden factor that makes both the expectation and the observed trend true.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, ask: “Does this option provide an offsetting mechanism linked to the same change, rather than a side effect, restatement, or unrelated alternative cause?”
Use when: Use for strengthen-explanation questions featuring an apparent contradiction between a theoretical prediction and aggregate empirical results.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is causal proof, numerical inference, or when an option merely shifts energy elsewhere without explaining unchanged total use.

Transfer rule: If an argument infers “not in subgroup X” from “lacks marker Y,” then require that every member of X could not have lost Y earlier.
Error pattern: I treated a majority/typicality claim as sufficient for a necessary-assumption question that needed an exception-free condition.
Diagnostic check: Negate the candidate assumption; if subgroup X could ever lose marker Y and the conclusion could still fail, that assumption is required.
Use when: Necessary-assumption questions involve classifying an item by presence/absence of a trait that can change over time or be destroyed.
Boundary: Ignore this when the conclusion is statistical, comparative, or explicitly about “most/some” rather than ruling out membership categorically.

Transfer rule: If a passage presents a finding and then emphasizes its broader implication, then choose the option capturing that implication, not the supporting detail.
Error pattern: I focused on the most concrete new fact and missed the author’s main takeaway or purpose.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state in 8–12 words the passage’s central claim; reject any choice that only restates one piece of evidence.
Use when: The passage includes background belief, new research, and a concluding “this means/may need to” statement.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific detail, data point, or direct finding rather than the main point.

Transfer rule: If someone passively gets an unneeded core item and later buys related extras mainly to justify or complete it, then classify it as this effect.
Error pattern: Mistaking one-off accessory or task-driven purchases for the broader escalation triggered by an accidental possession.
Diagnostic check: Verify all three: the first item was obtained unintentionally, it was not needed, and the later purchases were only linked to making that item usable or meaningful.
Use when: The scenario involves a gifted, won, or incidental item followed by additional category-related spending.
Boundary: Ignore when the first item was intentionally sought, already needed, or the follow-up purchase serves an independent practical purpose.

Transfer rule: If an argument opens with a broad claim and later uses “for instance” or examples, then treat the opening supported claim as the main conclusion unless later language overrides it.
Error pattern: Mistaking an illustrative premise or explanation for the author’s ultimate point.
Diagnostic check: Remove the example sentence(s); if the remaining claim still stands as the point being defended, choose that, not the illustration.
Use when: The stimulus includes a general thesis followed by evidence, causal explanation, or a concrete example introduced by indicator words.
Boundary: Ignore this when the opening statement is merely background or a definition and a later sentence receives the actual support.

Transfer rule: If a scenario involves an opponent in a zero-sum contest and one side changes its tactic based on predicted opposing moves, then classify it as a matrix game.
Error pattern: I overfocused on direct one-to-one matching rules and missed the adaptive best-response requirement under competitive opposition.
Diagnostic check: Verify three points: two competing sides, gains and losses are strictly opposed, and at least one side selects a strategy in response to the other’s expected action.
Use when: Apply this to contests, matches, or adversarial negotiations where lineup, order, timing, or choice can be strategically adjusted.
Boundary: Ignore this when outcomes allow compromise, shared benefit, or no reactive strategic adjustment to an opponent.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives one positive counterexample after a broad negative tendency, then infer only a limited “not all” exception, not a universal claim.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching quantifiers carefully and treating contrast words as signals that the second statement restricts the first.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, rewrite each claim as all/some/none/not all, then see whether the evidence supports existence, universality, or merely an exception.
Use when: Relevant in verbal-logic questions mixing general statements with anecdotes, exceptions, or contrast markers like however, but, although.
Boundary: Ignore this when the example is hypothetical, unrelated to the general claim, or the task asks for causal explanation rather than logical inference.

Transfer rule: If a definition contrasts ordinary orientation with an opposite one while rejecting unrestricted novelty, then choose the option showing a deliberate contrarian stance under specific conditions.
Error pattern: I overvalued a paraphrase of the wording instead of matching the operational features in the definition.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark whether it shows opposite direction to the usual approach and whether it is a disciplined small-probability strategy, not mere rephrasing or brainstorming.
Use when: Apply this on definition-matching questions involving “reverse,” “opposite,” “contrary,” or emphasis on uncommon-but-structured thinking.
Boundary: Ignore this when the definition targets creativity, causal backtracking, or broad divergence rather than opposition to common orientation.

Transfer rule: If a passage explicitly praises growth, influence, and social value while rejecting dismissive views, then choose a clearly positive attitude.
Error pattern: Success comes from aggregating evaluative cues across the whole passage instead of isolating one factual sentence.
Diagnostic check: Underline value-laden phrases; if most are approving and opposing views are criticized, mark the stance as affirmative.
Use when: Apply to attitude or tone questions about a subject discussed with trends, impacts, and judgments.
Boundary: Ignore this when the author mainly reports mixed evidence, quotes others without endorsement, or uses irony/sarcasm.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives category definitions by thresholds, then map all intervals and choose only what is explicitly entailed.
Error pattern: I overread quantifiers and exception claims instead of reasoning from the full partition created by the definitions.
Diagnostic check: Draw three bins—below lower cutoff, within range, above upper cutoff—and test each option against those bins word by word.
Use when: Definitions classify cases by numeric ranges, especially with terms like lower than, higher than, within, audible, or called.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task needs outside facts, causal mechanisms, or typicality judgments not fixed by the stated definitions.

Transfer rule: If an argument applies a gatekeeping principle to disqualify critics, then check whether using that principle already assumes the speaker can make the required qualification judgment.
Error pattern: Circularity by self-exemption—the arguer uses a standard that would also block the arguer’s own evidence or authority.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Under this rule, who is allowed to verify the key premise?” If the arguer must already be accepted to verify it, flag begging the question.
Use when: The argument defines who counts as a valid judge, expert, or member, then relies on its own assessment of that status.
Boundary: Ignore when the qualifying premise is independently established by neutral evidence not restricted by the same rule.

Transfer rule: If an argument moves from a group’s broad success or distribution to every member’s status, then test for an illicit whole-to-part inference.
Error pattern: Treating a property of a class as automatically applying to each constituent element.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the core claim as “All members share the group trait”; if that stronger statement was never supported, the reasoning is flawed.
Use when: Conclusions about each species, case, or item are drawn from facts about a taxon, category, population, or system overall.
Boundary: Ignore when the premise explicitly states every member has the property or gives member-level evidence.

Transfer rule: If a premise gives X-or-Y and one branch implies a contradiction with a stated fact, then eliminate that branch and force the other.
Error pattern: Success came from chaining conditionals with exclusivity instead of treating each statement as independent.
Diagnostic check: Assume each disjunct in turn, propagate all if-then consequences, and reject any branch that conflicts with a direct statement or one-to-one assignment rule.
Use when: Relevant in logic puzzles with either/or claims, conditional links, and unique-role constraints among several items.
Boundary: Ignore when the “or” is nonexclusive, assignments are not unique, or conditionals are defeasible rather than strict.

Transfer rule: If an argument cites what did or did not happen over time to justify a claim about what people value, then classify it as using a historical fact to support a preference claim.
Error pattern: Mistaking descriptive evidence about real-world developments for a normative principle or defense of taste.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is the premise mainly a value rule, or an observed historical outcome/trend?” If it references displacement, persistence, or change across time, mark it historical evidence.
Use when: The stimulus contrasts preferences with what happened to practices, media, or institutions over time.
Boundary: Ignore this when the argument truly states an evaluative standard instead of citing historical developments.

Transfer rule: If a passage lists conditions and ends with a normative takeaway, then choose the option stating that overall intended recommendation.
Error pattern: Mistaking supporting facts or background conditions for the author’s main purpose instead of the concluding call to action.
Diagnostic check: Mark premise sentences, then paraphrase the final sentence as “therefore, we should ___”; select the option matching that directive.
Use when: The text gives several scarcity or hardship facts, then shifts with words like “on the whole,” “however,” or an evaluative closing judgment.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for a specific fact, definition, or the primary topic rather than the author’s purpose.

Transfer rule: If two groups have equal sample sizes and the argument compares counts to claim one trait is more prevalent, then match an option using the same count-to-prevalence comparison.
Error pattern: I chased a tempting causal structure instead of preserving the argument’s quantitative comparison form.
Diagnostic check: Underline premise type and conclusion type; verify both are “equal-sized groups + different counts => more widespread/support,” not causation, composition, or set inclusion.
Use when: Relevant in parallel-reasoning questions built from survey, defect, infection, or preference data across matched groups.
Boundary: Ignore when group sizes differ, rates are explicit, or the conclusion depends on cause, definition, or whole-part quality.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what would make a proposed fix ineffective, then look for an independent cause that would keep producing the bad outcome even after the fix.
Error pattern: I focused on normal fluctuation/timing as an alternative explanation instead of testing whether the recommendation could still fail under the new policy.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Assuming the policy is implemented, what factor here would still directly lower the target population?” Prefer choices with a continuing causal mechanism over background variability.
Use when: An argument recommends an intervention to stop a decline and the task is to weaken efficacy, not merely question diagnosis.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices instead compare costs, ethics, feasibility, or only attack whether the decline happened at all.

Transfer rule: If a logic item asks what must be false, then enumerate the allowed values from any “either/or” statement and test each option against all linked conditions plus the all-different constraint.
Error pattern: Success came from exhaustive case-splitting instead of jumping from one conditional to a conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Build a tiny table for each possible assignment of the disjunctive variable, propagate every implication, enforce uniqueness, and mark each option possible or impossible.
Use when: Apply this to small assignment puzzles with conditionals, exclusive choices, and a question about must/cannot happen.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices are independent, quantities are continuous, or the prompt asks for likelihood rather than logical necessity.

Transfer rule: If an argument rejects one policy because it is politically blocked and concludes another is best, then require that the alternative faces less opposition or is more feasible.
Error pattern: Comparative-feasibility assumption checking in recommendation arguments; success comes from testing whether the preferred option is actually more implementable than the rejected ideal.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What hidden comparison must hold for ‘best way’ to follow?” Then negate it; if equal or greater resistance to the chosen policy breaks the conclusion, that comparison is required.
Use when: Policy, plan, or strategy arguments move from “optimal in theory” to “best in this setting” because of constraints.
Boundary: Ignore when the conclusion is purely about efficiency, causation, or ethics without any feasibility or implementation premise.

Transfer rule: If estimated duration conflicts with much faster actual completion, then look for hidden setup/procurement delays included for one performer but not the other.
Error pattern: Success came from separating administrative lead time from hands-on task time instead of comparing worker speed or general experience.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What nonwork steps occur before physical work starts for each party?” and test whether removing one party’s delay closes most of the gap.
Use when: Relevant in discrepancy questions comparing organizations, timelines, or methods where one side may face different procedural constraints.
Boundary: Ignore when the gap must be explained by on-task efficiency, capacity, or external conditions shared equally by both sides.

Transfer rule: If a passage contrasts officials’ legal duties with citizens’ obligations and repeatedly stresses cooperation/participation, then choose the option about public participation as necessary for legal effectiveness.
Error pattern: Overweighted a vivid concluding sanction statement and ignored the paragraph’s main argumentative center linking enforcement to citizens.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the subject of each sentence; if most sentences develop citizens’ role, reject options focused mainly on punishing power-holders.
Use when: Relevant in main-idea questions where the text balances authority conduct with mass participation in governance or enforcement.
Boundary: Ignore when the passage’s majority focus is specific institutional reform, official accountability details, or a narrow legal principle.

Transfer rule: If a passage builds context about a broad problem, then ends by highlighting one actor newly expected to act, choose the option capturing that emerging role shift.
Error pattern: Success comes from prioritizing the author’s main thrust over background facts, urgency statements, or partial descriptions of others’ weakness.
Diagnostic check: Ask: which option best matches the passage’s final emphasis and can explain why the earlier context was presented?
Use when: The text gives general trends, notes existing actors’ limits, then singles out another actor as the focus.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a detail, cause, attitude, or when the final sentence is merely an example, not the thesis.

Transfer rule: If force is used only to stop an ongoing unlawful attack and secure escape or recovery, then classify it as justifiable defense.  
Error pattern: Success came from tracking timing and necessity; self-defense fails when it becomes revenge, provocation, or force after the threat is neutralized.  
Diagnostic check: Ask in order: Was the infringement happening now? Was the response aimed at stopping it? Did force stop once safety/objective was achieved?  
Use when: Apply to criminal-law scenarios involving resistance to robbery, assault, trespass, or protection of self, others, or property.  
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the facts center on preemptive retaliation, mutual fighting set up by one party, or punishment after control is regained.

Transfer rule: If a stem contrasts two related factors as indirect/abstract versus direct/specific, then choose a conclusion about emphasizing both with added attention to the direct factor, not ranking or equating them.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: infer a practical policy recommendation from complementary roles; avoid jumping to superiority, identity, or exclusivity.
Diagnostic check: List each factor’s role, mark whether the relation is complementary or competitive, and eliminate answers that claim “more important,” “same thing,” or omit the recommended joint action.
Use when: Relevant in argument-completion items comparing functions, influence paths, or levels of immediacy between paired concepts.
Boundary: Ignore when the stem gives explicit comparative judgment, mutual exclusivity, causal proof for only one factor, or a definition statement.

Transfer rule: If people are said to do an activity together or live together, then treat those roles as belonging to different people and eliminate any assignment that merges them.
Error pattern: I made an unwarranted positive assignment from exclusions, turning “not X or Y” into “must be Z,” and failed to preserve all remaining possibilities.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, list each person’s forbidden roles from every clue, then verify each candidate option against all clues without adding new assumptions.
Use when: Apply this on logic-grid style assignment problems with identity, age, neighbor, or together/apart constraints.
Boundary: Ignore when clues explicitly allow one person to fill multiple referenced roles or when the question asks for probabilistic best-fit reasoning.

Transfer rule: If asked to weaken a causal claim, then prefer evidence naming a strong alternative cause of the same effect over later protections or access facts.
Error pattern: I chose a peripheral, time-shifted consideration instead of directly comparing causes for the observed decline.
Diagnostic check: State claim as “X caused Y”; for each choice, ask “Does this offer another cause of Y, block X→Y, or only discuss background/aftereffects?”
Use when: Relevant in causal-weaken questions about population change, environmental harm, or behavioral explanations with multiple plausible drivers.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is to strengthen, resolve chronology, or evaluate policy impact after the decline rather than its cause.

Transfer rule: If a passage gives a causal chain from an intervention to reduced precursor emissions to a later environmental effect, then infer the downstream reduction only when each link is stated.
Error pattern: Success pattern: following explicit cause-and-effect instead of choosing answers that add unstated mechanisms, rankings, or safety thresholds.
Diagnostic check: Map premise links as intervention -> emission change -> secondary effect; accept only an option that restates this chain without new claims.
Use when: Relevant in inference questions about policy, technology, science, or environment where one reduced factor is said to influence another outcome.
Boundary: Ignore when the answer requires outside knowledge, reverses causality, or introduces quantitative or evaluative claims not mentioned.

Transfer rule: If a principle makes morality depend on intention plus reasonably foreseeable effects, then test each choice against both required conditions.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating the rule into necessary/sufficient triggers instead of reacting to outcome alone.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark four boxes—benefit caused, benefit intended, harm intended, harm reasonably foreseeable—and accept only one matching the rule exactly.
Use when: Apply this on ethics questions contrasting motives, consequences, negligence, and unintended side effects.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the standard is purely outcome-based, purely motive-based, or asks for legal rather than moral judgment.

Transfer rule: If a passage balances two required elements and says one without the other fails the target, then choose the option stating their joint necessity.
Error pattern: I focused on a supporting prescription about maintaining one area while improving another, instead of the author’s defining conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark the target concept, list every condition tied to it, and reject choices that mention only one condition or only a background point.
Use when: Relevant in main-point questions using contrast words, “however,” “only if,” “without,” or statements defining what counts as the target system.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a detail, emphasis, or policy priority rather than the passage’s overall thesis.

Transfer rule: If an argument uses one finding to claim a feature was rare enough to identify source yet common enough to remove suspicion elsewhere, then test for inconsistency about how restricted that feature is.
Error pattern: I attacked an extreme claim not actually made, instead of checking whether the argument’s own interpretation of the evidence conflicts.
